documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large-load interconnection and reliability requirements directly affect hydro's strategic options for co-located load service and deliverability, and the tariff filing establishes new compliance obligations for generators in MISO.
documents.ai_summary: MISO presented updated Interconnection Reliability Requirements for large loads with a tariff filing targeted for the second half of August 2026. The framework defines which loads are subject to ride-through, performance, and telemetry requirements, with approximately 30 GW of large load potentially grandfathered under transition provisions. The revised tariff reflects stakeholder feedback on large-load definition, applicability, and transition language, and is consistent with recent FERC show-cause orders and NERC guidance. MISO clarified it would maintain visibility into large loads through PMU data, facility models, and forecasts, and noted a notwithstanding clause allowing flexible operational actions if requirements adversely affect system reliability. Stakeholders were invited to submit informal feedback on tariff updates by August 3, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, large-load interconnection and reliability rules establish the framework that will govern how existing hydro plants—especially those with firm transmission access or strategic location—can serve co-located large industrial or data-center loads behind the meter or through dedicated service. The reliability requirements and transition provisions (particularly grandfathering of ~30 GW) will shape the scarcity conditions and reserve margins against which hydro energy and ancillary-service revenues are set, and the telemetry and forecasting requirements signal MISO's operational reliance on detailed load visibility that could affect dispatch patterns and ramping obligations for all synchronous generators.

title: Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Market Performance
meeting_hydro_reason: EDAM is a foundational market-seams and governance choice for NHA members in the West, and a performance review would address pricing, participation rules, and strategic integration options affecting hydro revenue and market optionality in the CAISO footprint and beyond.

documents.title: Comments - WPTF - Extended Day-ahead Market (EDAM) Market Performance - Jun 25, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: EDAM market-design mechanics and performance reporting directly affect hydro's market revenue through energy price formation, resource participation rules, and multi-BAA market power mitigation affecting hydro's scarcity and capacity pricing in CAISO and partner balancing authorities.
documents.ai_summary: Western Power Trading Forum (WPTF) submitted comments on CAISO's May 2026 EDAM Monthly Performance Report, presented June 25, 2026. WPTF requests expanded reporting in future iterations on four areas: deployment scenarios' impact on congestion and real-time alignment; frequency and magnitude of BAA-level market power mitigation in PACE and PACW balancing authorities with pre/post-mitigation price comparisons; negative Reliability Capacity Up (RCU) and Reliability Capacity Down (RCD) clearing prices, which WPTF states were "not an intended outcome of the policy design" and should be addressed through reformulating requirement constraints; and clarification of how the EDAM Net Export Constraint applies to contracted transfers across external interties and internal BAA boundaries. WPTF emphasizes that performance reporting will become "an important tool for evaluating whether EDAM is achieving its intended policy objectives."
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, WPTF's focus on deployment-scenario design, BAA-level mitigation frequency in partner balancing authorities, and negative RCU/RCD prices is directly relevant to hydro owners. Deployment scenarios affect day-ahead energy dispatch and pricing—a primary hydro revenue stream. Negative reliability-capacity prices misrepresent the value of capacity provision and could depress revenue for dispatchable resources like hydro that are called upon for reliability. BAA-level mitigation in PACE and PACW matters because those authorities are expanding EDAM participation and any mitigation applied to hydro exports from CAISO into those regions would reduce realized energy revenue. The Net Export Constraint design is material to hydro's ability to contract firm deliveries across the EDAM footprint.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: SCE's comments on EDAM performance touch price formation (MEC convergence, transfer revenue, GHG cost treatment), ancillary-services procurement (IR and RC bidding and conversion), and interregional seams governance (WEIM/EDAM transfer capacity and market interaction), all mechanisms affecting hydro revenue and strategic options in the Western market.
documents.ai_summary: Southern California Edison submitted comments on CAISO's May 2026 EDAM Performance Report (presented June 25, 2026) requesting additional data and analysis on several market mechanics: transfer capacity availability in EDAM and WEIM markets; treatment of GHG costs in Imbalance Reserve (IR) and Regulation Capacity (RC) procurement; correlation between transfer revenue (marginal energy cost differences across balancing-authority areas) and GHG prices; the volume of $0-bid IR and $55-bid RC; and the real-time utilization of IR, including the percentage converted to Flexible Ramping Product and Energy by hour. SCE also questioned whether convergence bidding in CAISO drives price convergence in other EDAM balancing-authority areas when transfer capacity is sufficient versus congestion-constrained, and whether differences in Intra-day Financials Market versus real-time prices correlate with available transfer capacity.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not directly name hydropower or pumped storage. However, SCE's questions about GHG cost treatment in IR and RC procurement, MEC convergence across EDAM balancing areas, transfer-revenue dynamics, and the interplay between transfer capacity and price differences are central to how hydro revenue gets captured in EDAM's cross-market design. For hydro owners in California and WEIM, the answers to SCE's questions about GHG attribution in reserve pricing and how often and by how much locational energy prices diverge will materially affect both energy and ancillary-service revenue, and the transfer-capacity and congestion-driven price-wedge analysis directly determines the scarcity value hydro can monetize across the seam.

documents.title: Comments - PG&E - Extended Day-ahead Market (EDAM) Market Performance - Jun 25, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: EDAM is a cross-ISO market seam mechanism critical to hydro deliverability and revenue, and this comment directly raises operational and settlement transparency issues that affect price formation, imbalance-reserve accreditation, and real-time market volatility — all material to hydro scheduling and revenue realization.
documents.ai_summary: Pacific Gas and Electric submitted comments on the CAISO May 2026 EDAM Performance Report (meeting held June 25, 2026), raising seven questions on settlement transparency, platform scalability, congestion-price reporting in the PACW transmission zone, imbalance-reserve (IR) and resource-clearing (RC) procurement accuracy, and real-time price volatility. PG&E requests greater transparency on settlement-related issues and their upstream origins; faster turnaround on issue-specific responses; clarification on root causes of congestion or lack thereof in May; detailed breakdowns of capacity awarded IR only, RC only, both, or neither to assess contribution of new products relative to all real-time resources; and frequency comparison of FMM and RTD intervals at or above $1,000/MWh against pre-EDAM periods. The submission was due July 10, 2026 per the template instructions (note: metadata shows July 10, 2025, which appears to be an extraction error; meeting was June 25, 2026).
documents.hydro_read_through: EDAM is the operational and revenue framework for hydro generators exporting from the West; settlement accuracy, congestion pricing signals, and imbalance-reserve adequacy directly shape real-time revenue and dispatch incentives for flexible resources like hydro. PG&E's questions on IR procurement versus realized forecast error are especially relevant because hydro owners depend on accurate IR quantities to hedge their own ramping uncertainty and exposure to real-time prices—if procured IR is insufficient, hydro faces higher balancing costs. The request for granular capacity-award breakdowns and price-volatility trends identifies whether real-time markets are functioning efficiently under EDAM or whether technical/operational issues are creating artificial scarcity and uplift; this matters enormously to revenue stability.

documents.title: 20260820 MSC Item 01c Minutes 20260709.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document addresses multiple market-design mechanisms directly affecting hydro revenue and obligation: regulation-reserve deliverability and performance standards, ancillary-services demand curves, reserve-shortage pricing, transmission congestion management, and day-ahead settlement calculations—all canonical hydro-participation and compliance areas.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's July 9, 2026 Market Subcommittee meeting minutes cover six active market-design items with deadlines and next steps. (1) Enhance Reserve Deliverability (MSC-2026-2): MISO is evaluating Regulation reserve clearing location and performance standards, with plans to study Regulation RPE demand curves for day-ahead and real-time markets; feedback period closed. (2) Transmission Constraint Demand Curves (MSC-2026-6): MISO is evaluating congestion-management effectiveness and potential TCDC enhancements following recent reserve-shortage pricing changes, with recommendations and costs/benefits analysis planned for later in 2026. (3) FTR-ARR Market Enhancements (MSC-2025-5): MISO is performing holistic evaluation of ARR Nomination Process (Reference Year, Reserved Source Point, Long-Term Transmission Rights constraints) and transmission-outage reporting, with stakeholder feedback deadline July 23, 2026. (4) Up Ramp Capability demand curves (MSC-2026-1): MISO filed tariff revisions ER26-2705-000 on June 1, 2026 with requested effective date August 4, 2026 updating Regulation, Spinning Reserves, and Up Ramp Capability demand curves. (5) Improve Market Monitoring and Mitigation (MSC-2026-5): IMM shared revised tariff redlines addressing stakeholder concerns on Module D and Duty of Candor; goal is to return to MSC in August with revised redlines and implementation examples. (6) Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment Reduction Total (MSC-2026-7, new issue): MISO proposes fixing DAMAP and RSG Distribution calculations to prevent double-counting of MWs cleared across products, with draft redlines posted and Q3 2026 FERC filing targeted for 60-day effective date; stakeholder feedback deadline July 24, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Regulation-reserve clearing location and performance failures directly undermine hydro's core ancillary-services revenue, since hydro is the primary provider of this flexibility; MISO's planned demand-curve and performance-incentive changes will reshape how much hydro clears and at what price in these essential markets. Congestion management and TCDC-enhancement work affects the locational signals and out-of-market costs that constrain hydro's energy and reserve export economics. The Up Ramp Capability demand-curve update is likewise a direct pricing lever for a service hydro chronically supplies. The FTR-ARR process reform touches transmission-rights accreditation and congestion pricing that feed hydro's long-term revenue certainty. The DAMAP and RSG calculation fixes will correct settlement mechanics that currently overstate derated-unit revenue shares, benefiting all dispatchable resources including hydro. All of these items have tight feedback and filing deadlines in the next 6–8 weeks.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This MISO tariff/BPM revision proposal affects must-offer and dispatch rules for Resource Adequacy Charging (RAC) designated units during emergency events, which directly impacts how thermal and dispatchable resources—including hydroelectric plants operating in MISO—must respond to grid directives and manage fuel-cost risk recovery.
documents.ai_summary: Wabash Valley Power Alliance proposes that MISO adjust tariff and Business Practice Manual language to require all Resource Adequacy Charging (RAC) designated units to be dispatched during emergency events, rather than allowing designated units to remain undispatched. The proposal aims to prevent utilities from bearing unrecovered fuel-procurement costs when MISO directs fuel commitment for a RAC call that is not followed by dispatch. The submitter characterizes this as a middle ground between MISO's and PJM's current approaches, requiring minimal tariff revisions and promoting sufficient generation capacity during emergencies. The Market Subcommittee is asked to take up this issue for tariff/BPM revision.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although the document does not mention hydropower, MISO operates conventional hydro and PSH facilities alongside thermal units under the same RAC framework and dispatch obligations. Expanding the must-dispatch requirement during emergency RAC events could impose additional dispatch obligations on hydro owners' units when MISO designates them for RAC, potentially limiting their operational flexibility and ability to manage water and state-of-charge constraints during critical periods—conversely, if hydro plants are exempt from the tighter dispatch mandate, the rule would reset the relative obligation burden between thermal and hydroelectric resources.

documents.title: 2026-08-18-19 RC/TC A10.a Capacity Auction Reforms - Seasonal/Accreditation - Capacity Zone Formation - Presentation - Revision
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) restructure seasonal accreditation methods and capacity-zone testing that directly govern how non-energy-limited resources—including conventional hydropower—are accredited and valued in the forward capacity market, affecting accreditation-based revenue and zone-wide pricing.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presented updates to the Capacity Auction Reforms: Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal for capacity-zone development and accreditation methodologies, effective Q2 2027. The presentation updates stakeholder feedback on two objective-criteria tests: the import-constrained zone test now assumes 25% of winter gas-only capacity available (rather than 0%), and the export-constrained zone test now uses Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) for existing capacity and nameplate ratings for new capacity. The ISO continues stakeholder review of zone development, TSA calculation alignment, accreditation modeling, offer formation, transition mechanisms, and financial assurance policy through Q4 2026 before FERC filing. The two-step framework (identifying potential zones, then applying objective criteria) maintains the current timing sequence but introduces separate summer and winter assessments aligned with seasonal system conditions.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. The CAR-SA reform restructures accreditation of Non-Energy Limited Resources, which includes conventional hydro and includes pumped storage if it is modeled as a use-limited resource rather than as a battery. The shift from Qualified Capacity (QC) to Dependable Capability (DCap) in import-constrained testing, the addition of seasonal winter/summer splits, and the use of MRIC for export testing will reset the metrics by which hydro's seasonal capacity credentials are measured and thus how zonal requirements and clearing prices reflect hydro availability. The 25% winter gas-availability assumption affects the import test's boundary—if it moves zone trigger thresholds, it changes which resources compete in which auction zone, and thus the locational price signal for hydropower. Hydro owners should monitor which zones trigger and whether seasonal DCap curves materially alter their accreditation value.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO resource adequacy accreditation rules determine how transmission losses affect seasonal capacity requirements for all generation resources, including hydro; changes to loss-calculation methodology directly impact the megawatt obligations hydro owners must meet in the Planning Resource Auction.
documents.ai_summary: Hoosier Energy submits a new issue requesting MISO re-evaluate its transmission loss (TL) calculation methodology used in the Planning Resource Auction (PRA). MISO's current method uses a one-year lookback of State Estimator losses at the LBA level, with the percentage values based on Coincident Peak demand hour two years prior to the Planning Year (2024 data for 2026/27 PRA), creating year-to-year volatility that can require hundreds of additional megawatts of capacity procurement for individual LSEs. Hoosier proposes aligning the lookback period to average the prior three years of LBA transmission losses to reduce volatility while reflecting more consistent, reasonable loss levels, and is open to alternatives such as using Resource Adequacy Hours used for generation accreditation or hours proposed for PRMR Allocation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro directly. However, MISO's PRA transmission loss calculation method applies to all generation resources subject to capacity accreditation, including conventional hydropower. Transmission loss percentages directly affect the megawatt obligations each load-serving entity must procure; reducing year-to-year volatility in loss calculations stabilizes the capacity market requirements for hydro owners and improves predictability of revenue obligations. If MISO adopts a three-year lookback or alternative stability mechanism, it would dampen the procurement swings that currently force hydro owners to reassess seasonal capacity revenue and strategic bidding each year.

documents.title: 20260819 RASC Item 01c Minutes 20260708.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is reforming accreditation methodology for resource adequacy capacity markets, refining planning reserve margin allocation rules, and examining outage-notification thresholds — all of which directly govern how use-limited and variable resources including hydro are accredited, and how storage and conventional hydropower's seasonal capacity revenue is allocated across load-serving entities.
documents.ai_summary: MISO Resource Adequacy Subcommittee met on July 8, 2026, and discussed four major capacity-market design items affecting all resource accreditation and planning reserve margin (PRMR) allocation. (1) Solar accreditation for PY27-28: MISO retained existing fixed-window hours (HE 15-17 for non-winter seasons, based on Non-GADS data) despite observed shifts in reliability-risk hours, deferring updates to the planned Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) accreditation transition for PY28-29. (2) External Resource Accreditation (RASC-2019-2 and RASC-2024-5): MISO proposed distinguishing pseudo-tied resources (accredited via Schedule 53A) from non-pseudo-tied resources (accredited via day-ahead e-Tag offers with three-year lookback and 80/20 weighting between Tier 2 RA Hours and Tier 1 non-RA Hours); MISO also proposed eliminating Use-Limited Resources as a category from the Planning Resource Auction. Stakeholder feedback by July 27, 2026; tariff redlines in late 2026 with filing targeting PY 2029-30 or beyond. (3) 24-Hour Lead Time in Accreditation (RASC-2026-1): MISO presented three options to address resources that increase notification times within 48 hours of operating day, rendering themselves uncommittable while retaining full accreditation despite 3.1 GWs unavailability during Winter Storm Fern; options ranged from reducing max lead time to 12 hours, assigning zero availability to last-minute changes, or implementing a sliding-scale availability curve. Stakeholder feedback due July 22, 2026; FERC filing planned for October with October feedback. (4) PRMR Allocation (RASC-2020-4 and RASC-2019-2): MISO revised its proposal to allocate LSE PRMR based on settled load during Tier 2 RA Hours (three-year lookback), replacing previous CPDf-based approach; LSE RAHD is scaled by CPDf forecast ratio and weighted by effective margins, better aligning PRMR allocation with each LSE's contribution to system risk under the DLOL framework. Stakeholder feedback due July 24, 2026; tariff redlines in August and September; FERC filing by end of 2026 targeting PY 2029-30 or later implementation.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although the document does not name hydropower directly, three items materially affect hydro and pumped-storage asset owners: (1) the proposed elimination of Use-Limited Resources as a PRA category would remove a pathway through which run-of-river and some conventional hydro currently participate, forcing reliance on the new accreditation rules under Schedules 53A and 53B (the mechanics of which are still being finalized); (2) the DLOL transition and the related solar and external-resource accreditation reforms reset how seasonal capacity contributions are measured, directly affecting the ELCC-based availability factors and seasonal-risk-hour definitions that drive hydro's accreditation and hence its RA revenue, with implementation deferred to PY 2028-29 but tariff details due in late 2026; and (3) the PRMR reallocation from CPDf-based to risk-hour-based settled-load shares will shift how system-wide reserve margins are distributed among LSEs, which in turn changes the seasonal demand for hydro's capacity and the price signals hydro operators receive when optimizing dispatch timing and commitment—this is a high-impact revenue signal with PY 2029-30 implementation.

evidence.quote: MISO ultimately decided to maintain the status quo for PY27-28, given the planned implementation of Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) based accreditation in PY28-29... MISO will continue using the existing hours in the Non-GADS Performance Template and fixed accreditation for new solar resources during PY27-28.

evidence.quote: MISO requests written feedback by July 27, 2026... planning a FERC filing in late 2026 or early 2027, with an effective date for Planning Year 2029-30 or beyond.

evidence.claim: 24-Hour Lead Time: Winter Storm Fern case showed 37 thermal resources increased notification times, resulting in 3.1 GWs unavailable
evidence.quote: A case study from Winter Storm Fern illustrated the problem: 37 thermal resources increased their notification times, resulting in 3.1 GWs being unavailable for a morning capacity emergency.

evidence.claim: PRMR allocation will use three-year lookback of settled load during Tier 2 RA Hours, weighted by effective margins
evidence.quote: MISO's revised proposal allocates LSE PRMR based on actual demand during Resource Adequacy hours in last three years... Each LSE's Seasonal RAHD calculation will be scaled by the ratio of the LSE Coincident Peak Demand forecast (CPDf) to the lookback Planning Year's CPDf... documents.title: New Issue - Evaluation of Outage Policies in the Resource Adequacy Construct.pdf
documents.filename: New Issue - Evaluation of Outage Policies in the Resource Adequacy Construct.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Outage policies in MISO's resource adequacy construct directly affect how all dispatchable resources—including hydro and PSH—must plan and report outages, which touches compliance obligations and incentive alignment for meeting capacity commitments.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is evaluating its 31-day outage rule, replacement rules, and planned outage exemptions within the Resource Adequacy construct to assess whether current policies align with three intended purposes: incentivizing resources to meet capacity obligations, promoting prudent outage planning, and ensuring availability during periods of highest reliability risk. The issue relates to but is broader than prior work on RASC 2025-2A, which also addressed the 31-day rule and replacement rules. No specific resolution deadline is stated. The evaluation spans settlements, day-ahead and real-time energy and ancillary services markets, capacity accreditation rules, and operational performance standards.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, outage policies are compliance obligations affecting all dispatchable resources: how long plants can be down, which outages require replacement, and which are exempted shapes a hydro owner's operational flexibility and its accreditation treatment under capacity rules. If MISO tightens the 31-day rule or narrows exemptions, it would reduce the scheduling flexibility available to conventional and pumped-storage facilities during planned maintenance and refurbishment.

evidence.claim: MISO is evaluating the 31-day outage rule, replacement rules, and planned outage exemptions to assess whether current outage policies in the Resource Adequacy construct are aligned with the intended purposes: to incentivize resources to meet their capacity obligations, plan outages prudently, and be available during periods of highest reliability risk.
evidence.quote: MISO is evaluating the 31-day outage rule, replacement rules, and planned outage exemptions to assess whether current outage policies in the Resource Adequacy construct are aligned with the intended purposes: to incentivize resources to meet their capacity obligations, plan outages prudently, and be available during periods of highest reliability risk.

evidence.claim: The issue relates to RASC 2025-2A but is broader, also including planned outage exemptions.
evidence.quote: Yes, the proposed issue is related to RASC 2025-2A. Both issues include the 31-day outage rule and replacement rules within scope. However, the proposed issue is broader, also including planned outage exemptions.

documents.title: Large Loads - Straw Proposal - Aug 11, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large loads (especially data centers) and co-located generation/storage arrangements are strategic options affecting hydro's revenue, deliverability, and competitive positioning in California; this proposal also addresses flexible interconnection services and operational requirements that would apply to all dispatchable resources including storage.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Large Loads Straw Proposal (August 12, 2026) responds to FERC's June 18, 2026 Order to Show Cause by proposing tariff enhancements for transmission service and interconnection of large loads (defined as ≥50 MW at a single site). Key proposals include: (1) clarified application and study procedures with 60–90 day study timelines for large load interconnection studies; (2) new flexible interconnection service offerings—Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (FILI) for temporary flexibility during network upgrades and Flexible Load Interconnection–Permanent (FLIP) to avoid permanent upgrade costs; (3) rules for co-located large loads and behind-the-meter generation that align load and generator interconnection studies; (4) operational requirements including control technologies and protection systems for flexible loads; (5) data transparency and coordination with Participating Transmission Owners (PTOs) on cost allocation. CAISO declines to create separate transmission-service classes but proposes customized flexible interconnection configurations. The CAISO Board is scheduled to vote on October 28, 2026, with a draft final proposal expected September 21, 2026, and stakeholder comments due October 12, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage. However, the framework directly affects storage operators' strategic options: flexible interconnection services (FILI and FLIP) and co-location rules now extending to generating facilities serving large loads create precedent for how storage (including PSH) may participate in serving behind-the-meter or co-located loads with operational flexibility constraints. The proposed 60–90 day study timeline and customized protection-scheme requirements for flexible resources set operational and study-process benchmarks that would apply to any resource offering ramping or temporal flexibility, including storage. Large load growth forecasts (1.8 GW by 2030, 4.7 GW by 2035) drive scarcity and congestion where hydro's energy-and-flexibility value would compound.

documents.title: 20260817 LOLEWG Item 01c Minutes 20260623.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's LOLE study directly affects seasonal capacity accreditation (ELCC/DLOL) for all resources including hydro and storage, and determines Planning Reserve Margin Requirements that shape capacity-market outcomes, revenue adequacy, and seasonal reliability obligations for NHA members.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group met June 23, 2026, to review inputs and methodology for the Planning Year 2027–2028 LOLE study that determines seasonal resource-adequacy targets and capacity accreditation. Key updates include: adoption of enhanced wind profiles expected to alter wind and storage ELCC values, particularly in spring; shift from annual to seasonal LOLE targets (0.1 days/year overall, 0.01 days/year seasonal floor) to reflect year-round reliability risks; and refinements to load-forecast uncertainty modeling to capture increasing winter and spring peak-demand growth. MISO projects preliminary Capacity Import Limit (CIL) and Capacity Export Limit (CEL) results for September 2026. Stakeholders were invited to provide feedback by July 7, 2026, on load modeling, wind-profile treatment, and capacity assumptions.
documents.hydro_read_through: Seasonal LOLE accreditation directly sets the ELCC or DLOL percentage (effective capacity credit) that conventional hydro and pumped-storage units receive in MISO's capacity auction, determining revenue from the Planning Resource Auction. The enhanced wind profiles and shifted critical-hour distributions announced here will revalue storage accreditation—specifically reducing winter and spring storage DLOL percentages due to longer multi-hour high-risk periods—and alter the seasonal reliability targets against which all resources' contributions are measured. If winter/spring LOLE requirements tighten, hydro's ability to serve those seasonal peaks becomes more valuable; conversely, accreditation changes directly affect how much capacity hydro can offer and at what seasonal premium.

documents.ai_summary: The Transition Cluster Study 2024 (C24) Phase 2 report, issued in draft on August 13, 2026, evaluates interconnection facilities and system deliverability upgrades for 60 proposed projects (predominantly battery energy storage and wind) in NYISO. The study applies the Minimum Interconnection Standard (MIS) to determine System Upgrade Facilities (SUFs) required for Energy Resource Interconnection Service (ERIS) and the Deliverability Interconnection Standard (DIS) to evaluate whether each project requesting Capacity Resource Interconnection Service (CRIS) is deliverable at requested MW levels and what System Deliverability Upgrades (SDUs) are needed. Key findings include identification of critical buses classified as Bulk Power System (BPS) requiring special NPCC compliance; thermal ampacity constraints on NYPA's Uniondale Hub affecting the 1,321 MW Vineyard Mid-Atlantic West offshore-wind project; Short Circuit Ratio (SCR) and relay-protection upgrades required by National Grid for multiple battery and wind projects; and reactive-power capability assessments for LIPA-zone storage projects. The report is presented to the Interconnection Projects Facilities Study Working Group (IPFS WG), Transmission Planning Advisory Subcommittee (TPAS), and Operating Committee for approval.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although this document addresses battery energy storage and wind rather than pumped storage explicitly, it establishes interconnection deliverability and cost-allocation processes that govern the feasibility and revenue recovery of any capacity resource, including PSH. PSH owners competing for interconnection points in NYISO would face identical MIS/DIS standards, SUF/SDU cost allocations, and transmission constraints (thermal, SCR, reactive power) evaluated here; the findings on ampacity constraints, protection-scheme upgrades, and headroom calculations set precedent for how NYISO will evaluate PSH interconnection requests in future clusters. The battery projects here are near-term capacity competitors with PSH, so their queue position and deliverability constraints directly affect the scarcity and locational value of existing and proposed PSH capacity.

documents.ai_summary: The MISO-SPP Coordinated System Plan (CSP) 2024–25 study evaluated 70 proposed transmission solutions along the southern seam between the RTOs. One segment—Dora–Yell & Anthem–Dora–Yell—advances for consideration; it would cost $2.28B combined and deliver $2.8B–3.8B in 20–40 year benefits including increased SPP-to-MISO transfer capability and reduced congestion. Two other segments (Turk–McNeil and Sarepta–SW Shreveport) do not meet cost-allocation criteria for joint development but show strong reliability and transfer benefits. Benefits are calculated using Adjusted Production Cost (APC) savings, avoided reliability upgrades, and extreme-weather resilience. RTOs request stakeholder feedback on final recommendations by Friday, September 4, 2026, with final recommendations to be presented October 9, 2026. The 2026 CSP study is planned to initiate in late Q3 or early Q4 2026, per the Joint Operating Agreement timeline.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, interregional transmission expansion directly affects hydropower revenue and strategic flexibility: new seam transfer capability would improve the ability of SPP and MISO hydro to export generation into constrained load pockets, increasing locational pricing opportunities and capacity-accreditation value; expansion also reduces congestion rents and improves the feasibility of multi-RTO participation strategies. The APC-based benefit calculation shown here sets precedent for how interregional transmission projects will be justified and cost-allocated, which will influence future investment in lines that improve hydro's transmission access.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document addresses large-load interconnection processes and non-firm transmission service options that would affect how hydropower facilities compete for transmission access and interact with load-serving infrastructure, touching both strategic options and potential obligations under MISO's evolving interconnection framework.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group met on July 16, 2026, to advance several interconnection and service-delivery initiatives responding to a FERC Show Cause Order (EL26-70-000) issued June 18, 2026. The group accepted two new issues: (1) Generation and Large Load Alignment (LLWG-2026-6), proposing concurrent study of large loads ≥250 MW and paired generation with a 120-day study cycle, feedback due July 30; and (2) Non-Firm Large Load participation (LLWG-2026-5), allowing loads to connect without firm transmission service but subject to curtailment, feedback due July 31. Alliant Energy presented the Bridge Interim Transmission Service (BITS) proposal, a non-firm transmission product for large loads during network-upgrade construction, requesting feedback by August 7 with Q3/Q4 2026 filing target. MISO also refined the Firm Service Step Up process (LLWG-2026-1, feedback due July 30) and introduced a hub-and-spoke Business Practices Manual framework for large-load interconnection reliability (BPM-032, feedback due July 28), with October 1, 2026, implementation target. MISO's informational report on large-load resource adequacy was filed July 20, 2026. Next LLWG meeting scheduled August 27, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although this document does not mention hydropower, its proposals for large-load interconnection and non-firm transmission service establish new pathways that could alter how existing and future hydropower capacity competes for network access. The Generation and Load Alignment process and BITS non-firm service create preferential study tracks for loads paired with generation or loads willing to accept curtailment, potentially affecting transmission headroom available to conventional hydro plants seeking firm service upgrades or interconnection. The 120-day study cycle and 150% generation-capacity cap introduce new assumptions that could influence cost allocation and network-upgrade timing affecting hydro deliverability. Run-of-river and variable-output hydro facilities, as well as existing dams seeking uprates, may face either opportunity (non-firm service as a stepping-stone to firm service) or competitive pressure (transmission constraints absorbed by existing resources first). Monitoring how MISO treats hydro's own readiness requirements and how it ranks hydro against load-paired generation in network-upgrade prioritization will be essential.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's proposal for non-firm transmission service to large loads (FLITS) establishes transmission-participation rules, curtailment-obligation mechanics, and resource-adequacy treatment that would set precedent for how flexible use-limited resources like pumped storage negotiate firm-vs-non-firm service transitions, ARR exclusions, and demand-response ineligibility.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes Flexible Large-load Interconnection and Transmission Service (FLITS), a framework allowing large loads to obtain interim or permanent non-firm network transmission service (NITS) while pursuing firm service upgrades. The proposal—developed under FERC show-cause order direction (195 FERC ¶ 61,212, 2026) with a filing deadline of November 16—permits large loads to curtail on-demand under predefined reliability conditions without economic compensation, excludes FLITS-served load from Auction Revenue Rights (ARR) entitlements and demand-response resource registration, and requires curtailment to zero MW within 30 minutes of instruction (without violating 30 MW/minute ramp limits for loads >900 MW). Permanent FLITS is available for loads not meeting interim criteria. MISO is still evaluating resource-adequacy treatment options and requests stakeholder feedback by Wednesday August 19, 2026 on four specific questions: whether FLITS load should be included in LSE load forecasts, eligibility for Load Modifying Resource registration, differential treatment of loads that co-locate generation, and whether answers may differ by region (RERRA).
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not address hydropower or pumped-storage resources directly. However, the FLITS framework establishes a transmission-service and curtailment-obligation template for flexible resources—particularly the mechanics of interim non-firm service, mandatory curtailment without economic compensation, ARR/FTR exclusion, and demand-response ineligibility—that would become precedent if adopted across RTOs or extended to storage resources as markets design participation rules for duration-limited or use-limited resources. PSH owners choosing to serve large co-located loads via non-firm service or considering transition strategies from non-firm to firm transmission would encounter these curtailment obligations, revenue-entitlement restrictions, and RA treatment rules.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements Tariff establishes mandatory operational and modeling requirements for Large Load (≥50 MW demand at a single substation) and Computational Load (≥25 MW of IT equipment). Computational Load faces additional Phasor Measurement Unit, ride-through (voltage/frequency disturbance tolerance), and ramp-rate requirements, all to be implemented by September 1, 2027 at the latest. Transition provisions exempt Large Load with Service Commencement Date prior to December 4, 2026, and partially exempt projects approved in MTEP 2026 or earlier. Transmission Customer is responsible for providing real-time telemetry via ICCP, day-ahead and real-time load forecasts to support RAC and SCED, verified electrical models, and demonstrating compliance capability. Failure to comply may result in delayed service, operational limitations, or other remediation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not address hydropower or pumped storage. However, MISO's new Large Load reliability requirements will increase transmission-system modeling complexity and real-time coordination demands, potentially constraining system flexibility and raising dispatch coordination costs for existing conventional and pumped-storage resources. The ramp-rate requirements on Computational Load and the telemetry/forecasting mandates create a more tightly managed operating environment in which hydro's flexibility revenue (ramping, real-time co-optimization, reserve supply) may face tighter dispatch windows or reduced opportunity to provide fast-response products. Load-growth mechanisms also affect the scarcity value of existing hydro capacity — large IT loads competing for transmission interconnection reduce available transmission for hydro exports, a strategic concern for NHA members evaluating MISO membership.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's Protocol Revisions Subcommittee met on 2026-08-12 to review and vote on fourteen numbered protocol revision requests (NPRRs), several directly affecting storage and flexible-resource participation. Key items include NPRR1310 and NPRR1340, which establish Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service ancillary service with energy-storage-resource participation; NPRR1278, which creates Advanced Grid Support Service as an ancillary service; NPRR1214, which proposes a Reliability Deployment Price Adder to improve locational signals and reduce uplift; and NPRR1329, addressing resource-entity requirements for self-limiting facilities. The agenda lists these as up for review, impact-analysis consideration, and possible voting, with some items flagged as urgent (NPRR1310). One withdrawal (NPRR1284) and one tabled item (NPRR956, NPRR1255, NPRR1272, NPRR1278, NPRR1295, NPRR1296, NPRR1310, NPRR1312, NPRR1317, NPRR1332, NPRR1333, NPRR1334, NPRR1335, NPRR1336, NPRR1337, NPRR1340, NPRR1342, NPRR1343) are also noted.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although this agenda document does not name hydropower or pumped storage, ERCOT's creation of new ancillary-service products (Advanced Grid Support, Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service) and its rules for energy-storage-resource participation in those services signal how RTOs outside the Northwest and Northeast are beginning to value and compensate flexibility and storage differently. The Reliability Deployment Price Adder (NPRR1214) and resource-entity framework for self-limiting facilities (NPRR1329) are particularly relevant as precedent: if ERCOT moves toward locational uplift reduction and explicit opportunity-cost recognition for energy-limited assets, PSH owners in regions considering similar reforms would need to track whether those models extend eligibility or change compensation for storage resources generally. The energy-storage participation items (NPRR1310, NPRR1340) show how a major grid operator structures state-of-charge rules and AS-stacking constraints—frameworks NHA members planning multi-RTO strategies or advocating for storage rules in their own regions should monitor.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Business Issues Committee approved on June 10, 2026 proposed revisions to Attachment N of the ICAP Manual to implement seasonal translation factors for intermittent and limited control run-of-river resources, addressing their variable capacity contribution. The committee also reviewed the 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook, which assumes Smart Path and Smart Path Connect transmission upgrades in service and evaluates resource needs across multiple zero-emission scenarios; the study noted that new resources must include consideration of baseload, load-following, and peaking options to support system operations. The NYISO presented its compliance proposal for FERC Order No. 1920 long-term regional transmission planning, which introduces a new process for NYPSC-declared Long-Term Transmission Needs with solution solicitation and selection timelines of up to two years, modifies incumbent transmission owners' right of first refusal to include "right-size" projects, and requires consideration of alternative transmission technologies in existing planning processes.

Transmission planning upgrades (Smart Path, Smart Path Connect) and the new Order 1920 regional planning framework affect hydro's deliverability and export capability, particularly relevant to New York hydro and eastern US interconnections with multi-state transmission dependencies. Resource adequacy scenarios assuming different generation mixes and transmission investments shape long-term scarcity signals and will inform future capacity requirement resets, directly impacting all existing hydro assets through their bearing on CONE and demand-curve levels.

documents.ai_summary: The Broader Regional Markets Report documents NYISO's status on 34 multi-year initiatives governing interregional coordination, energy pricing, capacity imports/exports, and transmission interface operations. Key completed items include Market-to-Market Coordination with PJM (activated January 15, 2013), Coordinated Transaction Scheduling with ISO-NE (activated December 15, 2015), and implementation of FERC Order No. 831 energy-offer-cap rules (software implemented January 27, 2019). Pending initiatives include Five-minute Transaction Scheduling with Hydro Quebec via RTD at the Chateauguay proxy and 15-minute scheduling with Ontario/IESO. Recent completions affecting external capacity suppliers include Enhanced Deliverability Requirements for Hydro Quebec and Ontario capacity suppliers (approved stakeholders August 29 and September 11, 2019, effective August 12, 2019), and the Champlain-Hudson Power Express (CHPE) merchant HVDC facility (1,250 MW nominal capacity from Hydro Quebec, tariff revisions approved by FERC April 13, 2026, implemented May 13, 2026). The report also notes pending exploration of reserves and regulation participation across control areas and reciprocal capacity wheeling with New England. All items have been through multi-year stakeholder processes, with FERC compliance or approval where applicable.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name conventional hydro or pumped-storage facilities specifically, but NYISO's interregional coordination agenda directly affects how Northwest hydro and other external hydroelectric resources compete for capacity and energy revenue in the NYISO market. The Hydro Quebec deliverability rules and CHPE intertie implementation determine whether HQ's large seasonal hydro fleet can reliably sell capacity into NYISO and at what transmission-constrained pricing. Five-minute transaction scheduling with HQ and the pending 15-minute Ontario scheduling would improve dispatch efficiency for large hydro resources and flatten locational price spreads, directly raising their energy and reserve revenue. The broader M2M and CTS framework across PJM and ISO-NE likewise sets precedent for how NYISO treats external hydro imports and pseudo-tied generation from neighboring hydropower portfolios.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Market Operations Report for August 2026 meeting, covering market activity through July 31, 2026. LBMP energy prices (day-ahead load-weighted average) in July 2026 were $83.72/MWh, compared to $78.89/MWh in July 2025, a 6.1% year-over-year increase. Ancillary-service prices (10-minute spinning reserve, 10-minute non-synchronous reserve, 30-minute operating reserve, and regulation) are tracked across all five NYISO regions and three trading windows (DAM, RTC, real-time); regulation prices in July 2026 DAM averaged $23.54/MWh. Uplift costs (make-whole and bid-production-cost guarantees) totaled negative statewide in July 2026 (−$0.45/MWh statewide share, −$0.27/MWh balancing component), down from prior months. In-City energy mitigation in the NYC zone (Automatic Mitigation Procedure applied to committed generating units) mitigated 1.6% of unit-hours in DAM and 1.5% in real-time as of July 2026 YTD. The report includes external price comparisons with ISO-NE, PJM, Ontario IESO, and controllable interzone lines (Cross Sound Cable, Northport-Norwalk, Neptune).
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro owners operating in NYISO are directly affected by these price signals and by the mitigation percentages shown. The year-over-year increase in July LBMP (6.1%) reflects tightening energy scarcity; hydro operators benefit from scarcity pricing and from the ancillary-service market values posted here — regulation in particular, where conventional hydro typically competes. The in-city mitigation percentages show how often generating units' energy bids are capped by AMP in the constrained NYC zone; for hydro units committed there, this limits uplift recovery and revenue on high-priced hours. The uplift trend (negative in July, unlike prior months) is material because make-whole payments are a significant revenue stream for use-limited resources operating below their economic bid during shortage periods. External price comparisons inform hydro trading and interconnection strategies, especially the Ontario IESO and Quebec comparisons, which matter for Northeast hydro exports and import/export opportunity costs.

documents.ai_summary: This is the agenda for an August 11–12, 2026 joint meeting of the SPP Markets+ Design Working Group and Markets+ Resource Adequacy Task Force. Key action items include approval of co-located resource constraints (MIR8.2-R, comment deadline 8/3/2026), must-offer ceiling load exclusions (MIR74-R, comment deadline 4/20/2026), state-of-charge management for multi-state resources (MIR8.1, comment deadline 8/3/2026), ambient capacity derate submissions (MIR93-R, comment deadline 8/18/2026), null power designations in GHG transmission-and-recovery protocols (MIR94-R, comment deadline 8/7/2026), and dynamic multi-time-interval submissions in real-time balancing (MIR81-R, comment deadline 6/25/2026). Discussion items also include high-priority export system sales (MIR36.1-R, goal November MPEC), markets interchange transaction system point schedules (MIR60-R, goal August MPEC), quasi-pseudo-ties (MIR9.3-R, goal August MPEC), and MMU dispute resolution (MIR90-R, goal August MPEC). The meeting will be held by net conference; MDWG future meetings are scheduled for September 8–9, 2026 in Denver; October 7–8, 2026 by net-conference; and November 17, 2026 by net-conference.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although this document does not name hydropower directly, the agenda covers rule changes that bear directly on how hydro and multi-state storage resources—including pumped storage operating across state lines—register, bid, manage intra-interval state of charge, and stack ancillary services and energy products in SPP. Co-located resource constraints and state-of-charge rules reshape how these units can arbitrage across time and location; must-offer exclusions define what flexibility an operator can hold back or apply to loads; GHG null-power protocols affect revenue attribution in a carbon-conscious market; and the multi-time-interval framework governs how ramp and ramping-capability products are priced. For SPP members active in the Western markets, these decisions also influence choice of market platform (Markets+ vs. WEIM/EDAM) and the value of interregional export optionality.

documents.title: 05-MIR8.2-R Co-Located Resource Constraints submission.docx  [in Joint MDWG-MRAFT Meeting Materials 20260811.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This Markets+ Initiative Request establishes a participation model for co-located resources that allows MW-clipping between generation and storage (MSRs), directly affecting how pumped-storage and hybrid hydro facilities can offer energy and participate in capacity/flexibility markets, and setting operational and must-offer compliance rules that would apply to storage resources generally.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ Initiative Request 8.2-R proposes a new participation framework for co-located resources (two or more resources behind the same point of interconnection) by formalizing a "clipping" mechanism that allows the market clearing engine to transfer MWs between a generating resource and a Market Service Resource (MSR) when the sum of their registered capacities exceeds their shared injection limit. The proposal adds a Co-Located Resources Constraint definition and modifies Tariff Sections 4.2.9, 5.1, and 6.2 and Protocols Sections 4.2 and 9.1.1/9.1.16 to require individual registration and separate metering for each resource, integrate the constraint into Day-Ahead Market and RUC clearing, and adjust must-offer obligations when co-located resources plus self-committed charging exceed the shared constraint. The MIR ranks as High priority with desired MPEC approval in Q1 2027 and implementation in Q4 2027. Design, implementation, and operational complexity are all marked as High. The change is classified as a "New Protocol or Tariff" introducing new functionality rather than a correction or clarification.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage explicitly, but it establishes the participation model for co-located resources that would directly govern how pumped-storage facilities and hybrid generation-plus-storage arrangements participate in Markets+ capacity, energy, and flexibility markets. Pumped-storage owners operating behind a shared interconnection point would need to register their charge and discharge functions as separate resources, comply with the new co-located constraint in dispatch and must-offer calculations, and could benefit from automatic MW-clipping to maximize revenue when injection limits would otherwise curtail generation. The must-offer adjustments for self-committed charging (reducing load obligation when charging MWs are co-located and exceed the constraint) create a new operational tool for PSH operators managing charge-discharge cycles around flexibility and capacity obligations.

documents.title: 05-MIR8.2-R SPP Comments- 20260804.docx  [in Joint MDWG-MRAFT Meeting Materials 20260811.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Co-located resource participation rules directly affect revenue recognition, dispatch, and must-offer compliance for any market participant operating multiple generators at shared interconnection points, including conventional hydro, pumped-storage, and renewable-storage combinations common in hydro-rich regions.
documents.ai_summary: SPP's Markets+ Initiative Request 8.2 proposes formalization of a 'clipping' mechanism and Co-Located Resources Constraint to allow energy transfers between co-located generators sharing a point of interconnection, improving visibility of injection limits and enabling dispatch of generation that would otherwise be curtailed. The rule modifies Markets+ Tariff definitions and Sections 4.2.9, 5.1, and 6.2, plus Protocols Sections 4.2, 9.1.1, and 9.1.16. It requires individual registration and separate metering for each co-located resource, while allowing their combined offered capacity to exceed the shared interconnection constraint; the Market Operator will commit and dispatch such that collective output does not exceed the constraint. Must-offer obligations for day-ahead and real-time markets are recalculated to account for the constraint, with special carve-outs when co-located resources include market service resources (storage) managing self-committed charging. The proposal reflects stakeholder input from July 20, 2026 (MRATF) and July 29, 2026 (MORWG and MSR Subgroup) meetings; submitter document revisions are reflected in April 2025 Markets+ Tariff and 2.0a Markets+ Protocols.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention conventional hydropower or pumped-storage facilities by name. However, the rule directly affects any hydro owner or pumped-storage operator that co-locates multiple generation or storage assets at a single interconnection point—a common configuration in hydro-rich regions where a facility may combine run-of-river generation with downstream PSH units or co-locate solar and wind at a shared substation. The clipping mechanism and constraint formalization change both how such an operator's combined capacity is registered and committed, and which MWs are available to bid into energy and ancillary-service markets. The interaction between the constraint and self-committed storage charging could materially affect must-offer compliance and revenue stacking for combined-cycle hydro-storage complexes, requiring close attention to how storage charging eligibility and exemptions are modeled under the new tariff language.

documents.title: 06A-MIR74-R Must Offer Ceiling Load Exclusions submission.docx  [in Joint MDWG-MRAFT Meeting Materials 20260811.zip]
documents.filename: 06A-MIR74-R Must Offer Ceiling Load Exclusions submission.docx
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Must-offer obligation ceiling rules directly govern a Load Responsible Entity's (LRE) capacity-obligation mechanics, which is a core compliance obligation and revenue-preservation issue for hydro operators participating in Markets+ as resource providers or as entities with load obligations.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 74-R proposes revising the must-offer ceiling language in Markets+ Protocols section 4.2.1 and Tariff Attachment A, section 5.1.1(B) to require that physical loads explicitly excluded from the Western Resource Adequacy Program (WRAP) forward-showing obligation be added back into the Day-Ahead Must Offer Ceiling calculation. The stated objective is to ensure comprehensive accounting for all loads in the Markets+ footprint and prevent unintended shifts of capacity obligations to balancing authorities or other market participants. The MIR identifies a compliance and reliability risk: WRAP-excluded loads currently avoid bringing corresponding capacity into the market despite still requiring service, creating gaps in the must-offer obligation during peak demand when the ceiling is most likely to bind. Submitter John McCoskery (Bonneville Power Administration, jwmccoskery@bpa.gov) filed the initiative on 3/27/2026 as an enhancement under normal resolution timing; desired approval and implementation timelines are TBD.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never names hydro or pumped storage directly. However, the must-offer ceiling is a critical revenue-protection mechanism for Load Responsible Entities and resource owners participating in Markets+. If a hydro owner or PSH facility is registered to an LRE or has contractual load obligations in the Markets+ footprint, tightening the ceiling by adding back WRAP-excluded loads would increase the amount of capacity that LRE must offer into the market, effectively raising the must-offer obligation floor and potentially displacing higher-margin self-scheduled or economic-offer energy. Conversely, if the change reduces the ceiling's scope of exemptions, it could improve the market signal for capacity adequacy and reduce forced-offer requirements during non-binding periods, benefiting flexible resources. The outcome depends on whether the submitter's concern about capacity shortfalls reflects genuine systemic risk or an attempt to relax incentive-compatible omission of use-limited capacity.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 86-R, submitted by SRP on 7/17/2026, proposes enhancements to Attachment A sections 5.1.1(B) and 5.1.2(B) of the Markets+ Tariff and Protocols sections 4.2.1.1 and 4.2.1.2 to incorporate fleet performance changes (forced outages, derates, unplanned unavailability) for WRAP Qualifying Resources that are not registered in Markets+ as individual Resources—including imports, dynamic schedules, and internal interchange—into the day-ahead and real-time ceiling calculations for the must-offer obligation. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This submission proposes a new Market User Interface parameter for ambient derates below 50 MW, affecting how capacity and outage data are submitted in the must-offer obligation and fleet-performance calculations, which directly touches offer submission mechanics and resource capability representation for all dispatchable resources, including those with capacity-limiting ambient conditions.

However, any resource subject to ambient-temperature derating—a physical phenomenon affecting thermal generation but not limited to it—would be constrained by the current 50 MW threshold for derate recognition in must-offer calculations. This MIR would allow sub-50 MW ambient derates to flow into capacity and fleet-performance calculations, improving accuracy of resource-availability submissions for all resources experiencing such derations. Conventional hydropower with ambient-driven operating limits or facilities co-sited with load-serving thermal generation could benefit from more granular capacity accounting if they file ambient derates, though the document's silence on which resource types are affected or how derates factor into accreditation leaves the revenue and compliance implications unclear.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Markets+ Protocol revision defining validation and settlement rules for Load Responsible Entity system sales during export transactions, which directly affects how surplus seasonal resources are marketed and revenue is captured from exports—a strategic option and revenue stream for resource owners including hydro.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 36.1-R proposes Protocol language revisions (Sections 4.2.3.3 and 9.1.14) to clarify validation criteria for Load Responsible Entity (LRE) system sales associated with High Priority Export Interchange Transactions. The MIR, submitted by SPP staff on 6/4/2026, classifies exports as High Priority when they derive from an LRE's slice-of-system Resource during a WRAP Binding Season month and do not exceed the LRE's monthly seasonal surplus (defined as positive difference between total Resource QCC MWs less contract sales plus contract purchases minus Forward Showing Workbook obligation). High Priority exports also include those with NERC Priority 6 or 7 transmission service from internal sources or occurring during non-binding seasons outside an LRE, with pro-rata reduction of e-tag Energy profiles if cumulative High Priority exports exceed available seasonal surplus. The initiative is classified as medium complexity for design, implementation, and operations; target approval is Q3/2026 with implementation in Q1/2027.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or water-specific resources. However, the seasonal surplus and Forward Showing workbook mechanics directly apply to any dispatchable resource with seasonal capacity constraints. For conventional hydro and pumped storage participating in Markets+ as LREs or system-sale resources, this revision defines how much of their seasonal surplus can be marketed as high-priority exports—a material component of revenue for water-limited or contractually constrained resources during periods when they have generation above their forward commitments. The pro-rata settlement rule for over-subscribed exports and the monthly seasonal-surplus calculation affect how much revenue exposure a hydro or storage owner has in forward markets.

documents.filename: 10-MIR60-R Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) submission.docx
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document defines how Markets+ will handle interchange transactions at its boundary via generic system points (MPSPs), which affects how resources including hydro can export from or import into the platform, and establishes settlement and GHG attribution rules for those transactions—directly shaping the revenue and operational pathways for any hydro owner participating in or connected to Markets+.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 60-R establishes the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) framework, enabling Market Participants to schedule import and export transactions at the Markets+ boundary using generic Markets+ System Points (MPSPs) as sources and sinks rather than specific resources or loads. MPSPs are scheduling points located within each Participating Balancing Authority Area that facilitate transactions into, within, and out of the Markets+ footprint. The MIR revises Markets+ Protocols (sections including Glossary, definitions, offer submittal at 4.2.2.7 and 4.2.3.3, Day-Ahead Market inputs at 4.3.1.1, Real-Time inputs at 4.4.2.1.1, and settlement/GHG tracking at Sections 5.5.2.2, 8.2.6, and 9.4.2) to establish MPSPs as Settlement Locations, define import and export interchange limit controls per BAA, prohibit MPSP use for virtual transactions, and declare MITSPS transactions as non-attributed for GHG purposes. The document indicates desired MPEC approval in Q3 2026 and implementation in Q1 2027.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, MPSPs will become a key pathway for any resource (including hydro) in Markets+ to sell energy exported out of the footprint or purchase energy imported in, functioning as the generic source/sink point through which boundary transactions clear in the Day-Ahead and Real-Time markets. Hydro owners who operate in or interconnect to Markets+ will need to understand how MPSPs affect their ability to export in-region generation to external load or import purchases, and how the BAA-specific interchange limits (which can be set hourly by each Balancing Authority) constrain their external-trade flexibility. documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ Initiative Request 8.1-R proposes to enhance the MSR (Market Storage Resource) design by introducing time-coupled intervals within Day-Ahead Market and RUC studies. The proposed mechanism allows Market Participants with MSRs to elect for the Market Operator to calculate State of Charge by constraining each interval's starting State of Charge to the prior interval's ending State of Charge as calculated by the operator, rather than requiring the participant to forecast and submit a State of Charge for each interval. The proposal maintains the default policy that Market Participants manage State of Charge but introduces optionality to use market-calculated trajectories. Revisions affect Markets+ Tariff Sections 2.1.3, 2.2.3, and 4.2.2, and Protocols Sections 4.2, 4.3, and 4.4. The submission is ranked as High priority with desired MPEC approval in Q1 2027 and implementation in Q1 2027. Design, implementation, and operational complexity are all marked as High.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped-storage facilities, but MSR rules apply equally to any dispatchable storage resource in Markets+, including PSH. PSH owners benefit directly from this change because it removes the operational burden and financial risk of forecasting hour-ahead state-of-charge in their Day-Ahead offer when they elect the optionality—instead, the market operator will track actual dispatch and constraint each interval's state-of-charge to what was physically achieved in the prior interval, making their committed energy quantities feasible to deliver. This reduces the gap between Day-Ahead commitments and real-time capability that currently exposes storage to uneconomic dispatch or unearned start-up costs.

documents.ai_summary: MIR81-R, under discussion in SPP Markets+ MDWG, proposes to distinguish Normal MTI/MOTI (Market Transfer Interface / Market Opt-In Transfer Interface) constraints used in day-ahead, RUC, and pre-RTBM planning from Dynamic MTI/MOTI constraints used only in real-time balancing. documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly, but MIR81-R addresses transmission constraint handling in real-time dispatch, which affects how all dispatchable resources—including hydro—are economically dispatched in the balancing market. Hydro owners care about constraint treatment because it determines whether their plants face binding transmission limits in real-time that weren't present in the cleared day-ahead market, which can force real-time prices higher or prevent efficient utilization of already-committed capacity. The separation of normal and dynamic constraints could either improve or degrade real-time economics depending on how BAs apply the dynamic limits; hydro operators in SPP Markets+ should track whether the constraint logic preserves scarcity signals or creates artificial barriers to efficient dispatch.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC - NESCOE Conceptual Amendments - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NESCOE presents three conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's CAR-SA (Capacity Auction Reform / Seasonal Accreditation) capacity-market redesign, affecting how capacity resources are accredited, priced, and paid in a restructured auction with seasonal revenue recognition—directly touching capacity revenue and market design for all resources including conventional and storage hydro.
documents.ai_summary: NESCOE (New England States Committee on Electricity) proposes three conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's CAR-SA capacity-market redesign for implementation beginning 2028/29. Amendment 1 recommends aligning the CONE proxy resource performance assumption to a NERC class-average EFORd of 4.10% for combustion turbines, reducing the annual MRI-based Net CONE from $14.119/kW-mo to $11.432/kW-mo and seasonal payments from $8.501–$17.885/kW-mo to $7.372–$15.492/kW-mo. Amendment 2 proposes a four-period transition capacity price cap (stepping 1.0× to 1.6× annual Net CONE over the transition) to protect consumers from potential shortage pricing exceeding $3 billion in total seasonal market cost, versus ISO's three-period cap. Amendment 3 recommends phasing in the gas-only demand curve over three periods using proportional blending with today's zero-discount clearing, allowing more non-firm gas capacity (~3,000–3,500 MW) to clear in winter rather than the ISO's proposed hard limit of ~4,500 MW. The document indicates states' positions are still evolving and welcomes stakeholder feedback on these amendments.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not directly mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, CAR-SA's core mechanism—seasonal accreditation, marginal-reliability-impact-based capacity payment, and revised demand curves—governs how all dispatchable resources, including conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities, are credited and compensated for capacity supply. The CONE proxy resource (a combustion turbine) and its performance assumptions set the benchmark against which all non-energy-limited resources, including hydro, are measured for accreditation; NESCOE's lowering of that benchmark would reduce the capacity-payment floor for the entire fleet. The multi-year transition in the price cap and gas demand curve postpones the full revenue impact of seasonal accreditation, giving hydro owners longer visibility into how their seasonal availability and performance factors translate to capacity revenue under the new design. The $3 billion seasonal-cost volatility flagged in Amendment 2 matters to all capacity suppliers, not just gas resources.

The proposal builds on the FERC-approved CAR-PD reform and is slated for effect in 2027 ahead of the 2028-29 Capacity Commitment Period. Over 20 stakeholder meetings have been held focused on resource modeling, accreditation, gas constraints, seasonal auctions, and transition mechanisms. ISO-NE has deferred its vote request to the November 2026 Technical Committee meetings (November 4–5 for Markets Committee, November 17 for Reliability Committee, November 19 for Transmission Committee) and the December 3, 2026 Participants Committee meeting, with a planned FERC filing by end of December 2026. Amendment requests must be submitted by specified deadlines: August 4 for August meetings, August 28 for September meetings (posted by August posting date), and September 25 for October meetings (posted by October posting date).
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, CAR-SA's seasonality and accreditation reforms will reshape how non-energy-limited resources—the category into which most conventional hydro falls under ISO-NE's accreditation framework—are credited for capacity and revenue across seasons. Hydro owners need to monitor the accreditation modeling and seasonal-auction design to understand how median availability, performance factors, and seasonal deratings will be measured and applied to their units, as these drive capacity-market revenue. The deferred vote schedule and amendment-submission deadlines are critical for NHA members to coordinate with NEPOOL Counsel on tariff language that protects hydro interests in the accreditation methodology.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Advanced Energy United (AEU) proposes changes to ISO-NE's capacity accreditation model (CAR-SA) for storage resources, directly affecting how storage's seasonal capacity value (rMRI) is calculated and revenue streams established under the resource-adequacy framework.
documents.ai_summary: Advanced Energy United presents three proposed amendments to ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation and Resource Sufficiency Analysis (CAR-SA) for storage resources. Amendment 3 (Storage Charging Adjustment) argues that ISO-NE's proposed accreditation adjustment for storage resources understates available charging energy during multi-day events because it removes Type 3 hours from performance measurement without updating state-of-charge assumptions. AEU proposes reclassifying storage resources as EL3 (energy-limited, type 3) resource types in the GE MARS model as an interim solution, which would yield an rMRI value of approximately 0.253 rather than 0.187 under ISO's proposal. The amendments also address weather-year weighting (Amendment 1) and intertie modeling (Amendment 2) as they affect storage capacity accreditation. Amendment 1 proposes multi-day event metrics to replace peak-day weighting of tail events, and Amendment 2 proposes hourly import profiles instead of flat import-capacity blocks to capture when energy is available for storage charging. The presentation does not indicate a specific vote or filing deadline.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro directly. However, pumped-storage facilities operate under the same capacity-accreditation framework (CAR-SA and rMRI calculation) that governs other energy-limited resources in ISO-NE. The amendments AEU proposes—particularly the treatment of charging opportunities during multi-day winter events and the modeling of inter-regional energy availability for overnight charging—would directly affect how pumped-storage capacity value is measured and seasonal revenue is established. If ISO-NE adopts the reclassification of storage as EL3 resources, the ~18% upward adjustment to rMRI would flow through to capacity-market accreditation for any storage technology meeting that definition. The intertie and weather-weighting amendments also touch PSH revenue because they alter the assumptions about available energy during peak-risk periods when storage is needed most.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE economists Andrew Copland and Tami Ren present the Capacity Auction Reforms: Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal, with proposed effective date Q2 2027 (WMPP ID 185). The document addresses stakeholder follow-ups on offer formation and mitigation, including updates to intermittent-resource day-ahead must-offer rules, Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) methodology during the two-year transition phase (summer 2028 through winter 2030/31), and offer formulation when the Balancing Ratio is capped at 1. For the initial transition year (summer 2028–winter 2028/29), the ISO proposes a simple COPT equal to 37% of annual Net CONE; for subsequent transition years (summer 2029–winter 2030/31), a rolling-average methodology that incorporates seasonality by averaging historical seasonal capacity-price proportions and applying them to upcoming annual Net CONE values. The deck includes numerical examples showing COPT calculations, visual illustrations of Pay-for-Performance revenue under capped-BR rules, and a conceptual worked example demonstrating how a resource's expected performance during scarcity hours affects the cost of taking on a Capacity Supply Obligation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage. However, non-energy-limited conventional hydropower is subject to ISO-NE's accreditation and capacity rules, and this deck directly shapes the seasonal capacity revenue framework that hydro owners would use to formulate bids. The capped-BR analysis is particularly material: it shows how divergence between ePPR (earned) and PPR (charged) rates changes the cost of holding a capacity obligation, meaning a hydro plant's competitive capacity bid would depend on its expected performance relative to system scarcity ratios rather than just on general system parameters. Hydro's ability to ramp and respond during scarcity hours could either increase or decrease the perceived cost of a CSO depending on the realized ePPR/PPR split; the presentation does not model hydro performance characteristics specifically, leaving that gap for owners to evaluate.
