documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Capacity Auction Reforms—Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) directly reshape how non-energy-limited resources (the category that includes conventional hydropower) are accredited and compensated across summer and winter seasons, affecting hydro's capacity-market revenue and seasonal-payment-rate mechanics.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Markets Committee reviewed the Capacity Auction Reforms—Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) design at its July 7–9, 2026 meeting in Meredith, New Hampshire. The proposal replaces the current annual Qualified Capacity construct with seasonal accreditation based on Marginal Reliability Impact (rMRI) values, separating summer and winter auctions and introducing a winter demand curve for non-firm gas capacity. Key design elements include: Seasonal Payment Rates (SPR) anchoring method, a three-year transition glide path (blending Estimated Qualified Capacity with Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity through 2030–31), resource-specific corrections for storage and energy-limited resources, and firm-gas contract requirements for gas-only resources (16 hours per day across 20 days). The Committee raised extensive technical questions on the firm-gas requirement's relationship to modeled stress events, the storage adjustment's magnitude for short-duration resources, the applicability of class-average ratios to heterogeneous resources, the durability of transition-based investment signals, and the commercial feasibility of the assumed firming costs. The ISO committed to returning in August with remaining transition details and indicated it would consider sensitivities on import availability, storage-charging treatment, and phased gas-contract stringency. The activity schedule establishes a Qualification Data Submission Deadline roughly ten months before the seasonal auction, with resources able to enter through seasonal auctions, monthly reconfiguration events, or monthly bilateral periods even if they miss the primary seasonal deadline.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped storage directly. However, non-energy-limited resources—the category under which conventional hydropower participates—face fundamental changes in how their seasonal capacity accreditation is calculated (via rMRI rather than Qualified Capacity) and how their Dependable Capability and seasonal payment rates are determined. The storage and energy-limited-resource adjustment discussed here would not apply to conventional hydro but signals ISO-NE's evolving treatment of resource-class heterogeneity; the document's extended debate over class averaging (resource groups versus individual-resource ratios) and the interaction of material-change triggers with profile resets directly affects how hydro operators will qualify and update their accreditation attributes. The multi-year transition glide path and the uncertainty around seasonal reliability-risk splits, gas-constraint scope, and the Capacity Offer Price Threshold methodology will influence hydro's forward seasonal-revenue expectations and offer development—particularly because the framework anchors both seasons to a single Net CONE reference unit. The firm-gas framework, though targeted at gas-only resources, sets a precedent for how the ISO models fuel constraints and use limitations; if that approach were extended to other fuel-limited resources (oil, nuclear), hydro's competitive positioning and mitigation treatment could shift.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presents an update to the Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal, which will take effect Q2 2027 and modify how gas resources must demonstrate firm fuel contracts to qualify for capacity credits during winter, when regional natural gas supply is constrained. The ISO proposes to relax the LNG contract requirement from 20 days at 16 hours per day to 15 days at 16 hours per day (reducing required LNG volume by 25%), based on Analysis Group modeling showing 15 days would cover winter shortfall in all but 27 of 5,000 simulated winters. The ISO also clarifies that pipeline gas availability in its model is not modeled as a constant but varies day-to-day and across simulated winters, and explains that high gas prices during Winter Storm Fern reflect a physically binding regional gas constraint rather than unlimited availability at high price. Several gas resources reported forced outages exceeding 1 GW due to inability to procure gas during Winter Storm Fern. Questions or feedback should be sent to ISO-NE Markets Committee Secretary Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by August 24, 2026; tariff amendments and final design are expected in Q4 2026 and Q1 2027.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not address hydropower or pumped storage directly. The treatment of use-limited resources' seasonal availability—how their winter capability is measured and credited—is set by these same accreditation mechanics; the ISO's emphasis on physical constraints (gas supply bottlenecks) and on modeling availability variation across simulated conditions applies conceptually to hydro as well, whose winter capacity is itself constrained by water availability. Hydro operators should monitor how the ISO implements the accreditation and modeling principles articulated here, as they will shape how hydro's own seasonal contribution is quantified.

documents.ai_summary: Analysis Group, on behalf of ISO-NE, sets specifications for gas-only resources to qualify as 'Firm Capacity' under the Capacity Auction Reform (CAR) process for the three-month Winter Contract Period (December–February). Firm Capacity resources must hold either (1) primary or in-path secondary firm pipeline transportation capable of sustaining 16 hours of operations per day at elected capacity, with receipt points specified for each of five interstate pipelines serving New England, or (2) a minimum 15-day peaking contract with an LNG terminal with maximum daily quantity sufficient to sustain 16 hours of elected-capacity operations. Resources may sell pipeline firm gas rights during winter but must use firm transportation when nominating for day-ahead energy and capacity supply obligations. LNG contract call-option commodity charges are capped at the lesser of 125% of average Platts Gas Daily Algonquin City-gate December–February futures or $25/MMBtu. Resources elect MWs designated as Firm Capacity up to their Marginal Reliability Impact capacity. The document was originally posted April 15, 2026, and updated June 10, 2026, after stakeholder feedback; it is scheduled for implementation in Capacity Commitment Period (CCP) 19.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or storage resources. However, it establishes a two-tier accreditation framework in which gas plants can secure 'firm' status and command scarcity-driven capacity revenue during winter months by contracting for firm fuel supply, while plants without such contracts receive non-firm accreditation. This design parallels and competes with how ISO-NE accredits energy-limited resources (including conventional hydro and pumped storage) based on their seasonal availability and reliability contribution, meaning the gas-firm specifications effectively define the baseline against which hydro's seasonal capacity accreditation and winter-period energy-scarcity premiums will be benchmarked. Hydro owners should understand how ISO-NE is compensating competing dispatchable gas capacity and what operational requirements (16-hour daily sustained output, must-offer rules, use-when-nominated constraints) are being imposed on the gas fleet, as these set the performance and revenue standards the RTO may later apply to storage and hydro accreditation adjustments.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The proposal addresses capacity accreditation for resources with temperature-dependent output reductions—a mechanism that applies directly to conventional hydropower and other dispatchable resources whose summer output derates under elevated ambient conditions, affecting their seasonal capacity revenue and system responsibility shares in ISO-NE's Forward Capacity Market.
documents.ai_summary: Constellation proposes a Conceptual Amendment to ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation and Responsibility (CAR-SA) mechanism for resources with known and predictable output reductions at elevated ambient temperatures. The proposal would change the treatment from a delist-bid approach to an offer-based approach using the formula: Ambient MWs = rMRI × (Rating at 90°F – Rating at 100°F). Constellation argues this preserves current functionality and ensures a resource's capacity obligation corresponds accurately to its share of system requirements under stressed summer conditions, without double-counting ambient deratings that are excluded from both Resource Adequacy Analysis modeling and NERC GADS reporting guidance. The amendment is presented as addressing ISO's proposed CAR-SA rules and will proceed to further discussion.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never names hydropower, but it addresses capacity accreditation for resources with output reductions at elevated ambient temperatures—a physical characteristic conventional hydro shares with thermal units. Under ISO-NE's capacity market, a plant's seasonal-accreditation factor (rMRI) and resulting capacity obligation (Manifest Capacity Responsibility, or MRIC) determine its revenue and dispatch responsibilities; how ambient deratings are treated directly affects whether hydro is obligated to deliver more capacity than it physically can in peak-summer stress conditions, imposing financial penalties or forcing inefficient offer strategies. Constellation's proposal would scale the ambient-derate allowance with the plant's actual availability factor (rMRI) rather than capping it independently, which would restore the economic optionality of offering at true marginal cost. The outcome matters substantially to how often hydro owners must choose between overshooting their physical capability or accepting uneconomic obligation shortfalls.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02g.i: CAR-SA - FirstLight PFP BR - Presentation Rev. 1
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FirstLight proposes amendment to ISO-NE's Pay-for-Performance capacity mechanism to adjust the balancing-ratio cap governing over-performance payments for resources with capacity obligations, directly affecting how capacity revenue and performance incentives are calculated for all resource types including hydro.
documents.ai_summary: FirstLight proposes to amend ISO-NE's CAR-SA (Capacity Accreditation and Resource Supply Obligation - Special Accreditation) Pay-for-Performance mechanism by adjusting the Balancing Ratio (BR) cap to account for the lower fleet-wide resource rating under MRIC (Marginal Resource Impact) accreditation versus prior MCAP (Maximum Capacity) accreditation. FERC Order directed ISO-NE to cap BR at 1.0 times CSO (Capacity Supply Obligation), but FirstLight argues that BR cap of 1.0×CSO under current QC-based accreditation does not equate to the same cap under CAR-SA MRIC-based accreditation. FirstLight's preferred solution proposes a fleet-wide BR cap calculated as 1 divided by the fleetwide rMRI of CSO resources (e.g., 1/0.74 = 1.35), with resource-specific adjustments and shortfall allocation to ensure no resource's obligation exceeds its physical MCAP while maintaining sufficient funding for over-performance payments that incentivize performance beyond CSO levels. The proposal is presented to the NEPOOL Markets Committee for consideration.
documents.hydro_read_through: ISO-NE's accreditation transition from MCAP to MRIC-based capacity rating reduces the capacity obligation assigned to all resource types, but under a strict 1.0 BR cap this creates a structural funding gap in the Pay-for-Performance mechanism—over-performance payments would be severely underfunded even though the ISO explicitly wants to incentivize performance above the lowered CSO levels. Conventional hydro and other resources benefit directly from this mechanism because the balancing ratio cap determines the ceiling on over-performance payment rates available during scarcity events; if the cap is set too low relative to the accreditation methodology change, the PPR (Pay-for-Performance Rate) effectively collapses and hydro owners lose the revenue signal to perform. FirstLight's proposed adjustment of the BR cap upward (to ~1.35 in their example) is designed to restore the performance-incentive effect across the fleet, including for hydro and other non-CSO megawatts, by matching the cap to the lower accreditation baseline rather than capping at 1.0 absolute terms.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02g.ii: CAR-SA - FirstLight Conceptual Amendment on Risk Split - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FirstLight proposes an amendment to ISO-NE's capacity auction risk split and accreditation framework that would directly affect how non-energy-limited resources (including conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities) are accredited and receive capacity revenue based on system LOLE conditions rather than administratively fixed parameters.
documents.ai_summary: FirstLight proposes that ISO-NE's Capacity Auction and Related Services (CAR-SA) accreditation and risk-split parameters be set based on actual clearing outcomes and system LOLE from prior auctions rather than administratively set values. Under the proposal, resource accreditation would be based on the LOLE implied by clearing results from the prior same-season auction, and the risk split (used to calculate seasonal Net ICR) would be derived from the ratio of LOLE between the most recent winter and summer auction clearing results. The amendment includes a transition mechanism: until a full year of auction results is available, accreditation and risk split would use administratively set parameters (ISO's current proposal), with FirstLight accepting a 50/50 LOLE-based risk split for the first year. The presentation illustrates through two examples how an administratively set risk split misaligned with actual system conditions can distort pricing signals and new-entry incentives, and shows how improved resource accreditation could lower clearing prices and system costs.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the amendment addresses accreditation and capacity-market revenue for non-energy-limited resources (a category encompassing most conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities in ISO-NE). If adopted, shifting from fixed administrative risk-split to one derived from prior-auction LOLE would change the seasonal revenue signals that drive hydro owners' capacity-market revenue and entry/exit decisions. The amendment's rationale—that accreditation should reflect realistic system conditions rather than a static 50/50 split—suggests that in years when actual winter/summer risk differs materially from 50/50, hydro accreditation and clearing prices would increase or decrease accordingly, making capacity revenue more volatile but more aligned with actual seasonal scarcity.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02l: CAR-SA: Tariff Review - Redlines - Section III.1
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This tariff revision governs claimed capability audits and dispatchability requirements for all generation types, including conventional hydro and reversible (pumped-storage) hydroelectric units, affecting their accreditation, operational obligations, and dispatch treatment in ISO-NE's capacity and energy markets.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE Market Rule 1, Section III.1.5, establishes claimed capability audit procedures for generator assets and demand response resources, ending the audit requirement after August 31, 2027. The tariff specifies separate audit durations and methodologies: Establish Claimed Capability Audits (unannounced, with duration varying by technology type), Seasonal Claimed Capability Audits (summer and winter demonstration requirements), and ISO-Initiated Claimed Capability Audits (ISO-performed verification). Conventional hydro types—Daily Pondage, Run of River, and Weekly—require 2-hour durations for both Establish and Seasonal audits. Reversible (pumped-storage) hydraulic turbines also require 2-hour audit durations. The tariff exempts non-intermittent daily hydro from Establish Claimed Capability Audit requirements for newly commercial resources. Section III.1.11.5 requires intermittent hydro resources to either self-schedule at Economic Minimum Limit (if not cleared in Day-Ahead) or self-schedule with locked Economic Min/Max (if not committed by ISO), and permits market participants to elect dispatchability for hydro intermittent resources less than 5 MW on transmission below 115 kV, or as DDP Dispatchable if able to operate within a dispatchable range.
documents.hydro_read_through: These audit procedures directly determine how ISO-NE validates the seasonal capacity claims on which hydro owners' Forward Capacity Market revenues depend. The 2-hour duration for conventional and reversible hydraulic turbines and the separate treatment of daily pondage hydro from the new-resource Establish audit requirement create a specific compliance pathway that affects the timing and cost of demonstrating claimed output capability each year (until the audit obligation sunsets in 2027). For variable or run-of-river hydro resources, the self-scheduling and Do-Not-Exceed dispatch requirements shift dispatch control away from the owner's optimization, reducing strategic flexibility in real-time operations and potentially limiting revenue capture from high-price intervals. The option for small hydro to elect dispatchability or maintain non-dispatchable status introduces a participation-model choice with trade-offs in commitment obligations and settlement.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02l: CAR-SA: Tariff Review - Redlines - Section III.15
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's new Annual Seasonal Capacity Market structure (replacing the Forward Capacity Market starting June 2028) redefines how capacity is procured, priced, and accredited—core revenue mechanisms for all dispatchable resources including conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing a two-season Annual Seasonal Capacity Market effective June 1, 2028, replacing the Forward Capacity Market. The mechanism will conduct separate Summer and Winter Capacity Auctions each year, with Capacity Commitment Periods running June 1 through May 31. Capacity is procured using System-Wide and Capacity Zone Demand Curves adjusted for Seasonal MRI (Marginal Reliability Impact) values, and resources must qualify via a defined qualification process. Specific auction timelines include: Summer Capacity Auction Qualification Data Submission Deadline in February, Capacity Demonstration Deadline in March, and Auction in April; Winter Qualification Data Submission Deadline in June, Capacity Demonstration Deadline in September, and Auction in October. Resources failing to achieve critical path schedule milestones face termination of monitoring status and interconnection agreement termination via Commission filing. Capacity Auction Offer Price Cap is set at the greater of 1.6 times Net CONE or CONE; for the 2028–2029 period, CONE is $12.400/kW-month and Net CONE is $7.468/kW-month. Non-Commercial Capacity Resources transition rules require quarterly critical path schedule reporting with documentation of permits, financing, equipment orders, site construction progress (>20% of construction costs), equipment delivery and testing, commissioning, and transmission upgrade completion. Municipal utilities retain specifically allocated Capacity Transfer Rights (CTRs) for Pool-Planned Units (Millstone 3, Seabrook, Stonybrook units, Wyman 4) through December 31, 2040, with allocations based on ownership percentages shown in the tariff table; CTR value reflects zonal clearing-price differentials. Load obligations are assigned based on each Market Participant's Coincident Peak Contribution to system-wide annual peak load.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, ISO-NE's move from the multi-year Forward Capacity Market to annual two-season auctions materially affects capacity revenue and accreditation for all resources. Conventional hydro, which qualifies as a Non-Energy Limited Resource, will now compete in separate seasonal auctions using Seasonal MRI values—shifting how its seasonal availability profile translates to capacity obligation. Pumped-storage hydro will be subject to these same seasonal accreditation and auction mechanics, though the tariff excerpt does not detail how state-of-charge rules or cycling constraints interact with the new seasonal structure—those details are marked "[Revisions Forthcoming]" for at least one section. The shift to a two-season framework creates an opportunity for hydro owners to optimize seasonal bids around winter/summer reliability posture, but also introduces execution risk on qualifying timelines and potential loss of interconnection rights if projects miss critical path milestones. The CTR allocation for municipal-utility-owned Pool-Planned Units is a notable legacy carve-out that sets capacity-zone transfer rights through 2040 based on historical ownership percentages.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02l: CAR-SA: Tariff Review - Redlines - Section III.12
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE is revising its Installed Capacity Requirement calculation and Marginal Reliability Impact methodology in Section III.12, which directly affects how all capacity resources—including Energy-Limited and Energy Storage resources (explicitly named)—are accredited and valued in the capacity market, a core revenue stream for hydro and PSH operators.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is proposing tariff redlines to Section III.12 of its markets tariff, revising the calculation of Installed Capacity Requirement (ICR), Marginal Reliability Impact (MRI), and resource adequacy criteria for the capacity market. Key changes include: explicit treatment of Energy-Limited Generating Capacity Resources and Energy Storage Generating Capacity Resources in the MRI calculation methodology (Section III.12.1.2.2), where their resource-specific MRI values are determined by scaling both maximum capability and energy constraints proportionally when measuring reliability impact; updated LOLE standards from 0.1 days per year to 0.05 days per Capacity Commitment Period for the New England Control Area; and revised procedures for calculating tie benefits and local sourcing requirements in zonal capacity markets. The document also introduces provisions for a third annual reconfiguration auction beginning June 1, 2027. The redlines are under review at the NEPOOL Markets Committee meeting dated 2026-08-11, indicating stakeholder development is underway but no vote or filing date is stated in this excerpt.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage by name; however, it directly governs how all energy-limited and energy-storage capacity resources are accredited in ISO-NE's capacity market. Conventional hydropower is accredited as an Energy-Limited resource, and pumped-storage hydro as an Energy Storage resource, so the MRI and accreditation methodology shown here determines their seasonal capacity revenue and participation parameters. The explicit inclusion of proportional scaling of both capability and daily/seasonal energy limits in the MRI calculation is material to how hydro's use-limited nature affects its reliability value; changes to these formulas or the LOLE standard (from 0.1 to 0.05 days per Capacity Commitment Period) would shift the accreditation factors that set hydro's capacity payments. The reconfiguration auction framework and tie-benefits treatment also affect export capability pricing for hydro-rich zones. The document does not address how energy-limited resources' default energy bids or offer rules are treated, nor does it detail the penalty/performance framework applied to accredited capacity.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02f: CAR-SA: Impact Analysis: Resource Accreditation Modeling, cont. - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's CAR-SA proposal directly alters how capacity market accreditation is calculated and zonal requirements set for energy-limited and storage resources, affecting seasonal revenue and bid parameters for any such resource (including conventional and pumped-storage hydro).
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE staff (Chris Geissler, Fei Zeng) presented the Resource Accreditation Modeling Impact Analysis for the Capacity Auction Reforms: Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal, with proposed effective date Q2 2027 (WMPP ID 185). The presentation detailed capacity zone requirements and demand curves for Maine, Northern New England (export-constrained), and Southeast New England (import-constrained) under both current and CAR-SA rules; summer MRIC-based MCL values for Maine and NNE are lower than annual MCL under current rules, while winter MRIC-based MCL values are higher. ISO revised its rMRI adjustment calculation for energy-limited and storage resources by removing the EFORd term in response to stakeholder feedback. ISO assessed but declined to adopt FirstLight's alternate load-year weighting methodology and a profile-based tie-benefits approach incorporating NECEC impact, concluding both would require broader market design changes outside CAR scope. Contact for questions: Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by August 24, 2026. Next milestones: continued discussion of tariff redlines, transition mechanism, offer formation and mitigation, and financial assurance policy in August–September 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped storage. However, ISO-NE's accreditation framework applies to energy-limited resources (the category under which conventional and pumped-storage hydro are accredited), so these changes to rMRI calculation, seasonal zonal requirements, and demand-curve methodology directly set the parameters hydro owners face for capacity-market revenue. The removal of EFORd from the adjustment formula and the two-step rMRI process affect how energy-limited and storage resource availability translates into accredited capacity. Seasonal separation of MCL and demand curves creates seasonal revenue exposure that didn't exist under annual accreditation, and the shift from annual to MRIC-based MCL values will change clearing prices and accreditation outcomes for any energy-limited or storage resource depending on duration and outage characteristics. The ISO's rejection of an expanded tie-benefits calculation (which might have benefited storage charging) narrows the avenue for improving storage/hydro accreditation through external energy sourcing.

documents.title: 2026-08-11-13 MC/RC/TC A02l: CAR-SA: Tariff Review - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This presentation details ISO-NE's redesign of capacity accreditation (MRI-based methods replacing EFORd) and seasonal capacity auctions—directly affecting how all dispatchable and storage resources, including conventional hydropower and pumped storage, qualify for and are paid in capacity markets.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE Markets Committee presentation (August 2026) on Capacity Auction Reforms—Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) tariff revisions, effective Q2 2027. The proposal replaces the existing annual capacity auction and Qualified Capacity accreditation with seasonal (Summer and Winter) commitment periods and Minimal Risk Index (MRI)-based accreditation for all resource categories: Generating Capacity Resources (including Energy-Limited and Energy Storage), Intermittent Power Resources, Demand Capacity Resources, Distributed Energy Resources, and Import Capacity Resources. Key changes include: Relative MRI calculations based on demonstrated performance or assumed values for new resources; seasonal-specific resource adequacy planning criteria (0.05 LOLE per Capacity Commitment Period); a new Gas-Constrained Winter Capacity Demand Curve; revised zonal inputs including import-constrained and export-constrained Capacity Zone demand curves scaled to Seasonal MRI Capacity; and modifications to accreditation rules in Tariff Sections III.1, III.12, III.15, and II.K. The deck walks through accreditation and gas-firming methodology roadmaps and flags that Transition Mechanism, Passive Demand Capacity Resource accreditation, Financial Assurance Policy, and Billing Policy rules are forthcoming. Next steps: continued discussion in September Markets Committee on tariff redlines and transition mechanics, with Resource Accreditation Modeling and Market Clearing Impact Analysis ongoing.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, conventional hydropower is accredited as a 'Generating Capacity Resource' (specifically 'Energy Limited' for run-of-river and reservoir plants), and pumped storage as an 'Energy Storage Generating Capacity Resource,' and both are subject to the accreditation and seasonal auction mechanics described here. Seasonal MRI-based accreditation replaces the prior EFORd and Qualified Capacity approach, meaning hydro owners' capacity revenues will now depend on Relative MRI values (comparing each resource's seasonal availability to a perfect capacity resource, derived from resource-specific MRI and planned performance data). Energy-limited and storage resources face additional Relative MRI adjustments, and the split into seasonal commitment periods changes when and how much capacity must be offered and is paid. The mechanics of how seasonal median availability, forecasting, and qualified-energy inventory are measured for hydro (especially run-of-river and storage) will be critical to revenue impact but are not detailed in this high-level tariff roadmap.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group reviewed resource-adequacy assumptions and modeling for Planning Year 2027–2028. Key updates include: (1) MISO continues seasonal LOLE targets with an annual floor of 0.1 days/year and seasonal minimum thresholds of 0.01 days/year, applied since PY 2023–2024; (2) load-modeling methodology has been refined and is undergoing automation to standardize extreme-temperature adjustments, with feedback due July 7, 2026; (3) Capacity Import/Export Limit (CIL/CEL) studies have been posted for all four seasons (Summer 2027, Fall 2027, Winter 2027–2028, Spring 2028) with stakeholder model-review feedback due July 7, 2026; (4) wind-profile enhancements are being adopted for PY 2027–2028, using regression-based windspeed modeling that changes wind ELCC values (notably increasing Spring wind ELCC) and alters storage-resource accreditation under both ELCC and Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) frameworks; and (5) resource-availability assumptions for outyear LOLE models will no longer incorporate survey-based retirement suggestions, only approved Attachment Y filings. Next LOLEWG meeting is scheduled for August 11, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydropower's capacity-revenue accreditation—set by ELCC seasonal values and DLOL performance factors—is directly determined by MISO's LOLE and wind-profile modeling. Enhanced wind profiles systematically increase wind's ELCC accreditation (especially in spring) and shift critical-hour distributions, reducing multi-hour storage DLOL percentages. For conventional hydro owners, the shift in critical-hour timing and thermal outage-overlap analysis affects seasonal capacity-credit allocations; for pumped-storage operators, reduced winter and spring DLOL percentages may lower accreditation for use-limited multi-hour events, directly reducing capacity revenue. The automation of load-forecast uncertainty and the switch from survey-based retirement assumptions to only-filed retirements also reshape long-term adequacy signals that affect investment and mothballing decisions.

documents.title: Comments - CAISO DMM - Annual Summer Available Transmission Capacity Assessment - Mar 31, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO transmission planning and ATC methodology directly affects interregional wheeling and the Available Transmission Capacity available to hydropower exports from the Northwest (Malin intertie) into California — a core revenue and transmission-access issue for NHA members participating in CAISO markets and WEIM.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring comments on the 2026 Annual Summer ATC Assessment oppose retiring the Path 26 priority wheel-through (PWT) impact assessment, which evaluates how north-to-south high-priority wheeling reservations from Malin to Palo Verde affect internal CAISO transmission constraints. DMM argues that recent mild summers (2023–2025) are an insufficient basis for discontinuing the annual internal-constraint assessment, and that future conditions — including EDAM implementation and new transmission projects in Idaho and Nevada — may materially alter power flows and increase demand for wheel-through capacity, reinforcing the need for continued monitoring. The Path 26 assessment serves as a safeguard against oversubscription of CAISO transmission when wheeling-through transactions (which carry equal priority to CAISO load) could crowd out resource adequacy supplies during high-demand periods. For hydro owners exporting from the Northwest via the Malin intertie, this assessment directly informs how much wheel-through capacity remains available after CAISO load priority is satisfied — losing the assessment could leave external supply visibility and congestion risk unmanaged.

documents.title: Comments - Six Cities - Annual Summer Available Transmission Capacity Assessment - Mar 31, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Path 26 transmission-capability assessment affects interregional wheel-through reservations and deliverability of resources within CAISO, directly touching hydro export and interregional transfer capability—a strategic option for NHA members in the West (especially Northwest hydro exports via CAISO paths).
documents.ai_summary: Six Cities (municipal utilities in Southern California) oppose CAISO's proposal to discontinue the annual evaluation of Path 26 capability as part of the Summer ATC (Available Transmission Capacity) Assessment. Path 26 evaluation tracks the effect of wheel-through transactions on resource deliverability within CAISO and across interregional paths. CAISO cited limited wheel-through impact over the past two years under mild weather conditions, but Six Cities argue that this experience is insufficient to drop the evaluation, particularly given the startup of EDAM, which may change grid use patterns and wheel-through behavior. No comment deadline was stated in the June 2026 submittal; the deadline appears to have been April 14, 2026 (already passed). This matters to hydro owners using CAISO as an export corridor or relying on wheel-through transmission to reach Eastern demand — losing annual Path 26 visibility could obscure transmission constraints affecting their interregional sales options.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PG&E's critique of CAISO's proposed removal of Path 26 transmission sensitivity analysis directly affects interregional wheel-through transaction deliverability and the redispatch costs hydro owners would face when ATC assumptions fail — a transmission-planning and market-power issue for large hydro exporters.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposed retiring the Path 26 sensitivity analysis from its Annual Summer Available Transmission Capacity (ATC) assessment; PG&E opposes removal and argues the analysis should be retained and expanded. The Path 26 analysis is a safeguard designed to detect deliverability issues with high-priority wheel-through interregional transactions that the standard ATC process does not explicitly assess. PG&E contends that absence of recent congestion does not justify removal, that low wheel-through reservations may reflect constrained ATC rather than genuine capacity availability, and requests transparency on redispatch costs borne by CAISO when the unmonitored Path 26 constraint binds (citing six days in summer 2025 when flows exceeded 3,500 MW). Large hydro owners exporting to the Southwest and Pacific Northwest via interties depend on ATC availability and deliverability certainty; loss of Path 26 monitoring would increase redispatch cost exposure and reduce visibility into congestion that could strand available export capacity.

documents.ai_summary: The CPUC's Energy Division submitted comments on CAISO's March 31, 2026 Annual Summer ATC (Available Transmission Capacity) Assessment, requesting expanded system-wide power-flow analysis beyond the current Path 26 focus. ED staff opposes retirement of the Transmission Service and Market Scheduling Priorities Path 26 assessment and cautions against relying on mild 2024–2025 conditions to justify reduced congestion analysis. The CPUC specifically requests EDAM-wide power flows, South-to-North and North-to-South flow impacts (including SunZia), comparative year-over-year analysis, and analysis of how power flows will change with WEIM departures to Markets+ and dual-market DAM competition. For Northwest and California hydro exporters, this analysis directly shapes the transmission paths available to move energy into California during summer scarcity and determines whether EDAM expansion will ease or tighten internal constraints that affect pricing and deliverability for existing hydro resources.

documents.title: Presentation - Resource Interconnection Standards Fair 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document defines interconnection application requirements, technical data submissions, deposits, site control rules, and POI-constraint mapping that directly govern how hydropower and pumped-storage projects enter CAISO's queue, affecting deliverability, cost structure, and strategic timing of interconnection filings.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Resource Interconnection Standards (RIS) Fair presentation explains the Cluster 16 interconnection process for projects under Appendix KK, beginning with application window 10/1/2026–10/15/2026, with completeness review within 5 business days and opportunity for correction until 1700 PPT 10/15/2026. Applicants must submit deposits and fees at submission: Application Fee $5,000; Study Deposit (< 80 MW: $35,000 + $1,000/MW; 80–200 MW: $150,000; ≥200 MW: $250,000); Commercial Readiness Deposit (2× Study Deposit, due by end of customer engagement window); and for merchant projects, Merchant Option Deposit ($10,000/MW of deliverable capacity, minimum $500,000, maximum $5,000,000). Site control must cover 90% of acreage, with minimum acreage requirements by technology (Hydro: 10 acres/MW) and must extend through commercial operation date. Regulatory Limitation Site Control Deposit option ($10,000/MW, minimum $500,000, maximum $2,000,000) is available for projects on public or trust lands awaiting regulatory approval. Projects tied after cluster intake criteria review will proceed to auction ($/MW sealed bid via GRIP); auction winners must post auction deposit by end of customer engagement window. Cluster Study begins January 2027. The presentation also covers NDA requirements for transmission planning participation, POI-constraint mapping, and restricted POIs.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydropower and PSH owners in CAISO's queue must navigate substantially higher and more complex deposit requirements under RIS, with a $5,000 application fee, size-scaled study deposits up to $250,000, a Commercial Readiness Deposit equal to 2× the study deposit, and conditional Merchant Option or Regulatory Limitation deposits—all due at submission or by defined milestones—raising the cost of entry and liquidity required to compete in Cluster 16. The 10 acres/MW minimum site-control requirement for hydro is more stringent than most competing technologies (solar 6 acres/MW, wind 30 acres/MW, BESS 0.06 acres/MW), creating a specific land-siting challenge for conventional run-of-river plants and requiring clear documentation of long-term lease or ownership through COD. The auction mechanism for tied projects and the auction-deposit structure add execution risk: if a project ties on intake criteria, it must submit a competitive bid by a fixed deadline or withdraw, with the winning bid amount then determining the deposit owed to the PTO—a feature that could amplify capital requirements for speculative or flexible projects.

documents.title: 2a 2027 Proposed Market Project Descriptions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's 2027 market project pipeline includes multiple mechanisms directly affecting hydro revenue streams (energy price formation, ancillary services, capacity accreditation, flexibility products, storage participation) and strategic options (transmission planning, load growth, seams governance, water/reliability coordination), plus compliance obligations (Order 2222 DER participation, FERC transmission planning).
documents.ai_summary: NYISO released a draft 2027 market project candidate list organized into four categories: Prioritize (37 projects), Mandatory (4 projects), Continuing (2 projects), and Future (7 projects). Projects span energy and capacity market design, ancillary services, transmission planning, DER/hybrid aggregation, demand response, storage, and operational standards. Key prioritized projects include 5-minute transaction scheduling with Hydro-Québec (to improve ramping flexibility and price convergence in real-time markets), Balancing Intermittency Phase 2 (evaluating long-duration reserve needs), Capacity Zone Redesign (redefining ICAP zonal structure and locational pricing), Storage as Transmission (evaluating storage as alternative to transmission upgrades), and Time-Differentiated TCCs (granular congestion-hedging products). Mandatory projects include FERC Order 881 compliance (ambient-adjusted line ratings), FERC Order 2222 compliance (DER market deployment), FERC Transmission Planning Order 1920 implementation (long-term regional transmission planning reform), and a forthcoming Large Loads order. Continuing projects include Dynamic Reserves Phase 1 (moving from fixed to dynamic reserve requirements based on system conditions). The document was prepared by NYISO Product and Project Management as of June 30, 2026, for discussion at the Budget & Priorities Working Group.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro operators should track several mechanics: 5-minute scheduling with HQ will expand real-time balancing tools available to hydro, raising its role in price formation and intra-hour flexibility revenue. The Balancing Intermittency Phase 2 project—evaluating long-duration reserves and enhanced operating-reserve designs—directly targets products hydro has traditionally supplied; if the ISO adopts new duration or ramping products, hydro's accreditation and offer parameters may shift. Capacity Zone Redesign could reallocate seasonal and locational scarcity signals, affecting where existing hydro plants earn capacity revenue. Storage-as-Transmission exploration—though focused on batteries—will test regulatory boundaries on whether storage/hydro can substitute for wires; if storage gets that role, hydro may too. Hybrid Aggregation Model deployment (HSR by April 30, 2027) and Order 2222 compliance (2027 deployment) expand co-location and DER paths for small hydro. FERC Order 1920 transmission planning will open long-term interregional coordination, affecting Northwest hydro's export corridors. Time-Differentiated TCCs improve hedging granularity but do not directly change hydro's products. None of these projects are decisions yet—they are concept-stage or design-stage work—but the agenda signals where NYISO sees market friction in a high-renewables grid and where rule changes will concentrate.

documents.title: Regulation Phase 2 Settlement Impacts
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's Regulation Redesign Phase 2 directly changes how hydroelectric resources calculate and receive settlement compensation for regulation service — a core ancillary-services revenue stream hydro supplies, especially the opportunity-cost methodology that determines whether hydro is adequately paid for its service.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Regulation Redesign Phase 2, approved by FERC on June 14, 2024, splits the single-signal bidirectional Regulation product into two separate products—RegUp and RegDn—each with distinct requirements, offers, clearing prices, and settlements, effective December 1, 2026. Key changes include bifurcated performance metrics and clearing-price credits (both capability and mileage components) by product type; separate opportunity-cost calculation for RegUp and RegDn, with a single intra-commitment opportunity cost accounting for both assignments and 'Regulation signal bias' (energy produced while providing regulation); and new MSRS settlement reports including a dedicated 'Regulation Hydro Opportunity Cost Details' report for hydro units. The settlement changes take effect December 1, 2026, with the first billing statement issued January 8, 2027, following sandbox testing in August–September 2026 and education sessions in October–November 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro operators in PJM depend on regulation revenue, which is highly sensitive to how opportunity costs are calculated and whether deployment actually compensates them for forgone energy sales. Phase 2's bifurcation of RegUp and RegDn signals means hydro must now offer separately for each direction and will be paid separate clearing prices and opportunity-cost credits for each, potentially improving precision in compensation but requiring operational and bidding-system changes. The explicit treatment of 'Regulation signal bias' in opportunity-cost settlement is significant for hydro because it recognizes that regulation activity produces or consumes energy incidentally—a design nuance that directly affects how much uplift hydro receives when it isn't compensated by the clearing prices alone.

documents.title: 20260807 ERSC Item 04 IMM South Report.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The IMM report on MISO South market outcomes addresses energy price formation, ancillary-services cost recovery through uplift, and capacity-accreditation mechanics that directly affect the procurement and pricing of products conventionally supplied by dispatchable resources including hydro.
documents.ai_summary: Potomac Economics' Independent Market Monitor presents a February–June 2026 performance review of MISO South, finding the market remains competitive overall but identifying several design gaps. Energy prices are dominated by gas-cost correlation; capacity costs have risen significantly in summer as excess capacity conditions have resolved (2026–2027 Planning Resource Auction summer prices cleared at $412.10–$424.30/MW-day in Zones 8–10 and Zone 9 respectively). Out-of-market Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RSG) uplift payments, concentrated in MISO South for Voltage and Local Reliability (VLR) support in load pockets, would be better reflected in market products. The IMM recommends reaccrediting existing solar based on 4–7 pm output rather than 2–5 pm to better match evening peak reliability needs, which it estimates would have reduced existing-solar accreditation by 2.6 GW market-wide and raised summer prices by 50 percent; establishing local Short-Term Reserve requirements for load pockets to incentivize quick-start investment; and defining capacity zones reflecting electrical load pockets for more precise capacity procurement.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the report's findings on RSG uplift payments and capacity accreditation are directly relevant because conventional dispatchable resources, including hydro, are subject to the same cost-recovery and accreditation mechanics. The recommendation to replace the 2–5 pm solar accreditation window with 4–7 pm signals that MISO recognizes reliability needs persist after solar production drops steeply—the window where dispatchable resources including hydro are relied upon for evening ramps and reserves. Similarly, the recommendation to establish local STR requirements and redefine capacity zones based on load pockets could increase the value of quick-start and flexible capacity resources if implemented, affecting both the ancillary-services opportunities and seasonal capacity revenue available to hydro plants in MISO South's transmission-constrained regions.

documents.ai_summary: MISO and MISO Transmission Owners filed a motion in FERC Docket EL26-70-000 requesting a 90-day abeyance (through November 16, 2026) of a Show Cause proceeding to permit development of tariff proposals addressing large-load integration. The Show Cause Order (June 18, 2026) required MISO to address rules for application processes, study procedures, Network Upgrade cost transparency, rates and terms for co-location arrangements, and transmission services for large loads, co-located loads with behind-the-meter generation, and flexible loads. MISO proposes to file section 205 tariff changes including: Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement (ZGIA) for co-located generation by end of August; Interconnection Reliability Requirements (PMU, telemetry, forecasting, ramp/ride-through) for large loads; Load Addition and Resource Study (LARS) process for parallel study of generation and transmission (120-day timeline) by November 16; firm transmission service step-up option for staged energization; and non-firm large load service options. MISO will conduct six Large Load Working Group meetings between August 12 and November 16, 2026. MISO requests expedited Commission order by August 14, 2026, and a 5-day comment period (by August 10, 2026).
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, MISO's new interconnection procedures, co-location rules, transmission service options, and reliability requirements for large loads will apply to all resources and customers serving loads through MISO, including hydro facilities seeking to participate in co-located arrangements or serve large loads. The ZGIA process and LARS framework will establish the study and operational standards governing how any generation resource (hydro, gas, wind, solar) interconnects when serving proximate load; these rules will become the baseline against which hydro owners must compete or conform for speed-to-power opportunities and cost-allocation treatment. The firm step-up and non-firm service options may create new revenue or operational pathways for flexible resources, but will be available only under whatever terms MISO establishes—hydro owners must track the tariff language to understand whether flexibility value is captured or whether large-load priority preempts traditional hydro dispatch.

documents.filename: 20260807 ERSC Item 07 Entergys Presentaiton on LARS.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document addresses MISO's Load Addition Resource Study (LARS) — a new parallel study and interconnection process for large loads paired with generation, which directly affects how generation including potential co-located resources can participate in interconnection and transmission planning, and how resource developers secure injection rights.
documents.ai_summary: MISO has proposed the Load Addition Resource Study (LARS), a 120-day parallel study process that evaluates large load and associated generation together using aligned assumptions, rather than sequentially. The proposal requires a minimum load size of 250+ MW per study cycle, with up to 10 load-generation pairs per cycle; a $250,000 nonrefundable D1 application fee; and generation nameplate capped at 150% of identified load need. Generation must be geographically aligned to the load (same load resource zone but not co-located), have firm offtake agreements, and achieve commercial operation within 3 years. LARS outcomes include MTEP-approved transmission for reliable load withdrawal, allocation of generation injection rights (GIA), and a coordinated set of network upgrades. The framework addresses specified-source resource imports, export interchange transaction rules for legacy agreements, and how exports increase GHG load obligation in merit-order optimization.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the GHG pricing framework it is developing affects any resource that supplies energy to or imports into a GHG-constrained market zone; hydro in the SPP footprint and exports from the Northwest into SPP are potentially subject to emissions-based dispatch costs and tracking requirements. The protocol's treatment of specified-source resources, multi-configuration resource dispatch, export interchange deductions for legacy agreements, and emissions attribution to residuals all shape the marginal-cost offer curves and export-revenue recovery for hydro operators participating in or supplying into these markets. Unresolved items on hybrid-storage modeling and resource-attribution methodologies could materially affect how facility-level revenues are computed relative to market-wide dispatch optimization.

documents.title: Item 05 – Dominion July Loss Of Load Event – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The event documents load-shedding triggered by voltage-ride-through failure at large computational loads in PJM, and introduces NERC standards development for minimum ride-through requirements for data centers and computational loads — a precedent mechanism that will shape operational compliance and asset response rules for all dispatchable and grid-supporting resources including hydropower.
documents.ai_summary: On July 22, 2026, a 230 kV transmission-line fault in the Dominion zone caused approximately 3,800 MW of load to transfer to back-up generation due to voltage ride-through performance failure. PJM's presentation documents the event sequence, protection operation, voltage and frequency response, and generator behavior during recovery. NERC Project 2026-02 is developing reliability standards for large computational loads (defined as on-site data centers and similar facilities ≥50 MW at ≥100 kV) to establish interconnection requirements, modeling data standards, and minimum voltage and frequency disturbance-performance requirements. NERC's Large Load Working Group posted a draft whitepaper on July 30, 2026 for a 30-day comment period and expects standards to become part of a reliability standard in 2027. FERC directed NERC to file by December 31, 2026 (Docket RD26-7-000).
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the operational event and the NERC standards response matter to hydro owners because the new computational-load ride-through rules will set a precedent for how disturbance performance and voltage/frequency recovery requirements are structured across all grid-connected resources. Hydro operators providing voltage support and frequency response during such events will be evaluated against similar technical capability floors; generators' AVR and reactive-power response during the event (shown in the document) illustrate the performance standards that will likely propagate to conventional generation. Load-transfer mechanics and data-center load pockets also represent a strategic load-growth scenario where locational scarcity can raise energy and ancillary-service values for resources already positioned in tight zones.

documents.title: 09. Planning Working Group update 08_06_26
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PGRR 147 addresses non-consequential load-loss planning criteria and emergency load disconnection in ERCOT's transmission planning—a precedent-setting reliability and planning mechanism that informs how RTOs treat use-limited and dispatchable resources in resource-adequacy and operational-compliance contexts relevant to hydro's planning and dispatch obligations.
documents.ai_summary: The Planning Working Group reviewed PGRR 147 (Allowable Non-Consequential Load Loss Alignment), sponsored by Rayburn County Electric Cooperative, which proposes to expand ERCOT's allowance for non-consequential load loss in transmission planning. LCRA opposed the proposal, arguing that relaxed load-loss criteria could shift planning toward customer interruption as a reliability solution rather than transmission investment. ERCOT Operations agreed, noting that NERC requirements are minimum standards and ERCOT maintains stricter N-1-1 criteria to prevent non-consequential load loss during routine transmission outages. Rayburn and Oncor proposed a narrower approach limited to contractually interruptible customers on dedicated facilities, using predefined operational measures as an interim bridge pending long-term transmission upgrades. ERCOT Operations cautioned that widespread use of curtailment procedures for new large loads could be difficult to manage and blur the planning-operations boundary. Participants raised questions about contractual enforceability and quantification of costs under current criteria. The PGRR was tabled pending further language proposals from Rayburn, Oncor, and other stakeholders.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the debate over non-consequential load loss and emergency curtailment as a planning solution sets precedent for how ERCOT (and by extension other RTOs) may treat dispatchable and storage resources' operational flexibility as a substitute for firm transmission capacity. If load-loss exceptions expand, hydro operators may face stronger dispatch obligations during peak conditions and less certainty about when they can schedule maintenance or reserve capacity. Conversely, if transmission planning remains stringent as ERCOT Operations advocates, scarcity signals from load growth will support higher energy and ancillary-service prices where hydro can participate. The outcome also signals how the RTO will treat operational measures and state-of-charge flexibility in large-load interconnection decisions going forward.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT comparison content on frequency response and inertia management in a high-renewable-penetration grid — directly analogous to challenges hydro owners face in markets relying on variable renewables, and a reference point for how ERCOT procures and measures fast-frequency-response products that hydro supplies elsewhere.
documents.ai_summary: The PDCWG report to ERCOT's Reliability and Operations Subcommittee (August 6, 2026) documents ERCOT's frequency-control performance and inertia dynamics over a 10-year span. Key findings: CPS1 performance at 181.97% on a 12-month rolling average; minimum synchronous inertia declining from 143 GW·s in 2016 to 114.7 GW·s in 2026, measured at moments of peak non-synchronous generation penetration reaching 81% of system load in March 2026; Fast Frequency Response (FFR) awards increasing from 0 MW in prior years to 430 MW by March 2026. The report presents analysis of disturbances, frequency profiles, time-error corrections, and energy generation from wind and solar across the decade.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower directly. It illustrates the operational and stability challenges ERCOT faces as non-synchronous renewables grow, which mirrors conditions hydro-rich RTOs are entering. The declining minimum inertia (114.7 GW·s) despite growing load, and the rising FFR awards (430 MW), show how ERCOT is compensating for loss of synchronous support. Hydro owners in other regions should note how ERCOT structures and prices frequency-response products — the FFR mechanism is an alternative model for monetizing the fast-ramping capability conventional hydro provides, and comparison across RTOs can inform whether similar mechanisms could expand hydro revenue in markets without dedicated inertia or FFR markets.

documents.title: Item 02 1 – Offer Verification Exception Request Timeline Defintion – Problem Statement
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Offer Verification timelines and make-whole payment procedures directly affect hydro and storage operators' ability to submit cost-justified bids above $1,000/MWh—a core revenue-protection tool for use-limited resources during scarcity events.
documents.ai_summary: PJM staff identifies a gap in Manual 11 governing the submission timeline for Offer Verification exception requests supporting offers exceeding $1,000/MWh. Currently, Attachment D prescribes 11:00 AM EPT the next business day for Market Sellers to submit exception requests with supporting documentation when offers fail Markets Gateway validation. PJM notes this deadline was set in 2017 before current Markets Gateway functionality and has become burdensome during extended winter events when operators must manage both exception submissions and ongoing daily offers. The problem statement proposes updating the timeline to reflect current system capabilities and operational conditions. This touches hydro and pumped-storage operators directly: when water availability or dispatch constraints create genuine economic scarcity, both must justify offers above $1,000/MWh through documented cost or opportunity-cost cases, and tight submission deadlines during multi-day events can prevent recovery of legitimate incremental costs. The outcome of this charge will determine whether that recovery pathway remains viable during resource-constrained periods.

documents.title: Item 02 2 – Offer Verification Exception Request Timeline Defintion – Issue Charge
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: The issue charge concerns the after-the-fact make-whole payment timeline triggered by Offer Verification events under PJM Manual 11 — a key revenue-protection mechanism for resource-constrained or use-limited generators (prominently including hydropower and pumped storage) to recover costs when economically necessary offers are rejected in real-time dispatch, then manual dispatch is required. Updating the submission deadline and tools directly affects how hydro and PSH owners invoke make-whole relief and their ability to document opportunity costs.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising the timeline and procedural pathway in Manual 11 for Market Sellers to request after-the-fact make-whole payments following Offer Verification events, triggered by Winter Storm Fern in January 2026. The revision updates the deadline for invoking make-whole consideration to reflect new Markets Gateway functionality, replacing the prior 2017-era SharePoint submission process. The Quick Fix work is assigned to the Market Implementation Committee on a two-month timeline starting July 2026, with solution delivery targeted before winter operations when Offer Verification activity peaks. Hydropower and pumped-storage operators relying on make-whole recovery to justify economically necessary offers — especially during scarcity or high-opportunity-cost periods — should monitor the final timeline revision to ensure compliance with new notice and documentation submission windows.

documents.ai_summary: PJM's Manual 11 section 2.3.6.2 establishes a 60-calendar-day deadline for generation owners to submit exception requests justifying offers that failed offer screens, with supporting cost documentation submitted via Markets Gateway or, if unavailable, by email to designated PJM and Monitoring Analytics addresses. The process requires timely MMU input and evaluates requests in order received; incomplete submissions are queued for later processing once corrected. This redline update to the timeline definition affects any resource (including hydro and PSH) relying on after-the-fact make-whole recovery or LMP-setting eligibility in PJM—owners must meet the 60-day clock to preserve compensation rights when bids are initially rejected for non-compliance with PJM's Fuel Cost Policy, and procedural delays in submitting documentation can defer queue position.

documents.title: Item 02 4 – Offer Verification Exception Request Timeline Defintion – Executive Summary
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Offer Verification Exception Request timeline affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources justify high energy offers (>$1000/MWh) under PJM's make-whole payment process, directly touching revenue recovery for units that incur costs during scarcity events.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes updating PJM Manual 11 (sections 2.3.6.2 and Attachment D) to standardize the exception-request submission deadline for high-priced offers at 60 calendar days, with conforming updates to the Fuel Price Exceptions Markets Gateway tool. The change responds to extended winter events that required participants more time to document costs and to leverage improved Markets Gateway functionality available since the process's 2017 inception. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Hybrid resources market-model rules directly affect how pumped-storage and co-located hydro+storage systems can participate in capacity and energy markets; the problem statement identifies that current PJM rules requiring unified classification across capacity, energy, and ancillary-services markets prevent SIS (Surplus Interconnection Service) projects—including battery-added hydro facilities—from obtaining capacity accreditation, which limits the revenue pathway for storage additions at existing hydro POIs and constrains a strategic tool for new capacity deployment.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's existing rule requires Mixed Technology Facilities (MTFs) that participate in the capacity market as a Hybrid Resource to also operate as hybrids in energy and ancillary-services markets, creating operational and settlement complexity. The issue is particularly acute for Surplus Interconnection Service (SIS) projects—e.g., a battery added to an existing solar facility—which cannot obtain their own capacity interconnection rights (CIRs) and must become hybrids to leverage the host resource's CIRs and gain UCAP. PJM staff are flagging this as an impediment to capacity deployment and seeking stakeholder input on whether MTFs should be permitted to maintain one classification for capacity while using separate units in energy and ancillary services, consistent with how non-hybrid resources are treated. This directly affects pumped-storage and hydro owners considering co-location or additions via SIS, who currently face hybrid-operation mandates that may be technically infeasible or economically unviable when storage has separate offtakers or operational constraints.

documents.ai_summary: PJM staff is opening a work item to decouple how hybrid resources (mixed-technology facilities) are modeled in the capacity market from how they must operate in the energy and ancillary-services markets. Currently, a facility seeking capacity-market accreditation as a Hybrid Resource must also operate as a single hybrid unit in energy and AS markets, even when its components (e.g., pumped storage + conventional hydro) have different offtakers or could operate independently. This constraint is particularly binding for projects using Surplus Interconnection Service (SIS), which lack their own capacity interconnection rights and must be modeled as hybrids to obtain UCAP; once hybrid in RPM, they lose the option to bid energy and AS as separate units. The work will examine whether facilities can receive capacity accreditation as hybrids while electing to bid energy and AS as independent units, and map the downstream settlement, must-offer, and performance-assessment implications. Decision timeline is consensus-based on a single proposal, expected monthly work, priority level medium, starting August 2026. This proposal directly affects PSH owners considering co-location with conventional hydro under SIS and those seeking to optimize capacity accreditation without sacrificing energy-market dispatch flexibility.

documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes a transparent 'Advanced Scheduling' process for committing coal, gas, and other thermal units 1–2 days before the day-ahead market to mitigate winter performance risk—a practice PJM has expanded post-Winter Storm Elliott. The proposal requires units self-identified as 'at risk' (cold-weather, gas-procurement) to submit 'Indicative Offers' before the day-ahead deadline; PJM then evaluates which units to commit economically based on a multi-day minimization tool. Committed units' uplift is capped at the lesser of the Indicative Offer and final offer, and all uplift is allocated as reliability charges. Operating parameters allow committed units to set economic minimum to their advanced-scheduling MW level. The mechanism directly competes with hydro's natural slot as a dispatchable, lower-cost alternative to pre-committed thermal capacity, and the Indicative-Offer requirement (mandatory for self-identified at-risk units) mirrors offer-control rules that constrain use-limited resources. Pumped-storage and conventional hydro operators should monitor how PJM's risk-assessment criteria classify units and how the reliability-charge allocation burden (vs. energy-market-based cost recovery) affects the economics of flexible hydro participation. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this proposal document.

documents.title: Item 07 1 – PJM Energy Storage Resource Model Enhancements – Market Based Battery Operations – Brattle Group
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Market power mitigation rules for energy storage directly affect pumped-storage hydro's offer-pricing rights and real-time dispatch economics — the document analyzes how PJM's cost-based mitigation and offer-lock rules suppress opportunity-cost offers and cause inefficient discharge timing, a problem that applies equally to PSH as to batteries under PJM's offer-driven ESR model.
documents.ai_summary: Brattle Group presents PJM staff analysis of market-power mitigation (MPM) rules applied to battery energy storage, arguing that conventional fuel-based mitigation caps—designed for fossil generators—are poorly fitted to storage resources and cause two problems: (1) capping mitigated offers below inter-hour opportunity cost causes early, inefficient discharge and misallocates stored energy away from peak-scarcity hours, reducing reliability; (2) PJM's t-65-minute offer-price lock prevents sellers from updating offers as conditions change, locking in discharge decisions that become counterproductive when actual prices spike (illustrated by Winter Storm Elliott case study showing 42% of battery SOC misallocated). The document is preparing PJM Markets Implementation for a policy decision on whether to revise MPM and offer-timing rules to allow storage sellers to include opportunity costs in competitive offers and to permit real-time offer updates before dispatch. This affects pumped-storage hydro owners in PJM because PSH operates under the same ESR participation model and would be subject to identical MPM caps and offer locks; relaxing these constraints would restore PSH's ability to manage state-of-charge optimally for scarcity value, while tightening them further would suppress PSH revenue from peak-hour energy and ancillary services.

documents.ai_summary: MISO Advisory Committee met June 17, 2026 to discuss resource adequacy in a time of system transition. The session with the Board of Directors focused on maintaining resource adequacy as solar grows rapidly and large loads accelerate. Participants noted MISO's resource adequacy position has improved compared to a year ago, but the system remains tight and vulnerable to evolving risks. Members emphasized that MISO's recent resource adequacy reforms—including Reliability Based Demand Curve (RBDC), accreditation updates, and forthcoming Direct Loss of Load (DLOL) changes—are directionally sound but lack sufficient granularity in storage modeling, retirement assumptions, and queue-risk transparency. The Steering Committee approved redlines to incorporate the Large Load Working Group; the Large Load Working Group Chair reported seven Issues have been accepted and are being worked through, with the next meeting scheduled for June 29. MISO is delaying the FERC filing on Zero Generation Interconnection Agreements (ZGIA) and Interconnection Reliability Requirements to allow additional stakeholder input through the Large Load Working Group and to fully review FERC's Large Load ANOPR. Long-Range Transmission Planning (LRTP) work is picking up pace, and the Expedited Resource Addition Study (ERAS) process continues; storage is becoming increasingly important in capacity additions. Comments regarding the Current Issue draft questions are due to AC leadership by July 2.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not directly name hydro resources, but its focus on resource adequacy reforms, storage modeling, seasonal accreditation mechanics, and transmission-grid integration directly affects hydro owners. The emphasis on improved accreditation treatment and RBDC/DLOL rule changes will set seasonal capacity revenue; the stated gap in storage modeling and retirement assumptions signals ongoing uncertainty in how non-energy-limited resources (the accreditation category encompassing conventional hydro) are valued. MISO's delay of ZGIA/IRR rules and acceleration of LRTP work affect interconnection queue competition and deliverability for new and uprated hydro capacity. The discussion of shifting load patterns and rapid solar growth underscores scarcity conditions favoring existing dispatchable resources, though participants cautioned that reserve margins may be fragile—a signal relevant to hydro's long-run value in an uncertain transition.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's August 2026 Advisory Committee report covers multiple market and planning initiatives affecting resource participation. The Resource Adequacy Subcommittee is revising solar accreditation methodology and addressing a 24-hour lead-time rule for offline resources, with three alternative proposals (reducing threshold to 12 hours, assigning zero availability for 48-hour lead-time increases, or sliding-scale from 4-hour full availability declining 5% per additional hour to zero at 24 hours); FERC filing targeted for October 2026. PRMR allocation will be reformed to weight demand during Tier 2 RA hours over three years; tariff filing planned by end of 2026 for effective date Planning Year 2029/2030. The Planning Advisory Committee is revising Attachment GGG for merchant HVDC interconnection procedures and updating the ERAS (expedited resource adequacy) process to allow two quarterly study cycles with up to 15 projects each; Q3 2026 filing expected. The Large Load Working Group is advancing seven issues including zero-injection GIAs (filing by July 31, 2026), large load reliability requirements (mid-August filing), firm service step-up (Sept/Oct 2026), operational requirements, reserve enhancements, non-firm service options, and generation-load alignment for 250+ MW loads; multiple filings scheduled through Q4 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, the revisions to offline-resource lead-time accreditation rules and solar accreditation methodology establish precedent for how MISO will treat conventional hydro and other dispatchable resources' seasonal and daily-start-time accreditation—revenue that fluctuates sharply with lead-time design. The 24-hour threshold debate, particularly the sliding-scale option, would likely extend to how MISO accredits hydro's variable capability. Additionally, large-load interconnection reliability standards (ride-through, PMU, telemetry, ramp rates) and the zero-injection GIA rules will set operational and interconnection obligations for existing hydro plants and new uprates if they are co-located with or support firm service for large loads. The load-growth drivers (data centers, 31 GW in ERAS applications, unprecedented load growth noted in LOLE studies) increase near-term scarcity, raising the value of existing hydro's energy and flexibility products, but also create urgency for transmission and firm-service rules that may constrain how hydro can be scheduled and compensated.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's Wholesale Market Working Group (WMWG) is advancing three rule proposals affecting ancillary-services and reliability products. NPRR 1337 (Energy Response Service Enhancements) refines the Alternate Baseline Test methodology and is on track for September 2026 Board consideration; ERock and Generate proposed allowing resources to elect the alternate baseline if they pass the test, which ERCOT opposes citing concerns over resource availability and self-deployment. NPRR 1278 (Advanced Grid Support Service as an Ancillary Service) and NPRR 1333 (incentive program offering $1,500/MW capped at $25 million for AGS adoption) are tabled for additional discussion; ERCOT explained NPRR 1333 aims to accelerate near-term adoption while technical work continues on the market product. NPRR 1340 would allow Energy Storage Resources capable of sustaining maximum output for at least four hours to participate in the Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service (DRRS), consistent with PUCT guidance; TCPA (represented by Vistra) supports ESR participation but recommends evaluating whether the four-hour duration should be based on reliability needs rather than the statutory minimum. For 2027 ancillary-services methodology, ERCOT identified a 3,700 MW average underestimation in the 2026 probabilistic model for ECRS and Non-Spin and proposes increasing daytime risk credits to 50% for online/offline resources and 64% for batteries while maintaining 60% nighttime credits.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document never mentions hydropower or pumped storage. The 2027 ancillary-services methodology changes—particularly the distinction in risk credits by resource type (batteries at 64% daytime vs. 50% for generic online/offline resources) and the ongoing review of duration requirements—show how ERCOT values different storage characteristics in capacity accreditation; these distinctions would shape how longer-duration PSH or conventional hydro flexibility would be modeled elsewhere if the framework spreads.
