documents.title: 10. FFSS Offer Heat Rate Methodology
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT's FFSS (Fast Frequency Response Service) offer-cap methodology sets precedent for how RTOs determine heat-rate-based energy-cost caps for dispatchable thermal resources eligible to provide a fast-response service; the methodology's structure and data-sourcing choices (EPA operating data, percentile thresholds, verifiable-cost approaches) could inform how other RTOs including those with significant hydro exposure (PJM, NYISO, MISO) structure similar service definitions and price-setting, and thus affects market-design comparison of frequency-response compensation across regions.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT calculates FFSS Offer Caps ($/MW) using heat rate × fuel price × deployment hours for three resource categories under 16 TAC § 25.520: Category 1 (on-site fuel oil at 13.52 MMBtu/MWh, yielding $17,083/MW cap), Category 2 (resource-controlled natural gas at 11.36 MMBtu/MWh, yielding $14,163/MW cap), and Category 3 (contractual off-site using verifiable-cost data at 12.62 MMBtu/MWh, yielding $2,183/MW cap). Category 1 and 2 heat rates derive from EPA hourly generation data (2022–2026, 4 seasons) at the 90th percentile of actual heat rates in the 0.8–1.2 × midpoint output band; Category 3 relies on ERCOT-approved Verifiable Cost submissions and selects the Simple-Cycle average (12.62) rather than Combined-Cycle average (8.04) to preserve competitive incentives. The methodology applies a 48-hour deployment window and fuel-price adders ($0.05/Gl for Category 1, $0.50/MMBtu for Category 3).
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower or pumped storage directly; ERCOT has negligible hydro generation. However, the methodology illustrates how an RTO structures energy-cost-based offer caps for fast-response services using either historical EPA data with high percentile thresholds or verifiable cost data, rather than energy-limited or conditional capacity metrics. Conventional hydro and PSH owners in hydro-rich RTOs watch how frequency-response and ramping-service compensation gets anchored—whether to fuel cost, opportunity cost, or actual scarcity pricing—because hydro's high ramp rate and flexibility command premium revenue in these products when properly priced. ERCOT's approach of using 90th-percentile heat rates and deliberately conservative (SC over CC) benchmarks to preserve competitive bids may signal a regional tension between cost-recovery certainty and auction liquidity that hydro owners face in their own markets' ancillary-service and flexibility-product design.

documents.title: 09. NPRR1337_ERS_Enhancements
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Emergency Response Service (ERS) is a demand-response program that competes with supply-side resources for reliability-event revenue; tightening baseline qualification and availability scoring affects the competitive economics of demand response relative to dispatchable energy resources and reserves.
documents.ai_summary: NPRR 1337 proposes two changes to ERCOT's Emergency Response Service (ERS), a demand-side reliability tool that pays Qualified Scheduling Entities (QSEs) to curtail load or inject energy during emergencies. Change 1 tightens the Alternate Baseline test so that only loads that are genuinely unpredictable—not merely price-responsive—qualify to bypass the default baseline. Change 2 replaces a single QSE-portfolio-level availability factor per contract term with availability measured separately for each ERS Resource and each ERS Time Period, so high-availability periods no longer offset poor ones within the same term. ERCOT staff supports approval as enhancing reliability. The NPRR was posted May 26, 2026; WMS is voting today (August 5, 2026); PRS will be requested for urgent status and vote August 12, 2026; and TAC review is scheduled August 26, 2026, with ERCOT aiming for September Board review.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or storage, but it addresses demand-response program design in ERCOT, which sets precedent for how other RTOs and FERC evaluate the competitive positioning of demand-response versus supply-side flexibility and reserves. Tightening ERS qualification and making availability scoring resource-specific and time-period-specific reflects a move toward more granular performance accountability in demand response; similar logic could be applied to how storage and conventional hydro—both capable of delivering fast response and high availability in critical periods—are tested and compensated for ancillary services and flexibility products. The shift away from portfolio-level averaging to period-level evaluation mirrors the market-design principle (increasingly common in other regions) that capacity and performance should be credited only when it is actually available to meet the highest-risk operating conditions, not hidden in aggregate numbers.

documents.title: 09. FFSS Offer Heat Rate Methodology
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT's FFSS offer-cap and heat-rate methodology sets precedent for how offer caps are calculated for fuel-burning resources with supply constraints; the approach — using historical operating data, percentile thresholds, and cost-based substitutes — informs how similar mitigation and cost-recovery rules might extend to hydro and storage resources in other markets.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT has set heat-rate-based offer caps for the 2026–2027 Fuel-Fired Supplemental Service (FFSS) obligation period under 16 TAC § 25.520. The determination establishes three separate caps—one per resource category—using category-specific heat rates combined with fuel prices and a 48-hour deployment window: Category 1 (on-site fuel oil) heat rate 13.52 MMBtu/MWh and offer cap $17,083/MW; Category 2 (resource-controlled natural gas) heat rate 11.36 MMBtu/MWh and offer cap $14,163/MW; Category 3 (contractual off-site natural gas) heat rate 12.62 MMBtu/MWh and offer cap $2,183/MW. Categories 1 and 2 heat rates are grounded in EPA historical operating data at the 90th percentile from 2022–2026; Category 3 uses ERCOT-approved Verifiable Cost data, with ERCOT selecting the higher Simple Cycle average (12.62 MMBtu/MWh) over Combined Cycle (8.04 MMBtu/MWh) to preserve competitive incentives. The presentation to the Wholesale Market Subcommittee on August 5, 2026, describes the methodology but does not indicate next steps or stakeholder comment deadlines.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydro or pumped storage directly; Texas has no material hydropower fleet. However, ERCOT's approach to offer-cap methodology for use-limited fuel-burning resources—using historical operating data, percentile thresholds, and cost-recovery adjustments across heterogeneous resource types—illustrates how RTOs handle the canonical problem hydro faces: setting cost-recovery caps for resources with energy constraints and variable heat rates or opportunity costs. Hydro owners in other markets should note how ERCOT handles the tradeoff between accuracy (percentile thresholds, EPA data) and incentive preservation (selecting SC heat rate for Category 3 to prevent cream-skimming by CC resources); similar tensions arise in hydro mitigation and accreditation across WECC and the East.

documents.title: Item 04 A – 1 Fuel Switching Education – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Interconnection queue processes and fuel-type change policies directly govern how hydro and storage projects enter and navigate PJM's study queues; this presentation opposes allowing post-agreement fuel switching, which would affect strategic options for repowering or converting existing interconnection agreements.
documents.ai_summary: Brian Lynn (PJM Interconnection Construction Management) presented PJM's position opposing a proposal by Invenergy to permit post-agreement fuel-type changes based on Necessary Study results. PJM argues that such changes would increase study variability, require extensive restudy across Load Flow, Short Circuit, and Stability modalities, potentially affect headroom for subsequent projects, and violate the readiness expectations embedded in executed interconnection service agreements. The presentation states that fuel type is a fundamental term of signed agreements filed with FERC and affects permitting, power factor, equipment configuration, Schedule H requirements, and project milestones. PJM contends that projects seeking fuel changes should instead enter the next applicable cycle rather than modify post-agreement.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, it addresses the interconnection queue's handling of fuel-type changes, a rule that would apply to any resource seeking to repurpose an existing interconnection agreement—including hydro plants considering conversion to or from other fuel types, or PSH facilities changing their operational profile. The policy restricts switching after agreement execution, locking in the fuel type (and its associated dispatch parameters, as shown in Appendix A's ramping-limit table) as a binding project term. For hydro owners, this constrains the strategic flexibility to adapt existing interconnection positions if operational or market conditions change post-signing.

documents.title: Item 04 B – 2 Fuel Switching – Problem Statement
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's proposal to allow fuel switching for interconnected projects while retaining Capacity Injection Rights directly affects the strategic and commercial options available to hydro and storage developers competing in the interconnection queue, and sets precedent for how interconnection and deliverability rules adapt to changing resource preferences.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is proposing to establish a defined process allowing projects with completed interconnection studies and Capacity Injection Rights (CIRs) to change fuel type—such as from solar to storage—while retaining those CIRs, provided the change does not materially impact the transmission system. The rationale addresses PJM's capacity shortfalls, the accumulation of "stranded CIRs" at studied sites that are no longer being developed, and inefficiencies from duplicative restudies when market demand shifts. The proposal is framed as interconnection policy design and system planning efficiency, falling within the Planning Committee's scope. Other RTOs/ISOs have implemented similar fuel-change review processes through FERC-approved material modification frameworks; PJM would evaluate potential tariff or manual revisions to establish its own procedure.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, a fuel-switching rule that preserves interconnection positions and avoids re-study work affects all resources in the queue, including hydro and PSH developers. If PJM adopts a flexible fuel-change process that treats storage (including PSH) changes as non-material under certain conditions, or if it allows existing solar or wind positions to convert to storage without losing queuing priority or requiring full restudy, that would lower the barriers to PSH development at already-studied sites and could shift the strategic calculus for choosing between resource types given the same transmission infrastructure. Conversely, if the rule narrows (e.g., storage-to-non-storage changes are deemed material), it could lock in resource mixes that were planned years earlier and reduce flexibility for existing hydro or PSH projects considering upgrades or re-dispatch strategies.

documents.title: Item 05 – 3 Manual 21b Periodic Review – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM Manual 21b establishes ELCC classification rules and accreditation procedures that directly determine capacity-market revenue for hydropower and pumped-storage resources.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 21b (Revision 06, effective 06/24/2026) defines ELCC Classes and procedures for determining Accredited UCAP and capacity accreditation. The manual explicitly establishes two hydropower classes: Intermittent Hydropower Class for run-of-river generators that cannot appreciably store water, and Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage Class for facilities that can capture and store incoming flow with material control. Material control is demonstrated by evaluation of whether the resource can consistently produce power equal to or in excess of 110% of the daily average power baseline for at least 4 hours, assessed once per five years using the ratio of average output during the 4 highest load hours of summer afternoons versus all other hours over a five-year period. An existing Hydropower with Non-Pumped Storage resource that fails this evaluation will be reclassified as Intermittent Hydropower, unless PJM exercises discretion to retain the prior classification due to exceptional circumstances including recreational and public safety factors, unit outages, market prices, or ancillary-market participation. Capacity Storage Resource Classes include pumped-storage resources characterized by 4-, 6-, 8-, and 10-hour durations, defined by the ratio of modeled MWh energy-storage capability to modeled MW power capability. Testing requirements apply to hydro resources: Hydro with Non-Pumped Storage units must complete one (1) contiguous hour capability verification tests for summer and winter periods, with deadlines of September 20th and March 20th respectively. Data submission for hydro resources must include complete time series from June 1, 2012 through most recent May 31 unless previously submitted and unchanged.
documents.hydro_read_through: This manual is the foundational capacity-market accreditation document for PJM hydro owners. The Intermittent Hydropower versus Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage distinction directly determines ELCC Class placement and thus seasonal capacity revenue: storage-capable plants can claim higher ELCC factors through the controlled-output standard, while run-of-river plants are trapped in the lower-value Intermittent class. The five-year evaluation cycle and PJM's discretion to override a failed demonstration based on market participation or operational factors creates ongoing compliance risk and opportunity — owners of marginal plants must monitor their seasonal output ratios closely and may argue exceptional circumstances to avoid reclassification. Pumped-storage accreditation by duration class (4/6/8/10-hour) makes state-of-charge management and energy-balance assumptions critical to ELCC value; the manual does not here address charging-energy treatment or AS-stacking rules, which remain open in PJM's separate storage-participation framework. Testing obligations (annual summer/winter verification by September 20th and March 20th deadlines) are compliance-critical for all capacity resources and particularly onerous for multi-unit plants subject to simultaneous testing coordination.

evidence.claim: Intermittent Hydropower Class definition
evidence.quote: "Intermittent Hydropower Class" shall mean an ELCC Class consisting of Variable Resources that are run-of-river hydropower generators that must generally pass incoming water and therefore cannot appreciably store water to later increase the output of the facility.

evidence.claim: Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage Class definition and material-control standard
evidence.quote: "Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage" shall mean a hydropower facility that can capture and store incoming stream flow, without use of pumps, in pondage or a reservoir, and the Generation Owner has the ability, within the constraints available in the applicable operating license, to exert material control over the quantity of stored water and output of the facility throughout an Operating Day. A hydropower resource can exert material control over the quantity of stored water and over the output of the facility when it can consistently produce power equal to or in excess of 110% of the daily average power baseline for at least 4 hours.

evidence.claim: Material-control demonstration evaluation period and frequency
evidence.quote: This criterion is demonstrated by evaluating the ratio of the average actual output during the 4 highest load hours of all summer afternoons of the five year period starting with when the unit entered the applicable ELCC Class against the average actual output of all other hours on the same days. Such assessment and determination is once per five years.

evidence.claim: Reclassification from Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage to Intermittent Hydropower upon failed demonstration
evidence.quote: An existing Hydropower with Non-Pumped Storage resource that fails to demonstrate material control over the output of the facility through the foregoing evaluation will be reclassified as an Intermittent Hydropower Resource, provided that PJM may, at its discretion, retain the prior classification of the resource if, due to exceptional circumstances, such evaluation fails to capture the resource's capability to consistently produce power equal to or in excess of 110% of the daily average power baseline for at least 4 hours.

evidence.quote: Reasons that such evaluation might fail to capture such capability could include exceptional recreational and public safety factors, unit outages, locational market energy prices, ancillary market participation, and other exceptional operational factors or market factors that may limit a unit with material control capability from meeting the foregoing demonstration evaluation.

evidence.quote: The duration of acceptance, CAPMOD and capability verification tests shall be one (1) contiguous hour for Hydro with Non-Pumped Storage, simple cycle combustion turbine, fuel cell, and diesel (including other reciprocating engine type) units.

documents.title: Item 06 – 1 Manual 14h Revisions Ids – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Interim Deliverability Study (IDS) methodology directly affects interconnection deliverability determinations and capacity interconnection rights for generation projects, including storage and dispatchable resources—a core obligation and revenue driver for hydro and PSH owners seeking to interconnect or operate under provisional capacity rights.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14-H Section 4.10.1.3 to transition from a serial study approach to a cluster-based Interim Deliverability Study methodology, effective for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year. Under the new approach, IDS requests are grouped into two subclusters: Subcluster 1 (projects already provisionally operational from prior Delivery Years) receives priority allocation of deliverable capacity and energy, with remaining capacity allocated to Subcluster 2 (all other eligible projects). The methodology uses proportional allocation based on project MW impact and distribution factor (DFAX). The Planning Committee will hold first read on August 4, 2026, second read and voting in September 2026, and the MRC will conduct first read and voting on August 19, 2026, with IDS results due October 30, 2026. PJM states the proposal is intended to reduce project developer risk from curtailment or cessation of generation after provisional operation and to ensure operational continuity and Capacity Market alignment.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, IDS methodology is the mechanism determining whether generation projects—including hydro and PSH facilities—can deliver capacity and energy reliably before permanent network upgrades are complete, and whether they retain provisional capacity rights year-to-year. The cluster-based change prioritizes continuity for already-operational projects in the allocation queue, which would favor a provisionally operational hydro or PSH project in subsequent IDS determinations over new entrants competing for the same flowgate headroom. This affects both revenue certainty (capacity rights carry must-offer obligations in subsequent capacity auctions) and operational flexibility (projects deemed deliverable obtain protection against cessation-of-generation risk).

documents.title: Item 06 – 3 Manual 14h Revisions Ids – Problem Statement
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document addresses PJM's interim deliverability study (IDS) methodology for interconnection, which determines which generation resources—including conventional and pumped-storage hydro—receive firm transmission deliverability rights and capacity-market accreditation; changes to how deliverability is allocated across delivery years directly affect hydro owners' revenue certainty and capacity-market participation.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 14H proposes enhancements to the Cluster-Based Interim Deliverability Study methodology to address instability in deliverability allocations under the transition to cycle-based interconnection. The current IDS framework allocates system headroom on constrained flowgates sequentially, causing resources granted Provisional Interconnection Service to face uncertainty in maintaining deliverability status across delivery years; the problem statement identifies misalignment between planning study outcomes, operational reality, capacity-market obligations, and year-to-year reliability effects driven by study sequencing. The proposed improvement would provide greater stability in deliverability determinations, reduce risk that operating generation resources lose deliverability in subsequent years, enhance alignment between planning outcomes and operational needs, and support resources carrying must-offer obligations.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly; it concerns the general interconnection and deliverability framework. However, the instability problem it identifies—resources already operating and carrying capacity-market commitments losing deliverability status in later study years—is particularly acute for conventional and pumped-storage hydro, which have long lead times and often carry multi-year reliability obligations. Stabilizing deliverability across delivery years would directly reduce revenue and strategic planning uncertainty for existing hydro operators whose output and dispatch depend on firm transmission rights.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: interconnection-queue process manual for PJM establishing procedures, deposits, study phases, and agreements governing how new generation (including hydropower) and transmission interconnect to the transmission system—directly affects hydro developers' compliance obligations and strategic options for project entry.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 14H (Revision 05, effective 07/23/2026) governs the cycle-based interconnection process for new generation and transmission requests, applicable to valid new service requests submitted on or after 01 October 2021. The manual establishes three study phases (Phase I, II, III) with corresponding Decision Points, deposit requirements, cost-allocation methodologies for interconnection facilities and network upgrades, and site-control rules. Phase I consists of summer peak, winter peak, and light-load load-flow analysis completed within 120 calendar days from phase start. Project developers must pay 100% of interconnection-facility costs and share allocated network-upgrade costs. Study deposits are required; readiness deposits come due at Decision Points. The manual includes provisions for surplus interconnection service, replacement-generation requests, and affected-system studies. Revision 05 (effective 08/19/2026) updated Section 4.10.1.3 to reflect a new cluster-based methodology for the Interim Deliverability Study starting with the 2027/28 cycle, shifting from serial to cycle-based study methodology. Revision 04 incorporated FERC Docket ER26-403-000 (Replacement Generation process) and ER26-5-000 (elimination of 'first use').
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage resources by technology. However, PJM's interconnection manual directly governs how hydroelectric facilities—both conventional generation and any new pumped-storage projects—enter the transmission queue, recover their interconnection costs, and satisfy operational readiness. Developers of run-of-river or seasonal-flow hydro plants will face the same deposit, study, and three-phase approval timeline as any other generating resource. The shift from serial to cycle-based Interim Deliverability Study methodology in the 2027/28 cycle may affect deliverability accreditation for new hydro in that and subsequent cycles, though the manual text provided does not detail how deliverability is computed for energy-limited resources. Hydro owners considering upgrades to existing plants or surplus interconnection service at retired sites would also rely on these procedures.

documents.title: Item 03 – Market Efficiency Update
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Transmission-expansion planning and economic congestion analysis directly affects transmission deliverability of hydro resources and interregional export capability; congestion patterns identified here determine where hydro scarcity rents accrue and whether transmission investment accelerates or delays, changing the value of existing hydro MW.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's 2026/27 Market Efficiency (ME) cycle studies 2031 transmission congestion across its footprint using PROMOD IV simulation. Preliminary 2031 base case was posted July 15, 2026, with stakeholder feedback solicited through September 2026; PJM will finalize the base case and congestion drivers by January–February 2027, open a proposal window February–May 2027, and complete board approval by October–December 2027. The study identifies $1M–$50M+ annual simulated congestion on 40+ constraints across COMED, AEP-served West, MAAC, DOM, and external M2M tie lines, including several COMED–MISO and PJM–MISO interfaces. Per Operating Agreement Schedule 6 section 1.5.7(b), PJM will compare accelerating existing RTEP reliability projects, modifying them to relieve economic congestion, or building new projects solely for congestion relief—a process that can reprioritize transmission investment based on economic benefits. Hydro owners relying on eastbound or interregional export paths—particularly in the Carolinas (DOM), Virginia (COMED-adjacent), and MAAC regions with identified >$50M annual congestion—face the prospect of either relief via accelerated or modified projects (which could lower congestion rents) or delayed relief if no economic case is found, affecting scarcity pricing during high-value periods.

documents.title: Item 13 – Reliability Analysis Update
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: TRANSMISSION PLANNING: PJM's 2026 RTEP reliability analysis identifies multi-zone transmission constraints and load-growth drivers in 2031–2034 that affect hydropower deliverability, interregional transfer capability, and the scarcity conditions that support hydro revenue.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's 2026 RTEP Window 1 reliability update identifies transmission needs across its footprint in 2031 and 2034, driven primarily by load growth in ComEd (4 GW increase by 2031, now subject to a 1.3 GW reduction pending updated forecasts) and generation deactivations. ComEd faces numerous 345 kV and 138 kV overloads and fails to meet Capacity Emergency Transfer Objective (CETO) — a metric assessing power deliverability into stressed zones. Additional constraints identified in Dominion (transformer overloads, end-of-life violations), AEP (Columbus-area 138 kV clusters), ATSI (North Star Steel 345 kV load-loss violations), and MAAC (PECO-zone flow restrictions and CETL/CETO margin failures). Window 1 solutions are currently in evaluation; window closes September 21, 2026, with summary and short-listed solutions coming to TEAC November 2026–January 2027, and board approval expected Q1 2027. For hydro owners, constrained import corridors (especially PECO/EMAAC and PECO/DPL ties) reduce the economic value of exports into congested load centers and may limit the locational scarcity premiums that reward dispatchable hydropower during peak periods; conversely, transmission upgrades that relieve bottlenecks could extend the timeframe over which marginal hydro capacity commands scarcity pricing. The ComEd load-forecast reduction announced July 30, 2026, is expected to materially reduce transmission needs in that zone and may alter competitive solution selection.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is reforming its capacity accreditation methodology for Planning Year 2028/2029 and 2029/2030, with near-term tariff filings affecting how resources earn accreditation and PRMR-allocation design, which directly impacts hydro and other dispatchable resources' capacity revenue.
documents.ai_summary: The MISO Resource Adequacy Subcommittee reports three major accreditation and capacity-planning reforms in progress. First, MISO announced in July that solar accreditation will remain unchanged using current fixed hours until DLOL (Demand-Limited Operating Limits) takes effect in Planning Year 2028/2029. Second, for offline resources, MISO is addressing concerns that resources have changed their lead times near emergency conditions while still receiving accreditation credit; three options are under consideration—reducing the maximum lead-time threshold from 24 to 12 hours, assigning zero availability to offline resources increasing lead time within 48 hours before an operating day, or a sliding-scale approach reducing availability 5% per hour above 4 hours to zero at 24 hours—with a FERC filing planned for October. Third, MISO has proposed a new PRMR (Planning Reserve Margin Requirement) allocation methodology allocating to Load Serving Entities based on actual demand during Tier 2 Resource Adequacy hours over the last three years, weighted by effective margins, with a FERC tariff filing planned by year-end for an effective date of Planning Year 2029/2030. The Loss of Load Expectation Working Group separately met in June to discuss wind profile enhancements for LOLE accreditation calculations and unprecedented load-growth pressures on load-forecast assumptions.

documents.title: Presentation - Pre-Market Simulation Training for Inter-Scheduling Coordinators (SCs) Trades Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Enhancements 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Inter-SC trade mechanics in EDAM/WEIM touch settlement and bilateral procurement processes that hydro and other resource owners use to reconcile double-settlement exposures and manage revenue; the document trains SCs (scheduling coordinators, a role hydro operators typically hold) on the operational procedures for trades across the expanding regional markets.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO held a training session on July 7, 2026, introducing Scheduling Coordinators (SCs) participating in the Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) and Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) to inter-SC trade functionality for energy. Inter-SC trades are optional settlement services that allow two SCs to reconcile bilateral-procurement arrangements and "flip the money" to reverse double-settlement exposures, without affecting dispatch or scheduling of resources. The training covers three types of energy trades: Physical trades (PHY) backed by a generating unit, allowing submission seven days prior through 11:00 hours the day before; Aggregated Pricing Node trades (APN) at trading hubs or default load-aggregation points; and Converted Physical trades (CPT), where a PHY that exceeds the day-ahead schedule of its resource becomes a hub-based trade. Day-ahead trades are settled hourly at the resource pnode/apnode locational margin prices (Charge Code 6301); real-time trades are settled at the average of four fifteen-minute-market interval LMPs (Charge Code 6371). SCs must submit matching trades in the SIBR (Scheduling Infrastructure & Business Rules) application and continue to submit energy bids in the day-ahead and real-time markets per standard rules. A market simulation with structured scenarios is scheduled for July 20–August 1, 2026, with connectivity testing July 6–19, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources directly. However, inter-SC trades are a core settlement mechanism for dispatchable resources—including large conventional hydro and pumped-storage plants—that sell into bilateral contracts while also participating in WEIM/EDAM market-clearing. Hydro operators typically hold SC certification and use trades to manage the divergence between their contracted supply price and the nodal LMP at their resource location, a critical lever for revenue alignment across multi-zone markets. The expansion of this functionality from California ISO to WEIM and EDAM participants directly affects how hydro SCs in new member zones (PacifiCorp, Idaho Power, Puget Sound Energy, etc.) will reconcile bilateral sales with market settlement; getting the operational procedures right in simulation before the August activation date is essential to avoid settlement disputes and cash-flow mismatches on existing contracts.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to 2026–2027 winter ICAP market parameters to address misalignment caused by the Champlain Hudson Power Express (CHPE) project's entry into the ICAP market with Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights commencing July 2026. The proposal adjusts winter ICAP Demand Curve reference prices and maximum clearing prices to account for CHPE's assumed capacity availability (1,250 MW in shoulder-winter months November, March–April; 0 MW in peak-winter months December–February) and creates two separate Load Zone J Locational Minimum Installed Capacity Requirements for winter (86.4% for shoulder months, 82.6% for peak months). Manual revisions were filed with FERC on June 25, 2026 (Docket No. ER26-2959) with a requested effective date of August 25, 2026, and stakeholder approval of the manual changes is targeted for September 2026 via the Business Issues Committee. The Load Zone J winter reference price for the alternative demand curve is set at $10.18/kW-month to ensure revenue sufficiency for the proxy unit across both winter requirement sets.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped-storage resources by name. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The Balancing Intermittency project introduces Uncertainty Reserve Requirements (URR) for net load and variable renewable resources, which affects how reserves are procured and priced in NYISO markets — a revenue and operational obligation that extends to all dispatchable resources including hydroelectric units.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Balancing Intermittency project deploys Uncertainty Reserve Requirements (URR) at the end of August 2026 to account for forecast uncertainty in Net Load (load net of Behind-The-Meter Solar), Land-Based Wind, Offshore Wind, and Front-of-The-Meter Solar. The URR is a 24-hour requirement calculated before the Day-Ahead Market and procured in addition to existing reserve requirements. Historical forecast error metrics are calculated automatically after the first week of January using the prior calendar year's data, internally reviewed and validated, and posted by April 1 each year; the same set of metrics remains in use until the next annual update. FERC accepted the design in July 2025 (Docket ER25-1998), and manual revisions were approved by stakeholders in July 2026. The composite URR calculation uses mean and standard deviation of forecast errors across resource categories and applies a z-score (1.645 for the 95th percentile) to derive the requirement.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, URR is a procurement requirement in addition to existing reserves, which means NYISO will be demanding additional reserve capacity on top of spinning and operating reserves that hydro plants typically provide. If conventional or run-of-river hydro plants are dispatchable and capable of meeting these new uncertainty reserves, they will face a new compliance obligation and an opportunity to supply an additional product — but the document does not specify whether hydro is eligible to provide URR or how its physical constraints (inflow variability, state-of-charge limits) would interact with the requirement. The design's locational distribution (shown for NYCA, EAST, SENY, and LI) may also affect the revenue available to hydro at different transmission nodes.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO is updating capacity accreditation and resource adequacy modeling methodology, including design of de-rating factors, performance factors, and seasonal accreditation elections that directly affect how Energy Duration Limited resources (including storage and pump-back hydro) are credited in the capacity market and which revenues they can earn.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Installed Capacity Working Group is advancing a project to improve capacity accreditation and resource adequacy modeling, with a 2026 milestone of study completion. The updated 2026 objective refocuses on increasing transparency: NYISO proposes to publicly disclose resource-specific unavailability data (EFORd, performance factors, de-rating factors), 5-year averages used in adequacy modeling, capability-period averages, seasonal UDR/EDR elections, firm fuel elections, and Energy Duration Limitation elections beginning with the 2027–2028 Capability Year. The project will continue reviewing alternative marginal capacity accreditation methodologies (focusing on Marginal Reliability Improvement sensitivity) and will evaluate the impact of using Expected Unserved Energy (EUE) metrics; NYISO assessed stakeholder concerns about market-power risks from additional disclosure and found no incremental risk beyond existing mitigation provisions. Next steps include further ICAPWG discussion of tariff revisions needed to implement the transparency initiative, continued analysis of accreditation alternatives, and a Consumer Impact Analysis. Annual resource elections for 2027–2028 are due by August 1, with the IRM voted by the New York State Reliability Council Executive Committee in December.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities by name; however, it directly affects how NYISO will accredit and model Energy Duration Limited resources—a category that includes pump-back hydro. Public disclosure of resource-specific de-rating and performance data will increase transparency in the IRM and LCR-setting process that hydro owners depend on for revenue predictability, though it also exposes individual resource operating history. A hydro owner should monitor the alternative accreditation methodologies analysis—particularly the Marginal Reliability Improvement technique's sensitivity to resource and load changes—because changes to that methodology could materially reshape seasonal capacity values.

documents.title: 3a Draft ICAP Manual
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's Installed Capacity Manual governs how capacity is accredited, procured, and compensated in New York, directly affecting the revenue treatment of conventional hydro and pumped-storage resources through accreditation factors, duration adjustment, co-located storage rules, and external resource provisions.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Installed Capacity (ICAP) Manual (version 18.0, effective 07/07/2026, draft status as of 08/04/2026 working group meeting) establishes comprehensive rules for capacity accreditation, procurement, and settlement in the NYCA. The manual replaces duration adjustment factors with Capacity Accreditation Factors (CAFs) and Capacity Accreditation Resource Classes (CARCs) effective May 1, 2024; includes provisions for energy-limited resources such as hydro and intermittent power resources; governs co-located storage resources' UCAP calculation and bidding; addresses DER aggregations and their participation; requires Firm Fuel Characteristic Elections from natural gas and fuel oil resources; and establishes external capacity import rights with must-offer obligations. Key sections address DMNC/DMGC testing procedures, with recent updates (v12.0, 12/30/2024) to ambient adjustments for water-cooled fossil and nuclear units, and bidding requirements at Normal Upper Operating Limit. The manual is prepared by NYISO Capacity Market Products and is subject to ongoing revision and FERC filing.
documents.hydro_read_through: NYISO's manual directly addresses conventional hydro (through energy-limited resource provisions and Capacity Accreditation Factor methodology) and pumped-storage hydro (through co-located storage resource rules for charging, withdrawal scheduling, and state-of-charge constraints). The shift from duration adjustment factors to resource-class-based CAFs changes how seasonal capacity revenue is calculated for hydro—a critical input to long-duration storage economics. External hydro imports are governed by must-offer rules tied to Capacity Resource Interconnection Service (CRIS) rights, which affects Northwest hydro export revenues to NYCA. Co-located storage provisions allow PSH to bid withdrawal and injection limits by hour in the day-ahead market, directly addressing state-of-charge flexibility. Hydro owners should track revisions to the DMNC/DMGC test protocols and CAF assignment processes, which determine accredited capacity and performance penalties.

documents.title: Board Decisional Letter On Critical Issue Fast Path
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This board decision establishes a Reliability Backstop Procurement mechanism and Large Load Registry that fundamentally reshape PJM's capacity market and load-forecasting methodology, directly affecting how capacity revenue is procured, allocated, and priced across all resources including dispatchable generation.
documents.ai_summary: The PJM Board has approved a Critical Issue Fast Path decision addressing resource adequacy pressures from 70 GW of projected demand growth by 2038 and 15 GW of retirements since 2022. The Board will file with FERC by end of July 2026 a proposal that establishes: (1) a Large Load Registry to improve load-forecast accuracy; (2) a Reliability Backstop Procurement beginning September 2026 targeting the capacity shortfall identified in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, with costs allocated to Load Serving Entities by Peak Load Contribution; (3) an Interim Resource Adequacy Service requiring Electric Distributors to manage new Large Loads that cannot meet their resource adequacy needs at the 1-in-10 reliability standard; and (4) a compensation rate for Large Load customers directed to reduce consumption. New Large Loads beyond the 2028/2029 forecast will be excluded from RPM Auctions for delivery years starting 2029/2030, and included only when their new supply capacity is offered into the relevant auction.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, this decision restructures PJM's capacity-market demand baseline and procurement framework in ways that affect all generation resources' access to capacity revenue. By excluding new Large Loads from the demand used in future RPM Auctions until those loads bring dedicated new supply, the Board reduces the nominal capacity requirement against which existing dispatchable resources compete, potentially lowering system-wide capacity prices. Conversely, the backstop procurement—a direct FERC filing to secure capacity equal to the near-term shortfall—creates a procurement stream outside the normal RPM auction. Whether conventional generation (including hydro plants offering capacity) can participate in this backstop procurement, at what offer levels, and how it interacts with must-offer rules and energy bids is not addressed here and would be material to hydro owners' strategic options for securing capacity revenue in a tightening market.

documents.title: Item 02a – CIFP Reliability Backstop Procurement – PJM Board Decision
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement mechanism is a long-term capacity-procurement framework that directly affects capacity-market revenue streams, accreditation requirements, and strategic options for all capacity resources—including conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities—through changes to RPM participation rules, must-offer obligations, settlement structures, and cost allocation.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's Board has approved a two-path Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) mechanism to address a megawatt shortfall in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, combining a central procurement administered by PJM and a facilitated bilateral matchmaking process. The RBP will procure long-term capacity-only UCAP commitments for a fixed 15-year term from 2028/2029 DY to 2042/2043 DY, structured as pay-as-bid offers in $/MW-day with a maximum willingness-to-pay cap of $555/MW-day UCAP (Point 1 of the unconstrained 2028/2029 BRA VRR Curve). Eligible supply is defined as "new" resources—those bringing new ICAP, new MFO, or transferred CIRs from deactivated resources, with an online date no later than June 1, 2032—and includes new annual Demand Response and DER. Resources with RBP commitments become PJM capacity resources subject to a mandatory RPM Must-Offer Obligation at $0 (price taker) and are settled as contracts for differences against weighted-average RPM clearing prices. The central procurement window runs September 30 to October 21, 2026, with selection and results October 22 to December 2, 2026. Resources face a 20% shortfall-charge rate (based on RBP commitment price) if delayed or failing to come online, with a 3-year delay threshold triggering commitment rescission. Cost allocation is pro rata by zone/area based on load-growth megawatts, and resources must post collateral equal to 0.2 × (RBP Sell Offer Price × committed UCAP × 365 × 3 years). The framework includes provisions for Transmission Owner exit scenarios and default allocation among LSEs.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources. However, the RBP directly affects all capacity resources in PJM, including conventional hydro and PSH facilities, in several material ways: (1) the 15-year fixed commitment structure and $0 must-offer obligation fundamentally change the revenue-stacking and bidding flexibility that hydro owners use to optimize across RPM and energy markets, constraining how seasonal and intra-year dispatch strategies interact with capacity pricing; (2) the "new" resource eligibility rule—requiring online date by June 1, 2032, and excluding resources already holding RPM commitments—determines which existing hydro and PSH plants can participate, creating a cliff for resources without RBP coverage; (3) the settlement as a CfD against weighted-average RPM clearing prices rather than energy-market or hybrid-contract structures shifts risk allocation and may reduce revenue capture for flexible resources whose value depends on being held offline for scarcity events. Hydro and PSH owners operating in PJM need to understand whether their existing plants qualify as "new," what the mandatory $0 offer means for their forward contracting, and how the long-duration commitment interacts with their water-management and transmission constraints.

documents.title: Item 02b – CIFP Framework For Service During Periods Of Insufficient Resource Adequacy – Executive Summary – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The proposal creates a new load-curtailment regime (Interim Resource Adequacy Service) triggered when PJM clears short of capacity; it affects how resources compete for capacity revenue and how dispatch may be constrained during shortage, with implications for the market value and dispatch obligations of all resources including dispatchable generation and storage.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes the Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS), a framework to manage capacity shortages by requiring new Large Loads (≥50 MW at a single site) that do not 'Bring Your Own New Capacity' (BYONC) or have not received Reliability Backstop Procurement credit to reduce load during periods when PJM clears short of its Reliability Requirement. Large Loads must register by March 1, 2027 (existing) and before in-service date (new loads); PJM will maintain a registry and allocate Interim Resource Adequacy Service obligations by zone/area. When triggered, Interim Resource Adequacy Service load reduction will occur before Pre-Emergency Load Management actions. Loads subject to Interim Resource Adequacy Service will receive compensation at the Non-Performance Assessment Interval rate (50% of the existing Performance Assessment Interval rate, approved by FERC on June 26, 2026). BYONC-eligible supply includes new generation, uprates, surplus interconnection, and fuel-switching; Demand Response and Distributed Energy Resources are also eligible. New Large Loads incremental to the 2028/2029 BRA forecast will be excluded from future RPM auctions (starting 2029/2030) unless new supply sufficient to cover them clears an RPM auction. The Board integrated this proposal from stakeholder feedback; tariff language is being prepared for FERC submission.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro or pumped storage. However, the framework directly affects the competitive environment for all conventional generation: by allowing large new loads to interconnect without self-supplied capacity (subject to mandatory curtailment in shortage), PJM narrows the market-clearing price signal that would otherwise reward existing generation during tight periods. Hydro owners will see the scarcity premium dampened during events when Interim Resource Adequacy Service loads are curtailed instead of being served by costly-to-operate backup units. The framework also changes the dispatch rules—hydro will be dispatched normally in day-ahead and real-time markets, but it will not be exempt from system needs during Interim Resource Adequacy Service events, meaning its revenue during such events is exposed to a new form of involuntary dispatch constraint. Conversely, if Interim Resource Adequacy Service prevents deeper energy-market scarcity, hydro's expected energy prices will be lower than they would be under a regime that allowed all new load to clear at any price.

documents.title: 02 Local Transmission Planning Task Force
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FERC Order 1920 transmission planning process affects how Transmission Owners' local plans are updated and incorporated into NYISO's interconnection and transmission expansion processes, which directly govern hydro resource deliverability and interconnection eligibility.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is establishing a Local Transmission Planning Task Force to implement FERC Order 1920 requirements for Transmission Owners' annual Local Transmission Plan (LTP) updates. The process requires three publicly noticed meetings per year structured around assumptions, needs, and solutions, with minimum 25 calendar days between stages and 5 calendar days between paired meetings. The 2026 schedule runs September through December, with two cohorts of meetings starting September 17 (Assumptions 1) and September 24 (Assumptions 2), followed by Needs meetings October 19 and November 5, and Solutions meetings December 8 and December 14. Materials will be posted 5 business days prior to meetings, and David Dittman from NY Transco will chair initial sessions. TOs may consolidate meetings only for immediate Good Utility Practice updates or Short-Term Reliability Needs with documented justification for time constraints.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the Local Transmission Plan incorporation process governs when transmission upgrades affecting hydro plant deliverability and interconnection outcomes enter NYISO's formal planning and expansion processes. Hydro owners' ability to export power and secure stable deliverability to load centers depends on how transmission needs are identified and validated in this three-stage stakeholder review, so the timing and scope of TO updates and the assumptions used to assess transmission adequacy directly affect hydro's strategic and operational flexibility.

documents.title: 04 Q2 STAR Near Term Reliability Need Explanatory Statement
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO Short-Term Reliability Process decision to solicit transmission and non-generation solutions for a Lower Hudson Valley deficiency, including consideration of RMR agreements and interim service providers — directly affects generation-retirement triggers, fleet retention decisions, and compensation mechanisms for dispatchable resources serving reliability.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO has identified a Near-Term Reliability Need in the Lower Hudson Valley arising from the proposed retirement of Danskammer units 1–4, observed in the 2026 Quarter 1 Short-Term Assessment of Reliability (STAR). The deficiency ranges from 184–201 MW in summer 2029 and 291–309 MW in summer 2030, lasting 3–5 and 4–5 hours respectively. NYISO reviewed alternative operating procedures and Local Transmission Owner Plans but concluded they would not sufficiently address the need. By September 2026, NYISO plans to issue a solicitation for solutions, including market-based and regulated non-generation solutions, from Central Hudson, Con Edison, Orange & Rockland, and NYSEG for their respective Transmission Districts. If proposed solutions prove insufficient, NYISO may retain Danskammer as an Interim Service Provider under a Reliability Must Run (RMR) Agreement. Stakeholder comments are due by August 7, 2026, and must be submitted to stakeholder_services@nyiso.com.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although this document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage, it directly engages NYISO's RMR process — a critical mechanism for generator compensation when reliability needs exceed market-driven retention. The decision to solicit non-generation solutions first, and only resort to RMR for Danskammer if those fail, establishes the order and burden of proof for an interim service provider agreement. Conventional hydro and PSH owners in NYISO who may face retirement-driven reliability determinations or RMR opportunities should track how NYISO applies this precedent: the threshold for declaring sufficiency of planned projects, the timeline for solicitation-to-RMR escalation, and whether the RMR agreement price-setting methodology (OATT Section 38 terms not detailed here) favors use-limited or peaking resources.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO issued its 2026 Q2 Short-Term Assessment of Reliability (STAR) on July 14, 2026, finding continued transmission deficiencies in New York City and Lower Hudson Valley without CHPE (Cross-Hudson Power Express) demonstrating planned capability, and extremely narrow margins on Long Island (projected to tighten to less than 40 MW in summer 2027). Danskammer 1-4 was prohibited from deactivating on August 1, 2026, and must remain in service until at least January 15, 2027, pending permanent solutions. NYISO will solicit solutions for Lower Hudson Valley reliability needs following a stakeholder comment period (deadline August 7, 2026), with developers having 60 days from solicitation (approximate due date mid-to-late October 2026) to submit proposals; NYISO will evaluate proposals October–November 2026 and issue findings by December 2026. The 2026 Q3 STAR will assess bulk power transmission facilities using base cases from the 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment (RNA) for the study period July 15, 2026–July 15, 2031, incorporating updated generation assumptions (Wheelabrator Hudson Falls generator deactivation effective December 31, 2026; withdrawal of two solar projects from queue; use of zonal-average EFORd for thermal units; NYPA small gas plants modeled out of service from January 2031) and transmission outage extensions (Plattsburgh transformer outage extended from September 2026 to May 2027; Station 23–42 outage extended from December 2026 to May 2027).
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or hydro-specific rules. However, it establishes the reliability-constrained operating context and scarcity signals that directly shape energy and ancillary-service prices in NYISO: transmission congestion in NYC, Lower Hudson Valley, and Long Island—and the forced retention of fossil-generation capacity (Danskammer) to maintain security margins—indicate sustained scarcity premiums and high opportunity costs during peak periods. Conventional hydro and pumped-storage resources in the NYISO footprint benefit from these scarcity conditions, but they also face dispatch pressure and potential energy-imbalance exposure from the generator-deactivation assessment process and transmission-outage assumptions; understanding the multi-year reliability forecast (through July 2031) and the near-term procurement timeline (solicitation in late August, proposals due October) is material to hydro owners' bidding strategy and revenue modeling.

documents.title: 06a 2026 RNA: Scenarios - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's 2026 RNA scenario planning establishes assumptions about imports, demand, aging generation, and transmission constraints that will shape resource adequacy assessments and transmission-expansion decisions directly affecting hydro's deliverability and the scarcity signals hydro supplies into.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO presented five selected scenarios for its 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment, modeling uncertainties in demand growth, large-load development, generator aging, renewable buildout, and imports through 2036. Scenario A assumes higher demand (32,607 MW vs. 30,713 MW) and increased planned projects (10,900 MW vs. 6,300 MW); Scenario B models widespread large-load expansion (4,113 MW vs. 2,717 MW) with reduced imports (1,460 MW vs. 2,920 MW) and emergency assistance (2,000 MW all years vs. 3,400–2,500 MW); Scenario C models slower growth with 5-year project delays; Scenario H tests inverter-based resource reliance on voltage control with reduced reactive capability and higher imports from PJM and HQ; Scenario J aligns with contracted projects (7,000 MW). Analysis will continue through August 2026 and results will be presented with the RNA draft in September 2026. Stakeholders had requested removal of a 1 GW nuclear assumption from selected scenarios; NYISO removed it and will address it as a sensitivity. Other sensitivities including "Loss of All Imports" and demand-response flexibility testing are planned as time permits.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro directly, but RNA scenario assumptions directly shape how transmission-constrained systems will procure dispatchable generation and flexibility during scarcity events. Scenario B's assumption of reduced imports (1,460 MW vs. 2,920 MW baseline) and Scenario J's focus on contracted projects will influence which transmission and generation capacity gets built, which in turn affects how much locational and temporal scarcity rent flows to hydro located on congested interfaces. Scenario H's treatment of inverter-based resources controlling voltage at lower reactive-power levels introduces operating conditions under which synchronous generators (including large hydro units) may see higher-value dispatch and ancillary-service opportunities. The RNA results will inform NYISO's long-term transmission and resource-adequacy framework, directly affecting the strategic value of existing hydro capacity and the economics of relicensing or strategic retirement decisions.

documents.title: 06b Scenarios for Analysis in the 2026 RNA
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The 2026 RNA scenario analysis establishes demand, resource availability, and transmission assumptions that directly shape capacity accreditation, seasonal adequacy, and the value of hydro deliverability and flexibility in NYISO's market.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO selected five scenarios for the 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment (RNA) to be analyzed in accordance with Section 3.3.4 of the NYISO Reliability Planning Process Manual. Scenario A assumes higher demand (32,607 MW summer peak in 2036 vs. 30,713 MW base case) and increased aging generation at risk (3,036 MW vs. 2,585 MW), with 10,900 MW of planned projects included. Scenario B models accelerated large-load development (4,113 MW vs. 2,717 MW base case) with reduced emergency assistance (2,000 MW vs. 3,500 MW) and reduced firm imports (1,460 MW vs. 2,920 MW). Scenario C reflects supply-chain delays and lower demand (28,719 MW vs. 30,713 MW base case) with reduced large loads (1,211 MW vs. 2,717 MW). Scenario H assumes new inverter-based resources with lower reactive capability and increased PJM imports with Hydro-Québec export flows (1,100 MW export to HQ, 965 MW PJM import vs. 643 MW base case). Scenario J represents the contract case with 7,000 MW of planned projects and local transmission projects added. Additional sensitivities including nuclear generation and flexible demand will be analyzed as time permits.
documents.hydro_read_through: These scenarios define the resource, demand, and transmission conditions under which NYISO will assess capacity adequacy and seasonal energy sufficiency through 2036, directly shaping the basis for accreditation, seasonal reserve requirements, and the scarcity value of hydro ramping and energy flexibility. Scenario B's reduced emergency assistance and firm imports are particularly relevant to New York hydro owners, as they model a future with tighter interregional transfers—reducing access to emergency assistance that has historically supported winter peak and scarcity conditions. Scenario H's modeling of HQ export flows and increased wind generation availability during light load conditions signals potential changes in hydro dispatch patterns and opportunity costs.

Key items include: (1) NERC Project 2025-03 on FERC Order No. 901, requiring inclusion of Inverter-Based Resource (IBR) performance in operational assessments and real-time monitoring both individually and in aggregate, as well as aggregate Distributed Energy Resources (DERs), with balloting and comment periods ending 8/7/26; (2) a Level 3 Essential Action Alert on computational load modeling and control to address risks from large loads, with entity responses due by August 3, 2026; (3) a Small Group Advisory Session (August 10-14, 2026) for registered entities on mandatory IBR compliance standards (PRC-028-1, PRC-029-1, PRC-030-1, MOD-026-2) with 2026-2027 compliance dates; (4) the 2026 Registered Ballot Body Self-Select Attestation Process (deadline August 18, 2026); and (5) announcements of upcoming NERC technical conferences and ReliabilityFirst events in fall 2026.

Because conventional hydropower plants are synchronous resources and pumped-storage systems are dispatchable and often equipped with converter technology, the expansion of operational assessment and real-time monitoring rules to aggregate-level performance and the new IBR/DER compliance regimes may create new compliance obligations or provide precedent for how hydro facilities' operational behavior will be monitored and validated. documents.title: Item 06 – July 22 Dominion Load Transfer Event – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document addresses load-transfer events, voltage ride-through requirements, and NERC standards development affecting synchronous units and large loads, which establish operational and interconnection obligations that apply to all dispatchable generators including hydropower facilities.
documents.ai_summary: On July 22, 2026, approximately 3,800 MW of load transferred to backup power following a 230 kV transmission line fault in PJM's Dominion zone, causing high voltage conditions and triggering additional load transfers. Frequency reached 60.092 Hz and ACE excursion recovered within 9 minutes, meeting the BAL-001-2 R2 requirement of recovery within 30 minutes. The event prompted NERC to accelerate Project 2026-02, developing new reliability standards for computational load integration onto the bulk power system. Draft standards are expected to address interconnection requirements and modeling data requirements for transmission operators and operators of large load sites; NERC is on track to file with FERC by December 31, 2026. A separate NERC Large Load Working Group whitepaper on minimum voltage and frequency ride-through requirements for computational loads was posted for 30-day industry comment on July 30, with expected incorporation into a reliability standard in 2027.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower directly; however, it establishes precedent and context for synchronous unit ride-through and disturbance-recovery obligations. Hydropower plants are subject to generator ride-through standards (such as NERC FERC Order 2023-02 requirements) and frequency response obligations. The voltage and frequency ride-through performance standards being developed here for large computational loads may inform or become precedent for broader generator disturbance-response requirements that would apply to conventional hydro and synchronous condensers. Additionally, the 3,800 MW load-transfer event and the stress it placed on voltage control illustrates how the integration of large uncontrolled loads can create acute scarcity in voltage support services—ancillary services that synchronous hydro stations supply and for which this event may drive increased procurement or higher performance standards.

documents.title: Presentation - Market Seams Workshop - Jul 31, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Market seams coordination between CAISO's EDAM and SPP's Markets+ and RTO expansion directly affects hydro transmission deliverability, interregional trade revenue, congestion-management cost allocation, and loop-flow settlement — core strategic and financial concerns for Western hydro owners choosing between market footprints.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO convened a workshop series on Western market seams coordination (July 31–October 2026) to address inefficiencies arising from multiple non-contiguous day-ahead markets: EDAM (PacifiCorp entering 2026, BANC/LADWP/PSNM/TID planned 2027) and SPP Markets+ wave 1 (APS, Powerex, PSCO, SRP, TEC planned 2027). The workshop addresses loop-flow management, congestion allocation across three markets, transmission commitment and reservation conflicts under differing rules, and cost-shifting. CAISO and SPP jointly directed to submit a seams coordination plan and schedule to FERC by September 30, 2026 (per AD26-10), covering operational coordination, loop-flow management, congestion settlement, and import/export transaction efficiency. Presenters noted that the West has an opportunity to learn from Eastern RTO experience: Eastern seams arrangements have used transmission-loading-relief (TLR), market-to-market coordinated flowgates, and redispatch mechanisms with varying success; however, coordinated transaction scheduling (CTS) implemented in the East has left over 40–50% of seams trades uneconomic, whereas intertie optimization has been more efficient (yielding $160–300M annually in Eastern estimates). Future workshops (August 18, September TBD, October TBD) will address transmission operations, congestion mechanics, and cross-border transaction examples.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, Western hydro owners and pumped-storage operators are materially affected by seams coordination design because their generation and storage is geographically dispersed across multiple market footprints and interties: loop-flow rules, congestion-settlement cost allocation, and transmission-reservation protocols will determine how efficiently hydro can export power and access arbitrage opportunities, and whether loop-flow costs are borne fairly or shifted to outside parties. The choice between coordinated transaction scheduling and intertie optimization (noted in the expert panels as a live question for the West) will significantly affect the realized revenue from cross-border flexibility trading. Additionally, since many Northwest hydro owners are choosing which market to join or how to participate in EDAM, seams governance, loop-flow entitlements, and redispatch-cost allocation are direct inputs to those strategic decisions.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Market Performance and Planning Forum (January 27, 2026) reviewed 2025 market outcomes and 2026–2027 release plans. Storage resources saturated CAISO's upward regulation market (accounting for over 100% of requirements) and have increasingly bid capacity and provided spinning reserves; they accrued 2.8% of day-ahead bid-cost recovery while gas resources accrued 96.7%. Storage charging during midday solar hours is shifting peak demand to earlier in the day, and storage resources are dispatched to meet both morning and evening peaks via energy arbitrage. CAISO reduced load-conformance use through process improvements (including a December 2025–January 2026 real-time pilot showing significant reduction in HASP conformance) and implemented enhancements to mitigate real-time market disruptions and improve long-start unit commitment. The Forum reported five active market issues, including incorrect transmission-constraint mitigation designations, off-grid charging indicator clarifications for co-located energy storage, and telemetry data-quality impacts on demand forecasting.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never names hydropower or pumped-storage facilities. However, it documents CAISO market mechanics directly governing use-limited storage resources: regulation markets where storage now dominates bid (saturating upward regulation procurement), state-of-charge management and load-conformance processes that constrain dispatch, and the revenue and dispatch implications of co-optimization with solar (midday charging shifts peak demand and reduces night peak generation value). Pumped-storage hydro participates in these same procurement and dispatch processes as a storage resource class; the saturation of regulation and changes in daily load profile shift what scarcity prices and storage dispatch revenue pumped-storage operators face. Load-conformance pilots and market disruption mitigations affect all storage assets' real-time economics.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) began May 1, 2026, covering CAISO and PacifiCorp East/West BAAs. The June 2026 performance report (the second of six monthly reports) shows robust market outcomes with results posted before 1:00 p.m. on 77% of days (up from 61% in May). Two new products were implemented: imbalance reserves up/down (IRU/IRD) and reliability capacity up/down (RCU/RCD), plus greenhouse-gas allocation pricing. Resource sufficiency evaluation passed across all participating areas except PACE, which failed a single hour on June 17. Energy prices rose seasonally into summer; imbalance reserve and reliability capacity prices stabilized and declined in June versus May with lower volatility. The report identifies ongoing issues including negative RCD prices, infeasible solar RCU awards (fixed July 6, 2026), storage resources unable to provide RCD, missing shift factors in the Market Participant Portal and CRR system, and missing IR deployment scenarios in CRR clawback. PACW and PACE areas are sourcing imbalance reserves primarily from transfers and hydro resources, while CAISO relies on gas and solar. Settlement data are preliminary and subject to adjustment through T+70 true-up.
documents.hydro_read_through: The report reveals that hydro is now explicitly relied upon as a supply source for the new imbalance reserve product in PACW and PACE areas—a flexibility revenue stream that did not exist in pre-EDAM day-ahead design. However, the document identifies an unresolved technical issue preventing storage resources (which would include pumped-storage hydro) from offering reliability capacity down (RCD) despite having economic incentive and available state-of-charge. This bug suppresses a revenue opportunity for any PSH fleet in the footprint. The IRU/IRD pricing mechanics and the apparent stability of IR prices in June suggest the product may be functioning for hydro participation, but the missing shift factors and clawback deployment scenarios are settlement issues that could delay or distort revenue collection for all resources, including hydro.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This MIR establishes Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS), a mechanism for scheduling import/export transactions across the Markets+ boundary and within its footprint, which affects how generators including dispatchable resources manage interchange scheduling, settlement location treatment, and GHG attribution — all operational and revenue-stream mechanics that apply to hydro and storage operators participating in Markets+.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 60-R (MIR60-R), submitted by SPP staff on 5/29/2026, establishes the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) framework. This MIR creates Markets+ System Points (MPSPs)—generic scheduling points neither resource nor load-specific—to enable Market Participants to schedule import and export transactions across the Markets+ boundary and within its footprint via e-Tag with confirmed OATT transmission. MPSPs will function as sources for export e-Tags and sinks for import e-Tags; participating Balancing Authority Areas may establish one or more MPSPs with optional hourly import/export/net limits (default 99,999 if not provided). MITSPS transactions are classified as Uncommitted Interchange Transactions, excluded from Market Participants' net position and must-offer obligations, and are non-attributed for GHG purposes (meaning their emissions treatment differs from source-specific exports). The framework revises Markets+ Protocols across multiple sections (Glossary, offer submittal, Day-Ahead and Real-Time inputs, settlement locations, and GHG tracking). Desired MPEC approval is Q3 2026 with implementation in Q1 2027. Design, implementation, and operational complexity are all rated Low; no separate Impact Analysis is required as MITSPS is already included in base Markets+ design.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the MITSPS framework establishes how generic system points facilitate interchange scheduling and settlement across the Markets+ boundary—mechanics that affect how any dispatchable resource or storage operator in the region manages bilateral and market-cleared export/import transactions, their settlement-location assignment, and GHG attribution. For hydro and PSH operators exporting across the Markets+ footprint, the treatment of MITSPS as Uncommitted Interchange Transactions (excluded from must-offer obligations) and as non-attributed for GHG purposes creates a distinct scheduling pathway; the optional per-BA hourly limits on net MPSP interchange may constrain export capability or create opportunities for intra-day flexibility sales depending on how each BA sets those limits.

documents.ai_summary: SPP submitted comments on behalf of the MSWG on behalf of the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) MIR (Markets+ Initiative Request). The MIR establishes Markets+ System Points (MPSPs), generic scheduling points within Markets+ Balancing Authority Areas, to facilitate interchange transactions into, within, and out of the Markets+ footprint that are market-cleared rather than pre-scheduled bilateral transactions. The framework allows Market Participants to e-Tag export transactions from an MPSP source to Markets+ boundary export points, and import transactions from boundary import points to an MPSP sink, enabling unscheduled interchange to non-Markets+ load sinks and from non-Markets+ sources. The SPP/MSWG comments propose revisions to the Markets+ Protocols governing MPSP definitions, offer submittal rules for uncommitted import and export interchange transactions, Day-Ahead and Real-Time Market inputs, congestion-management scheduling limits, and settlement-location treatment; the document shows protocol text with tracked changes across multiple sections (Glossary, sections 4.2–4.5) and indicates the MIR submission date as 7/15/2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the MITSPS framework governs how all generation resources, including those in hydro-heavy regions, schedule market-cleared exports across RTO boundaries—a core revenue-protection issue for hydro operators exporting from SPP or considering Markets+ membership. The rules for MPSP interchange limits (submitted hourly by Balancing Authority), e-Tag confirmation requirements, and treatment in Day-Ahead RUC and Real-Time market runs will determine whether a hydro facility's output can be freely scheduled to external markets or faces coordination constraints. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Market Storage Resource (MSR) state-of-charge management touches PSH revenue through dispatch accuracy, offer feasibility, and potential reliability-driven penalties in Markets+ energy and ancillary-services markets.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ Initiative Request 8.1-R proposes enhanced state-of-charge management for MSRs by introducing time-coupled intervals in Day-Ahead Market and RUC studies. Market participants will have the option to elect whether the Market Operator calculates MSR state of charge within these studies, constraining it to the end-of-prior-interval value computed by the MCE; if not elected, participants submit state-of-charge forecasts in their offers. The design aims to reduce forecast burden on MSR participants, prevent infeasible dispatch outcomes between Day-Ahead and real-time, and mitigate reliability and financial penalties. Requested MPEC approval is Q1 2027 with implementation target Q1 2027. Revisions to Markets+ Tariff (Definitions, Sections 2.1.3, 2.2.3, 4.2.2) and Protocols (Sections 4.2, 4.3, 4.4) are required.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, PSH operators participating as MSRs in Markets+ face direct consequences from state-of-charge rules: under current design, they must forecast SOC in offers, creating dispatch-feasibility mismatches between day-ahead commitments and real-time capability that expose them to reliability penalties and financial losses. This MIR's time-coupling option would let PSH operators delegate SOC calculation to the market, reducing their forecast risk and improving operational accuracy in markets where PSH is the canonical use-limited, long-duration storage resource.
