documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Co-located resource participation rules and must-offer obligations directly affect how multiple resources at the same point of interconnection (common for hydro/battery co-location and PSH plants) clear energy and register capacity in SPP Markets+, touching both revenue accreditation and dispatch mechanics.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ Initiative Request 8.2-R proposes new tariff and protocol language to formalize market treatment of Co-Located Resources—two or more resources behind the same point of interconnection that jointly utilize an injection-limit constraint. The MIR introduces a Co-Located Resources Constraint mechanism allowing the market-clearing engine to transfer MWs between resources when their combined registered capacity exceeds their shared injection limit, and modifies must-offer obligations in Day-Ahead Market, RUC, and Real-Time Balancing Market to use the lesser of individual-resource-offered-capacity sums or the co-located constraint. Changes affect Tariff sections on Definitions and Sections 4.2.9, 5.1, 6.2, and Protocols sections on Definitions, 4.2, 9.1.1, and 9.1.16. The MIR is ranked High priority with desired MPEC approval in Q1 2027 and implementation in Q4 2027. SPP staff identified Design, Implementation, and Operational Complexity as High.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or hydro-specific applications. However, the co-location constraint mechanism is directly relevant to PSH and conventional-hydro owners who co-locate generation with battery storage or other resources at the same interconnection point. The formalized 'clipping' mechanism allows injection-limited facilities to reallocate output between co-located resources dynamically within market dispatch, which could improve revenue capture when one resource is curtailed by interconnection limits; conversely, the modified must-offer language (using the lesser of individual capacity sums or the joint constraint) may tighten must-offer obligations for co-located participants during binding seasons. The mechanical change to how co-located resources are committed and dispatched warrants watching for its interaction with seasonal hydro operations and PSH charge/discharge scheduling.

documents.ai_summary: MIR9.2-R defines the Markets+ tariff and protocols for Dynamic Schedule Resources—resources coupled to generators that dynamically serve load in non-participating balancing authorities. The proposal clarifies that the output of a Dynamic Schedule Resource must be 100% e-tagged (with one dynamic transaction type and optionally normal transaction types); establishes a Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface offset between resource dispatch and normal e-tag layoffs; and specifies different treatment in day-ahead, pre-real-time, and real-time settlement—the dynamic e-tag energy profile is used as a fixed value in day-ahead/RUC/pre-RTBM, while the resource interface governs real-time export quantities. SPP posted MIR9.2-R on April 13, 2026 with comment deadline May 1, 2026; the Markets Deployment Working Group approved it July 8, 2026; MORWG approval is pending July 29, 2026, and MPEC approval is pending August 25, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped storage. However, conventional hydroelectric plants and pumped-storage facilities that self-schedule dynamic power transfers across balancing authority boundaries would fall under these Dynamic Schedule Resource rules. The distinction between fixed dispatch quantities used in pre-real-time processes and dynamic adjustment via the Resource Interface in real-time settlement is material to how real-time balancing directives and settlement payoffs flow to dispatchable resources—a hydro owner operating such a facility would need to understand whether these rules align or conflict with their operational capabilities and revenue accreditation.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ filed a comment (July 2, 2026) on MIR9.2-R, proposing tariff and protocol language to clarify how Dynamic Schedule Resources—internal resources whose output is allocated to an Attaining Balancing Authority via a Dynamic Schedule—are registered, e-Tagged, and settled across the Day-Ahead Market, RUC, Pre-RTBM, and RTBM. The proposal requires all output of a Dynamic Schedule Resource to be 100% e-Tagged with one Dynamic transaction-type tag and, if applicable, one or more Normal transaction-type tags. For self-scheduled Dynamic Export Interchange Transactions, the Day-Ahead Market, RUC, and Pre-RTBM will use the e-Tag energy profile as a fixed value and settle at external interface LMP; the RTBM will ignore the e-Tag and use the Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface to set the export quantity, settled based on the updated Dynamic e-Tag at interface LMP. The proposal also specifies that Dynamic Schedule Resources may represent imports or exports for Multi-Service Resources (MSRs) and that separate e-Tags will be required depending on MSR dispatch. No vote date or decision deadline is stated in the comment form.

The distinction between Day-Ahead/RUC fixed settlement versus real-time interface-based settlement also affects how inter-BA hydro dispatch and pricing is calculated.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Markets+ protocol change for external resource registration and pseudo-tie modeling affects how resources including potential storage and external resources participate in the SPP footprint, setting operational registration precedent relevant to multi-state resource positioning.
documents.ai_summary: This Markets+ Market Implementation Request (MIR 9.3-R) establishes a registration and modeling framework for dynamically scheduled pseudo-ties — external resources represented in the Markets+ network model as pseudo-tied into an Attaining Balancing Authority while continuing to be scheduled as Dynamic Schedules under NAESB and WECC standards. The proposal creates two forms of external-resource pseudo-ties: formal pseudo-tie agreements (electronically tied per NAESB standards) and dynamically scheduled pseudo-ties (modeled as pseudo-ties in Markets+ but scheduled as Dynamic Schedules between Native and Attaining BAs). Market Participants must designate the resource type, obtain Attaining BA attestation, and designate a Meter Agent responsible for submitting export pseudo-tie quantities. The MIR targets Markets+ Protocols sections 9.1.1, 9.1.9, 9.1.9.1, and 9.1.9.2 (new) for revision. SPP Staff submitted the MIR with desired MPEC approval in Q3 2026 and implementation in Q1 2027; no Impact Analysis is required because the enhancement is already included in Markets+ base design.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, external resources seeking to participate in SPP Markets+ must register through pseudo-tie pathways, and the formalization of dynamically scheduled pseudo-ties—allowing resources to participate in the Markets+ model while remaining scheduled outside it—creates an operational precedent for how external storage, variable resources, and multi-BA-spanning assets including potential PSH facilities could enter SPP's energy and ancillary-service dispatch. For hydro owners considering participation in Markets+ from outside the SPP footprint or exploring co-location across BA boundaries, the clarity around pseudo-tie registration, Meter Agent responsibilities, and the distinction between formal and dynamic pseudo-ties will shape feasibility and administrative burden.

documents.title: 09 - MIR79-R MIR Process document-SRP Comments-20260526.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260729.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document establishes the Markets+ Revision Initiative Request (MIR) process for changing Markets+ tariff, protocols, and governing documents — the procedural framework through which all market-design changes affecting hydro and storage revenue and obligations are proposed, reviewed, and approved in SPP Markets+.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ has adopted a Revision Initiative Request (MIR) process (formerly called MRR) governing submissions, routing, review, and approval of changes to Markets+ Tariff, Markets+ Protocols, and the MIR Process itself. Qualified entities—including any Markets+ Market Participant, SPP staff, the Market Monitoring Unit, SPP Members, and governmental authority staff—may submit MIRs using an online submission form. All MIRs except those from SPP staff must be submitted via the Request Management System (RMS). Submissions must include submitter information, objectives (problem, proposed solution, expected benefits), identification of affected documents and sections, and proposed language changes if known. SPP has three business days to request additional information; incomplete submissions are not processed. Upon receipt of a complete MIR, SPP posts it to the website and distributes it within three business days to the MIR and Primary Working Group email exploders. The Markets+ Design Working Group (MDWG) is the primary responsible body for Markets+ Tariff and Protocols changes. The process includes a 15 business-day comment period before Primary Working Group review; comments must be submitted using the MIR Comment Form no later than five business days before the Primary Working Group's initial review. Secondary Working Groups provide secondary approval; all Secondary Working Group changes must be accepted by the Primary Working Group before Markets+ Participant Executive Committee (MPEC) and Markets+ Independent Panel (MIP) review. SPP conducts Impact Analysis (IA) assessing system, process, and staffing impacts, budgetary costs for implementation and ongoing operations, implementation timeline, and possible workarounds; IA results are posted for review, and SPP will issue completed IA within thirty calendar days after Primary Working Group approval unless longer review is warranted. The Primary Working Group may rank MIRs (high, medium, low) if they are more than Correction or Clarification, and SPP Staff schedules drafting based on rank, staff availability, and vendor availability. The Primary Working Group may approve (as submitted or modified, potentially contingent on IA review), reject, table/postpone (with optional additional 15 business-day comment period), withdraw, or refer an MIR. Primary Working Group-approved MIRs route to Secondary Groups, MPEC, and when necessary MIP. Process effective date November 13, 2025; document version 2.0 as of May 12, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, this MIR process is the formal governance structure through which all substantive market changes in SPP Markets+ are proposed and decided—including changes to energy pricing, capacity accreditation, ancillary-services design, storage participation rules, and must-offer/operational compliance obligations that directly affect hydro and PSH revenue and obligations. Hydro and PSH owners active in SPP Markets+ need to understand the comment deadlines (five business days before Primary Working Group initial review), the routing path (MDWG as primary, with secondary groups and MPEC/MIP review), and the Impact Analysis process to anticipate when significant rule changes are under consideration and when comment windows open. Changes to tariff and protocols documents flow through this procedure, making it the chokepoint for all substantive market design that touches dispatchable and storage resources.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This Markets+ initiative modifies e-Tag and Market Transfer Interface rules that govern interregional energy scheduling and transmission capacity allocation, which directly affects hydro owners' ability to move power across balancing authority boundaries and their exposure to real-time redispatch risks when scheduling constraints change post-day-ahead.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 81-R proposes to distinguish Normal and Dynamic transaction types for Market Transfer Interfaces (MTIs) and Market Operator Transfer Interfaces (MOTIs), with Dynamic transactions eligible only in RTBM and Normal transactions fixed after the Pre-RTBM SCED run thirty minutes before each operating hour. The proposal allows Balancing Authorities to create separate BAA Scheduling Constraints around MTIs/MOTIs with different transaction types, preventing unilateral changes to scheduling limits after DA Market and RUC clearing that would force redispatch and artificial price separation. SPP staff submitted the MIR with desired MPEC approval in Q4 2026 and implementation in Q1 2027; the change is classed as an Enhancement with Low complexity across design, implementation, and operations.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage resources. However, as a general matter, hydro and PSH owners participating in Markets+ depend on stable transmission-scheduling windows to plan and commit dispatch resources across RTO seams—particularly in the West, where hydro generators use interregional transfer capability to monetize flexibility. By locking Normal MTI quantities after Pre-RTBM SCED and reserving Dynamic MTIs only for the five-minute RTBM, this rule prevents a Balancing Authority from unilaterally tightening scheduling constraints in real time in ways that would force costly redispatch of units already committed in the day-ahead and RUC. That protection is particularly valuable for hydro, which is use-limited and chronically exposed to opportunity-cost penalties when forced to spill or shift dispatch away from optimal conditions.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Transmission scheduling constraints and market-transfer interfaces affect hydro's ability to move power from high-generation to high-load basins and interact with intraday market dispatch; MIR81-R's distinction between Day-Ahead (fixed) and Real-Time (flexible) scheduling transfers directly touches hydro's operational flexibility and revenue exposure to real-time pricing.
documents.ai_summary: MIR81-R introduces a two-tier scheduling system for Market Transfer Interfaces (MTIs) and Market Opt-In Transfer Interfaces (MOTIs) in SPP Markets+. Normal MTI/MOTI flows, submitted by Day-Ahead Market close and used in the DA market, RUC, and Pre-RTBM SCED, become fixed quantities in the Real-Time Balancing Market. Dynamic MTI/MOTI, submitted only for RTBM, allows Balancing Authority Areas to impose separate scheduling constraints on the same transmission path in real-time without undermining the prior DA commitment plan. The proposal updates protocol sections 4.2.7 (MTI Tagging by transaction type), 8.2.1.1 (MTI Limit communication), 8.2.2.1 (MOTI Limit communication), 8.2.6 (BAA Scheduling Constraint timing), and 9.4.1 (MTI/MOTI registration requirements). Limits for Dynamic MTI/MOTIs must be submitted via the Market User Interface (MUI) and default to 99999 MW unless a BA-to-BA or TSP-to-TSP restriction applies; BAA Scheduling Constraint limits must be submitted by DA Market close but may be updated for RUC, Pre-RTBM SCED, and RTBM.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never mentions hydro directly. However, the mechanism matters for conventional hydro and PSH operators because hydro's value hinges on moving water-driven generation from run-of-river or reservoir locations to load centers via transmission interfaces. Locking in Normal MTI flows at DA-market close reduces real-time flexibility but protects the operator's commitment position; the new Dynamic MTI tier allows real-time constraint tightening on the same path, which would force incremental dispatch to occur at more expensive local generation or reduce the real-time price signal hydro captures on already-committed transfers. The BAA Scheduling Constraint update timing—now allowing updates post-DA and through RTBM—could create adverse real-time transmission congestion that was not priced into hydro's DA-market position, reducing expected revenues on fixed transfers or forcing hydro to curtail generation behind a newly binding constraint. Whether this change expands or constrains hydro's strategic dispatch options depends on how MTSPs and BAs exploit the Dynamic MTI feature in practice.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MIR82-R modifies SPP Markets+ transmission-service queue management during day-ahead market settlement, affecting the timing and coordination between market clearing and interconnection-request processing that hydro and storage resources depend on for transmission service acquisition and scheduling.
documents.ai_summary: MIR82-R revises the Markets+ Tariff and Protocols to replace a mandatory OASIS Queue Pause (during which transmission requests cannot be processed) with a more flexible queue-management framework allowing individual Transmission Service Providers (MTSPs) to pause, limit, or otherwise manage request processing between day-ahead market close and energy-schedule publication. The change aims to accommodate NAESB WEQ 001-4.13 timing-requirement compliance without requiring blanket waivers; each MTSP retains responsibility for its own OATT compliance. The revision permits MTSPs to determine "specific conditions" of queue management consistent with their operational requirements, provided coordination with market-operator timelines and public documentation of procedures. MTWG approved MIR82-R on June 25, 2026, MDWG on July 8, 2026, with MPEC scheduled for approval August 25, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, the queue-pause revision affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources secure transmission service for the next operating day relative to market-settlement timing. Hydro plants and pumped-storage units competing in day-ahead energy and ancillary-services markets depend on timely transmission-request confirmation to finalize their operating schedule and manage intraday dispatch; a more flexible queue-management regime could either accelerate or delay that confirmation depending on how individual MTSPs implement their procedures. The shift from mandatory pause to individual MTSP discretion introduces variability in queue-processing timelines across the SPP footprint, which could affect the certainty and speed with which hydro resources confirm transmission service availability for market participation.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MITSPS establishes the technical and scheduling framework for interchange transactions at generic system points within the Markets+ footprint, which affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources can export and import energy across regional boundaries and participate in internal market transfers — a direct application to hydro's access to revenue-generating market participation and transmission utilization.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 60-R implements the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS), creating a framework for generic Markets+ System Points (MPSPs) to function as source and sink locations for uncommitted import and export interchange transactions within and across the Markets+ boundary. MPSPs are generic scheduling points (neither resource- nor load-specific) located within Markets+ Balancing Authority Areas that facilitate e-Tag scheduling and tagging of transactions not pre-scheduled as bilateral interchanges but resulting from market clearing. The MIR amends Markets+ Protocols sections covering glossary definitions, offer submittal (4.2.2.7, 4.2.3.3), day-ahead and real-time market inputs (4.3.1.1, 4.4.2.1.1), congestion management (new 4.4.2.5.3), settlement locations (5.5.2.2, 8.2.6), and GHG tracking for import/export transactions (9.4.2). Participating BAAs may establish one or more MPSPs with optional hourly interchange limits (defaulting to 99999 if not submitted); MITSPS transactions are non-attributed for GHG purposes. Implementation is desired for Q1 2027, with MPEC approval targeted for Q3 2026. Design, implementation, and operational complexity are all rated as low; no separate impact analysis is required as the work was already included in the base Markets+ design.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, MITSPS establishes the operational and settlement infrastructure for interchange transactions that hydro operators will use to export renewable energy across regional boundaries or import low-cost energy during periods of constraint within Markets+. By establishing generic system points rather than requiring resource-specific tagging, the framework reduces administrative friction for hydro exports and enables participation in both day-ahead and real-time market transfer mechanisms — directly affecting the ease and cost of monetizing hydro's geographic location advantage and flexible capacity. The GHG tracking treatment (non-attribution of MITSPS transactions) will influence how Northwest hydro exports are counted under any future carbon-pricing linkages between Markets+ and other GHG programs.

documents.ai_summary: SPP filed comments on behalf of the Markets+ Steering Working Group (MSWG) on MIR60-R, which implements the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) framework. MITSPS enables Market Participants to e-Tag import and export transactions using generic Markets+ System Points (MPSPs) as sources or sinks to facilitate interchange from market-cleared transactions (not pre-scheduled bilaterals) into and out of the Markets+ footprint. The MIR establishes MPSP definitions, integration into the Day-Ahead Market, Real-Time Balancing Market, and settlement logic, including hourly interchange limits that participating balancing authorities submit via the Market User Interface; these limits are enforced in the DAM, RUC, and RTBM. SPP's proposed revisions modify Markets+ Protocols sections governing import/export interchange transaction offer eligibility, day-ahead and real-time market inputs, coordinated interchange scheduling limits, and settlement locations to incorporate MPSP mechanics.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, MITSPS framework design touches three strategic dimensions for hydro owners: (1) how they schedule energy exports and imports across BA boundaries in a way that recognizes both market-cleared and bilateral flows — MPSP limits submitted by each BA will constrain net interchange and may tighten the locational scarcity signals hydro receive; (2) the treatment of MPSP transactions as "Uncommitted" (not counting toward must-offer obligations) creates a separate participation pathway for hydro seeking to arbitrage or balance across BA lines without commitment consequences; (3) the interaction of MPSP limits with transmission e-Tag capacity allocations determines effective transmission access, which is relevant to hydro's ability to deliver to non-home-BA load and to multi-BA portfolio optimization. Whether MPSP limits are set too tight will reduce scarcity pricing and flexibility revenue; too loose, they impose no meaningful constraint. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Market Storage Resource (MSR) state-of-charge management rules in SPP Markets+ affect how pumped-storage and battery-storage facilities compete on revenue terms, forecast burdens, and feasibility constraints—directly touching the participation model and dispatch-prediction obligations for storage-based flexible supply.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ Initiative Request 8.1-R proposes to enhance MSR participation by introducing time-coupled intervals in Day-Ahead Market and Reliability Unit Commitment (RUC) studies to address reliability and financial risks. Currently, MSRs must predict state-of-charge in their Resource Offers, creating a burden not placed on other resource types and risking infeasible commitments if Day-Ahead forecasts cannot be achieved in real-time. The proposal gives MSRs the option to elect, on a daily basis, that the Market Operator constrain state-of-charge within study windows to the calculated end-of-prior-interval value rather than relying on Market Participant forecasts. The change applies to definitions and MSR offer parameters in Markets+ Tariff sections 2.1.3, 2.2.3, and 4.2.2, and Protocols sections 4.2, 4.3, and 4.4. Desired MPEC approval and implementation are both Q1 2027. The proposal was developed collaboratively with the Markets+ MSR Subgroup and is classified as a High-complexity, New Protocol/Tariff initiative.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the rule addresses Market Storage Resources (MSRs), a category that includes pumped-storage hydro and battery storage. The change would materially reduce the operational risk and prediction burden on PSH operators: instead of forecasting the exact state of charge at each interval (which physical and market conditions may render infeasible), an MSR owner could elect to have the Market Operator enforce consistency between Day-Ahead and real-time commitments by constraining state-of-charge to what the market actually achieved in the prior interval. This reduces the likelihood of over-commitments that would cause financial penalties or reliability shortfalls and shifts forecast responsibility from the MSR owner back to the market model—benefiting any long-duration or constrained-availability storage asset.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 8.2-R (MIR 8.2-R) proposes formal market rules for co-located resources — multiple generating units behind the same point of interconnection operated by the same market participant. The proposal adds a Co-Located Resources Constraint mechanism that allows the market-clearing engine to transfer energy between generating resources and Market Service Resources (MSRs) when generation would otherwise be curtailed due to injection limits. The MIR modifies the Markets+ Tariff (Definitions, Sections 4.2.9, 5.1, 6.2) and Protocols (Definitions, Sections 4.2, 9.1.1, 9.1.16) to provide visibility and operational coordination for Day-Ahead Market, Reliability Unit Commitment (RUC), and Real-Time Balancing Market processes. The proposal is marked High complexity for design, implementation, and operations; desired MPEC approval is Q1 2027 with Q4 2027 implementation target. Submitted by Nick Foss (SPP) on 7/14/2026, with the work characterized as a collaboration between SPP and the Markets+ MSR Subgroup.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the co-located resource constraint framework applies to any dispatchable generating unit co-located with other generation or storage behind a single interconnection point. For pumped-storage facilities that co-locate generating and charging assets, or for hydropower plants paired with battery or thermal resources, this mechanism could alter dispatch sequencing and revenue capture by explicitly allowing the market to 'clip' (curtail) one resource to make room for another to reach the injection limit — a form of implicit market power over use-limited resources that would require careful evaluation of how offering requirements and penalties are calibrated under the new must-offer rules.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ tariff and protocols modification MIR9.2-R establishes rules for Dynamic Schedule Resources that are coupled to physical generation resources and export energy via self-scheduled dynamic e-Tags to non-participating balancing authorities. Key changes effective in RTBM and day-ahead/RUC/pre-RTBM processes distinguish between dynamic e-Tag energy profiles (used as fixed values in day-ahead and RUC) and Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface values (used in RTBM to set export quantity). For internal dynamic transfers, the DSR and its interface offset the native BA's power balance; for dynamic exports, the DSR is included in native BA power balance only during RTBM, not during day-ahead planning. The distinction between day-ahead fixed e-Tag values and real-time dynamic adjustment of export quantities through the DSR Interface could affect settlement accuracy and real-time dispatch signals for such resources; hydro owners with cross-BA operations or considering Markets+ participation should monitor how this framework treats variable dispatch versus pre-scheduled exports and whether the RTBM dynamic adjustment creates opportunities or constraints for flexible ramping.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Initiative Request 81-R proposes to distinguish Normal and Dynamic transaction types for Market Transfer Interface (MTI) and Market Operator Transfer Interface (MOTI) e-tags and BAA scheduling constraints. Normal MTI/MOTI transactions will be allocated in day-ahead and RUC markets and become fixed for real-time; Dynamic transactions will be RTBM-only and updated by participating BAs at 5-minute intervals. The proposal modifies Markets+ Protocols sections 4.1.4.4, 4.2.7, 6.1, 6.2, 8.2, and 9.4 to prevent post-clearing BAA scheduling constraint changes that would force redispatch and price separation. MIR submitter is Garrott Granholm (SPP Staff). Desired MPEC approval is Q4 2026 with implementation in Q1 2027.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never explicitly mentions hydropower or storage. However, this rule change directly affects how dispatchable resources—including conventional and pumped-storage hydro—face commitment certainty and redispatch risk in the real-time balancing market. By fixing Normal MTI quantities after pre-RTBM and confining Dynamic transactions to RTBM-only status, the rule reduces the operational exposure to unplanned constraint-tightening that would force costly redispatch away from the DAM/RUC unit commitment. For hydro operators with limited energy and high opportunity costs, the ability to rely on a fixed commitment band through pre-RTBM, without late BAA constraint surprises, materially reduces revenue volatility and artificial binding-constraint risk in real-time dispatch.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MIR81-R establishes dynamic transmission scheduling constraints that can differ between day-ahead/pre-RTBM and real-time markets, affecting transmission availability and congestion pricing hydro faces in real-time dispatch — a direct application of transmission-dispatch mechanics to locational price formation and access.
documents.ai_summary: MIR81-R introduces a two-tier Market Transfer Interface (MTI) tagging system that allows Balancing Authorities in Markets+ to register separate Normal MTIs (used in day-ahead market, RUC, and pre-RTBM) and Dynamic MTIs (used only in real-time market). Normal MTI quantities are locked in once set; Dynamic MTIs can be adjusted in real-time to prevent large swing in net scheduled interchange between dispatch intervals while preserving the day-ahead commitment plan. The proposal updates protocol sections 4.1.4.4, 8.2.1.1, 8.2.2.1, 8.2.6, and 9.4.1 to define transaction types, require registration of at least one Normal and one Dynamic MTI per interface, and allow limits to be submitted or updated via the Markets Operations Interface (MUI) throughout the operating day for Dynamic MTIs in RTBM. Protocol language specifies that Dynamic MTI limits default to 99999 MW unless constrained by BA-BA or TSP-TSP scheduling restrictions per WEQ-023 Standard Business Practices.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage resources directly. However, hydro and PSH operators participating in Markets+ face transmission constraints that shape real-time dispatch and locational pricing. This rule change creates a mechanism by which BAs can lock in normal (day-ahead optimized) transfer limits while using dynamic MTI constraints to manage real-time transfers on the same physical paths. The effect for a hydro operator is that transmission access in real-time could be tighter or looser than what the day-ahead model assumed, changing the locational price signals and potentially the revenue hydro can capture from real-time generation or from flexible ramping services. Operators need to understand how their home BA or interconnected BAs are likely to use these dynamic constraints — whether to preserve day-ahead schedules or to create real-time scarcity — and how that will feed through to nodal prices and reserve activation.

The comment proposes revisions to Markets+ Protocols sections 4.1.4.4, 4.2.7 (new), 6.1, 6.2, 8.2, and 9.4 in version 2.0a (June 2026). The objectives are to allow BAA Scheduling Constraints that do not impact day-ahead or RUC markets but constrain real-time transfer changes, and to avoid North-South Interface (NSI) swings while preserving the optimized commitment and dispatch plan from day-ahead and RUC processes. The document establishes separate protocols for Normal and Dynamic transaction types, with Dynamic transfers updated by participating BAs on 5-minute dispatch intervals and Normal transfers adjusted and fixed after Pre-RTBM SCED.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not directly address hydropower or pumped-storage resources. However, the MTI/MOTI scheduling and BAA constraint framework affects how variable or controllable generation—including flexible and dispatchable resources—can schedule energy across Markets+ balancing authority boundaries in both day-ahead and real-time markets. By allowing real-time BAA constraints to be established separately from day-ahead limits without disrupting the commitment plan, this rule shapes the transmission corridors and interface limits that determine where energy can flow and therefore which resources capture price spreads and congestion signals. This particularly matters for resources with the ability to respond to intra-day transmission changes and provide ramping or flexibility into congested interfaces.

documents.ai_summary: MIR82-R proposes to revise the Markets+ Tariff and Protocol queue-pause requirements for Transmission Service Providers (MTSPs). The current rule mandates that MTSPs pause all transmission service request processing between day-ahead market close and when day-ahead energy schedules are updated. The proposed revision allows each MTSP discretion to pause, limit, or otherwise manage queue processing according to its own operational requirements and procedures, provided coordination with Market Operator timelines is maintained and queue prioritization is preserved. The change responds to NAESB WEQ 001-4.13 timing-compliance concerns by creating operational flexibility for individual transmission providers. documents.ai_summary: EKPC, a PJM Load-Serving Entity, presents a proposal for mandatory LSE hedging requirements and a return to RPM's original residual-market design. EKPC argues that LSEs relying solely on the wholesale RPM capacity market to meet growing load (including data-center loads) create unequal burden and load-shed risk for entities that self-supply or bilaterally contract. The proposal includes three concepts: guardrails on market leaning, state partnership to clarify state vs. PJM resource-adequacy roles, and mandatory bilateral hedging outside the wholesale market. The framework would require LSEs to identify confirmed load before auction and provide proof of bilateral or owned supply, with penalties for noncompliance and revenue returned to compliant LSEs. EKPC references FERC technical conference findings on July 23, 2026, that state vs. PJM responsibility for resource adequacy remains undefined, particularly in retail-choice jurisdictions.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, it addresses the demand-side structure of PJM's capacity market—specifically, how LSE portfolio obligations and hedging behavior shape the wholesale-market clearing and residual-auction mechanics that set capacity revenue for all available resources, including dispatchable supply. If LSEs are required to hedge bilateral capacity positions rather than rely on RPM spot procurement, that shifts when and how much capacity supply enters the wholesale market, which would affect the accreditation value and bidding strategy for hydro capacity resources. The proposal also touches ELCC accreditation volatility as a source of LSE hedging risk, which is directly germane to how seasonal and annual capacity value is determined for hydro facilities.

documents.ai_summary: Dominion Energy presents PJM's 'Powering Reliability Through Market Design' process (Phase 1 initial for Delivery Year 2028/29), proposing reforms to incentivize resource-adequacy investment by restructuring the Base Residual Auction as a residual rather than centralized auction, introducing a Load Entity Large Load Addition (LLA) Sufficiency Incentive with penalties at 50% in Year 4 and 100% in Year 5 (2031/32–2032/33) if entities do not procure 70% of their new large-load capacity needs, and expanding capacity-equivalent credit options (demand-response reforms, provisional interconnection service). The proposal includes coordination mechanisms between transmission, generation, and load planning modeled on SPP processes, as well as enhancements to energy and ancillary-services markets to provide investment signals and mitigate uplift. The Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) sunsets in 2027; Reliability Backstop Procurement is scheduled for September 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities are dispatchable resources whose revenue depends critically on capacity-market structure, ancillary-services pricing, and uplift mitigation. Restructuring the Base Residual Auction to function as a residual auction, expanding bilateral contracting, and strengthening price signals in energy and ancillary-services markets would reduce reliance on central procurement and uplift—mechanisms that often undervalue use-limited dispatchable resources relative to their true contribution to reliability. The LLA sufficiency penalties and coordination reforms may also shift load-procurement patterns in ways that affect where and how much dispatchable capacity (including hydro) is valued; the timeline extending to 2032/33 suggests a multi-year transition in which existing units' capacity accreditation and ancillary-services revenue opportunity could shift materially.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Reliability Imperative is a multi-year strategic program addressing operational risks, market design, transmission, operations modernization, and digital systems through initiatives running 2026–2029+. Key mechanisms affecting storage and dispatchable resources include: (1) Market Redefinition — accreditation alignment with peak-risk periods, storage-resource participation optimization, dynamic reserves, demand-response product standardization, and congestion-pricing reform; (2) Transmission Evolution — enabling large-load interconnection with reliable speed-to-power, expedited generator interconnection (ERAS approved), and updated futures; (3) Operations of the Future — centralized control-room operations, ambient-adjusted-ratings integration (FERC Order 881), and large-load grid integration; (4) System Enhancements — AI/automation, new day-ahead market clearing, cloud-enabled settlements. The presentation invites stakeholder feedback with a submission deadline of September 4, 2026. Storage integration is explicitly listed as an in-progress initiative with optimization phases planned through 2029+.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly; however, the storage-participation and accreditation initiatives are core to hydro operators' revenue and compliance. Accreditation alignment with peak-risk periods and seasonal accreditation refinement will reshape how conventional and pumped-storage hydro are credited for capacity — a foundational revenue lever. Storage optimization in markets and dynamic-reserves design will affect both energy and ancillary-service pricing for storage resources. The large-load integration, expedited interconnection queue, and transmission-evolution work create both scarcity signals (raising hydro's energy value) and integration challenges. Congestion-pricing reform and new market-clearing mechanics will change locational signals and real-time coordination. Conversely, the deck says nothing about how hydro's use-limited nature or multi-year water conditions are reflected in accreditation or operational planning — a gap worth monitoring.

documents.ai_summary: The California Public Utilities Commission Energy Division presented findings from the SB 1174 (2025 Transmission System Assessment) requirement to report on changes to in-service dates of transmission and interconnection facilities needed to serve eligible renewable energy and energy storage resources. Analysis identified approximately 40.5 GW of new generation and storage resources with signed interconnection agreements in PG&E and SCE service territories; approximately 8.9 GW (~22%) are expected to be delayed due to transmission delays, with an additional 4.4 GW (~11%) at risk. PG&E's key delays stem from bundling dependencies (2.5 GW) and financing/design delays; SCE's from materials procurement (4.5 GW delayed, 2 GW at risk), bundling dependencies (4.4 GW), and unknown customer-initiated causes (3.7 GW). The CPUC recommended that transmission owners allocate more planning time for realistic in-service-date estimates, engage in proactive long-lead-material procurement, improve permitting-timeline data collection, and work with CAISO and state agencies to develop consistent metrics for high-impact project identification. Next steps include highlighting key issues through the 2026 Transmission Development Forum and state agency workshops on accelerating interconnection.

The CPUC's push for better scheduling, material procurement planning, and transparent high-impact-project tracking directly affects whether a hydro plant can reach its commercial-operation date and begin generating revenue.

documents.ai_summary: Constellation presented root-cause analysis of PJM's resource adequacy challenges at the July 29, 2026 Powering Reliability Through Market Design Workshop. The presentation identifies structural obstacles (doubled construction timelines, escalated capital costs, regulatory uncertainty, lack of revenue certainty) and exogenous drivers (unprecedented load growth from large data centers, political price sensitivity, continued retirements) as factors affecting resource viability. A specific example cited is the cost of relicensing a hydroelectric unit at $100 million or more. Constellation argues that PJM's capacity market design should allow scarcity prices to signal high-cost resources (including those facing opportunities to export capacity off-system) that their capacity is needed, and recommends hedging mechanisms to shield ratepayers from price volatility while preserving market-clearing price signals. The presentation also notes BRA (Base Residual Auction) clearing-price volatility, ranging from $28.92/MW-day (2024/25) to $329.17/MW-day (2026/27), and flags that load "riding" the spot market (rather than being hedged through bilateral transactions) undermines both revenue certainty for suppliers and public confidence.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro owners depend on the capacity market for revenue certainty and on scarcity-price signals to justify retaining aging units or investing in upgrades and relicensing. Constellation's argument that market design must preserve price discovery while adding hedging mechanisms directly affects how PJM would structure incentives for retention of existing hydro (including relicensing decisions at $100M+ cost) and competition for new capacity investment. The presentation's concern that out-of-market interventions (price caps, RMR bidding as price-takers) undercut both price signals and long-term adequacy is especially relevant to hydro, which is often a high-opportunity-cost use-limited resource susceptible to market-power mitigation and price-suppression rules; designing hedges that don't collapse the scarcity signal is central to maintaining hydro revenue.

documents.ai_summary: Toller Energy presents a framework for completing PJM's capacity-market evolution toward transparent long-term risk transfer. Similarly, bilateral contracting and long-term project finance — mechanisms the document argues have weakened — are principal hedging pathways for storage and conventional hydro owners seeking to lock in capacity revenue; restoration of transparent forward pricing would lower the risk premium they pay and improve their investability.

documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 11 (Energy and Ancillary Services Market Operations) is being revised effective April 1, 2026, per FERC Order ER26-846-000 and ER26-846-001, with changes to sections 10.2.2 and 10.2.3 governing Economic Load Response Regulation Only resources. The revision requires Curtailment Service Providers (CSPs) to identify when locations registering as Economic Load Response Regulation Only contain customers on Net Energy Metering with the ability to inject, and requires Electric Distribution Companies to review NEM-customer locations and confirm the ability to inject safely; if not confirmed by an EDC, PJM will deny the registration. The Markets and Reliability Committee voted on the changes on July 28, 2026, after a first read on June 24, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. The revision governs how demand-response and behind-the-meter resources (potentially including co-located solar or storage with demand) qualify for PJM's regulation service market. Expanding and clarifying eligibility pathways for distributed resources in regulation services can increase the supply of competing regulation products, which may pressure the price and utilization rate for hydro's regulation revenue. Conversely, if NEM injection creates operational or safety barriers that limit those resources' usability, the net effect on hydro's regulation share depends on how many locations are disqualified.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Reactive power control requirements for synchronous generators, including voltage regulation modes and D-curve definitions, directly affect how conventional hydropower plants must operate and what ancillary-service revenue they can realize; new NERC registration thresholds also affect compliance obligations for mid-sized hydro.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual M14D Revision 71 clarifies voltage and reactive-power control requirements for generators 20 MVA and above, establishing that only automatic voltage control mode (AVR controlling voltage) is acceptable without documented exception. The revision defines volt-var boundaries at ±32.87% of maximum MW output, specifies acceptable reactive-control range per MW output, and requires PJM approval for any deviation from automatic voltage mode. A three-party investigation process is established for reactive-control performance issues. The changes respond to NERC's May 15, 2026 lowering of IBR registration thresholds to 20 MVA (bringing mid-sized inverter-based resources under Category 2 GO registration) and PJM's stated concern about increasing low-voltage risks, exemplified by the 2025 Spain blackout in which insufficient synchronous-generator voltage support contributed to a major outage.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, conventional synchronous hydropower plants—especially large run-of-river and reservoir facilities—are among PJM's primary sources of dynamic voltage support and will be directly subject to these tightened automatic-voltage-control requirements and the new D-curve boundaries. Hydro owners operating in PJM must now ensure their AVR equipment is configured to automatic voltage mode unless they obtain explicit documented exemptions from both PJM and the transmission owner; plants already running in constant-MVAR or constant-power-factor mode will require engineering review and possible operational changes. The higher clarity on volt-var boundaries may also change how hydro operators bid reactive-power capability into PJM's voltage-schedule process, affecting both revenue opportunities and compliance risk if their equipment cannot meet the new boundaries.

documents.ai_summary: PJM has implemented a new Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) process as a parallel track to the standard interconnection queue for generators meeting three criteria: (1) written support from a Primary Siting Authority, (2) commercial operation within 36 months, and (3) at least 250 MW of Accredited UCAP. The EIT process compresses interconnection review into three phases—Application Review (~180 days), Study (~60 days), and Final Agreement Negotiation (~60 days)—operating outside but parallel to the PJM Cycle Adequacy Process to expedite state-sponsored generation projects. PJM filed EIT tariff revisions with FERC on April 9, 2026 (Docket No. ER26-1563) and submitted a Limited Effective Date Answer and Amendment on July 31, 2026. Manual 14H revisions to implement the EIT process were endorsed by the Planning Committee on June 24, 2026, and received first reading at the Markets and Reliability Committee on July 7, 2026, with final endorsement scheduled for July 28, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the 250 MW UCAP threshold and tight 36-month development timeline make the EIT track potentially accessible to larger run-of-river or peaking hydro plants and pumped-storage projects with state backing seeking to qualify for resource-adequacy accreditation faster than standard-queue timelines allow. The elimination of milestone-extension options (blocking the one-time postponement available in standard GIA processes) imposes stricter compliance discipline on expedited applicants, which would tighten capital and permitting schedules for hydro developers pursuing this path versus the standard process.

documents.ai_summary: PJM GDECS (Governing Document Enhancements Cleanup Series) April 2026 package proposes seventeen tariff revisions to Attachment DD (Reliability Pricing Model), Operating Agreement, and interconnection procedures. Key changes: (1) Capacity Storage Resources and Intermittent Resources must now offer as annual (not seasonal) into RPM Auctions, with the categorical must-offer exception removed per FERC 190 FERC ¶ 61,117 (2025); (2) Commercial aggregation of these resources limited to those granted additional winter Capacity Interconnection Rights; (3) UCAP definition revised to align with effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) analysis per Schedule 9.2; (4) Planned Generation Capacity Resources that clear an RPM Auction become Existing Generation Capacity Resources for subsequent Incremental Auctions in the same Delivery Year; (5) Mixed-Technology Facility definitions clarified for participation as single ELCC Resource or multiple stand-alone resources, with five-year modeling election periods. DER Capacity Aggregation Resources subject to MOPR Floor Offer Price and Market Seller Offer Cap per March 1, 2023 FERC Order (paragraph 87). Locational UCAP bilateral transactions now explicitly subject to Test Failure Charges under section 11B. Document appears on PJM MRC consent agenda for 2026-07-28 meeting; no comment deadline stated in excerpt.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities by name, but the revisions directly govern resource types to which hydro and PSH are subject or compete with. Removal of the must-offer categorical exception for Capacity Storage Resources and Intermittent Resources means PSH and conventional hydro's seasonal flexibility value faces heightened must-offer obligations for annual capacity commitments—affecting their auction bidding strategies and accreditation calculations. The ELCC-aligned UCAP definition will rebase how hydro's seasonal and peak-period capacity is accredited: owners will need to track effective load-carrying capability analysis rather than EFORd-based forced-outage rates, directly changing seasonal accreditation factors and thus capacity-market revenue. The aggregation limits and five-year modeling elections for mixed-technology facilities also matter if hydro co-locations with solar or battery storage are pursued. MOPR and Market Seller Offer Cap rules applying to DER aggregations set a pathway and precedent affecting how small hydro may participate in future Order 2222 aggregation pilots.

documents.ai_summary: PJM Legal presents 43 proposed clean-up, clarifications, and corrections to Tariff Parts VII through IX as part of the Interconnection Reform Process (IPRTF GDECS III), dated April 17, 2026. Changes span definitions in sections 300 and 400 (Application and Studies Agreement, Business Day, Cancellation Costs, Decision Points, Default, Eligible Customer, Merchant Network Upgrades, Merchant Transmission Provider); modifications to Generation Interconnection Agreement (GIA) form provisions in Part VII, Subpart D and Part VIII, Subpart C; clarifications to the GIA form in Part IX, Subpart B (including Energy Storage Resources specifications for maximum load capacity and state-of-charge); revisions to Wholesale Market Participation Agreement (WMPA) form in Part IX, Subpart C (as-built documentation, interconnection facilities capitalization, Energy Storage Resources sizing language, and Cancellation Cost responsibility); and one correction to Upgrade Construction Service Agreement (UCSA) form in Part IX, Subpart E (replacing 'Developer Party' with 'Upgrade Customer'). Most changes are grammar corrections, capitalization fixes, and clarifications; substantive additions include Energy Storage Resources language requiring maximum load capacity and state-of-charge specifications in WMPA and GIA forms (mimicking provisions across both agreement types). documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped-storage resources directly. However, it addresses the tariff definitions and agreement forms that govern how all generation, including hydro and storage facilities, interconnect to PJM's system and participate in wholesale markets. Most revisions are technical clean-ups, but three have strategic weight for storage-heavy operators: (1) the insertion of Energy Storage Resources specifications into the WMPA form—requiring documentation of maximum load capacity and maximum state-of-charge—signals that PJM is aligning participation templates across agreement types and may shape how PSH and battery resources model their physical and operational constraints in future interconnections; (2) the clarification of Cancellation Costs responsibility through revised Default definitions and WMPA Appendix 2 language affects how resource developers manage withdrawal risk and upgrade liability, a chronic pain point for use-limited resources; (3) the expansion of the Default definition to include Wholesale Market Participation Agreement, Engineering and Procurement Agreement, and Necessary Studies Agreement broadens the trigger for automatic termination and may tighten the compliance envelope for participants across the development lifecycle.

The tightening of the definition to require flexibility across all available schedules could reduce the ability of units with operational constraints (e.g., those that are flexible only on certain cost-based schedules) to claim LOC credits when curtailed, affecting the risk-reward calculus for committing inflexible capacity day-ahead.

documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes tariff changes to Sections 1.10.2 and 3.2.3 governing pool-scheduled resource selection and lost-opportunity-cost settlement. The revision explicitly carves out hydropower from pool-scheduling eligibility except for pumped-storage units scheduled via PJM's hydro optimization tool in the Day-ahead Market. Section 3.2.3(f-2) specifies that hydroelectric resources (pool-scheduled or self-scheduled) whose output is altered by PJM dispatch instructions due to transmission constraint or reliability issue shall be compensated for lost opportunity cost per sections 3.2.2(d) and 3.2.3A(f) as detailed in PJM Manuals. The document also establishes new Section 3.2.3(e-2) on Uplift Reform for flexible resources and Section 3.2.3(o) listing conditions under which resources are not assessed deviations in real-time settlement. The explicit reference to a 'hydro optimization tool' for Day-ahead scheduling of pumped-storage units suggests PJM is operationalizing a water-constrained commitment model, which could improve PSH scheduling but requires owners to understand the tool's inputs and constraints. The carve-out of run-of-river and conventional hydro from standard pool-scheduling rules underscores their non-dispatchable treatment in PJM's market design, whereas pumped storage is increasingly treated as a flexible, committable resource—a distinction with revenue implications for PSH owners choosing operating strategy.

documents.ai_summary: PJM's redlined tariff amendment to Attachment DD, Section 5.3, modifies the treatment of Generation Capacity Resources committed through Reliability Must Run Service Agreements or transmission-retention rate schedules. Resources that do not clear the Base Residual Auction but meet specified criteria—including obligation to operate throughout the Delivery Year and FERC acceptance of the rate schedule at least three months prior to planning-parameter posting—are deemed to submit a Sell Offer at $0/MW-Day for their full Accredited UCAP (up to Capacity Interconnection Rights) in the Base Residual Auction. The amendment extends these provisions through the 2028/2029 Delivery Year (unless extended by the Office of Interconnection and accepted by FERC). Additional UCAP accruing after Base Residual Auction posting is deemed to clear at $0/MW-Day in the Third Incremental Auction; any shortfall is sought through the same auction. Capacity revenues from these resources are credited to the Transmission Owner or zones assigned financial responsibility for reliability upgrades associated with the resource's deactivation. The revision establishes that such retained resources clear at $0/MW-Day (administratively set, not market-competitive), which locks out revenue through the auction mechanism and channels all capacity revenues to load in zones paying for transmission upgrades rather than to the resource owner. For a hydro or PSH facility retained under a transmission-reliability rate schedule, this means capacity-market revenue flows are predetermined and administratively controlled, not responsive to scarcity or demand-curve clearing. The through-2028/2029 sunset also creates scheduling risk for post-2029 operations if the provision is not extended.

documents.ai_summary: PJM presented revised tariff language for Part V (Generation Deactivation) at the 2026-07-28 Markets and Reliability Committee meeting. The revision establishes notice periods (12 months minimum prior to deactivation, with specified date windows), reliability-impact assessment timelines, and compensation mechanisms for units required to continue operating beyond their desired deactivation date. Generation owners continuing to operate receive either a monthly Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit with escalating multipliers (110% first year, 120% second year, 135% third year, 150% fourth year), or a cost-of-service recovery rate. Avoidable costs are calculated from operations and maintenance labor, administrative expenses, maintenance, variable expenses, taxes/fees/insurance, carrying charges, and corporate-level expenses incurred in the 12 months prior to the deactivation notice. Generators providing reactive supply and voltage control must satisfy additional Schedule 2 requirements. The document is a redline for first read with no voting scheduled in this excerpt.
documents.hydro_read_through: This deactivation framework directly affects hydro owner decisions to retire, mothball, or continue operating aging plants. The 12-month notice windows and reliability-impact assessment timelines create administrative hurdles for exit; the Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit formula—particularly the escalating multipliers and deduction of actual net revenues—will determine whether an owner can justify keeping a marginal unit online during transmission-upgrade periods. Run-of-river and storage hydro plants with low marginal operating costs may face artificially low avoidable-cost credits under the formula's net-revenue deduction. Conversely, hydro units critical to reactive support or voltage stability may be forced to execute must-run agreements and recover costs under the cost-of-service rate instead, shifting risk and limiting exit optionality.

The stated goal is to allow states and PJM to get ahead of reliability issues caused by state-law retirements, avoiding contentious RMRs and improving planning certainty. Conversely, if deactivation-driven scarcity would otherwise trigger RMRs on existing hydro units, this framework's success in avoiding RMRs reduces that revenue risk and cost for hydro operators in PJM.

documents.title: Item 03a – 1 Periodic Review Of Default CONE And Acr Values – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's periodic review of Default CONE and ACR values directly affects how use-limited resources like hydropower calculate their minimum offer prices and capacity-market mitigation thresholds under MOPR and MSOC rules.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is updating its Default Gross CONE (Cost of New Entry) and Gross ACR (Avoidable Cost Rate) values applicable for the 2030/2031 delivery year, used to set the floor offer price for planned and existing resources respectively under the Minimum Offer Price Rule and Market Seller Offer Cap. The update uses financial assumptions (55% debt ratio, 5.8% debt rate, 16.0% equity rate, 9.506% ATWACC, 27.7% tax rate, 2.2% inflation, 20-year asset life) from the approved 2025 Quadrennial Review and overnight capital and fixed O&M costs from EIA's 2026 Annual Energy Outlook. PJM retained The Brattle Group and Sargent & Lundy to analyze Gross ACR. Preliminary Gross CONE values for 2030/2031 range from $298/MW-day (Fixed Solar PV) to $4,403/MW-day (Nuclear). The tariff will be updated to remove bonus-depreciation escalation factors that are no longer accurate under current 100% bonus-depreciation tax law. The Markets and Reliability Committee is scheduled to take an advisory vote in August 2026 on the updated CONE and ACR values and tariff changes, with filings at FERC targeted for no later than October 1, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, Default ACR is the mechanism by which existing use-limited resources like conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities calculate their minimum offer caps in capacity auctions; updating the financial assumptions and reference-resource cost structure underlying ACR directly impacts what existing hydro/PSH units are permitted to bid. The ATWACC (9.506%), debt cost (5.8%), and equity return (16.0%) in these calculations flow through to the avoidable-cost mitigation screen, affecting whether a hydro owner's opportunity-cost-based offer will clear the MSOC floor or trigger default-offer requirements. The August MRC vote and October FERC filing are the hard deadlines for stakeholder commentary on these parameters.

documents.title: Item 03a – 2 Periodic Review Bonus Deprection Factor Tariff Change – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM is adjusting the Minimum Offer Price Rule (MOPR) floor offer prices for new resources using a bonus-depreciation factor that applies to multiple resource types including storage, which sets precedent for how energy-limited and storage resources are treated in capacity-market offer development — a direct cost-of-entry benchmark that hydro and PSH owners monitor for competitive positioning.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's tariff change adjusts the methodology for calculating default New Entry MOPR Floor Offer Prices, effective with the 2023/2024 Delivery Year Base Residual Auction. The Office of the Interconnection shall post preliminary estimates by 150 days prior to each auction's offer period. For combustion turbines and combined-cycle resources, PJM applies the same BLS Composite Index used for the Variable Resource Requirement Curve CONE adjustment; for all other resource types including solar, wind, and storage, a different BLS Producer Price Index component (Final Demand, Goods Less Food & Energy, Private Capital Equipment) is used. The adjusted gross costs are then modified by a factor of 1.022 for nuclear, coal, combustion turbine, and combined-cycle resources or 1.01 for solar, wind, and storage resource types to reflect annual changes in bonus depreciation under federal corporate tax law. Net energy and ancillary service revenues from the three most recent calendar years are subtracted to determine the final MOPR floor price.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the bonus-depreciation adjustment methodology PJM is adopting—specifically the 1.01 factor applied to 'solar, wind, and storage resource types'—will influence the entry-level thresholds used to screen competitive offers from storage resources including PSH. Since MOPR floors are set relative to these default costs of new entry, changes in how depreciation is factored into that benchmark affect the competitive bids PSH operators face and the reference levels against which their own offers are evaluated in capacity auctions.

documents.title: Item 03b – PJM Draft Avoidable Costs – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document establishes PJM's avoidable-cost methodology for 2026, which directly affects capacity-market revenue accreditation and retirement economics for hydro and pumped-storage resources, since avoidable costs are used to determine Must-Run and peaking-unit economics under FERC's resource-scarcity rules.
documents.ai_summary: The Brattle Group and Sargent & Lundy present PJM's 2026 draft Gross Avoidable Costs, a benchmark used to evaluate whether existing generation units should remain in service. The analysis covers eleven technology types (natural gas combined cycle, coal, nuclear, simple-cycle CT, solar, wind, steam oil & gas) at representative plant cost levels, plus a new battery energy storage system (BESS) category added for 2026 based on PJM's Fast Lane IX queue. Pumped storage and hydro are flagged for unit-specific treatment rather than generic representative costs, reflecting their heterogeneity. The document establishes representative plant avoidable costs in $/MW-day (e.g., natural gas CC at $133/MW-day vs. $113 in 2022, coal at $135 vs. $94), driven by plant aging, capacity factors, and configuration. Next steps include consolidating stakeholder feedback and presenting final avoidable costs at the PJM Market and Reliability Committee meeting scheduled for August 19, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although the document names hydro and pumped storage, it defers their cost treatment to unit-specific analysis rather than establishing representative benchmark costs as it does for dispatchable thermal resources. This reflects a structural gap in cost-screening methodologies applied to use-limited resources: seasonal and run-dependent hydro plants cannot be fairly evaluated against fixed daily avoidable costs that apply to plants with flexible dispatch. The deferral to unit-specific treatment means hydro owners will need to engage separately on their cost assumptions when plants approach retirement screens or resource-adequacy tests, rather than having transparent, RTO-endorsed benchmarks. The lack of a hydro-specific representative-cost band also means hydro may be at a procedural disadvantage in disputes over whether a unit's retirement threat is credible under FERC's scarcity-pricing and RMR rules.

documents.title: Item 04 – 1 Planning Parameter Deadlines – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM is changing the timing of Forecast Pool Requirement (FPR) and Installed Reserve Margin (IRM) calculations and posting deadlines that directly affect capacity-accreditation inputs (ELCC values) used to set hydro and storage resource capacity revenue in RPM auctions.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes to shift the Base Residual Auction (BRA) Planning Parameter due date from February 1 to March 1, and align final ELCC values posting with the third Incremental Auction (3rd IA) Planning Parameters deadline to resolve sequencing and timing pressure in the RPM planning-parameter process. The change addresses a constraint that PJM staff need approximately 12 weeks to complete FPR/IRM/ELCC analysis but currently have only 9 weeks between when key supply/demand data becomes available (mid-December) and the posting deadline. Per RAA Schedule 9.2, final ELCC Class Rating values must be posted no later than five months prior to the start of the target Delivery Year and communicated to Capacity Resource Providers. The MRC first read is scheduled for August 19, 2026, with same-day MC endorsement planned.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, PJM's planning-parameter timeline establishes when ELCC values—which determine the maximum unforced capacity that ELCC resources, including conventional hydro and most non-energy-limited storage, can offer in capacity auctions—are finalized and posted. By shifting the BRA deadline from February 1 to March 1 and synchronizing final ELCC posting with the 3rd IA, PJM is creating more time for technical review and reducing the risk of deadline misses that could delay accreditation results and compress bidding windows for the next delivery year's RPM auctions.

documents.title: Item 04 – 2 Planning Parameter Deadlines – Problem Statement
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's reform of RPM planning-parameter deadlines and Installed Reserve Margin / Forecast Pool Requirement calculation processes directly affects capacity-accreditation timing and UCAP computation for all resource types, including hydro and storage, touching both revenue-stream accreditation mechanics and compliance scheduling obligations.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes to reform RPM Planning Parameter deadlines starting with the 2030/31 delivery-year Base Residual Auction to address workload and timing pressures introduced by post-ER24-99 compliance requirements. The problem statement identifies three workflow challenges: (1) aligning the resource portfolio used in Installed Reserve Margin and Forecast Pool Requirement computation with expected RPM participation; (2) incorporating the most recent PJM Load Forecast into demand-side uncertainty analysis; and (3) expanding Effective Load Carrying Capability analysis and UCAP calculation to all resource types. PJM notes that timing between data availability and analysis-due deadlines is currently "at best tight and at worst unworkable," creating risk of missed mandated deadlines and insufficiently verified data if reforms are not made to Governing Documents.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or storage directly, but the three-part reform touches capacity-accreditation mechanics that govern all participating resources. Conventional hydro and pumped storage are accredited through the UCAP pathway; expanding ELCC analysis and UCAP calculation to all resource types means the deadline and verification pressures PJM is flagging will directly affect when and how hydro's seasonal capacity revenue is finalized. If deadlines slip or data-verification requirements remain unworkable, hydro owners face uncertainty in advance of the 2030/31 auction, and if the reforms compress timelines further, hydro (being weather- and hydrology-sensitive) may face tighter windows for seasonal and real-time availability data submission.

documents.title: Item 05a – 1 Manual 14h Ieee 2800 Revisions – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM is adopting IEEE 2800 interconnection standards for inverter-based resources, including frequency and voltage ride-through requirements; this establishes operating standards that apply to all resources interconnecting to the transmission system, directly affecting synchronous hydro units' compliance obligations and potentially their interconnection costs and timelines.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14H to adopt IEEE 2800-2022 interconnection requirements for inverter-based resources (IBRs) in Phase 1, covering definitions, ride-through specifications, and primary frequency response parameters. The revision creates new Section 9.15 and Attachment K, effective June 22, 2027, and applies to IBRs interconnecting with transmission and sub-transmission systems. Key technical parameters include enter-service voltage thresholds (0.9–1.05 p.u.), frequency ranges (58.8–60.12 Hz), and voltage ride-through times ranging from 0.16 to 1800 seconds depending on voltage magnitude; frequency disturbance ride-through requirements exclude fast frequency response. PJM Markets and Reliability Committee is scheduled for first read July 28, 2026, with Planning Committee first read May 8, 2026 and endorsement votes on June 2 and August 19, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention conventional hydropower or pumped-storage resources. However, the ride-through and frequency-response standards being adopted apply to the general category of synchronous and grid-forming resources interconnecting at the transmission level, which includes conventional hydro units. Hydro owners in PJM would need to assess whether existing units meet the mandated voltage and frequency ride-through envelope (particularly the 0.16–0.32 second ride-through times at very low voltages) and the primary frequency response droops and deadbands; units falling short could face retrofit costs or operational restrictions. The June 22, 2027 effective date would establish new technical requirements for any plant modifications or uprates proposed by that deadline.

documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 18 Revision 63 (effective September 1, 2026) updates the PJM Capacity Market operational procedures across multiple areas. Key changes include: periodic-review updates to the Variable Resource Requirement curve parameters and cost-of-new-entry (CONE) methodology for delivery years 2025/2026 through 2028/2029; new penalty frameworks for capacity-resource derates caused by reductions in accredited AUCAP (Accredited Unforced Capacity) factors; billing and credit-requirement changes for bilateral transactions; revisions to accommodate forecast-load adjustments through RPM and Fixed Resource Requirement processes; and updates to generation-resource classification (existing vs. planned), must-offer-exception administration, and aggregate-resource rules including seasonal capacity performance and DER-aggregation compliance. The manual addresses resource-performance assessments, settlement-charge calculations, load obligations, and locational reliability charges. The redline document reflects conforming changes and clarifications to existing tariff filings (ER26-455-000, ER25-783-000, ER25-2002, ER24-2447-003, ER26-980) that are in compliance phases with FERC.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, Manual 18 establishes the accreditation, capacity-pricing, and settlement rules that apply to all dispatchable and use-limited resources in PJM's capacity market. Conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities are subject to the ELCC-based accreditation mechanics, VRR-curve-driven clearing prices, seasonal capacity performance rules, and non-performance penalties documented here—changes to AUCAP derating, forced-outage treatment, and aggregate-resource rules materially affect hydro's accredited capacity and capacity revenue. The shift in VRR-curve parameters and CONE methodology for 2026/2027 forward also directly resets the demand curve that determines hydro's capacity clearing price, making the specific curve equations and reference-resource ELCC divisors (sections 3.3–3.4) critical revenue drivers.
