documents.title: Item 05c – 3 Manual 21b Periodic Review – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This periodic review of PJM Manual 21B updates the procedures for calculating ELCC accreditation and capacity ratings across all ELCC resource classes, including explicit definitions and testing requirements for Intermittent Hydropower Class and Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage, which directly affect hydro owners' capacity-market participation and revenue accreditation.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 21B Revision 06 (effective June 24, 2026) specifies the rules and procedures for determining generating capability and ELCC accreditation across all resource classes in the PJM capacity market. The manual defines two hydro-specific ELCC classes: Intermittent Hydropower Class (run-of-river resources that cannot appreciably store water) and Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage (resources that can capture and store incoming streamflow and exert material control over output—demonstrated by producing at least 110% of daily average power baseline for 4 hours during the four highest load hours of summer afternoons over a five-year rolling period). Existing Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage resources failing this evaluation may be reclassified as Intermittent Hydropower, though PJM may retain the prior classification for exceptional circumstances including "recreational and public safety factors, unit outages, locational market energy prices, ancillary market participation, and other exceptional operational factors or market factors." Testing requirements differ by class: Hydro with Non-Pumped Storage units must conduct one-hour contiguous capability verification tests (summer June 1–September 1, deadline September 20; winter December 1–March 1, deadline March 20), while Limited Duration Resources' test duration must equal their applicable ELCC Class characteristic duration. The manual also defines Hybrid Resource Classes (including combinations of storage with variable or unlimited resources) and Component DER frameworks for distributed energy resources, all subject to ELCC-based accreditation.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro owners' capacity-market accreditation and seasonal revenue now turn critically on ELCC class assignment. The material-control test for conventional (non-pumped) storage hydro—requiring 110% of daily average output for 4 hours in the four highest summer load hours over five rolling years—creates a measurable but stringent threshold; failure triggers reclassification to intermittent status and a steep loss of accredited MW. PJM's discretion to retain prior classification for "exceptional circumstances" including ancillary-market participation and market-driven operational constraints opens a compliance and advocacy pathway, but the burden is on the owner to document and request relief. Testing deadlines (September 20 summer, March 20 winter) and single-hour duration for conventional hydro are tighter than multi-hour Limited Duration Resources, reflecting the traditional assumption that hydro can ramp quickly; owners must plan annual test coordination with PJM Dispatch. Hybrid resource rules now formally accommodate co-located storage and variable resources at a single point of interconnection, expanding options for hydro owners seeking to blend storage or renewable capacity into a single market-accredited asset—a significant strategic opening if ELCC accreditation for hybrids is favorable.

documents.title: Item 06 – 2029 2030 BRA Fpr IRM Results – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's 2029/30 Capacity Accreditation determination directly affects how hydro and storage resources earn capacity revenue through ELCC ratings and FPR calculations.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Resource Adequacy Planning presented the 2029/30 BRA Installed Reserve Margin (IRM), Forecast Pool Requirement (FPR), and Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) results to the Markets and Reliability Committee on July 28, 2026. The 2029/30 BRA assumes FERC approval of PJM's proposal to extend RMR recognition to Brandon Shores units (1 and 2) and Wagner units (3 and 4) through 2030/31. Hydro Intermittent resources received a 35% ELCC rating (unchanged from 2028/29); Hydro With Non-Pumped Storage received accreditation credit for 1,945 MW of its 2,015 MW nameplate capacity. Storage resources saw ELCC rating changes: 4-hr Storage declined from 59% to 57%, 6-hr Storage from 68% to 67%, 8-hr Storage from 71% to 69%, and 10-hr Storage from 78% to 77%, driven by higher winter risk share. The FPR decreased from 0.9401 to 0.9248, and the UCAP Surplus margin compressed by 1,635 MW due to higher peak load forecast (up 5,963 MW ICAP) and higher winter extreme loads.
documents.hydro_read_through: The ELCC ratings directly determine what capacity credit hydro and storage resources receive in PJM's capacity auction, influencing their annual capacity revenue. Winter risk now dominates the seasonal adequacy picture—the LOLH winter share jumped from 60.5% to 77.4%—which systematically depresses accreditation for resources with weaker winter performance and benefits those that contribute in winter. Run-of-river (Hydro Intermittent) holds steady at 35%, but the compression in storage ratings and the widening winter-risk share signal a market tightening around seasonal scarcity where dispatchable hydro and pumped storage (if present) could gain strategic value, while variable hydro faces ongoing accreditation pressure in peak-risk hours.

documents.title: Item 07 – Storage As A Transmission Asset Informational Report – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Storage-as-transmission asset (SATA) design sets operational, metering, settlement, and transmission-planning rules that would establish precedent for storage participation models, which is directly applicable to pumped-storage hydropower considering deployment as a transmission asset rather than a market participant.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's Storage As Transmission Asset (SATA) Combined Package, developed over Phase 1 (2020–Planning Committee) and Phase 2 (August 2025–Operating Committee), prescribes design and operational rules for storage resources deployed to solve RTEP transmission violations. SATA assets operate automatically to discharge for intended violations and charge afterward (coordinated with PJM), use revenue-grade metering and telemetry matching energy-storage standards, operate at voltages studied in RTEP, and are excluded from the interconnection queue and PJM markets with no capacity value. Cost recovery occurs through Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits (TEC) in a separate sub-account. The combined Planning and Operations package moved to Markets and Reliability Committee in June 2026; MRC first read occurred in July 2026, with endorsement and FERC submission (conforming language changes) targeted for October–November 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage hydro directly. However, SATA framework and operational design—automatic discharge for identified transmission needs, state-of-charge telemetry, revenue-grade metering, exclusion from market participation, and TEC cost recovery—establish a participation pathway and settlement model that pumped-storage developers could adopt as an alternative to conventional energy-market participation. The design constrains SATA to transmission-only operation and forbids energy-market revenue, which trades off capacity-market and ancillary-service revenue for transmission-asset certainty; a PSH owner evaluating deployment would need to compare that trade against conventional merchant or resource-adequacy paths. The tariff and manual language under FERC review will set the template for how storage-as-transmission is metered and billed in PJM, affecting any PSH considering that role.

documents.title: 2026-07-28 PAC A07.0 2025 LTTP RFP – Preliminary Preferred Solution
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's selection of transmission solutions affecting Maine–New Hampshire and Surowiec–South transfer capability and onshore wind accommodation directly impacts interregional resource deliverability and scarcity pricing on interfaces where hydro exports compete; selection of preferred solution LTP A1 sets 2032–2035 timeline for new capacity that changes transmission constraints affecting hydro dispatch value and locational energy prices.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has selected LTP A1, led by Central Maine Power (an AC transmission project with $2.20B cost and Q4 2032 in-service date), as the preliminary preferred solution from six Longer-Term Proposals submitted in response to NESCOE's December 2024 request. The RFP required three capabilities by December 31, 2035: increase Maine–New Hampshire interface to ≥3,000 MW (LT-1), increase Surowiec–South interface to ≥3,200 MW (LT-2), and accommodate ≥1,200 MW of onshore wind in northern Maine at Pittsfield or alternate location (LT-3). LTP A1 passed all three objective tests (transfer analysis and wind accommodation energy/capacity standards); LTP A2 (also CMP-led AC, $2.14B, Q4 2032) performed identically. Four other proposals (B1, C1, D1, D2) were excluded for failing thermal, voltage, stability, or wind-accommodation criteria. LTP A1 benefits total $3,388.53M in 2025-present-value terms (2033–2052), primarily from production-cost and congestion savings ($1,420.43M), avoided capital cost ($1,301.97M), and avoided transmission investment ($694.42M), yielding a benefit-to-cost ratio exceeding 1.0 and establishing it as financially justified. The document flags potential adverse-impact issues (N-1 thermal overload in northern Maine, low voltages in Portland area, overduty circuit breakers at West Medway and Larrabee Road) that apply equally to A1 and A2. Next steps are not stated in the excerpt.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, transmission expansion on Maine–New Hampshire and Surowiec–South interfaces materially affects the scarcity-pricing and locational-revenue environment for all dispatchable resources on those interfaces, including conventional hydro and pumped-storage facilities competing to export during peak scarcity. The Q4 2032 in-service date for LTP A1 will increase transfer capacity precisely on the corridors where hydro-based exports encounter binding transmission constraints; earlier-than-expected relief of those constraints could reduce locational price adders that currently compensate for congestion, directly affecting the energy-market and possibly ancillary-services revenue of Northeast hydro owners. The parallel capacity-expansion modeling (which projects solar, wind, and battery buildout post-project) influences near-term market entry and retirement decisions by other resources, potentially crowding out or increasing dispatch volume for hydro depending on regional scarcity. NHA members in Maine or New England should monitor the adverse-impact issues (thermal overload, voltage, circuit-breaker duty) for their own facility constraints during 2033–2035 construction phases.

documents.title: Briefing on Spotlight Initiative - Price Formation Enhancements - Oct 2025

documents.ai_summary: CAISO staff briefing on the Spotlight Initiative—Price Formation Enhancements, presented to the WEM Governing Body on October 28, 2025. The briefing explains two foundational mechanisms: (1) BAA-level Market Power Mitigation (MPM), which detects and mitigates uncompetitive pricing when a balancing authority area becomes import-constrained and depends on a small number of suppliers; and (2) Scarcity Pricing, which allows prices to reflect the reliability value of reserves when available capacity is tight. The straw proposal discussed includes three BAA-level MPM changes: shift to a grouping approach testing connected BAAs together, include CAISO BAA in the test, and mitigate only pivotal suppliers to avoid unnecessary mitigation of fringe participants. For scarcity pricing, proposed changes include preserving scarcity signals to reflect opportunity cost of capacity from contingency reserves in the 5-minute market, triggering scarcity pricing for load-shedding events, and developing a comprehensive scarcity pricing design through stakeholder working groups. The briefing notes that CAISO will bring formal policy proposals to the WEM Governing Body and ISO Board of Governors for consideration in 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the price-formation mechanisms described directly shape how hydro's energy sales are valued in scarcity conditions and how its bids are treated under market power rules. Scarcity pricing's focus on opportunity cost of capacity and use of contingency reserves is particularly material for run-of-river and storage-constrained hydro, which face chronically imperfect pricing of their flexibility value; changes to how CAISO reflects reserve scarcity could significantly alter the energy prices hydro receives during tight conditions. BAA-level MPM changes that shift from individual-supplier tests to grouping approaches and pivot-supplier logic may reduce unnecessary mitigation of hydro bids in constrained zones, but the document does not specify how the revised framework treats use-limited resources or whether it alters the opportunity-cost reference-price methodology that has historically undervalued hydro's strategic value.

documents.title: Briefing on Spotlight Initiative - Price Formation Enhancements - Vitol Presentation - Oct 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Vitol's presentation directly addresses scarcity pricing and operating reserve demand curves (ORDC) as core mechanisms of energy price formation in CAISO, which govern how hydro's energy and reserve revenues are determined during shortage conditions—a foundational revenue stream for dispatchable resources.
documents.ai_summary: Vitol presented to CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements initiative on October 28, 2025, advocating for implementation of an enhanced operating reserve demand curve (ORDC) in both real-time and day-ahead markets. The proposal calls for scarcity pricing to reflect the reliability value of reserves using a Loss of Load Probability multiplied by Value of Lost Load (LOLP×VOLL) framework before reserve shortages occur, rather than only during load-shed events. Key design elements outlined include scarcity detection methodology (one-hour-ahead LOLP measurement), VOLL valuation based on customer data segmented by load class and outage duration, minimum contingency reserve thresholds, and reserve types to be included in the requirement. Vitol supports CAISO's initial proposal to ensure energy prices reflect shortage costs during involuntary load-shed events but argues that an enhanced ORDC would improve price signals ahead of shortages, enabling supply and demand response before constraints tighten.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or PSH, but it directly affects how dispatchable resources including conventional hydro are compensated for energy and reserve provision during tight system conditions. Enhanced scarcity pricing through LOLP×VOLL would raise energy prices more gradually and predictably as reserves tighten, creating higher and earlier price signals that reward hydro's ability to ramp quickly and sustain output. This contrasts with CAISO's current design where prices spike sharply only during declared emergencies; a continuous ORDC would increase hydro's revenue in the 10–100 hour window before physical shortages occur—precisely where hydro's marginal value is highest. The outcome depends on CAISO's adoption of this proposal and the VOLL magnitude it chooses; understating VOLL would limit the benefit.

documents.ai_summary: WPTF submits comments on CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements (PFE) initiative, criticizing the current proposal as insufficient to meet reliability objectives established in 2021 following the August 2020 blackout events. WPTF argues that the proposal delays meaningful price signals until scarcity is already occurring, rather than allowing prices to rise gradually as supply tightens, and contends that relying solely on future Flexible Ramping Product (FRP) and Ancillary Services (AS) enhancements risks another five-to-ten-year delay in developing robust scarcity pricing. WPTF also objects to CAISO's plan to apply BAA-level market power mitigation to the CAISO footprint absent forward-looking competitiveness analysis, arguing that such mitigation without counterbalancing robust scarcity pricing would artificially suppress prices during tight conditions when accurate pricing is essential to attract additional supply and maintain reliability. WPTF requests that the WEM Governing Body direct CAISO to fully develop a scarcity-pricing design with gradual price-rise mechanisms in the current PFE phase and to conduct a robust competitiveness study before implementing BAA-level mitigation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, scarcity pricing is a primary revenue driver for dispatchable resources during system stress, and gradual price signals as supply tightens would directly affect energy revenues for conventional hydro and the opportunity-cost basis for pumped-storage offer development. Conversely, BAA-level market power mitigation applied without offsetting scarcity-pricing enhancements could suppress the very high prices during tight periods when use-limited resources like hydro generate marginal value; hydro owners depend on those scarcity rents to justify investment and operation of flexible capacity. The five-year delay cited by WPTF in implementing robust scarcity pricing since 2020 also reflects a broader strategic risk—that lack of timely price signals extends the period during which hydro revenue adequacy depends on out-of-market mechanisms or capacity markets rather than energy markets themselves.

documents.ai_summary: Joint LSEs (CalCCA, Six Cities, NCPA, PG&E, SCE) filed comments opposing adoption of expansive scarcity-pricing revisions to CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) and Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) design, specifically rejecting Vitol's and WPTF's proposals to enhance scarcity pricing using Value of Lost Load (VOLL) methodology. documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage explicitly. If VOLL were adopted at the high levels cited from the MISO example, hydro with storage capability would benefit from higher scarcity events; if scarcity pricing remains moderate and uniform, hydro's revenue upside is lower but its market risk is more predictable and its investment case remains aligned with regional adequacy goals rather than peak-event windfall.

documents.ai_summary: Appian Way, an energy-trading firm, comments on CAISO's proposed CRR Enhancements Phase 1 tariff changes to explicitly authorize loop-flow modeling in the annual CRR (Congestion Revenue Rights) allocation process. Appian Way supports the loop-flow modeling itself, noting that the Simultaneous Feasibility Test cannot fulfill its intended purpose without it, but argues that CAISO staff has not adequately analyzed a deeper market-design problem: how much transfer capacity on congested paths (particularly Path 15) is consumed by external entities sourcing in the Desert Southwest, and whether the current allocation of CAISO transmission network usage between CAISO ratepayers and EDAM/Market+ participants is fair. Appian Way states that external loop flows "flow 40% over CAISO's transmission network" per CAISO staff analysis (December 11, 2025) and claims these flows "restrict CAISO ratepayers and market participants' ability to use the CAISO network through revenue inadequacy and reduced CRR allocation." The comment positions the issue at the intersection of CRR Enhancements, EDAM Congestion Revenue Allocation, and Western Markets Seams policy initiatives, and calls on CAISO staff to analyze historical usage patterns and propose a business solution for fair allocation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, loop flows and congestion revenue allocation are foundational to how western transmission scarcity is priced and allocated across generators. Reduced CRR allocations from improved loop-flow modeling could lower congestion revenues available to hydro operators selling into congested corridors (e.g., Pacific Northwest hydro exporting south on Path 15), while the underlying seams-governance question—how much transmission capacity CAISO hydro and external resources each consume—will shape whether future EDAM/Market+ designs favor or disadvantage hydro in interregional trading. The comment also surfaces a strategic risk: if external desert-southwest resources are consuming 40% of certain congested paths without commensurate transmission charges, CAISO ratepayers (including hydro) may face revenue dilution, making the allocation methodology a material issue for hydro operators evaluating long-run market participation in the integrated western market.

documents.title: Decision on Congestion Revenue Rights Enhancements Phase 1 - Presentation - Jul 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Congestion revenue rights (CRR) are financial instruments that hedge transmission congestion costs; changes to CRR modeling and revenue adequacy directly affect the value of transmission rights held by hydro and other generators, especially those in constrained areas.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO management proposes to expand the ISO's authority to model loop flows in the annual congestion revenue rights (CRR) process, effective for the 2027 annual CRR process. The proposal addresses revenue inadequacy in the CRR market by improving the accuracy of the CRR model to better align with power flows observed in the day-ahead market. A root-cause analysis identified three sources of CRR revenue inadequacy: missing power flow contributions from injections below the 2% shift factor threshold, loop flows consuming transmission capacity without contributing to congestion rent collection, and divergence between the CRR network model and the day-ahead market. Stakeholders expressed support for the proposed expansion of ISO authority, though they requested additional detail on the loop flow modeling approach to be provided through the annual CRR process. Phase 2 will continue discussions on auction efficiency, product definition, and additional revenue adequacy measures in Q3 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never mentions hydro specifically. However, CRRs are a primary financial hedge for generators—including hydro—that are exposed to transmission congestion costs, particularly in the California grid's constrained zones. Improving the accuracy of CRR modeling by capturing loop flows and correcting for missing power-flow contributions would reduce "revenue inadequacy" (the shortfall between modeled and actual congestion rents), directly increasing the value of CRR auctions to holders. Hydro generators with exposure to constrained interfaces would see improved hedging effectiveness and more accurate price signals if the model more closely tracks real power flows.

documents.ai_summary: The ROWE Board Selection Process and Formation Committee Update outlines the establishment of the Western Energy Markets Governing Body (ROWE) as a new regional organization that will assume sole authority over CAISO energy market rules through a three-part regulatory structure: an Integrated CAISO Tariff (under ROWE sole authority for market rules, CAISO sole authority for balancing/transmission), a ROWE Governance Tariff, and a CAISO-ROWE Coordination Agreement. documents.ai_summary: On May 1, 2026, CAISO launched the extended day-ahead market (EDAM) expanding to include PacificCorp East (PACE) and PacificCorp West (PACW) balancing areas. EDAM employs a temporary congestion revenue allocation methodology that allocates day-ahead congestion revenues to the balancing area where transmission rights were exercised, rather than where the constraint is located. In May, total EDAM congestion revenues were $39.9 million, with $38.2 million (96 percent) from constraints in the CAISO balancing area and $1.7 million (4 percent) from PACE; no congestion occurred in PACW. Congestion allocation to PacificCorp balancing areas totaled $1.34 million, with $36.9 million remaining in the CAISO balancing area. The document analyzes congestion patterns and reports that congestion revenue allocation to PAC was consistent with projections.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the EDAM congestion revenue allocation rule shown here directly affects how hydro resources monetize energy trades across the expanded footprint. Hydro owners exercising transmission rights or transacting between balancing areas will realize different revenue under this temporary allocation rule compared to what they would receive if congestion revenues stayed with constraint locations; the rule effectively shifts revenue flows based on where self-schedules are dispatched. Hydro owners in all three participating zones should understand this allocation mechanism, since their revenue from congestion relief or congestion contribution will depend on which balancing area incurs the transmission-rights cost, not necessarily where their generation physically congests the line.

documents.ai_summary: The WEM Governing Body Market Expert briefs on Comprehensive Scarcity Pricing (CSP) design for the Western Electricity Market, discussing how scarcity pricing increases electricity prices when supply is insufficient to meet load and reserve targets, thereby eliciting incremental supply and demand reductions. The document examines two competing approaches—an Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) linked to reserve deficiency, and a latent supply margin design that creates a price adder as available supply tightens—and notes that the CAISO had planned CSP discussion concurrently with incremental enhancements proposed in August 2025, but stated on July 2, 2026 it would "resume discussion of [comprehensive scarcity pricing] ... after the governance decision on current [scarcity pricing] changes." documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities. However, CSP design is directly relevant to hydro revenue: scarcity pricing mechanisms determine how much additional energy and reserve prices rise during physically constrained periods—the conditions when hydro's flexibility and stored energy command the highest marginal value. Hydro's participation in ancillary-services and reserve products under either ORDC or latent-supply-margin designs would depend on the co-optimization assumptions, reserve product definitions (10-minute vs. 30-minute), and whether scarcity prices flow through those products. The status statement (CSP discussion deferred pending governance decision on current changes) means hydro owners should monitor when that governance decision occurs and CSP re-enters the formal proposal stage.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO presented a spotlight briefing on the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) congestion revenue allocation Phase 2 initiative to the WEM Governing Body in June 2026. Phase 1 design, approved June 2025, allocated congestion revenues to the EDAM balancing area where congestion occurs and provided congestion hedges tied to firm transmission rights. Phase 2, launched December 2025, evaluates enhancements and long-term design to address potential self-scheduling incentives and asymmetry between CAISO and EDAM allocations. Three design concepts are under evaluation: (1) enhanced allocation based on cleared schedules, expanding eligibility beyond balanced self-schedules to economically bid and cleared schedules with reciprocal treatment for ISO balancing area; (2) historical baseline rights framework establishing historical transmission rights eligible for expanded congestion hedges; and (3) ongoing simultaneous feasibility framework using annual and monthly feasibility tests to assign financial entitlements to congestion revenues. Four stakeholder working groups met from December 2025 onward with an average of 117 attendees, producing 49 comments. Targeted milestones are Q4 2026–Q1 2027 for proposal development and Q2 2027 for WEM Governing Body decision presentation.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower directly. However, EDAM congestion revenue allocation is fundamental to hydro export economics in the Western market: congestion hedges allow hydro owners to recover transmission rights value when exporting from generation-rich to load-rich areas. The Phase 2 redesign—shifting from balanced self-schedule eligibility to economically bid schedules, and potentially using simultaneous feasibility or historical baseline frameworks—would change which hydro resources qualify for hedging and how much value they recover per MW of transmission right. Hydro operators participating in EDAM as either balancing-area resources or external participants depend on clarity around congestion-hedge rules to model inter-temporal dispatch value and transmission-dependent export strategies.

documents.title: NV Energy Perspective - Spotlight Briefing on Extended Day-Ahead Market Congestion Revenue Allocation - Jun 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NV Energy's perspectives on EDAM congestion-revenue allocation touch hydro's strategic options for market participation in the West — the design and implementation schedule directly affect EDAM go-live, which is a major governance choice for western hydro owners, and the treatment of OATT transmission rights and load-ratio-share allocation of congestion revenues affect how non-participating entities (including hydro) manage transmission costs and benefits.
documents.ai_summary: NV Energy presented its perspective on CAISO's Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Congestion Revenue Allocation Phase II design to the WEM Governing Body. NV Energy stated its core position: treat all OATT customers equally, hold them harmless from financial consequences of congestion costs from intra-day transmission schedule changes, and allocate congestion shortfalls or surpluses on a load-ratio share after firm transmission is protected. NV Energy expressed that the design and implementation schedule have material impact to EDAM go-live, requested CAISO analysis showing proposed congestion revenue allocation against current methodology under major upcoming transmission projects (Greenlink and SWIP-N), and stated preference for Option 1 as an incremental enhancement that captures congestion hedge for self-schedules and market awards without delaying EDAM tariff alignment or creating costly Grid Management Charge increases. NV Energy emphasized that the design must be implementable by existing and future EDAM Entities given limited vendor resources.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not directly address hydropower. However, EDAM participation and congestion-revenue treatment are strategic choices for western hydro owners joining the day-ahead market; the allocation methodology and implementation timeline affect how non-market-participating hydro entities (particularly those using OATT transmission) manage transmission-cost exposure and the financial incentives for or against EDAM accession. NV Energy's insistence on protecting OATT customers from congestion consequences of intra-day schedule changes and its preference for load-ratio allocation speaks to how transmission use and congestion revenues flow to entities that remain outside EDAM — a material consideration for hydro owners evaluating market membership.

documents.title: PacifiCorp Perspective - Spotlight Briefing on Extended Day-Ahead Market Congestion Revenue Allocation - Jun 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Congestion revenue allocation under EDAM directly affects how transmission-constrained hydro plants, which are use-limited and depend on congestion rent, can monetize their output and exercise transmission rights in the Western interconnection.
documents.ai_summary: PacifiCorp presents three design concepts for congestion revenue allocation (CRA) under the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM), evaluating their operational complexity, system-change requirements, feasibility timelines, and long-term durability. Concept #1 (enhancement to Phase 1, allocating congestion revenues for cleared balanced schedules) is recommended for continued exploration despite potential operational complexity. Concept #2 (historical baseline of entitlements) is not recommended as it does not reflect forward-looking system changes. Concept #3 (common simultaneous feasibility test for eligible OATT rights and CRRs) is recommended for continued exploration as a potential long-term solution but requires substantial additional analysis. PacifiCorp notes that CRA is not the only reason entities use self-schedules and calls for CAISO to evaluate options through a systems-impact lens, including mock simultaneous feasibility testing and analysis of congestion and revenue across the wider EDAM footprint and constraint interactions across balancing authority areas.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although the document does not mention hydro directly, congestion revenue allocation is critical to use-limited resources like conventional hydropower and pumped-storage plants, which earn congestion rent through transmission-constrained paths and depend on transmission-rights structures (CRRs and eligible OATT rights) to monetize their output. The design chosen for CRA—particularly whether it honors historical OATT rights, CAISO CRRs, or requires recalculation via simultaneous feasibility testing—will determine whether hydro owners retain or lose congestion revenues they currently collect, directly affecting project economics and revenue certainty in EDAM. This is especially material for PacifiCorp, itself a major hydro operator, as the outcome reshapes how congestion rents flow to use-limited generators across the Western footprint.

evidence.claim: Three design concepts for congestion revenue allocation under EDAM, with PacifiCorp recommending continued exploration of Concept #1 and #3 but not #2.
evidence.quote: Design Concept #1 – Enhancement to Phase 1 design, CRs allocated for cleared balanced schedules associated with eligible rights...PacifiCorp recommendation: Continue exploring...Design Concept #2 – Established historical baseline of CR entitlements for CRRs and eligible OATT rights...PacifiCorp recommendation: Do not move forward...Design Concept #3 – CR financial entitlements established for eligible OATT rights and CAISO CRRs based on a common SFT...PacifiCorp recommendation: Continue exploring

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: EDAM transmission pricing and congestion revenue allocation directly affect how all market participants—including hydropower as a dispatchable resource—pay for transmission use and recover revenues from it, with implications for cost shifts and strategic transmission planning.
documents.ai_summary: SCE presents a framework for allocating EDAM congestion revenue that treats CAISO-BAA and non-CAISO (OATT-based) BAAs differently. SCE proposes Option 3 ('Simultaneous Feasibility'), which would guarantee congestion-revenue backing only for transmission sales that are simultaneously feasible with all other EDAM transactions. Additional transmission sales would be allowed but without expectation of full EDAM congestion-revenue funding. SCE frames the change as preventing cost-shifts among EDAM transmission providers and creating a path for willing EDAM BAAs to migrate from OATT transmission contract rights to CAISO-style CRRs (Congestion Revenue Rights).
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower directly. However, EDAM congestion-revenue allocation affects all market participants' transmission-use costs and revenue recovery from transmission rights. Hydropower plants, particularly those in non-CAISO footprints joining EDAM, would face changes in how their transmission costs are calculated and how any transmission rights they hold are backed by congestion revenue. The shift toward physics-based transmission pricing rather than contract-right-based allocation could alter the locational signals and cost-recovery mechanisms that hydro operations depend on, especially for plants relying on existing transmission contract positions.

documents.title: Department of Market Monitoring Update - Jun 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This market-monitoring report directly evaluates EDAM operational performance in May 2026, including imbalance-reserve design and pricing that hydro supplies, residual unit commitment procurement and cost changes, and hydro's specific shares of upward and downward reserve schedules—all core revenue streams and market-design mechanisms affecting hydropower participation.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO Department of Market Monitoring reports on May 2026 EDAM operations covering California ISO, PacifiCorp East, and PacifiCorp West. Hydro resources contributed to imbalance reserve procurement: gas resources made up 43 percent of upward imbalance reserve schedules while hydro made up an unspecified share, and wind and solar combined made up 81 percent of downward imbalance reserve schedules. Average hourly reliability capacity up procured in May 2026 was around 1,500 MW (up from 900 MW in May 2025), with CAISO accounting for 93 percent; reliability capacity down averaged 470 MW. Total residual unit commitment costs in May 2026 were $13.5 million (14 percent above May 2025's $11.8 million). Weighted average residual unit commitment prices fell to $15/MWh in May 2026 from $17.50/MWh in May 2025 despite resource adequacy resources being permitted to bid above $0/MWh. Imbalance reserve prices remained low overall—less than $5/MWh in over 90 percent of hours in CAISO and PacifiCorp East, but above $5/MWh in 53 percent of hours in PacifiCorp West. Total imbalance reserve payments were $2.2 million upward and $1.6 million downward in May.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro's ramping and flexibility value is captured in imbalance-reserve procurement and pricing, shown here disaggregated by fuel type and hour. The document does not isolate hydro's share of upward imbalance reserve or explicitly state hydro's downward reserve contribution, but the comparison to solar and gas penetration (and the intra-day hourly variation peaking at solar-ramp hours 7–8 and 18–19) suggests hydro's dispatch flexibility is being called upon during high-uncertainty periods. The drop in residual unit commitment prices month-over-month, despite allowing RA resources to bid above zero, signals a shift in how scarcity is being priced in the expanded EDAM footprint; if hydro is accredited or participates as RA capacity, this price compression affects its guaranteed-revenue expectations. The transfer-limit constraints described (156–939 MW between balancing areas) also constrain hydro's ability to arbitrage or export across the EDAM region.

documents.title: Market Design Initiatives Update - Jun 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document covers CAISO market design initiatives affecting price formation, storage modeling, demand flexibility participation, congestion revenue allocation, and resource adequacy—all mechanisms that affect hydro and PSH revenue, compliance, and strategic options, particularly in the EDAM-inclusive West.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's June 2026 Market Design Initiatives Update covers eight active work streams under WEM Governing Body authority: (1) Commitment Cost Bidding Flexibility—revisiting 2018 changes to expand resource commitment-cost bidding with a market-power test, education workshops running Q1–Q3 with implementation timing TBD; (2) Demand and Distributed Energy Market Integration—designing aggregation rules, demand-flexibility models, reliability-triggered demand response, and real-time demand/pumped-load bidding, with Track 1 and Track 2 straw proposals posted in March and decisional authority with WEM Governing Body; (3) Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Congestion Revenue Allocation Phase 2—establishing long-term design and near-term enhancements, with Phase 2 started December 2025 and conceptual alternatives under evaluation as of April; (4) Intertie Schedule Modeling Enhancements—FERC approved tariff clarifications April 8 supporting transitional EDAM design, with monthly stakeholder workshops since March discussing modeling evolution and RA impacts; (5) Storage Design and Modeling—addressing outage management, uplift/default energy bids, state-of-charge management, and mixed-fuel/distribution-level resources, with second revised straw proposal on outage management posted May 2026 and June straw proposal targeting state-of-charge and default energy bids; (6) Price Formation Enhancements—two-track framework with Track 1 advancing near-term balancing-authority-area market-power mitigation and scarcity rules, and Track 2 developing comprehensive scarcity pricing, with revised straw proposal planned for June and March 3 spotlight briefing on scarcity pricing; (7) Resource Adequacy Design—Track 1 and 3A approved by FERC May 11, Track 2 straw proposal published May 12, covering loss-of-load-expectation modeling, planning-reserve-margin and counting-rule updates, outage/substitution reforms, visibility and backstop enhancements; (8) Congestion Revenue Rights (CRR) Enhancements—refining product definitions to align with hedging needs including time-of-use granularity and storage locations as sinks, with straw proposal on near-term auction-efficiency and revenue-adequacy improvements published June 1. Decisional classifications vary across primary WEM Governing Body authority, ISO Board authority, and TBD items, with implementation dates marked 'no sooner than' specified windows.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly, but addresses core mechanisms that affect conventional hydro and PSH revenue and dispatch: storage state-of-charge and default-energy-bid rules reshape PSH's ability to maintain economic flexibility; commitment-cost bidding and scarcity pricing changes redefine energy uplift and energy-bid treatment for all dispatchable resources including hydro; demand-flexibility and aggregation rules (including 'pumped load' bidding) create new competition for the flexibility product hydro traditionally dominates; EDAM intertie modeling and congestion-revenue allocation changes affect how Northwest hydro exports are priced and hedged; resource-adequacy and outage-management reforms shift how seasonal hydro availability is credited. The June-targeting state-of-charge straw proposal and commitment-cost workshop series are near-term items requiring owner attention; CRR storage-sink and time-of-use hedging updates directly affect PSH revenue certainty.

documents.ai_summary: GridLab consultant Ed Smeloff submits comments supporting CAISO's Draft 2025-2026 Transmission Plan and proposes a Granular Scenario Planning approach for future cycles to address concentrated load growth in specific grid locations. The proposal uses historical locational marginal price (LMP) data from CAISO's OASIS platform as a vulnerability filter, applies three load-growth scenarios to production-cost models to generate predictive shadow prices, and recommends a "least-regrets" decision matrix to prioritize non-wires alternatives, hybrid battery, or reconductoring investments based on whether congestion appears across all scenarios or only extreme cases. Smeloff recommends the Board support a Special Study of the Los Angeles Basin in the upcoming planning cycle to operationalize this framework through collaboration with the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never names hydropower. Hydro's high capital cost and low marginal cost make it chronically dependent on scarcity pricing at binding transmission interfaces; the extent to which CAISO's planning explicitly models future LMP risk at specific nodes, and whether it commits transmission solutions to alleviate high-shadow-price nodes, will reshape the set of locations where hydro generators can expect sustained margin in the decade ahead.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's 2025–2026 Transmission Plan proposes a policy-driven Trout Canyon–Lugo 500 kV line (approximately 180 miles, $1,270–$1,800 million, in-service June 1, 2035) to be competitively solicited under CAISO's non-incumbent-transmission-owner framework. The line interconnects at Great Lakes Water Authority's (GLW) Trout Canyon 500 kV substation (Clark County, NV) to Southern California Edison's Lugo 500 kV substation, with 70% series compensation and functional specifications for protection, ampacity (3,800 A continuous, 5,130 A emergency 30-min), and coordination with existing 500 kV transmission. Because the project directly expands interregional transmission capacity to the Nevada/California border (a critical hydro-export corridor) and uses competitive solicitation (allowing non-incumbent developers to own and operate major transfer paths), it reshapes the transmission-constrained deliverability of hydro and storage resources on both sides of the CAISO seam—particularly PSH and large reservoir hydro whose value depends on interregional pricing spread and transmission-congestion rents. The functional specifications (impedance, series-cap location, line reactors, protection) will influence the electrical characteristics of hydro dispatch and may create opportunities for storage-as-transmission or co-optimization of hydro ramping into constrained corridors. Competitive solicitation rules and in-service milestones are embedded in the plan approval process; no explicit member comment deadline is stated in this appendix, but the plan itself would typically face board action and stakeholder input windows.

documents.title: Decision on Consent Agenda - Attachment 2 - Apr 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ROWE start-up funding via cost-recovery tariff amendment establishes a new charge mechanism that will be allocated to all market participants, including Western hydro operators in CAISO, WEIM, and EDAM footprints, affecting settlement costs and potentially revenue adequacy in the expanded regional markets that hydro generators will depend on.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes a tariff amendment to establish a cost-recovery mechanism for Regional Organization for Western Energy (ROWE) start-up debt financing. The ROWE is a new independent entity that will assume governance responsibilities over regional energy markets operated by CAISO, with the goal of promoting broader participation in WEIM and EDAM and reducing electricity costs. Start-up costs are projected at $7–8 million, to be incurred from early 2026 through early 2028. The ISO would guarantee a commercial loan or line of credit not to exceed $8.5 million, with repayment scheduled to begin and end during 2028. The cost-recovery mechanism establishes two new settlement charges—a market services charge and a real-time dispatch charge—modeled on existing Grid Management Charge components, allocating 68% to market services and 32% to real-time dispatch. Based on 2026 forecasted volumes, combined charges would be less than 2 cents per MWh. The charges will be collected like other settlement charges and adjusted monthly beginning February 1, 2028. California utilities (PG&E, SDG&E, SCE, and Six Cities) and the CPUC Energy Division expressed concern that the day-ahead/real-time combined allocation could disproportionately affect California ratepayers and create inequitable outcomes for WEIM-only participants; Management rejected this position. The Western Energy Markets Governing Body is asked to approve the tariff amendment, and the ISO Board of Governors will consider it on its consent agenda at the April 30, 2026 meeting.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although the document does not name hydropower or pumped-storage facilities, conventional hydro operators in the Western Interconnection—particularly those in CAISO, WEIM, and EDAM—will face direct settlement impacts from this mechanism. The new ROWE charges will be allocated to all market participants based on their day-ahead and real-time market volumes, meaning every MWh of hydro generation and ancillary-service supply in the Western markets will carry a proportional portion of ROWE start-up debt service. For hydro owners, this is structurally a fixed cost per unit energy output (less than 2 cents per MWh) over the 2028 repayment window, reducing effective energy revenue and raising their all-in operational costs in those markets. The allocation methodology—blending day-ahead and real-time volumes—means hydro's contribution is weighted by its participation in both timeframes, a departure from pure real-time-only cost allocation that some participants opposed on equity grounds.

documents.title: Decision on Interconnection Process Enhancements 5.0 - Memo - Apr 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document modifies CAISO's interconnection queue process, deliverability allocation rules, and queue-management practices, which directly govern how generation projects including hydropower and storage facilities access transmission capacity and participate in resource adequacy and energy markets.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Board approved interconnection process enhancements (IPE 5.0) effective April 22, 2026, reforming the interconnection request intake process, deliverability allocation, and queue management. Key changes include: removal of corporate-sustainability attestation requirements for non-load-serving-entity projects; revision of the full-allocation election cap to the lesser of 50% of an LSE's resource-adequacy load or 500 megawatts; inclusion of distribution-system interconnection projects in cluster scoring and deliverability allocation; allowance for operational energy-only projects to seek deliverability after commercial operation; application of commercial-viability criteria to all projects (not just deliverable ones), with a one-time one-year safe harbor for projects lacking an executed power-purchase agreement; and process efficiencies including streamlining of affected-system studies, modification of commercial-readiness deposit timing, discontinuation of pre-application reports, and enabling alternate Vice Presidents to serve on the Executive Dispute Resolution Committee. Stakeholders expressed general support; a few larger LSEs objected to the 500 MW limit (which CAISO justified as the 95th percentile of service capacity for projects reaching commercial operation), and some stakeholders requested future exploration of allowing energy-only projects to fund network upgrades and to seek deliverability transfers. The ISO will monitor implementation during cluster 16 and consider additional enhancements in future initiatives.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities by name. However, the interconnection reforms are of direct concern to hydro owners because they govern how any generator—including hydro and storage projects—enters CAISO's queue and qualifies for deliverability status and capacity-market accreditation. The lowering of barriers to energy-only projects seeking deliverability post-operation, and the tightening of commercial-viability criteria with queue-withdrawal consequences, will affect how existing hydro and storage facilities manage queue positions if they face extensions or re-entry. The broadened inclusion of distribution-system projects in cluster scoring and deliverability allocation may also affect the competitive landscape for smaller hydroelectric and storage projects. Conversely, hydro's flexibility in supplying deliverable capacity is not addressed here; the document focuses on intake and allocation mechanics, not on how dispatchable resources are priced or accredited for their capabilities.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: EDAM design and tunable parameters (reserve products, storage state-of-charge envelope constraints, imbalance-reserve rampability limits) and congestion revenue allocation methodology directly affect storage resources' participation incentives, energy costs, and locational pricing signals — the revenue framework for all dispatchable resources including pumped storage.
documents.ai_summary: The Market Surveillance Committee briefing reports on CAISO's refinement of Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) ahead of Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) launch. Key findings: (1) DAME design limitations include a 30-minute rampability requirement for imbalance-reserve eligibility and state-of-charge "envelope constraint" complexities for storage resources that could limit supply and raise prices; (2) CAISO has proposed conservative adjustments to DAME implementation through summer 2026, including reductions in imbalance-reserve procurement levels (shifting from 2.5/97.5th to 10/90th percentile coverage) to manage uncertain price impacts; (3) the June 2025 Congestion Revenue Allocation (CRA) methodology masks loop-flow costs and creates perverse incentives favoring rigid self-scheduling over flexible market participation, with estimated monthly impacts of $2–$7 million on CAISO-PacifiCorp transactions; (4) a Phase 2 CRA revision is underway to address self-scheduling incentives and support economic bidding, with proposed flow-gate entitlements as a foundation for longer-term financial congestion-hedging design. MSC supports the cautious DAME rollout approach.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, the tunable parameters under review—especially the 30-minute rampability gate for imbalance reserves and state-of-charge envelope constraints on storage—set operational and revenue boundaries that would apply to any storage or flexible resource, including pumped-storage hydro. The CRA methodology change is material to all generators' locational incentives: by rebating congestion revenues to self-scheduled resources, it weakens the link between congestion prices and the costs actually paid, reducing the value of flexible market participation (which is how PSH typically maximizes revenue from spatial scarcity). Conversely, Phase 2 CRA work toward flow-gate entitlements could restore stronger nodal price signals and reduce penalties for energy-limited resources that manage dispatch to reflect true scarcity costs.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes tariff amendments to establish a cost recovery mechanism for the Regional Organization for Western Energy (ROWE) start-up debt financing. The ROWE is a new independent entity that will assume governance responsibilities over CAISO's regional markets, including WEIM and EDAM. Management proposes two new settlement charges—a market services charge (68% allocation) and a real-time dispatch charge (32% allocation)—mirroring existing Grid Management Charge allocation methodologies and assessed on all market participants in the ISO BAA and WEIM/EDAM footprints. The combined charges for loan repayment are projected at less than 2 cents per MWh based on 2026 forecasted volumes. California utilities (PG&E, SDG&E, SCE, Six Cities) and the CPUC Energy Division opposed the allocation methodology, arguing that day-ahead market charges disproportionately burden California ratepayers and create inequitable outcomes for WEIM-only participants, while Management argues the allocation is justified because day-ahead participants realize greater ROWE benefits. The WEM Governing Body approval is sought, with ISO Board of Governors consent required, conditioned on FERC acceptance of the tariff amendment. Rates will be calculated using estimated volumes and adjusted monthly starting February 1, 2028, with final rates posted in December 2027.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the per-MWh settlement charges proposed will apply to all generation resources in the ISO BAA and WEIM/EDAM footprints, including hydro operators. Because the allocation mirrors the Grid Management Charge methodology (68% to market services, 32% to real-time dispatch), hydro generators will be subject to these pass-through costs regardless of their participation mix; the allocation methodology and its fairness across day-ahead versus real-time participation is structurally the same issue utilities raised here, and hydro owners operating across both markets will bear the per-MWh burden starting in early 2028.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO presented the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) benefits methodology developed by a cooperative working group, with draft methodology published in Q1 2025, finalized in Q2 2026, and benefits estimation completed in Q3 2026 with quarterly reporting to begin. The methodology estimates economic benefits as the difference between no-EDAM and EDAM production costs across three components: energy production cost savings, imbalance reserve savings, and greenhouse gas market revenues. The document notes that due to complexities of hydro resource management, benefits will be estimated using default energy bids rather than settlement data, and CAISO will run both EDAM and counterfactual scenarios daily, provide monthly benefit estimates to each entity, and publish quarterly reports.

documents.title: Briefing on Day-Ahead Market Enhancements Configurable Parameters - Mar 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: DAME/EDAM implementation is setting configurable market parameters (reserve deployment factors, constraint multipliers, bid caps) that directly affect how imbalance reserves and ancillary services are priced and deployed — mechanisms central to hydro's revenue from flexibility and reserve provision in the day-ahead market.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO is tuning five configurable parameters for its Day-Ahead Market Enhancement (DAME) ahead of EDAM integration, with implementation staged through market simulation (Oct 2025–Jan 2026), parallel operations (Feb–Apr 2026), and post-go-live ramp-up. First-stage sensitivity analysis found significant impacts on imbalance reserve pricing and deployment from envelope multipliers (currently 85%) and reserve deployment factors (currently 100%), with results tuned during parallel operations before go-live. The ISO proposes a two-phase go-live strategy: Phase 1 at moderate settings to limit early impact, Phase 2 post-ramp-up with more robust configuration based on actual operational data.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not name hydropower or pumped storage. However, DAME's imbalance-reserve architecture and the parameters being tuned — multipliers on reserve envelopes, deployment factors, and bid caps — directly structure how quickly and at what price reserves are called and paid in the day-ahead market. Hydro's revenue from reserve supply depends on these prices and dispatch signals; aggressive multiplier and deployment-factor settings increase reserve activation rates and prices, while moderate settings compress them. The two-phase go-live with initial conservative settings followed by post-ramp operational tuning suggests the ISO expects significant learning curves in reserve-market behavior — changes to those parameters after go-live could substantially shift the revenue hydro realizes from the flexibility and reserves it supplies during the parallel and live periods.

documents.title: Department of Market Monitoring Update - Mar 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Market-monitoring report on WEIM price formation, generation mix, transfers, and resource adequacy trends directly relevant to hydro revenue and dispatch — hydro's role as a dominant supply source (22,120 MW average) and its interactions with solar, batteries, and load patterns affect pricing, congestion signals, and strategic positioning across Western markets.
documents.ai_summary: DMM report on WEIM market performance in 2025: 15-minute market prices averaged $34/MWh, down 14% from 2024 despite higher natural gas prices; regional variation was significant (PNW down 26%, Intermountain West down 16%, CA down 7%, Desert Southwest down 6%). Average hourly hydro generation was 22,120 MW, up about 920 MW from 2024; natural gas averaged 23,110 MW, down 1,900 MW; solar reached 10,410 MW. Battery capacity grew to 25,600 MW (+42% YoY), with net battery discharge during evening hours (18–23) up 2,540 MW, displacing natural gas generation. Transfer constraint congestion on WEIM paths decreased: Pacific Northwest impact down $4.28/MWh, Intermountain West down $2.59/MWh. California GHG compliance costs remained the largest driver of regional price differences. Total WEIM system load was nearly flat year-over-year at 78.3 GW, but regional load shifted: CA down 2% (concentrated in solar and evening peak hours), while PNW, Intermountain West, and Desert Southwest all grew slightly. WEIM transfers averaged 4,480 MW (up 100 MW), with mid-day exports from CAISO and evening imports to serve peak load.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro's average output (22,120 MW) remains the WEIM's second-largest fuel source, but the document reveals two structural headwinds: battery growth (42% YoY to 25,600 MW) is now systematically capturing mid-day solar surplus and displacing evening gas generation, which pressures the high-value evening peak market where hydro has historically commanded premium prices. Second, declining transfer congestion on key WEIM paths ($4–$6/MWh improvement) reduces the scarcity premium hydro could earn when transmission-constrained; lower PNW prices (−26% YoY) suggest reduced scarcity in hydro-rich regions. Together, these trends compress the value stack for existing hydro — the report does not address seasonal energy adequacy or drought/water conditions, which remain critical unknowns for hydro positioning.

documents.title: Policy Initiatives Update - Mar 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This policy update addresses multiple market-design mechanisms affecting hydro and storage revenue: commitment-cost bidding and mitigation for use-limited resources; storage design encompassing uplift, default energy bids, and state-of-charge management; EDAM congestion-revenue allocation; price-formation scarcity and fast-start rules; and capacity/resource-adequacy accreditation — all core axes for hydro and PSH operators in the CAISO footprint.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's WEM Governing Body is advancing six policy initiatives affecting hydro and storage participation in 2026. Commitment-cost bidding flexibility, approved in 2018 but not yet filed with FERC, will be implemented or revised to address market-power mitigation for resources offering commitment costs; policy development with stakeholders is underway in 2026 with decisional classification TBD. Storage design and modeling encompasses four topic groups: outage management (policy development in Q1–Q2, implementation enhancements Q3–Q4), uplift and default-energy-bid treatment (policy development Q1–Q2, decision Q3–Q4), state-of-charge management (policy development Q1–Q2), and mixed-fuel and distribution-level resources (policy development Q1–Q2). EDAM congestion-revenue allocation Phase 2 launched in December 2025 and focuses on long-term durable design and near-term enhancements, with decision expected Q4 2026. Price-formation enhancements on scarcity pricing and market-power mitigation are scheduled for policy development Q1–Q2 and decision Q4 2026; fast-start pricing is postponed. Intertie scheduling and modeling on CAISO balancing-area interties will be addressed in a new stakeholder process launching March 2026. Resource adequacy tracks are advancing: Track 1 (modeling and default rules) approved for implementation; Track 2 (outage, substitution, and performance incentives) in policy development with decision Q3–Q4; and Track 3 (visibility and backstop reform) split between implementation (3A) and policy development (3B). Congestion revenue rights enhancements on product definition and revenue adequacy are under development, with an initial straw proposal expected to move to ISO Board decision.
documents.hydro_read_through: Although the document does not name hydro or pumped storage, it directly governs several critical revenue and operating rules. Commitment-cost bidding flexibility directly affects how use-limited resources (the canonical case for which is conventional hydro and pumped-storage generators) can recover their minimum-generation and start-up costs and how market-power tests apply to those offers — a long-standing source of revenue uncertainty for hydro. Storage design and modeling, particularly the uplift and default-energy-bid topic group, sets the framework for how PSH (and eventually hydro) costs are recovered and how their bids are treated in commitment and dispatch — a principal pain point for use-limited resource operators. EDAM congestion-revenue allocation Phase 2 determines how PSH and conventional hydro can hedge their wheeling and congestion exposure in the multistate market. Scarcity-pricing and market-power-mitigation policy shapes whether hydro's high marginal-cost periods trigger scarcity-signal pricing or are suppressed by mitigation rules, affecting both energy revenue and the incentive to maintain reliability flexibility. Resource-adequacy outage and substitution processes and performance-incentive design will determine how forced and planned outages are accredited and penalized, influencing how PSH and conventional hydro participate in capacity markets and how their availability is measured.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's 2026 budget sets the Grid Management Charges that all market participants, including hydropower and storage resources, pay to CAISO, and documents rate reductions driven by EDAM volumes and market design changes affecting energy market pricing and access.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's 2026 Grid Management Charge (GMC) revenue requirement is $249.9 million, up 5% from 2025, driven by a $14.3 million increase in Operations & Maintenance spending (primarily new EDAM-supporting positions, SaaS costs, and telecom expenses), while the project budget of $26 million will be funded from existing capital reserves rather than new cash-funded capital. Market Services and System Operations Real-Time Dispatch rates are projected to decrease in 2026 due to higher day-ahead volumes from EDAM launch, despite overall revenue requirement growth: Market Services Charge drops from $0.1615 to $0.1416 per MWh, System Operations Real-Time Dispatch Charge falls from $0.1122 to $0.0901 per MWh, and WEIM Market Services and System Operations rates also decrease (from $0.1042 to $0.0913 and $0.1004 to $0.0901 per MWh respectively). O&M budget increases include 13 additional headcount (to 790 total), with the primary driver being EDAM operations and supporting groups in System Operations (+9) and Market Design and Analysis (+3). The 2026 operating cost reserve adjustment of $3.9 million credit reflects favorable 2024 operations. Other revenues decline $17.4 million, principally because WEIM administrative charges shift from $18.4 million to $5.3 million due to EDAM rate design changes approved in the 2023 Cost-of-Service Study, and the phase-out of Nodal Pricing Model revenue from PacifiCorp's May 2026 EDAM entry.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, CAISO's GMC rates fund all ISO operations and directly affect dispatch signals and real-time market outcomes that influence hydro energy revenue and flexibility pricing. The projected decrease in Market Services and Real-Time Dispatch charges per MWh, driven by EDAM volume growth, signals lower administrative cost recovery per unit of market activity — a potential benefit to high-volume market participants like hydro. The $7 million intermittent-resource forecasting fee revenue (collected from wind and solar generators but absent from hydro) shows CAISO's reliance on variable-resource user fees rather than broad GMC spreads, which can affect how cost allocation evolves as more variable resources enter the market and hydro's accreditation and reserve-provision roles shift. The significant EDAM-related spending increases (new positions, system development, rate design shifts away from WEIM's legacy model) suggest CAISO is restructuring how it prices market access and grid services; hydro owners should monitor whether future rate design changes will affect ancillary-service or ramping-product revenue as EDAM matures.

documents.ai_summary: The Energy Authority (TEA) comments on CAISO's Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) intertie scheduling framework and tariff clarifications for EDAM go-live on May 1, 2026. SP-Tie versus GAP-Tie modeling affects whether existing forward-market conventions can accommodate large scheduled transfers (typical for hydro-rich footprints moving output to load centers), and congestion-reversal and NETC timing rules reshape the margin available on otherwise economic trades. A hydro operator wheeling power daily across multiple BAAs, as TEA's description suggests its clients do, would face material changes to transaction efficiency and economic exposure depending on which scheduling framework CAISO adopts.

documents.title: Joint Public Comment Letter - Briefing on Policy Roadmap - Dec 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Transmission Access Charge (TAC) structure reform would reshape how transmission costs are allocated across users and resource types; cost-allocation changes drive revenue distribution between generators with different locational and demand profiles, directly affecting where hydro and other resources earn margins.
documents.ai_summary: California Department of Water Resources, Bay Area Municipal Transmission Group, and State Water Contractors request that CAISO Board of Governors revive the Transmission Access Charge (TAC) Structure Review initiative. The TAC review was developed 2016–2018 and produced a Draft Final Proposal in 2018, but was shelved to focus on EDAM development. Commenters argue the current volumetric-only TAC approach fails to reflect cost causation and system utilization, and that the proposal aligns with CAISO's Resource Adequacy obligations and California's load-flexibility and climate goals. They note that MISO, SPP, NYISO, ERCOT, ISO-NE, and PJM already factor coincident peak demand in transmission-charge allocation. CAISO staff dismissed the initiative at the September 25, 2025 Transmission Planning Process stakeholder meeting, citing stabilized behind-the-meter solar levels. Commenters request a stakeholder process in 2026 to evaluate adjustments to the 2018 recommendations and cite the Sector Sponsor Pilot Program as an alternative venue.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, transmission cost allocation fundamentally affects revenue by changing the geographic and temporal incentives embedded in charges that hydro and other generators face. A shift from purely volumetric charges to one reflecting coincident peak demand and cost causation would alter the locational and temporal value of energy delivery, potentially raising or lowering the effective price hydro receives depending on its generation profile and network position. Whether this favors or penalizes hydro depends on how the coincident-peak methodology treats seasonal, run-of-river, and storage-capable resources—details the document does not address.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO management briefed the Board of Governors and WEM Governing Body on tariff revisions required to support Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) and Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) launch. The revisions address intertie scheduling and modeling rules: at ISO balancing area interties with non-EDAM areas, current intertie scheduling and modeling approaches are retained; at EDAM Entity balancing area interties, generation aggregation point modeling continues consistent with WEIM design. Resource adequacy rules are aligned to allow system resources at ISO balancing area interties that are transfer locations with EDAM areas to bid at resource locations, with transitional provisions allowing resource adequacy imports into the ISO balancing area not sourced in an EDAM area to bid at an ISO intertie that is also an EDAM transfer location. Additional revisions clarify congestion revenue rights funding, DAME/EDAM design ambiguities, and provide day-ahead contingency analysis tools to EDAM entities. FERC tariff filing is scheduled for Q1 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not directly name hydropower or storage resources. However, the revisions to intertie scheduling, aggregation point modeling, and resource adequacy import bidding rules directly affect how hydro and storage resources monetize multi-balancing-area transactions and recover scarcity rents from congestion—a primary revenue stream for western hydro exports and storage resources participating across the EDAM footprint. The transitional resource adequacy provisions that permit non-EDAM imports to bid at ISO interties are particularly material for hydro operators managing resource adequacy positions across market seams.

documents.title: Briefing on Extended Day-Ahead Market and Day-Ahead Market Enhancements Implementation Details and Associated Tariff Revisions - Memo - Dec 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: EDAM/WEIM implementation tariff changes affecting intertie modeling, resource adequacy scheduling, and congestion-revenue settlement — core market-design mechanisms that alter how external resources and imports participate in California's day-ahead market and interact with transmission pricing and capacity accreditation.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO management is filing tariff revisions in early 2026 to clarify EDAM (Extended Day-Ahead Market) and DAME (Day-Ahead Market Enhancements) implementation details ahead of the May 1, 2026 launch. Key changes include: (1) transitional intertie modeling at ISO balancing-area scheduling points will continue modeling injections at the scheduling point itself rather than aggregate generation locations, preserving existing commercial arrangements while CAISO works with stakeholders on future transitions; (2) resource adequacy imports at EDAM transfer locations will be subject to new reassignment rules allowing unspecified system resources sourced from EDAM areas to bid capacity; (3) congestion-revenue-rights (CRR) funding from EDAM constraints will be clarified to zero dollars at EDAM start, with revenue instead allocated to EDAM balancing authorities; and (4) technical clarifications on imbalance-reserve charging, firm transmission service availability, and day-ahead contingency analysis tools for EDAM operators. The revisions received mixed stakeholder feedback during November–December 2025 workshops, with some stakeholders opposing intertie modeling and resource adequacy scheduling requirements; management's proposed revisions represent a compromise to preserve current ISO intertie practices on a transitional basis.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro or pumped-storage resources. However, EDAM's intertie modeling and resource-adequacy-import rules are directly material to how dispatchable external resources—including hydro-based system resources from neighboring balancing areas—can participate in CAISO's day-ahead market and reserve their transmission capacity to support day-ahead dispatch and RA import obligations. The transitional preservation of current ISO intertie modeling (rather than aggregation) protects existing commercial pathways for out-of-state system resources to compete in CAISO's market; any future shift to aggregation modeling could alter the locational granularity and congestion signals that external generation (hydro included) faces when bidding into California. Additionally, the CRR revenue treatment (allocating parallel-flow congestion to EDAM balancing authorities rather than the ISO) affects the overall congestion-cost landscape and uplift allocation that load-serving entities pass through or absorb, influencing the competitiveness of external versus internal resources.

documents.title: Market Surveillance Committee Update - Dec 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The Market Surveillance Committee addresses gas resource cost-recovery mechanisms and offer-price flexibility in EDAM participation; these are precedent for how use-limited and dispatchable resources generally (including hydro) manage cost-recovery and bidding, and the MSC's critique of mitigation design and market-power testing extends to the reference-level framework that governs hydro's default-energy-bid calculations.
documents.ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issued a formal Opinion on December 12, 2025, on the ISO's Gas Resource Management initiative's Final Proposal. The Opinion addresses three enhancements: (1) changes to reference-level calculations for gas-fired generators with high fuel-cost variability, permitting greater offer-price flexibility in EDAM conditioned on ISO evaluation of historical cost variation; (2) additional rules for after-the-fact gas-cost recovery during supply disruptions; and (3) improvements to advisory market runs to provide day D+2 fuel-procurement forecasts within gas nomination timelines. The MSC supports these changes if implementation costs are not significant, but flags ongoing concerns: complexity of the Reference Level Change Request process, inability to account for fuel-switching costs, imperfect cost recovery allocations that shift costs to balancing-area loads and exports, and the absence of a supplier market-power test for commitment-cost caps, which the MSC characterizes as 'overdue' and calls for resolution 'on a fast track' in a stakeholder process the ISO committed to hold in the coming year.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro directly. However, the MSC's critique of the reference-level framework and offer-price flexibility mechanics applies to any dispatchable or use-limited resource subject to mitigation rules. The MSC emphasizes that blanket commitment-cost mitigation applied to units without market power can create inefficient constraints, whereas insufficient flexibility for legitimate cost management may deter market participation — both problems afflict hydro operators under existing EDAM mitigation design. The MSC's call for a 'workable test for market power in commitment cost' and its acknowledgment that 'the flexibility offered in this proposal may provide units that truly possess market power with overly generous offer bounds' foreshadow potential redesign of mitigation reference levels, a foundational revenue mechanism for use-limited resources including hydro.
