documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document examines market power mitigation rules applied to gas-fired generators in CAISO and EDAM markets, particularly the capping of commitment costs and default energy bids—mechanisms that set precedent for how use-limited resources (including pumped-storage hydro) are mitigated, and it addresses gas-cost recovery frameworks and offer-price flexibility that directly parallel storage participation design debates.
documents.ai_summary: The Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO issued a final opinion in December 2025 on the Gas Resource Management (GRM) proposal, examining how CAISO's mitigation of commitment-cost and energy-offer caps affects gas-fired resource participation in EDAM (Extended Day-Ahead Market), which launches in 2026. The opinion identifies four core challenges: enabling EDAM participants to reflect current gas costs in offer prices given morning-market gas purchasing deadlines, providing after-the-fact cost recovery when afternoon gas markets force higher purchases, improving day-ahead schedule forecasts (D+2) to inform morning gas procurements, and preventing locational market power abuse. The MSC finds that existing Reference Level Change Request (RLCR) processes are underused by Western EIM entities due to tight 8 a.m. submission deadlines, complex SIBR interface requirements, and poor approval rates (only 8 of 72 manual requests approved since 2021); supports proposed improvements to RLCR and after-the-fact recovery mechanisms as long as implementation costs remain low; but expresses deep concern that absent a market-power test for commitment-cost caps, all gas units continue receiving blanket mitigation regardless of market position, creating both inefficient suppression of competitive offers and potential over-generous bounds for units with genuine market power. On D+2 forecasts, the MSC concludes that historical data show considerable day-to-day error in CAISO's forecasts, and questions whether the CAISO will achieve sufficient accuracy at the individual balancing-area level before EDAM go-live to support morning-market gas purchasing decisions, particularly on days with volatile gas prices or when supporting EDAM exports. The opinion recommends treating D+2 forecasts as unreliable at launch and ensuring EDAM participants retain offer-price flexibility to manage gas-market risk; highlights that cost-recovery allocations would shift unrecovered afternoon-market gas losses onto balancing-area load rather than the exporting resource; and calls for developing a workable market-power test for commitment costs as a high priority.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not address hydropower or pumped-storage hydro directly. However, it examines the foundational market-power mitigation and cost-recovery frameworks that govern how use-limited resources are constrained in offer formation and whether their actual costs can be recovered when system schedules exceed prior expectations—the same category of rules that shape pumped-storage participation and accreditation in CAISO and EDAM. The MSC's core finding—that blanket commitment-cost caps applied without a market-power test simultaneously suppress competitive offers from resources lacking market power while potentially tolerating inflated offers from those with power—has immediate relevance to how storage resources accreditation, dispatch incentives, and cost recovery would be designed under parallel EDAM frameworks. The opinion also surfaces the tension between requiring resources to forecast operating costs far in advance (8 a.m. for day-ahead market) and the market's inability to reliably forecast dispatch schedules and prices days ahead—a problem that applies equally to any dispatchable resource, including storage, attempting to manage its state-of-charge and charging cost in a co-optimized day-ahead-plus-real-time market design.

documents.ai_summary: The CAISO Department of Market Monitoring (DMM) supports Management's proposed enhancements to gas-resource cost recovery and bidding flexibility in CAISO, WEIM, and the upcoming extended day-ahead market (EDAM). The package includes: (1) more flexible options for determining gas cost inputs in energy bid mitigation and commitment-cost bids; (2) expanded after-the-fact cost recovery for physical supply disruptions occurring after the 8 a.m. day-ahead bidding deadline; (3) changes to two-day-ahead advisory market runs to improve fuel-procurement forecasts; and (4) gas nomograms to manage system limitations. documents.ai_summary: Middle River Power comments on CAISO's Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design (RAMPD) Track 1 initiative, submitted October 23, 2025 to the CAISO Board of Governors. MRP supports CAISO's effort to modernize default qualifying capacity (QC) methodologies and planning reserve margin (PRM) but disputes the final Unforced Capacity (UCAP) proposal, which includes all outages except those caused by transmission constraints or force majeure in the UCAP calculation. MRP contends that certain outage types—specifically fuel insufficiency due to gas-pipeline maintenance and short-notice opportunity outages approved by CAISO operators—fall outside generator management control and should be excluded from UCAP calculations, particularly where no substitute capacity is required. MRP urges the Board to modify the UCAP proposal to exclude outage types that are both beyond management control and currently exempt from substitute-capacity requirements.

The dispute over outage inclusion affects how forced outages and operational unavailability reduce a hydro plant's credited capacity; hydropower operators typically have limited control over some outage types (e.g., reservoir conditions, transmission-system constraints, operator curtailments) and would benefit if CAISO excludes outages beyond their control from the accreditation floor. The treatment of opportunity outages is especially material for hydropower, which is routinely curtailed or asked to hold water for grid reliability; if such curtailments are treated as plant unavailability rather than system-requested events, seasonal and annual accreditation will be suppressed.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO is updating its default resource adequacy qualifying-capacity criteria and planning-reserve-margin rules, with specific new accreditation methodologies for dispatchable hydro, run-of-river hydro, and pumped-storage hydroelectric resources that directly affect how their capacity is credited toward ISO resource adequacy requirements and thus their participation revenue.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Board of Governors voted in October 2025 to update the ISO's default resource adequacy rules (last revised in 2006) to modernize qualifying-capacity criteria and planning-reserve-margin methodology. The proposal replaces one-size-fits-all accreditation with differentiated approaches: dispatchable hydro and run-of-river hydro will now be accredited using Average Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) based on forced outage rates and generation during critical periods respectively; pumped-storage hydroelectric resources will use Unforced Capacity (UCAP) calculated from three years of historic outage data (Winter: November–April; Summer: May–October). The ISO will conduct an annual transparent process to establish values, with stakeholders (including local regulatory authorities such as CPUC, Northern California Power Agency, and Six Cities) able to adopt these defaults or set their own methodologies. The Board authorized Management to file tariff amendments with FERC. Concurrent Track 2 and Track 3 efforts will address resource adequacy availability incentives and other related provisions.
documents.hydro_read_through: Conventional hydro owners face a material shift in capacity accreditation. The shift from historic net-dependable-capacity (NERC GADS) to average ELCC for dispatchable hydro and to ELCC based on critical-period generation for run-of-river hydro changes how much capacity a plant can offer into the market; the values will now reflect dynamic system conditions and the resource's actual contribution to meeting peak needs during scarcity events, rather than nameplate or historical-average metrics. Pumped-storage operators benefit from direct UCAP accreditation (a more straightforward outage-rate adjustment) rather than being bundled with thermal or nuclear. Annual recalculation introduces some uncertainty for multi-year revenue planning, but the transparent modeling process and CPUC coordination create opportunity to influence methodology design. The new framework is designed to align with CPUC's pending UCAP framework for 2028 implementation.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design (RAMPD) Initiative Track 1 establishes default qualifying capacity (QC) criteria and planning reserve margin (PRM) rules for California's resource adequacy program. documents.ai_summary: The California ISO Department of Market Monitoring (DMM) submitted comments supporting two proposals (Track 1 and Track 3A) from ISO Management on resource adequacy modeling and program design. Track 1 proposes updating default methodologies for planning reserve margin and qualifying capacity to meet a 0.1 LOLE (one loss-of-load event every 10 years) standard; DMM supports this and the inclusion of a resource-specific unforced capacity framework for some resource types, including a methodology for storage resources that includes a measure of energy sufficiency. DMM notes that the Track 1 proposal defers net-qualifying-capacity finalization to the California Public Utilities Commission and cautions that capacity accounting differences across local regulatory authorities could incentivize additional capacity sales. Track 3A proposes informational enhancements to improve ISO visibility into available capacity for procurement through the capacity procurement mechanism; DMM supports this as a reliability tool to facilitate bilateral procurement when competitive solicitation is unavailable. DMM recommends the ISO address seasonality of default values, unforced capacity, and interactions with outage substitution, resource-adequacy availability incentive mechanism, and capacity procurement mechanism as parallel policy processes conclude.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the DMM comments address resource-adequacy accreditation methodology and qualifying-capacity rules that apply to all dispatchable resources, including conventional and pumped-storage hydro. The energy-sufficiency measure for storage resources is particularly significant: it recognizes that storage value depends on both power capacity and energy availability, a distinction central to hydro operations and central to how correctly accounting for PSH—which faces binding state-of-charge constraints—differs from energy-unlimited resources. The unforced-capacity framework and default qualifying-capacity rules also govern how hydro's seasonal and intermittent contributions are accredited for system reliability, directly affecting seasonal and annual capacity revenue. DMM's caution about cross-jurisdictional capacity-accounting arbitrage (note 3) suggests default values may create incentives to source capacity from areas with favorable qualifying-capacity treatment, a concern hydro operators should monitor as the default framework is finalized.

documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities. However, PG&E's generator interconnection network-upgrade pipeline directly affects hydro deliverability and transmission-access economics. Each of these 100+ projects either enables new generation to export (deliverability-driven reconductoring and transformer upgrades) or mitigates reliability constraints that would otherwise curtail existing generators during peak loading. For conventional and run-of-river hydro already in the queue or operating in CAISO, delays in completion (many projects slip 1–3 years as shown in the schedule updates) mean longer wait times to achieve full deliverability rights, while accelerated completion benefits existing hydro by widening transmission windows for export. Cost allocations and timing sequencing also set precedent for how CAISO allocates network costs to future generation, including hydro interconnections; the dominance of reliability-driven and RAS-based projects (rather than pure headroom expansions) suggests the queue is hitting physical and dynamic-stability limits that may constrain the value or feasibility of marginal hydro capacity in this region. Owners of existing hydro plants in northern California (PG&E territory, including any small generators on PG&E transmission) should monitor the in-service delays on reconductoring and bus upgrades that could affect their real-time transmission headroom and interconnection-service charges.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Regulatory Report for October 2025 surveys FERC orders and other regulatory filings through October 22, 2025. Key items affecting market-design frameworks include: FERC acceptance of PacifiCorp and Portland General Electric tariff amendments for Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) implementation (August 29, 2025); FERC approval of CAISO's congestion revenue allocation methodology for EDAM (August 29, 2025), which modifies how day-ahead congestion revenues from point-to-point and network transmission service rights are allocated among participating balancing areas; FERC approval of CAISO's June 6, 2025, Subscriber PTO tariff amendments allowing conversion of subscriber rights to congestion revenue rights (August 5, 2025); a second FERC Order 2023/2023-A compliance filing on revised Large Generator and Small Generator Interconnection Agreements (July 14, 2025, supplemented October 3, 2025); and FERC decisions to explore elimination of the WECC soft price cap framework (July 15, 2025 section 206 proceeding, with CAISO filing reply comments August 14, 2025). Additional items include WEIM expansion agreements with Power Watch, LLC (filed September 29, 2025) and Imperial Irrigation District (accepted August 25, 2025), extension of the Assistance Energy Transfer feature in WEIM (filed September 23, 2025), and FERC approval of reliability standards on extreme cold weather preparedness (EOP-012, September 18, 2025) and cybersecurity (CIP-003-11, CIP-015-1, September 18, 2025). The report also notes FERC Order 912 on supply-chain risk management standards and CPUC rulemakings on demand response enhancement and integrated resource planning procurement framework.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not address hydro or pumped-storage resources directly. However, it reports FERC progress on interconnection-queue reforms (Order 2023-A LGIA/SGIA) and EDAM expansion governance that affect where hydro generators can interconnect and trade across western balancing authorities. The congestion revenue allocation redesign for EDAM may shift the financial treatment of parallel flows on long-term transmission rights that hydro operators rely on for export; the soft price cap elimination proceeding, if successful, would remove a price floor that has historically constrained revenue upside in scarcity conditions where hydro typically earns its highest margins. Reliability standards on cold-weather preparedness and cybersecurity may extend to synchronous hydro units' operational and physical-security obligations. The extension of WEIM Assistance Energy Transfer and addition of new balancing authorities (Power Watch, IID) expands the geographic scope in which hydro operators in member and adjacent areas can participate.

documents.title: State, Regional, and Federal Affairs Update - Oct 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: AB 825 authorizes CAISO to operate voluntary energy markets governed by an independent Regional Organization, fundamentally reshaping CAISO's governance and market structure, which directly affects hydro's strategic options and market participation pathways in California and the West.
documents.ai_summary: On September 19, 2025, California signed Assembly Bill 825 into law, authorizing CAISO and California electrical corporations to participate in voluntary energy markets governed by an independent Regional Organization (RO) if specified requirements are met. AB 825 requires CAISO to maintain technical capability to operate energy markets, continue its functions as a balancing authority, develop an annual report on ISO and independent RO activities with annual legislative presentation, and by December 31, 2026, conduct a study of the independent RO's impacts on job retention and creation in California. The Western Energy Markets Governing Body celebrated the passage and CAISO is working with the Pathways Initiative Formation Committee to implement AB 825 requirements. PacifiCorp and Portland General Electric received FERC approval in August 2025 to join EDAM in 2026, with PacifiCorp on track for May 2026 activation following successful EDAM Market Simulation launch in early September; Nevada Energy plans to file its EDAM application on October 22, 2025.
documents.hydro_read_through: AB 825 and concurrent EDAM expansion reshape California's energy-market governance by creating an independent Regional Organization parallel to CAISO, which directly affects where California and Western hydro resources can participate and how their products are priced and accredited. Hydro owners must track whether the independent RO will adopt different capacity accreditation, ancillary-service pricing, or ramping-product designs than CAISO, and whether EDAM's May 2026 launch in PacifiCorp's territory (which includes significant hydro) alters incentives for participating resources or creates new obligations for existing plants. The West-Wide Governance Pathways Initiative framework and job-impact study deadline of December 31, 2026, will determine whether the RO operates a unified market or carve-outs that fragment hydro's revenue opportunities.

documents.ai_summary: CEO Elliot Mainzer reports on CAISO's winter readiness, EDAM expansion, and market governance. FERC issued three orders on August 29, 2025 approving EDAM congestion-revenue allocation and tariff changes enabling PacifiCorp and Portland General Electric to join EDAM next year; FERC also accepted an agreement integrating Imperial Irrigation District into WEIM and EDAM in October 2028, and NV Energy plans to file with Nevada's Public Utilities Commission this month to join EDAM in 2028. Governor Newsom signed Assembly Bill 825 (AB 825, "Pathways" legislation) on September 19, 2025 with overwhelming legislative support (101-2 combined vote), requiring the ISO to establish independent West-wide governance and submit an annual report to the Legislature by February 1 each year. Battery storage on the CAISO grid grew from 101 MW at end of 2020 to 14,428 MW as of mid-October 2025, with an additional 2,406 MW expected by April 2026; SunZia transmission line (551-mile HVDC/HVAC connecting 3,600 MW New Mexico wind) is nearing commissioning this year under a new subscriber participating transmission owner model. A new GHG emissions accounting framework, launching after EDAM's 2026 operational start, will match market results to hourly consumption using residual emissions rates for net market purchases, supporting state reporting requirements and voluntary corporate climate goals.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, the governance transition codified in AB 825 and the accelerating EDAM accession of multiple Western utilities will reshape the markets in which CAISO-connected hydro and pumped-storage operators compete for energy revenue and ancillary-services pricing. Battery-storage deployment at 14,428 MW and rising 2,406 MW/year will intensify competition for evening peak revenue and scarcity-pricing opportunities, compressing the margins hydro historically earned in those hours. Transmission additions and multi-utility EDAM membership growth affect interregional locational signals and hydro's ability to arbitrage scarcity across the West.

Hydro owners in the West will be strategically choosing between WEM, WEIM continuation, and other market pathways; the bylaws, board composition, and tariff framework under development here will be material to those decisions.

documents.title: Briefing on Spotlight Initiative - Gas Resource Management - Oct 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Gas resource management framework proposes changes to default energy bid and reference-level processes, which are market-power mitigation tools that directly apply to use-limited resources including hydro and PSH; expansion of EDAM participation rules and cost-recovery mechanisms also affects all dispatchable generation.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO presented a proposal to recalibrate gas resource management tools for the EDAM, addressing cost estimation and fuel procurement challenges faced by gas resources outside the ISO balancing authority area. The initiative modifies the reference-level change request process to allow more frequent use and adjusts cost thresholds for market participants whose gas hubs are more volatile than ISO calculated estimates. CAISO proposes providing additional flexibility during periods of significant forecast uncertainty (D+2→D+1 or D+1→real-time) to reflect costs of unexpected unit commitments, and creating after-the-fact cost recovery eligibility when physical supply disruptions occur after the adjustment deadline. The proposal also seeks expanded authority to use gas constraints as a reliability tool across the full ISO market footprint (currently limited to the southern part), and enhancement of the D+2 advisory market to better inform fuel procurement decisions. A 2018-approved commitment cost and default energy bid policy that was never implemented is being revisited for potential activation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or PSH directly. However, the changes to default energy bid and reference-level adjustment processes are the same mechanisms used to govern offer behavior and cost recovery for all use-limited resources in the ISO and EDAM. Hydro and PSH operators use these same reference-level and default energy bid tools to reflect operational costs and scarcity conditions; any liberalization of cost thresholds, frequency of adjustment requests, or after-the-fact recovery eligibility would apply to them as well. Additionally, the expansion of these tools to full EDAM participation and the relaxation of cost-recovery eligibility rules during supply disruptions could improve revenue flexibility for hydro and PSH in stressed conditions, though the proposal's primary focus on gas procurement volatility means the specific mechanics may not be optimized for hydro seasonal or hydrologic variability.

documents.title: Department of Market Monitoring Update - Sep 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Energy price formation and market-wide transmission congestion affect the locational value and revenue opportunities for hydro exports and imports across the WEIM; load growth and transfer patterns reveal shifting demand and scarcity conditions that influence when hydro generation is most valuable.
documents.ai_summary: The Department of Market Monitoring's September 2025 report summarizes Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) pricing, load, and transfer patterns for the second quarter of 2025 (April–June). Overall 15-minute market prices averaged $26/MWh, up 12 percent year-over-year; regional variation was significant, with Desert Southwest prices up 40 percent, Pacific Northwest up 14 percent, and Powerex down 18 percent, driven by natural gas price changes and transmission congestion. Total system load averaged 74.7 GW, a 1.4 percent increase; during mid-day solar hours, south-to-north congestion suppressed prices in California and Desert Southwest while raising them in the Pacific Northwest and Powerex. Average WEIM transfers were around 4,730 MW, relatively flat year-over-year, with mid-day exports from CAISO and morning/evening exports from the Intermountain West.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never mentions hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, it establishes the regional price signals and congestion patterns that determine the value of hydro flexibility across the WEIM. Hydro owners benefit from high prices during afternoon peak net load and from geographic price spreads created by transmission constraints; the report's finding that mid-day solar hours suppress prices in the Southwest while raising them in the Pacific Northwest, and that south-to-north congestion persists, shows where and when hydro generation captures scarcity rents. Load growth of 1.4 percent year-over-year and the shift in transfer patterns—particularly increased Intermountain West exports during non-solar hours—signal growing demand for flexible generation from the Northwest and other supply zones, which raises the implicit value of hydro's dispatchability and energy storage.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Congestion revenue allocation mechanisms under EDAM directly affect how transmission-based revenues are divided among balancing areas and rights holders, with implications for how use-limited resources like conventional hydro and pumped storage accrue financial hedges on constrained interfaces.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Congestion Revenue Allocation Phase 2 working group (meeting July 28, 2026) evaluates three design concepts for allocating Day-Ahead congestion revenues across the broadened EDAM footprint. Concept #1 would allocate revenues to EDAM entities based on cleared balanced schedules associated with firm OATT transmission rights (long-term firm PTP and NITS), with reciprocal treatment for CAISO's CRRs; stakeholder feedback showed qualified support for this incremental improvement but concern about implementation feasibility and persistent self-schedule incentives. Concept #3, with broader stakeholder support, proposes a common Simultaneous Feasibility Test (SFT) to evaluate CRRs and eligible firm OATT rights' effectiveness on constraints across the entire EDAM footprint, with annual and monthly nomination cycles mirroring current CRR processes; Concept #2 faced broad opposition for relying on historical baselines. Stakeholder comments are due August 10, 2026, and the next working-group meeting will be scheduled in August following comment review.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources. However, congestion revenue allocation mechanisms set the financial hedges that use-limited resources (hydro's canonical category) receive on transmission paths. Concept #1's broadening of allocation from self-schedule-only to cleared balanced schedules could affect how a generator with firm OATT rights monetizes simultaneous market bids; Concept #3's common SFT across the EDAM footprint would establish congestion entitlements jointly with other transmission rights, potentially changing the baseline against which a hydro owner with legacy OATT capacity competes for congestion revenue funding. The shift from internal-balancing-area allocation (Phase 1) toward footprint-wide constraint effectiveness testing could either improve or degrade congestion hedges depending on how parallel flows and network topology changes interact with a given plant's transmission path.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: EDAM congestion revenue allocation (CRA) directly affects locational price signals and transmission-driven congestion costs that hydropower operators face when exporting across the expanded footprint; the analysis quantifies transmission constraints and parallel flows that will shape hydro plant economics and hedging strategies.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Director of Market Performance presented analysis of congestion cost patterns in the prospective Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) footprint spanning nine balancing authorities (BANC, CAISO, IPCO, LADWP, PACE, PACW, PNM, PGE, TID). The analysis found that on average 137 congestion constraints are active in the CAISO area—about 86 percent of all constraints—with approximately 34 percent impacted by parallel flows from EDAM-area transactions. Key constraints like Path 26 experience up to 40 percent flow impacts from transactions between PacifiCorp east and west. Congestion is concentrated during solar hours and increases during evening peak hours in summer months. CAISO constraints drive most congestion pricing across EDAM areas, while constraints in non-CAISO EDAM areas have negligible frequency of congestion and minimal price impact on other EDAM regions. The analysis used historical 2024 WEIM congestion data and shift factors as a proxy for projected EDAM congestion patterns.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydropower plants exporting power across the EDAM footprint—particularly from the Pacific Northwest into California—will face transmission congestion charges shaped by the parallel-flow patterns and locational price spreads this analysis documents. The finding that CAISO constraints generate the largest price separations (e.g., negative prices in Southwest desert areas, positive in PNW) directly affects the value of hydro at different locations and the revenue from selling energy into different nodes. Hydro operators need to track which transmission paths are most frequently congested and how parallel flows from other EDAM regions will influence the congestion rent distribution that determines their payment or charge per MWh.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to its ICAP Manual to implement the Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements tariff provisions, which became effective June 28, 2026. The revisions establish seasonal (summer and winter) NYCA minimum capacity requirements, seasonal locational minimum requirements, and revised ICAP demand curves with separate zero-crossing-point and level-of-excess parameters for each season, replacing the previous summer-to-winter and winter-to-summer conversion ratios. Revisions also implement seasonal elections for Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights (UDRs) and External-to-Rest-of-State Deliverability Rights (EDRs) with accompanying must-offer requirements. These manual changes are scheduled to take effect for the Capability Year beginning May 1, 2027, with approval targeted for the September 16, 2026 Business Issues Committee meeting.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the seasonal capacity-requirement and demand-curve design directly affects how all capacity resources—including conventional hydro and PSH—are accredited and procured. Hydro owners in NYISO must respond to the seasonal minimum-requirement structure and the revised demand-curve parameters that now have independent winter parameters rather than ratios applied to summer values; this changes how their winter capacity can be monetized and whether their winter availability translates to matching winter-peak capacity credit. The mandatory UDR/EDR elections with must-offer requirements also constrain hydro's ability to withhold external-import capacity optionality if it relies on external deliverability rights for compliance.

documents.title: 3 Firm Fuel Characteristic Elections: MMA Overview and Monitoring
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's Firm Fuel Characteristic Election mechanism directly governs capacity accreditation and revenue treatment for dispatchable resources meeting winter firm-fuel requirements, establishing must-bid rules, sanctions for non-performance, and outage-scheduling constraints that affect any resource type (including hydro) participating in that accreditation class.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO requires gas/fuel-oil generators electing the Firm Fuel Capacity Accreditation Resource Class to submit elections by August 1, 2026 for the 2027–2028 capability year and to maintain fuel-supply documentation by December 1 to satisfy a Firm Fuel Performance Availability Requirement (eight consecutive hours of operation daily during the December–February winter period, within a 56-hour-per-7-day rolling constraint). Generators must bid their elected firm MW in the day-ahead market, respond to supplemental resource evaluations, and notify NYISO within five business days of any change to fuel-supply agreements. Failure to maintain fuel, bid the firm capacity, or meet documentation requirements triggers annual firm-fuel sanctions and settlement adjustments, with FERC referral possible for false claims or misleading data. Proposed outage-scheduling changes would require resources to return to service within three days during winter and summer peak periods (exempt for non-firm-accredited units during winter). The document is a technical overview and monitoring framework for participants; no vote or action item is scheduled.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the Firm Fuel Characteristic Election mechanism applies to any 'Installed Capacity Supplier that operates by utilizing natural gas and/or fuel oil'—a category that in principle could include dispatchable hydro with dual-fuel backup or co-located thermal capacity. More broadly, the accreditation, must-bid, notification, and sanction framework establishes precedent for how NYISO polices capacity resource performance and commitment. Conventional hydro (not reliant on fuel oil or gas) would not participate directly, but if NYISO were to extend similar accreditation or performance-assurance rules to non-fuel-limited resources, the enforcement mechanics shown here—rolling availability targets, bid requirements, ex-post settlement adjustments—would define the model.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Manual 04 is a draft revision of the Installed Capacity (ICAP) manual effective for the Capability Year beginning May 1, 2027. The draft incorporates revisions to capacity accreditation procedures, unforced-capacity (UCAP) calculation methodologies, and demand-curve mechanics. Key revisions referenced in the revision history address Duration Adjustment Factors sunsetting in May 2024, new Capacity Accreditation Resource Classes (CARCs) and Capacity Accreditation Factors (CAFs) effective May 2024, DMNC (Demonstrated Maximum Net Capacity) test procedures for energy-duration-limited resources, and DER/aggregation participation rules. Specific updates to LCROR Hydro Resources' UCAP calculation are noted in version 6.54 (effective 01/03/2023). The manual was approved by the Business Issues Committee on 06/18/2026 and issued for discussion on 07/07/2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: This manual revision directly affects how NYISO calculates and credits hydroelectric capacity in the ICAP market. Conventional and run-of-river hydro are accredited as Non-Energy Limited or Energy Limited Resources depending on their characteristics, with accreditation factors that now tie to seasonal CARCs rather than duration-adjustment factors. Pumped-storage resources appear as Co-Located Storage Resources subject to their own UCAP calculation and DMNC requirements. The revision history confirms explicit updates to LCROR (Low-Capacity-Run-Of-River) Hydro Resources' UCAP methodology as of May 2024, and new sections address how DER aggregations and storage resources are treated in capacity accreditation and auction participation—matters central to revenue recognition for hybrid and aggregated hydro projects in the NYCA.

documents.title: 2 Q1 State of the Market Review
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Pumped-storage and hydro revenue is directly affected by NYISO's capacity-market design, energy-price formation under scarcity and cold-weather conditions, ancillary-services dispatch, outage-scheduling rules for firm-fuel resources, and out-of-market actions that depress spot prices and inflate uplift — all covered in this State of Market review.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Q1 2026 State of Market Review (authored by Potomac Economics MMU) analyzes energy and capacity market outcomes, with focus on the January 24–February 9 cold spell. Key findings: (1) All-in energy prices ranged $101–$135/MWh across regions, up 5–48% year-over-year; hydro generation averaged 2.64 GW and set prices as a marginal fuel in 26% of intervals. (2) Out-of-market commitments were extensive: SRE commitments on 14 days and SCR activations on 8 days, driven partly by oil-inventory management rather than minimum reserve requirements; 580 MW of pumped-storage capacity was excluded from NYISO's SRE adequacy evaluation. (3) Market power mitigation: SRE-committed gas generators generated ~$80M in uplift during the cold spell, with fuel costs under investigation; generators with delayed startup times on dual-fuel units were flagged for potential physical withholding. (4) Outage scheduling: 1.2 GW of firm-fuel capacity was on scheduled outages during the cold spell, with ~800 MW on non-recallable outages lasting ≥3 months; MMU recommends NYISO limit firm-fuel units from scheduling such outages during peak winter. (5) Capacity market: spot prices $6.25/kW-month in NYC (down 23% YoY), $3.37/kW-month Rest of State (up 30% YoY); prices driven by ICAP requirement changes and administrative parameters rather than supply reductions. No formal vote or comment deadline stated; document is published June 2026 for 2026-Q1 outcomes.
documents.hydro_read_through: Hydro owners should note three direct revenue and operational impacts: (1) Pumped-storage units were systematically undercounted (580 MW excluded) in NYISO's real-time SRE adequacy assessment, which means the ISO committed expensive gas units instead of tapping cheaper storage, compressing storage arbitrage value and suppressing energy prices; this exclusion should be corrected to let PSH compete fairly in reliability procurement. (2) The report documents how out-of-market actions and SRE commitments during scarcity depress energy prices while inflating uplift, shifting margin from energy-market winners (including low-cost hydro) to OOM recipients — this is a long-standing hydro complaint that the data here validate quantitatively. (3) The restriction on outage scheduling for firm-fuel units reflects a broader principle (reliability and dispatch precedence for dispatchable resources) that could tighten scheduling windows for any unit with low inventory risk, including run-of-river and seasonal hydro; conversely, relaxing outage rules for firm-fuel generators without symmetry would advantage gas over hydro.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: SPP on behalf of MSWG is submitting tariff protocol changes to Markets+ that establish system points (MPSP) and interchange scheduling limits affecting how resources can import/export energy and manage interchange transactions with non-Markets+ areas — a direct governance change to seams coordination and transmission-deliverability mechanics that affects strategic options for interregional energy positioning.
documents.ai_summary: SPP submitted protocol change comments on behalf of the Markets+ Steering Working Group (MSWG) on July 15, 2026, to implement Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) and Markets+ System Points (MPSP) — generic, non-resource-specific scheduling points located within Balancing Authority Areas to facilitate interchange transactions into, within, and out of the Markets+ footprint. The MIR establishes that MITSPS transactions (imports and exports using an MPSP as source or sink) are classified as Uncommitted Interchange Transactions and do not count toward must-offer obligations. Interchange Limits on MPSP transactions (import-only, export-only, and net interchange) are submitted hourly by each BA via the Market User Interface and enforced in Day-Ahead Market, RUC, and real-time balancing market runs, with default limits of ±99999 if not provided. MPSP are used for administrative energy accounting and shift-factor calculations but have no associated market settlement; all settlement for MITSPS uses the External Interface Settlement Location LMP. The document proposes revisions to Markets+ Protocols sections spanning definitions, offer submittal, market inputs, congestion management, and settlement locations to incorporate MPSP and MITSPS mechanics into the day-ahead, RUC, real-time, and post-operating-day processes.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources. However, MITSPS and MPSP establish a new interchange pathway across the Markets+ seams that could materially affect how a hydro owner positioned in one BA exports energy to or imports from non-Markets+ areas (or other Markets+ BAs). The ability to use MPSP as a generic source or sink for scheduling and e-Tagging, rather than tying interchange to a specific resource location, could simplify hedging and arbitrage opportunities across the footprint boundary; conversely, the hourly MPSP interchange limits set by each BA create a potential congestion bottleneck independent of transmission capacity that could constrain the revenue opportunity from seasonal energy trading. The treatment of these transactions as Uncommitted (and thus exempt from must-offer) and the use of External Interface LMPs for settlement (rather than internal nodal pricing) are structural choices worth understanding as they affect how a hydro operator models the profitability of interchange strategies.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Markets+ transmission opt-in/opt-out rules govern how transmission service reserved outside the Markets+ tariff can be made available or withheld from market optimization, directly affecting transmission deliverability and interregional transfer capability for resources including hydropower.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Transmission Working Group reference guide (July 2026, version 0.1) documents procedures for Markets+ Transmission Contributors to opt-in and opt-out transmission service. Opt-in allows transmission customers to designate transmission service acquired from non-participating providers as available for Markets+ optimization via day-ahead and real-time markets; monthly-or-longer service triggers Congestion Rent Eligible Transmission Service Request (CRETSR) review and Service Flow Constraint coordination with Participating Balancing Authorities. Opt-out applies to Point-to-Point transmission supporting pseudo-tied generation/load or bilateral wheels not registered in Markets+ (wheel-through transactions); opt-outs require approval by both market participant and the individual transmission service provider and exclude opted-out segments from Markets+ settlement unless combined with Markets+-available transmission in the same schedule. The guide establishes registration, e-Tag profiling, and settlement workflows for both opt-in and opt-out scenarios but does not specify an adoption or implementation deadline.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, Markets+ transmission governance affects hydro deliverability and the ability to serve external load or other balancing authorities through interregional transfers. The opt-in framework determines whether transmission reserved by a hydro owner under legacy bilateral contracts or non-MTSP tariffs can be embedded in real-time market optimization; opt-out rules affect whether third-party wheel-through transactions consume transmission paths that a hydro owner's own transactions would otherwise use. For a hydro owner making strategic choices about Markets+ membership versus remaining outside, these transmission rules define the practical cost and operational flexibility of either position.

documents.title: 07-MIR9.2-R Dynamic Schedule Resources_MTWG 20260727.pptx  [in MTWG Meeting Materials 20260727.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Defines how dynamic schedule resources (dispatchable and non-dispatchable) are treated in Markets+ tariff and settlements, affecting how flexible resources serving load across balancing-area boundaries are dispatched, settled, and valued — a direct governance change to participation models for any dispatchable resource including hydro.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ (SPP) is updating MIR9.2-R to clarify how resources that dynamically serve load in other balancing areas (Dynamic Schedule Resources) are managed in dispatch, power balance, and settlements. The proposal distinguishes resource-coupled (dispatchable by Markets+) and non-resource-coupled (not dispatchable) options across five use cases spanning internal dynamic transfers and export/import interchange transactions. For resource-coupled dynamic exports to non-participating balancing areas, the day-ahead and pre-real-time markets use the normal e-Tag energy profile as a fixed value and exclude the Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface, while real-time uses the Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface to set export quantity; settlements mirror this split treatment. MDWG approved the proposal July 8, 2026, and MTWG is receiving second education on July 27, 2026; MORWG and MPEC approval votes are pending July 29 and August 25, 2026 respectively.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not address hydro or pumped storage directly. However, dynamic schedule resources are a dispatch and settlement model for any use-limited or dispatchable resource serving variable load across balancing-area boundaries. A hydropower plant with seasonal or daily flexibility could be deployed under this mechanism to serve dynamic demand outside its home balancing area; the treatment determines how its real-time dispatch interacts with day-ahead commitment, how it is accounted in power balance, and what energy profile drives settlement — all material to revenue and operational obligation. The distinction between resource-coupled (dispatchable by Markets+, echoing output) and non-resource-coupled (self-scheduled with fixed day-ahead and variable real-time profile) models would be available to hydro operators choosing to participate in Markets+.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Markets+ tariff and protocol rules for Dynamic Schedule Resources directly affect how dispatchable generation—including conventional and pumped-storage hydroelectric plants—can register, offer energy across balancing-authority boundaries, and participate in day-ahead and real-time market clearing; these are core revenue and operational participation rules for multi-state hydro export and interchange operations.
documents.ai_summary: SPP submitted comments on Markets+ Initiative Request MIR9.2-R (Dynamic Schedule Resources), proposing tariff and protocol changes to clarify how Markets+ will process dynamic schedules within and across participating balancing authorities. The MIR defines Dynamic Schedule Resource and Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface constructs and specifies registration, e-Tagging, and ICCP requirements. Key proposed changes include: (1) requiring 100% of Dynamic Schedule Resource output to be e-Tagged with one Dynamic transaction type and zero or more Normal transaction types; (2) modifying the day-ahead market, RUC, and pre-RTBM to use the e-tag energy profile as a fixed value for self-scheduled Dynamic Export Interchange Transactions, with settlement at the external interface LMP; (3) in real-time, ignoring the e-tag in RTBM solution and instead using the Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface to set export quantity, with settlement based on updated Dynamic e-Tag. The proposed revisions affect Markets+ Tariff sections I (Definitions A, D, H) and 4.2.9, and Markets+ Protocols sections 1 (Glossary), 4.2.2.5.9, 4.2.3.3, 4.2.6, 4.2.6.1, 4.4.2.1.3, and 9.1.8. SPP stated this clarifies market processing, maintains balance without excessive regulation burden, decreases over/under commitment in RUC, reduces regulation burden on Markets+ BAs, and reduces the need to pseudo-tie resources between BAs.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydroelectric or pumped-storage resources by name. However, Dynamic Schedule Resources are dispatchable generation assets that can participate in multi-BA energy transfers, and the rules here define how their output gets allocated, scheduled, and settled—mechanisms that directly determine revenue recognition and operational flexibility for any owner managing export of generation across balancing-authority boundaries. For hydro owners participating in Markets+ (SPP footprint), these rules establish whether a plant can remain dispatchable for market optimization under a dynamic schedule or must be locked into a fixed export profile, and whether settlement occurs on forecasted or actual real-time dispatch—material questions for revenue and state-of-charge management of storage resources.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ has formalized the Revision Initiative Request (MIR) process, a unified procedure for submitting proposed changes to Markets+ Tariff, Protocols, and system enhancements. Any qualified entity—including Markets+ Participants, SPP staff, the Market Monitoring Unit, and governmental authorities—may submit an MIR on an SPP form to the Request Management System. MIRs are routed to Primary and Secondary Markets+ Working Groups according to routing criteria; the Markets+ Design Working Group (MDWG) holds primary responsibility for Tariff and Protocols changes. Submitted MIRs are posted within 3 business days and must receive written comments no later than 5 business days prior to the Primary Working Group's review. SPP performs an Impact Analysis assessing budgetary, implementation-timeline, staffing, and system impacts; the Primary Working Group ranks MIRs as high, medium, or low and may approve, reject, table, or refer them. Approved MIRs proceed through Secondary Working Groups, the Markets+ Participant Executive Committee (MPEC), and the Markets+ Independent Panel (MIP) for final review. The document (v2.1, effective 07/08/2026) reflects updates in response to comments by SRP.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or storage directly, but it establishes the gating process through which all future Markets+ tariff and protocol changes—including any affecting energy pricing, ancillary-service accreditation, storage participation rules, capacity-market mechanics, or transmission interconnection—will be submitted and reviewed. Hydro and PSH owners evaluating whether to join Markets+ or participate in its governance need to understand the MIR timeline and structure (15+ business days for drafting review, working-group and MPEC approval gates, mandatory Impact Analysis) to assess how quickly market-design problems can be escalated and whether the process favors or delays changes in their interest.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document establishes the Markets+ Revision Initiative Request process—the governance pathway through which market-design changes affecting all participant classes, including hydro and PSH owners, are submitted, routed, reviewed, and approved; this process directly governs how market rules affecting revenue, obligations, and strategic options are developed and adopted in the SPP/Markets+ footprint.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ has finalized version 2.0 of the Markets+ Revision Initiative Request (MIR) Process document (effective date November 13, 2025, updated May 12, 2026). The document establishes the formal governance pathway for submitting, reviewing, and approving changes to Markets+ Tariff, Markets+ Protocols, and the MIR Process itself. Qualified entities—including any Markets+ Market Participant, SPP staff, the SPP Market Monitoring Unit, rostered working-group members, governmental authorities with SPP jurisdiction, and designated entities—may submit MIRs via the SPP Request Management System using a standardized MIR Submission Form. SPP reviews submissions for completeness within three business days and posts complete MIRs to the SPP website within three business days of receipt. Written comments on an MIR must be submitted using the standardized MIR Comment Form no later than five business days prior to the Primary Markets+ Working Group's initial review; all complete comments received in proper format are posted to the SPP website within three business days and distributed to relevant email exploders. SPP performs an Impact Analysis assessing budgetary impacts, implementation timelines, alternatives, interim workarounds, and system/staffing needs; unless greater complexity warrants, the IA is issued within thirty calendar days of Primary Working Group approval. The Primary Markets+ Working Group (for Markets+ Design matters, the Markets+ Design Working Group / MDWG) ranks MIRs as high, medium, or low and may approve, reject, table/postpone, or withdraw them; approved MIRs are routed through Secondary Markets+ Working Groups, the Markets+ Participant Executive Committee (MPEC), and where necessary the Markets+ Independent Panel (MIP). Draft MIRs ready for Primary Working Group review are posted for a 15-business-day comment period prior to the meeting; MIRs with shorter notice may be expedited or deferred to the next regularly scheduled meeting. This process applies to all Markets+ participant classes and replaces the prior Markets+ Revision Request (MRR) nomenclature.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the MIR process it describes is the direct governance mechanism through which SPP Markets+ members—including hydro and PSH operators—propose, comment on, and collectively decide changes to the Markets+ Tariff and Protocols that determine how their resources are priced, accredited, required to operate, and interact with the market. Understanding this process is essential for hydro/PSH participants: the five-business-day comment deadline, the fifteen-business-day draft review period, and the sequence of working-group review → MPEC → MIP approval determine how quickly market-design changes affecting energy pricing, ancillary-service accreditation, ramping products, storage participation, and operational compliance rules are developed and implemented. A hydro owner in SPP/Markets+ territory needs to know these deadlines and routing rules to participate effectively in market-design decisions that shape their revenue and obligations.

documents.ai_summary: SPP developed this training presentation to explain Markets+ transmission capacity opt-in and opt-out processes for Market Participants. The document covers: (1) Background on Markets+ Transmission Service Providers (MTSPs), Transmission Contributors, and how transmission capacity is designated as opted-in or opted-out; (2) Opted-in transmission capacity within and outside Participating BAAs, including Market Opt-in Transfer Interfaces (MOTIs) that utilize transmission service across non-participating TSPs to optimize energy transfers between Participating BAAs; (3) Opted-out transmission capacity, including capacity on MTSP systems and previously opted-in non-participating TSP transmission; and (4) Bilateral schedule processing, wheel-through scenarios, and special considerations. By default, all MTSP transmission assets within a Participating BAA are available for Markets+ optimization; transmission service with monthly or longer duration from non-participating TSPs may be opted in via RMS ticket submission, with Firm or Conditional Firm classes eligible for Congestion Rent treatment; service less than one month must be coordinated with the Participating BA for Service Flow Constraint inclusion.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, it establishes the transmission participation framework under which conventional hydro and PSH owners must operate in Markets+—specifically, how their own transmission rights and those of third parties are either automatically included or must be explicitly opted in for use in day-ahead and real-time market optimization. Run-of-river and reservoir-constrained hydro typically rely on firm or conditional-firm transmission service to deliver output; the requirement to opt-in (or coordinate if sub-monthly) and the distinction between CRETSR-eligible and non-eligible service will determine whether their transmission reserves are remunerated under the Markets+ Tariff and included in network optimization, directly affecting their dispatch priority and revenue. The MOTI mechanism allowing transmission across non-participating systems to link Participating BAAs is also material to hydro facilities located in or serving multiple BAA areas.

documents.ai_summary: SPP's comment on Markets+ Initiative Request 9.3 proposes to formalize registration and operational rules for dynamically scheduled quasi-pseudo-ties—external resources (generators located outside Markets+ but serving load within it) that remain e-tagged as Dynamic Schedules between their Native Balancing Authority and the Attaining Balancing Authority while being modeled as pseudo-tied into the Markets+ Network and Commercial Models. The proposed rules in Markets+ Protocols sections 9.1.9.1–9.1.9.3 require: (1) Market Participants to designate the Resource as a dynamically scheduled quasi-pseudo-tie in the registration workbook; (2) the Attaining BA to provide an attestation letter confirming it understands the Resource will be modeled as a pseudo-tie in Markets+; (3) the MP to ensure Max ECOL (Maximum Economic Capacity Obligation) submitted in Day-Ahead and Real-Time offers accounts for any tagged off-system sales; and (4) no other e-tagged transactions from the quasi-pseudo-tied Resource may sink into any other Markets+ Participating BAA. The Market Operator will limit dispatch to the lesser of the Max ECOL and the energy profile on the dynamic tag if they differ in any market timeframe. The submission was filed July 20, 2026, for the Markets+ Transmission Working Group meeting on July 27, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or pumped storage directly. However, it clarifies participation mechanics for external generation in Markets+, a regional market platform that NHA members (particularly in the Southwest and potential entrants) are evaluating as an alternative or complement to existing RTOs. The rules codify how dispatch limits apply when external resources' Max ECOL differs from their dynamically scheduled tag, which affects offer strategy and revenue certainty for any dispatchable external generator. More broadly, the attestation and modeling requirements standardize a capability 'already included in the Markets+ base design,' suggesting this MIR is removing ambiguity that could otherwise constrain external resource participation and revenue reliability in the footprint.

documents.ai_summary: PJM's Engineering and Procurement (E&P) Agreement mechanism allows Project Developers to expedite procurement of long-lead-time items necessary for interconnection in Phase III of the interconnection process. documents.title: ERS_Alternate Baseline Test_Concept_Paper_V2
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document establishes ERCOT's baseline methodology for Energy Response Service (ERS) loads, which is the settlement and performance-tracking rule for demand-response participation; the Alternate Baseline Test (ABT) directly affects how demand-response resources are credited and penalized, which sets a precedent for how storage and other flexible resources may be treated under similar settlement frameworks.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's Alternate Baseline Test (ABT) Concept Paper describes a two-step process for assigning baselines to ERS Loads. Step 1 evaluates resources against five default baseline methods (M810, MDP, REG, MBMA, NEAR20); a method passes if P95 is 20% or less and absolute bias is 5% or less. Step 2 applies ABT only to resources failing all five defaults. ABT compares actual load against a reference load calculated from the 10 most recent qualifying same-day-type, non-price historical intervals at the same time of day; an interval is counted as reduced when actual load is at or below 50% of reference load. A resource fails ABT only when the high-price reduction rate exceeds 50% AND the non-price reduction rate is below 20%. The final baseline becomes the single approved baseline used for ERS offers and performance analysis.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage resources directly. However, ABT's framework for distinguishing deliberate load-reduction behavior from normal variation establishes how ERCOT settles and validates demand-response performance. The methodology—using high-price versus non-price interval comparison and a 50% load-reduction threshold—could serve as precedent if ERCOT or other markets adopt similar baseline-validation rules for storage or other flexible resources whose value derives from strategic state-of-charge or load-shedding decisions. The design choice to require corroborating non-price-interval behavior before accepting demand-reduction patterns as eligible for settlement is relevant to how storage charging, discharge timing, and use-limited-resource settlement might be validated in future frameworks.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is filing tariff language in mid-August 2026 establishing interconnection reliability requirements for large loads (50+ MW), with differentiated treatment based on load type. Computational loads (data centers, AI, cryptocurrency mining) must meet Phasor Measurement Unit (PMU) requirements, ride-through criteria for voltage and frequency disturbances, and ramp-rate limits; non-computational industrial and agricultural loads face less stringent behavioral requirements. A transition provision exempts large loads already in service as of the effective date from all requirements unless subject to a 25+ MW upgrade, while previously MTEP-approved loads not yet receiving service must meet visibility and behavioral requirements. The tariff targets filing in mid-August 2026 with a November 1, 2027 effective date. Stakeholders may provide informal comments by August 3, 2026.

The forecasting requirements and real-time telemetry mandates for large loads also signal MISO's growing reliance on granular data feeds and minute-to-minute coordination, which may extend to hydro's dispatch and reserve-delivery obligations.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes a new Section 37A to its tariff establishing interconnection and operational reliability requirements for Large Load (defined as load of 50 MW or more associated with any facility or aggregation owned or coordinated by a single or group of entities). Computational Load (data-center and IT-equipment load) is subject to additional Phasor Measurement Unit, ride-through, and ramp-rate requirements. All Large Load must provide basic facility data, modeling, telemetry via ICCP (to be operational by September 1, 2027), load forecasts, and audit documentation to MISO. Computational Load must remain connected during voltage and frequency disturbances and meet transmission-provider-determined ramp limits. Transition provisions exempt Large Loads that achieved Service Commencement prior to the effective date, except upon a Qualified Change (modification increasing demand or repurposing the load). The Transmission Provider may require full compliance if material adverse reliability effects are determined. Failure to provide information may result in delayed Service Commencement, operational limitations, or disconnection.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. However, the Large Load requirements establish technical and operational standards—PMU telemetry, ride-through performance, ramp-rate constraints, and demand forecasting—that MISO may extend to or use as precedent for other dispatchable and storage-like resources. The requirement for Computational Load to maintain stable ramp rates and ride-through capability mirrors flexibility and stability obligations hydro operators face; if applied to storage-as-load (behind-the-meter charging), or to distributed generation and battery resources, these standards would shape how quickly any co-located or aggregated resource can respond and how its output must be forecast, setting compatibility rules that affect hydro's ability to serve or compete with these loads. documents.ai_summary: MISO is revising its Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements tariff to take effect November 1, 2027, establishing mandatory facility-data, modeling, telemetry, forecasting, and ride-through and ramp-rate requirements for loads ≥50 MW. The framework differentiates between computational loads (≥25 MW of IT equipment) and non-computational loads, applying the full suite of requirements (including Phasor Measurement Units, voltage/frequency ride-through at specified performance criteria, and up/down ramp limits) only to computational loads and loads not yet approved in MTEP planning. Loads already approved but not in service by December 2026 face visibility and behavioral (ramp/ride-through) requirements. Existing operating loads are grandfathered unless modified by ≥25 MW. MISO plans to file the tariff in August 2026 and is requesting stakeholder feedback by August 3, 2026. Informal comments focus on slides 7, 9, and 12 covering definitions, applicability, and transition provisions. The Business Practices Manual is to be developed June 2026–December 2026 to detail implementation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the ride-through, ramp-rate, forecasting, and PMU requirements set an industry template for how MISO will treat real-time dispatch behavior and dynamic performance of dispatchable resources during grid stress. If a pumped-storage plant is located at or behind a large computational load's point of withdrawal, or if MISO later applies these standards to other dispatchable resources as precedent, the facility-level modeling, telemetry, and dynamic-response requirements would constrain PSH operational flexibility and create new compliance costs. The ramp-smoothing provision allowing "reduction/ramp smoothing provided by generation or other resources" suggests MISO may eventually credit storage or distributed generation co-located with large loads to mitigate their variability—a potential revenue mechanism if hydro or PSH can contract to provide it, but only if the tariff explicitly extends that role.

documents.title: 2026-07-23 RC A03.b Capacity Auction Reforms - Seasonal/Accreditation - Post-RAA Accreditation - Presentation - Revision
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE is reforming its capacity auction accreditation methodology for resources not included in the RAA model, explicitly covering energy-storage resources (pumped hydro and batteries) and intermittent-resource classes (hydro by load zone and SOG/non-SOG type), which directly affects how PSH and run-of-river hydro are accredited for seasonal capacity revenue.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms—Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) project introduces post-RAA accreditation methodologies for resources not modeled in the Resource Adequacy Assessment (~10 months before seasonal auctions), including newly-commercial resources, Passive Demand Resources, Import Capacity Resources, and Intermittent Power Resources. For energy-storage resources (including pumped hydro and batteries), ISO-NE will estimate representative rMRI using a proxy ES curve developed seasonally, expressing rMRI by energy duration (1 to 100 hours), with MCap of 0.5 MW, max discharge rate 0.5 MW, round-trip efficiency 84%, and EFORd of zero; the resource's rMRI is then adjusted by incorporating EFORd and an rMRI adjustment factor. For Intermittent Power Resources, ISO-NE will use class-weighted average rMRI by MCap, with hydro classes delineated by SOG/non-SOG type and load zone. The ISO plans to publish representative rMRI information ~5 months prior to each seasonal auction, with the approach effective Q2 2027. Stakeholders should submit follow-up questions to the RC Secretary by July 31, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document never names conventional hydropower explicitly, but ISO-NE's IPR accreditation explicitly delineates hydro classes by settlement-only vs. non-SOG type and by load zone, meaning run-of-river and variable hydro will receive class-weighted representative rMRI values seasonal accreditation based on historical fleet performance. Pumped storage is directly addressed as an energy-storage resource: its accreditation will use a proxy curve with specified round-trip efficiency (84%), energy duration range (1–100 hours), and availability/forced-outage adjustments—this methodology replaces or supplements direct RAA modeling for any PSH resources that miss the ~10-month RAA submission window or are post-qualified. documents.title: 2026-07-23 RC A01.1 MC/RC June 9-11, 2026 Meeting Minutes
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal Accreditation directly affects hydro and storage accreditation, revenue recognition under seasonal MRIC, offer mitigation, and modeling of energy-limited resource contributions to reliability.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presented preliminary design for Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal Accreditation (CAR-SA), a major capacity market restructuring moving from annual auctions to seasonal (summer/winter) auctions and replacing annual Qualified Capacity (QC) accreditation with seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values. Key elements include: (1) a proposed two-year transition allowing resources to sell weighted-average of current QC and seasonal MRIC values; (2) resource accreditation modeling using optimized subsets of 70-year weather data; (3) a post-modeling adjustment increasing accreditation for energy-limited and storage resources (approximately 18% winter adjustment) to address Reserve Adequacy Assessment model limitations in charging representation; (4) deactivation mitigation redlines conforming existing rules to seasonal MRIC framework; (5) seller-side offer mitigation including Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) methodology estimated at approximately $5/kW-month; (6) buyer-side mitigation floors and recalculation procedures; (7) Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (Capacity IBTs) for price hedging using floating seasonal clearing prices. Committee raised extensive concerns about weather-year weighting potentially overstating multi-day winter events affecting storage accreditation, modeling of energy-limited resource charging and duration assumptions, at-criteria versus expected-conditions assumptions, and transparency of transition mechanics and demand-curve changes. FirstLight Power and Flatiron Energy presented alternative load-weighting methodologies and risk-modeling approaches; Advanced Energy United proposed weather-year weighting refinements and intertie modeling changes. The ISO indicated it would consider technical engagement on multi-day event representation and would provide additional detail on transition formulas, COPT derivation, and seasonal offer construction in July. Next steps include further stakeholder engagement on accreditation modeling, transition mechanics, and Tariff redlines.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document addresses the single largest change to hydro revenue recognition in ISO-NE's capacity market: the move from annual Qualified Capacity to seasonal MRIC accreditation, which will establish how much seasonal capacity each hydro and pumped-storage facility can offer and be paid for. The proposed transition mechanism (weighted average of QC and seasonal MRIC for two years) affects investment certainty during the changeover. The 18% winter adjustment for energy-limited resources is critical to pumped-storage accreditation, as the base MRIC methodology may understate PSH's reliability contribution by failing to model storage charging from other generators during stressed hours. The weather-year weighting and at-criteria modeling choices will materially affect both the seasonality of accreditation values and their absolute levels — stakeholders representing storage interests are flagging that the ISO's current approach may overstate winter scarcity duration, artificially boosting winter accreditation but misaligning market signals with actual resource-constrained periods. Offer mitigation rules (COPT at ~$5/kW-month, cost-based opportunity-cost testing) will govern whether hydro owners can clear their true economic value or be forced to offer below avoidable cost. The seasonal design will also create new hedging needs (Capacity IBTs) for resources whose value now depends on highly variable seasonal prices rather than a single annual clearing price. Directness: these are not general market changes; they are hydro's accreditation and revenue framework for the coming decade.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Markets and Reliability Committee met 9–11 June 2026 to advance the Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal. The ISO presented transition mechanics for resource accreditation (moving from Qualified Capacity to Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity or MRIC), covering a proposed two-year glide path using weighted averages of current and seasonal MRIC values; a post-modeling adjustment to boost energy-limited and storage resource accreditation by approximately 18% in winter to correct for Reserve Adequacy Assessment model limitations; and proposed Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (Capacity IBTs) as a new price-hedging instrument to address the shift from 40-month forward auctions to seasonal auctions one month ahead. Stakeholders including FirstLight Power and Advanced Energy United offered alternative load-weighting methodologies claiming the ISO's optimized weather-year sampling understates multi-day winter events critical to storage and energy-limited resource modeling. The Committee flagged concerns that seasonal accreditation differences could produce materially different revenue impacts across resource types, that modeling at "at-criteria" rather than expected system conditions may misalign market procurement, and that the adjustment for energy-limited resources lacks permanent modeling fixes. The ISO stated it does not currently propose to model all 70 years of winter hourly loads, intends no delay of core auction timing or deactivation changes, and acknowledged it would provide additional impact analysis, tariff redlines, and technical engagement on multi-day event representation.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not name hydropower or pumped storage explicitly, but energy-limited and storage resources are a central topic. The accreditation methodology and the 18% winter adjustment apply to any resource with multi-hour duration and energy limitations, including pumped-storage hydro and run-of-river generators during high-flow seasons. The stakes are direct: the weighting of historical weather years, the model's treatment of multi-day charging windows, the baseline MRIC calculation, and the final adjustment formula will set the seasonal capacity prices (MRIC values) on which PSH and energy-limited hydro depend for seasonal revenue. Stakeholder pushback on the ISO's load-weighting approach suggests the current proposal may undervalue storage and energy-limited resources relative to firm resources, which could depress PSH capacity accreditation and hence clearing prices. If the ISO's methodology is adopted unchanged, owners of PSH and long-duration hydro facilities should expect lower seasonal-accreditation values than competitors whose input-cost structures align better with the model's assumptions about multi-day event frequency.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Order 2222 compliance filing addresses Electric Distribution Company (EDC) override of Distributed Energy Aggregated Resources (DEARs) and individual DERs during normal operations for distribution safety and reliability. MISO filed tariff language (38.1.1.aa) enabling EDCs to override DEAR physical operation and require the Distributed Energy Resource Aggregator (DERA) to update bidding parameters (economic limits, emergency limits, ramp rates, dispatch and commitment status) in response. The document discusses when EDC override should be used (FERC cites distribution line faults/outages; stakeholder feedback added safety, equipment protection, voltage/thermal limits, outage restoration, and planned work), the format and timing for EDC-to-DERA notification, and after-the-fact validation and dispute resolution via meter data and Schedule 12/38.7.D. documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, Order 2222 aggregation rules apply to DERs including small hydropower facilities when enrolled in a DEAR. The EDC override framework creates a new operational constraint: a DERA managing small hydro (or any aggregated resource) must respond to distribution-level dispatch orders that may conflict with RTO scheduling, reducing the aggregator's ability to optimize dispatch for energy or ancillary-service revenue. The update-offer-parameters requirement means small hydro or other DERs lose dispatch autonomy during override periods, and metering/settlement disputes under the new Schedules could create revenue-recognition or performance-assessment risks for small aggregators not previously subject to this level of distribution-system intervention.

documents.ai_summary: NAESB is developing business-practice standards for DER registry interoperability in coordination with RTO/ISO working groups. Following April 2026 discussion at NERC working groups, NAESB decided to proceed with business-practice standards first and reconsider a centralized registry later in the year. The September 2026 completion date may influence when RTOs finalize their own Order 2222 compliance rules affecting small hydro.
