Projects must submit one-line diagrams with detailed electrical component data, steady-state models (PSSE 35.6.4 .sav/.raw/.idv/.sld files), short-circuit models (ASPEN 15.9 .olr/.chf files), and dynamic models (PSSE 35.6.4 .dyr files using standard library models or documented exceptions). Usability tests include 20-second flat-run tests at nominal and reactive-power-limit conditions, 9-cycle three-phase fault ride-through tests at two short-circuit ratios (SCR=3 and SCR=10), and short-circuit criteria requiring non-tripping performance for single-phase, two-phase, and three-phase faults. Projects must also satisfy NERC PRC-024 protection settings, transmission operator (LIPA and Con Edison) specific fault ride-through and reactive power capability requirements, and primary frequency response droop and deadband criteria. Where modeling data is inconsistent with the validated Interconnection Request, the request is the data of record.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydro directly but establishes mandatory modeling and testing standards that apply to all generator and storage projects entering NYISO's interconnection queue, including hydro and pumped-storage facilities. Hydro operators must ensure dynamic models capture ride-through behavior, frequency response capabilities, and reactive-power injection characteristics at specified fault levels and short-circuit ratios to pass usability testing before cluster study advancement. The requirement that projects not trip during fault events and meet specific VCCS and frequency-response parameters will affect project design and control-system development, potentially requiring equipment upgrades or detailed transient modeling for conventional hydro units.

documents.title: 03 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment: Preliminary Results - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's Reliability Needs Assessment identifies a multi-GW resource-adequacy deficiency driven by large-load growth and aging-generation risk, affecting long-term supply scarcity and the value of available generation resources; transmission constraints in NYC and Lower Hudson Valley also raise locational value of existing resources.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2026 RNA presents preliminary base-case results for years 2030–2036 showing statewide resource-adequacy LOLE violations beginning in 2033 (0.115 event-days/year) and worsening to 0.596 event-days/year by 2036. Key drivers include approximately 2,700 MW of proposed large-load additions by 2036, planned retirement of 517 MW of NYPA small gas plants after 2030, and approximately 2,600 MW of aging-generation risk. NYC transmission security margins are deficient by ~130 MW in 2031, growing to over 1,800 MW by 2036; Lower Hudson Valley shows ~300 MW deficiency in 2032 growing to over 2,000 MW by 2036, primarily following NYPA small-plant retirement and unavailability of Gowanus and Narrows barges. Statewide, approximately 1,850 MW of compensatory capacity would be required to meet the adequacy criterion if distributed proportionally across zones. The RNA study timeline shows draft report and stakeholder review in September, with final approvals scheduled for October–November 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Long-duration resource scarcity—driven by load growth, retirements, and aging risks—raises the energy and capacity value of all available dispatchable generation including conventional hydro and pumped-storage resources. The NYC and Lower Hudson Valley locational deficiencies, which persist even accounting for emergency assistance and operating procedures, suggest that resources capable of serving those constrained zones will attract higher locational revenues in capacity and energy markets. Hydro owners should monitor whether these identified needs drive either accelerated investment in new resources (raising competition) or preferential accreditation/valuation of flexible, available capacity in the deficient zones (raising hydro value).

documents.title: 04 Large Load FERC Show Cause Order: Updated
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document establishes interconnection and operational procedures for large and co-located loads in NYISO, which affects transmission service availability, cost allocation, operational requirements, and strategic positioning for all resources including conventional and pumped-storage hydro.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO issued procedures responding to FERC's June 2026 Show Cause Order on large load integration. The procedures establish two new interconnection pathways: Bulk Electric Large Load (BELL) for loads ≥50 MW at voltages >69 kV, and Bulk Operating Load Tracking (BOLT) for loads 10–50 MW. BELL includes a 90-day screening and modeling period, 90-day system impact study, and alternative upgrades evaluation; loads may take firm withdrawal service (no curtailment restrictions) or non-firm withdrawal service (subject to $200/MWh mandatory bid cap curtailment). Co-located loads with generation at the same point of interconnection can net injection and withdrawal, though FERC directed elimination of cross-subsidy by requiring gross-demand charging for regulation and black-start service. Transmission customer must provide hourly load forecasts, real-time telemetry, and accept remote-disconnect capability and ramp-rate constraints. Large loads may partner with proposed generators in the same capacity region to mitigate resource-adequacy impacts. NYISO's compliance filing deadline is August 17, 2026, but may request an abeyance extending it to November 16, 2026. Written feedback requested by July 27, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or pumped-storage resources. However, the order has direct implications: (1) non-firm withdrawal service with a $200/MWh mandatory bid cap creates a new curtailment product that will compete for scarcity rents with ancillary services and energy revenue from conventional and pumped-storage resources during tight conditions; (2) the requirement that co-located loads be charged on a gross-demand basis for regulation and black-start eliminates a netting opportunity that may have previously allowed hybrid or adjacent generation to offset costs, establishing precedent for how NYISO treats co-located and adjacent resources more broadly; and (3) the firm versus non-firm distinction allocates transmission rights based on resource adequacy screening, which may pressure legacy generation (including existing hydro plants serving regional adequacy) if load growth accelerates faster than modeled. The operational requirements (ramp rates, ride-through, remote disconnect) are general rules applied to large loads; they set the operational bar for grid-following devices and may inform future standards for synchronous and energy-limited resources.

documents.title: 20260722 PSC Item 04a MTEP26 Voltage Stability Analysis Results
documents.filename: 20260722 PSC Item 04a MTEP26 Voltage Stability Analysis Results.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Voltage stability constraints on interregional transfer capacity directly affect hydro's dispatchability and revenue opportunity, especially when coal retirements upstream eliminate reactive-power support that hydro and synchronous resources normally provide.
documents.ai_summary: MISO completed voltage-stability analysis for MTEP26 under two transfer scenarios: Manitoba Hydro/US Interface (export from Minnesota and North Dakota to Manitoba, 2031 winter, limiting voltage-stability transfer level 540 MW) and Illinois Import (MISO Classic to Illinois under Illinois' 2040 coal-retirement mandate, 2031 and 2036 summer peak). Illinois Import study built two retirement scenarios (best-case: smallest reactive-power generator retires first; worst-case: largest retires first) to show voltage-stability transfer-level sensitivity. Results showed worst-case scenario in 2031 summer reduces voltage-stability transfer level to 4,780 MW (less than half the best-case 10,250 MW). Next steps: March 11 MISO proposes voltage-stability scope to PSC, March 27 stakeholder feedback deadline, April 29 scope finalized, April 30 study begins, July 22 results presented (today), September 2 remaining results presented, September 30 final report posted.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower resources by name; it addresses voltage stability as a transmission-constraint mechanism. Voltage-stability binding in Illinois Import scenarios driven by coal-unit retirement reflects loss of synchronous-machine reactive-power supply. Where synchronous coal units retire, voltage support must come from other sources—hydro and pumped-storage units are the primary existing synchronous resources in the footprint. Tighter voltage-stability constraints reduce maximum transfer limits into load pockets, which can reduce arbitrage revenue for generators selling into importing regions and may increase must-dispatch pressure in export regions where hydro assets are concentrated (particularly Manitoba interface scenarios). The worst-case vs. best-case spread (4,780 MW vs. 10,250 MW in 2031) shows how sensitive transfer capacity is to reactive-resource composition, raising the question whether MISO will compensate synchronous-resource owners for reactive-power provision as coal exits the system.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's proposal to expand transmission service exemptions for electric storage resources (ESR) charging when economically dispatched establishes precedent for how use-limited resources like pumped-storage hydro are treated in transmission charges and market participation rules.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to exempt Electric Storage Resource (ESR) charging from transmission service requirements (TSR) when ESR transactions are offered with Economic dispatch status and provide grid services such as regulation, ramping, or energy-market participation—distinguishing economically-dispatched ESR from self-scheduled or traditional load. ESR charging with Self-Schedule dispatch status will continue to require TSR. The proposal aligns with FERC Order 841 and 841-A guidance that ESR providing grid services should not bear the same transmission charges as end-use load. MISO will move the proposal from the Planning Subcommittee to the PAC in August 2026, with a feedback deadline of August 7, 2026, and targets tariff filing by end of 2026. MISO will separately record and audit ESR charging and discharging to ensure operation continues as a grid service, with potential penalties including market removal for violation.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage hydro. However, it establishes a precedent for how use-limited resources that charge from the grid are treated under transmission-cost causation principles. PSH operators face similar questions about when charging should be exempt from TSR—the distinction MISO draws between economically-dispatched ESR (exempted) and self-scheduled ESR (charged) may serve as a model or comparison point if PSH participation rules are revisited. The principle that charging for grid services differs from load consumption could favor PSH revenue under future market-design changes, but the audit and penalty provisions for verifying grid-service operation also signal tighter compliance monitoring for storage-type resources generally.

documents.filename: 20260722 PSC Item 04c Revising MTEP Sensitivities for NERC TPL.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's revision of 2-year MTEP winter-peak sensitivities to incorporate low renewable scenarios (wind at 30%) directly touches transmission planning and capacity-adequacy modeling, which shape the location and timing of transmission-dependent resources' access to markets and scarcity conditions affecting hydro revenue.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to update its 2027 MTEP (Multi-Year Transmission Plan) sensitivities for NERC TPL (Transmission Planning and Protection) compliance by incorporating a winter peak scenario with reduced wind output (30% capacity factor vs. the prior 67% baseline), while maintaining 0% solar. The analysis demonstrates that lower wind output increases the severity of reliability violations in the 2-year winter case. MISO will implement a full set of revised sensitivity scenarios across 2-year, 5-year, and 10-year time horizons, with updates to the Planning Model Manual redlines presented to the Market User Group; no Business Practice Manual updates were identified as required. The contact for this work is Joseph Dunn at MISO.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's BAL-001-TRE evaluation process establishes a rolling 12-month performance scorecard for all generating units' primary frequency response during Frequency Measurable Events (FMEs). Resources must maintain a rolling average PFR score of 0.75 or above; those failing to meet this threshold or scoring below 0.75 for three consecutive FMEs become subject to reduction in their Ramping Reserve Service (RRS) MW allocation based on past performance. Market participants have 30 days from MIS posting to request exclusions for legitimate operating conditions that impaired normal PFR performance; ERCOT makes final determinations, though the PDCWG may be asked to advise. This scheme links frequency-response performance directly to reserve-service capability — a dispatchable resource's ability to provide RRS is capped by its demonstrated PFR capability during disturbances, creating a performance-based ratchet on flexibility services.

documents.title: Revised Straw Proposal - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track-2 - Jul 17, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The proposal directly changes hydro's resource-adequacy availability incentive mechanism (RAAIM), outage definitions, must-offer obligations, and substitute-capacity procurement processes that govern how conventional hydropower and PSH operators get paid for and manage their RA capacity and forced/planned outages.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design (RAMPD) Track 2 Revised Straw Proposal (July 17, 2026) proposes replacing the current static, monthly RAAIM structure with an event-based availability framework that assesses availability during periods of elevated reliability risk rather than averaging across all availability assessment hours in a month. The proposal introduces three outage classifications — planned (maintenance/construction with advance notice), urgent (increased risk but still operable), and forced (little/no notice) — and eliminates short-notice opportunity outages. It proposes a "shopping cart" workflow for substitute-capacity trading among scheduling coordinators (displayed in CIRA with seller confirmation) rather than ISO-centralized matching, and revises must-offer and RAAIM settlement rules so resources are penalized only on shown RA capacity, not on capacity above their shown RA. Comments on the proposal are due August 5, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: Conventional hydropower, being inherently use-limited and weather-dependent, is highly sensitive to changes in when availability is assessed and how forced outages are treated in RA revenue. The shift from monthly averaging to event-based assessment during stressed-system conditions could concentrate RAAIM penalties on the hours hydro actually needs to be on-line (typically summer peaks), rather than diluting them across the whole month; this could either increase or decrease a hydro owner's exposure depending on how the final "elevated reliability risk" periods are defined. The new urgent-outage category and elimination of short-notice opportunity outages may reduce hydro's flexibility to take unplanned maintenance on short notice without RA penalty, making forced-outage rates and substitute-capacity costs more material to revenue; conversely, the revised RAAIM rule limiting penalties to shown RA (not MOO) could reduce exposure if a plant shows less than its full nameplate. The substitute-capacity shopping-cart mechanism replaces bilateral searching with a platform tool, but the document does not specify whether hydro, as a fast-ramping resource, would face different availability-assessment hours or outage-substitution priorities than thermal or battery resources.

documents.title: Presentation - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track 2 - Jul 22, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's revised RAAIM (Resource Availability and Accuracy Incentive Mechanism) directly reshapes penalty exposure and revenue-recovery allocation for hydropower and storage resources during stress events, moving from a monthly netted assessment to per-event tiered triggers that substantially increase payoff volatility and compliance burden for use-limited resources.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes overhauling its RAAIM availability-penalty mechanism, replacing a $4.40/kW-month fixed charge assessed over monthly AAH windows with event-based tiered pricing: Tier 1 (Elevated Reliability Risk) at day-ahead LMP, and Tier 2 (Critical Capacity Insufficiency, keyed to EDAM RSE failures) at $2,000/MWh. Hydro, storage, VERs, thermal, and DR would receive technology-specific treatment: hydro and thermal face shown-RA-based availability assessment against bids and outage status; storage's obligation is tied to SDM-modeled feasibility limits and SOC nonlinearity (not automatic outage exposure); VERs are exempted from low-wind/solar/ambient variability but remain exposed for forced equipment outages. Co-located and hybrid resources receive configuration-specific rules. The proposal eliminates the <1 MW exemption and tightens exemptions overall. Stakeholder feedback flagged that storage and hydro need duration, state-of-charge, and hydrologic limits recognized; that Tier 2 exposure should reflect cost causation not any EDAM failure; and that penalty exposure must not exceed shown RA. No vote or comment deadline is stated in this presentation; next steps are listed as pending.

documents.title: WPTF Presentation - UCAP Implementation and RAAIM - Jul 22, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: UCAP implementation and RAAIM redesign directly affect how CAISO accredits and pays hydro/PSH capacity in resource-adequacy showings, and how availability is measured and penalized — touching both the accreditation revenue stream (through changes to counting rules, must-offer obligations, and deliverability ceilings) and compliance obligations (RAAIM performance metrics and penalty exposure).
documents.ai_summary: WPTF presents CAISO's path to implement CPUC-adopted UCAP (Unforced Capacity) methodology for 2028 RA year, arguing that CAISO must define separate capacity values post-UCAP — Pmax, PmaxRA (deliverable accredited capacity), LRA-specific QC, maximum NQC, and shown RA — because one value cannot serve every CAISO function (forward counting, deliverability studies, must-offer formulas, RAAIM exposure, exports, and backstop procurement) without double-counting or losing capability. On RAAIM, WPTF argues the current design does not need redesign: forced-outage data show no correlation with load or prices, UCAP itself does not justify price increases, and a 94.5% monthly availability floor is conceptually consistent with UCAP's removal of expected outages from the forward MW value. The presentation urges CAISO to establish demonstrated failure (via resource availability trends, substitution-request analysis, and event-level causation) before changing RAAIM penalties or exposures. This touches hydro and PSH by redefining which capacity value applies to RA accreditation, must-offer, and RAAIM calculations — especially for partially deliverable resources and storage with variable seasonal contribution — and by proposing to keep RAAIM pricing unchanged while clarifying what 'shown RA' means, which will determine both the compliance exposure and the RA revenue hydro owners receive in forward showings.

documents.title: Straw Proposal - Storage Design and Modeling - Uplift, Default Energy Bids, and State-of-Charge Management - July 15, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO straw proposal on storage default energy bids, uplift, and state-of-charge bidding paradigms directly addresses revenue mechanisms (bid cost recovery, default energy bid methodology, opportunity-cost pricing) that apply to storage resources generally, including pumped-storage hydro, and establishes market-design precedent for how dispatchable, use-limited resources participate in the ISO market.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes enhancements to storage resource participation in energy and ancillary-services markets through three pathways: (1) replacement of the current static storage default energy bid with a time-of-day approach that incorporates temporal cost differentiation while remaining administratively implementable; (2) extension of default energy bid rules to hybrid resources using a "greater-of" method based on the highest-cost component with minimum-share guardrails; and (3) a reframing of non-generator resource bidding to allow storage to submit a single terminal state-of-charge bid reflecting willingness to pay/accept for ending an optimization period with higher or lower energy stored, relative to a reference state, rather than interval-by-interval bid curves. The ISO sequences default energy bid and bidding-structure improvements as near-term work, with a comprehensive uplift (bid cost recovery) redesign to follow by end of 2026. Comments are due August 5, 2026, following stakeholder discussion on July 22, 2026.
documents.hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly; however, it addresses storage resource market participation rules that apply categorically to all use-limited storage, which includes conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities. The three proposed changes would affect how storage operators recover costs and value state-of-charge opportunity costs: default energy bid improvements would permit more frequent cost reassessment reflecting daily price variation (directly important for run-of-river and seasonal hydro), the hybrid framework would govern hydro paired with solar or wind, and the terminal state-of-charge bidding concept would replace the current hourly bidding structure with a single value-of-energy offer that propagates backward through dispatch optimization. The sequencing of default energy bid reform ahead of uplift redesign signals that CAISO is treating marginal-cost recovery as foundational to any future changes to bid cost recovery policy—a framework within which conventional hydro has historically received mitigation treatment as a canonical use-limited resource. The reframing concept would also change how day-ahead and real-time dispatch treat state-of-charge deviation, potentially affecting the price-following incentives that hydro operators currently use to manage storage-like flexibility.

documents.title: Presentation - Storage Design and Modeling - Jul 22, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO is redesigning default energy bids for storage and hybrids, which directly affects the opportunity-cost offer framework for pumped storage and creates a precedent being leveraged across EDAM/WEIM; storage DEB is the primary mitigation-compliant bidding pathway for PSH and energy-limited resources.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO is evaluating two methodologies to reform storage default energy bids (DEBs): a time-of-day approach that incorporates hydro DEB elements with hourly multipliers (1.4 pre-opportunity-cost hour, 1.0 after) and a static hydro-based approach. The time-of-day approach, currently preferred by CAISO, applies upward-only scaling of price proxies and addresses a core PSH challenge—that current static DEBs using day-ahead LMPs become 'stale' in real-time and prevent WEIM-only storage from accessing the DEB option at all. The time-of-day approach enables WEIM-only resources to use real-time DGAP and LMP scaling, and extends this framework consistently across EDAM and WEIM. A revised straw proposal is due September 2, 2026, with comments due September 30, 2026; final proposal is targeted for October 28, 2026. Pumped storage operators reliant on negotiated DEBs or using stale price proxies gain material upside if the time-of-day approach adopts the 1.4 multiplier on opportunity cost; conversely, stakeholders opposing time-of-day multipliers below 1.0 or favoring simpler hydro-based static methods will shape whether the structure is simplified or retained.

No immediate member action specified, but the summary establishes operational baseline and BAA governance context for West-region hydro owners.

documents.ai_summary: SPP filed for an April 1, 2027 go-live date for FERC Order 881 (Attachment AJ), deferring the October 2027 date ORWG had recommended. Order 881 introduces Advanced Auctioning and Ramping Interchange Tool for Flexibility (AARs), a grid-enhancing technology that co-optimizes energy and ramping products in real-time. SPP reports 89% production-readiness for April implementation and cites data showing most transmission assets can operate with AARs, capturing monthly reliability and market-efficiency benefits sooner than October. Key implementation risks remain: software delivery and system integration (HIGH), member participation and readiness (MEDIUM), and sufficient parallel-operations duration to validate system reliability (WATCH). Hydro operators in SPP will see energy and ramping prices reformulated under AAR logic beginning April 2027 — the primary revenue mechanism changes; most affected are reservoir and run-of-river hydro supplying flexibility during real-time dispatch.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal, with Q2 2027 effective date, introduces seasonal capacity procurement tied to accreditation reforms and a winter gas constraint. The document clarifies offer-formulation principles for resources whose accreditation (MRIC) differs from installed capacity, showing that resources exiting energy markets without a capacity sales obligation would face higher per-MW offer prices under MRIC-based accreditation than under prior QC methods. For imports and energy-limited resources, CAR-SA requires demonstration of 16-hour fuel availability for accreditation; external resources using stored fuel must show historical usable-inventory measures over past three like-seasons. Capacity Offers may include risk premia for pay-for-performance (PFP) costs, and the ISO is publishing offer-formulation guidance (contact: Jasleen Singh, jsingh@iso-ne.com) with questions due by the August Markets Committee. Most exposed are operators of energy-limited hydro and storage whose accreditation drops relative to summer nameplate, forcing higher per-MW asks in seasonal auctions to recover fixed obligations.

documents.title: 2026-07-21 MC A03b - CAR-SA: Offer Formulation Memo
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This memo directly addresses offer formulation rules for ISO-NE's Capacity Auction and Resource (CAR) market, which determines how resources—including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities—calculate and submit capacity bids; the rules govern the cost basis (incremental costs, opportunity costs from Pay for Performance, annual-cost allocation) that hydro operators must use to stay competitive and avoid mitigation challenges, and it explicitly addresses the interaction between offer formulation and market-power mitigation thresholds.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has issued a detailed guidance memo on how Capacity Resources should formulate competitive offers under the CAR-SA (Seasonal Accreditation) framework. The memo teaches that a competitive offer must equal the resource's expected incremental cost of accepting a Capacity Supply Obligation, including the opportunity cost of the PfP (Pay for Performance) scarcity-condition obligation and the cost of any annual-basis expenses allocated across seasonal offerings. The guidance explicitly advises market participants to consult the Internal Market Monitor (IMM) before submitting offers that may exceed the Capacity Offer Price Threshold or involve resource-specific concerns such as risk modeling or annual-cost treatment; the IMM cannot direct offer prices but can validate cost assumptions and whether expectations are reasonably justified. This creates a new compliance pathway for hydro and PSH owners in ISO-NE: operators allocating multi-year capex or seasonal energy availability into capacity-offer costs will need to pre-clear their methodology with the IMM to avoid triggering mitigation and price caps. The memo is comprehensive reference material (no vote or deadline stated) suitable for long-term corpus use by NHA members evaluating ISO-NE's cost-substantiation regime.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's Internal Market Monitor reports that Winter 2026 (Dec 2025–Feb 2026) saw record $6.5 billion wholesale costs, with energy prices reaching $147.99/MWh day-ahead and $137.66/MWh real-time, driven by a 19-day cold snap in late January and 31% year-over-year rise in natural gas prices to $17.79/MMBtu. Opportunity-cost adders (EMOC) preserved 433 GWh of oil generation by allowing offers over the soft cap to $460/MWh day-ahead during scarcity. The NECEC transmission line (in service Jan. 16) initially improved day-ahead prices but caused poor day-ahead-to-real-time convergence during the cold snap; Quebec imports reversed during peak cold, forcing New England to export briefly. For hydro operators, the data illustrates how scarcity pricing and opportunity-cost mechanisms reward withholding of use-limited resources, how transmission reconfigurations (NECEC, LNG injection swings) reshape import/export flows and local clearing patterns, and how interregional cold events can reverse import directions — all material to hydro's revenue and positioning in regional exchange markets. documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes adding an optional MUI/API parameter called 'Ambient Capacity Adjustment' to allow market participants to submit hourly ambient derates (such as temperature-dependent derate for thermal generators, but applicable to any resource with ambient sensitivity) rather than forcing them through the CROW system, which has technical volume limits. Currently, derates affecting must-offer calculations must be submitted in CROW at high frequency, risking dataflow congestion; the MUI already handles hourly resource data for Markets+, so SPP recommends shifting hourly/frequent ambient derates there while keeping longer-term forced outages in CROW. The proposal was presented to MORWG on May 27, 2026, and will be presented to MRATF on July 20, 2026, with protocol updates and an MIR (Markets+ Issue Resolution) to follow. The analysis follows NEPOOL's 2025 priority request and builds on FERC Order 2023 compliance filings (May 2024, accepted by FERC in 2025) that allowed surplus service to be used immediately upon interconnection agreement execution. Part 1 identifies rule gaps; Part 2 (separate document) addresses market participation models for co-located resources. Current rules limit surplus service to affiliates or third parties with original customer consent, exclude retiring/repowering facilities, and require commercial operation status for CNR (capacity) service. Hydro owners considering uprates, pumped-storage additions, or hybrid development at existing sites should review stakeholder discussions at NEPOOL Transmission Committee and watch for gap-analysis conclusions and proposed tariff solutions, which will shape interconnection timelines and costs for co-located projects.

documents.title: 2026-07-16 TC A04.2 New England Large & Co-Located Loads Show Cause Order (EL26-72) Compliance: Informational Report on Resource Adequacy
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large-load growth and co-located load interconnection directly expand the addressable market for hydro's energy and flexibility products, while capacity-market and energy-price signals discussed here determine hydro's revenue sustainability and new-entry incentives.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE filed a FERC compliance report (EL26-72) on resource adequacy for large loads (particularly data centers) entering New England. The report affirms that existing competitive energy and capacity markets are well-positioned to attract new supply and retain the existing fleet, citing forward energy prices currently near or at cost-of-entry for new generation. ISO-NE describes several market-refinement projects underway: reductions to the Pay-for-Performance penalty rate (which disproportionately burdens slow-start resources), Capacity Auction Reforms affecting accreditation methodology, improvements to Surplus Interconnection Service, probabilistic forecasting, and uncertainty reserves. For hydro owners, the key mechanics are (1) large-load growth will tighten energy markets and raise scarcity pricing, especially in winter when data centers compete with heating load; (2) co-location rules and interconnection protocols being developed will determine whether hydro can serve load behind-the-meter or tap surplus interconnection at existing plants; (3) PFP rate reduction and CONE updates directly affect the capacity revenues hydro operators depend on for fleet retention; and (4) probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty reserves may create new ramping/flexibility product opportunities. The report signals ISO-NE's expectation of tariff amendments to facilitate large-load entry and expects these changes to be completed within the ongoing stakeholder process.

documents.title: New Issue - Non Firm Large Load
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Non-firm large-load participation design directly affects hydro's resource adequacy accreditation, curtailment exposure, and transmission service value; load growth and co-located demand are strategic options that amplify scarcity and change the value of existing hydro capacity.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes a new Non-Firm Large Load participation option allowing large loads to interconnect ahead of firm transmission-service availability, with the understanding that these loads would be curtailed under grid-reliability-risk conditions. The proposal covers energy and ancillary service participation, resource adequacy accounting, transmission and planning, cost allocation, and curtailment procedures — currently at issue-submission stage with no stated deadline. MECHANISM: Non-firm load participation raises two direct concerns for hydro owners. First, if non-firm large loads are NOT counted toward resource-adequacy requirements (or counted with heavy discounts), the RA bar for other resources including hydro rises, while loads receiving scarcity benefit bear no capacity obligation — this inverts normal cost-allocation. Second, if non-firm loads ARE curtailed preferentially during scarcity events, hydro operators face reduced dispatch value in real-time scarcity periods, since the non-firm load absorbs the curtailment instead of pushing higher locational prices. MISO's design choices on RA treatment and curtailment-dispatch rules will determine whether non-firm loads are free-riders on hydro's scarcity value or are appropriately penalized. This affects all hydro in MISO, particularly reservoir and run-of-river operators in tight seasonal periods.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: BITS enables large loads to interconnect and ramp into service on an interim basis while transmission upgrades are constructed, directly affecting hydro's strategic options for co-located load service, behind-the-meter arrangements, and the economics of load growth as a driver of scarcity value.
documents.ai_summary: Alliant Energy proposes Bridge Interim Transmission Service (BITS), a non-firm interim transmission product for large loads in MISO that allows service to begin once load interconnection studies are complete and local facilities are built, while required network upgrades are under construction—automatically converting to firm Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) when upgrades finish. BITS requires load to have metering and telemetry in place, 24/7 contact availability, and ability to reduce load in 30 minutes if curtailed; loads are backed by accredited capacity resources and included in Module E forecasts. This removes a timing mismatch that has deterred large-load interconnection: hydro owners co-locating loads or offering behind-the-meter service can now ramp customers into service faster, capturing scarcity premiums from load growth without waiting years for transmission buildout. The proposal aligns with FERC's Large Load Show Cause Order (EL26-70) for MISO; Alliant seeks stakeholder feedback by August 7, 2026, and proposes FERC filing in Q4 2026 with implementation March 2027.

Stakeholder feedback on tariff language and process details is due July 30, 2026, with filings on interconnection reliability requirements and ZGIA registration expected July 31, 2026. The Firm Service Step-Up and non-firm service options, combined with co-location rules, could enable pumped-storage and conventional hydro operators to participate as flexible resources backing large-load commitments or to co-locate generation with load behind a single point of interconnection—expanding the strategic toolkit for hydro assets in MISO, particularly those seeking firm transmission service without full generation-only interconnection costs.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes a new streamlined process for studying large loads (250+ MW+) paired with associated generation in parallel, rather than sequentially, aiming to achieve MTEP approval and full study completion within 120 days (vs. 180+ days in current serial process). Outcomes include allocation of generation injection rights, transmission service for reliable load withdrawal, and optimized network upgrades; the proposal harmonizes with FERC's show-cause order (Paragraphs 114–118) on efficient infrastructure build to support large loads. The process imposes a $250,000 nonrefundable application fee per party, requires generation ≤150% of identified load need with firm offtake agreement, full site control through point of interconnection, and ability to reach commercial operation within 3 years; generation must transition to normal interconnection queue if load goes away. This is particularly relevant to pumped-storage and large hydro operators evaluating co-location with industrial or data-center loads—the faster study and clearer transmission-cost allocation could unlock new partnership models—and to all hydro owners tracking transmission-planning acceleration and the precedent it sets for generation-load nexus outside traditional firm-injection assumptions. Stakeholder feedback due July 30, 2026; tariff filing expected September 2026.

The redline governs how all generators—including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities—qualify for interconnection, achieve Commercial Operation Date certainty, manage contingent facilities in the interconnection queue, and access surplus capacity from existing generators. For hydro owners, the GIP redline is material to understanding cost responsibility for upgrades, queue certainty, and whether existing hydro plants can offer surplus interconnection service to new resources—critical for uprate projects and for existing plants seeking revenue from hosting junior queued resources.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is developing a new Large Load BPM-032 (Business Practices Manual) and related tariff framework to govern interconnection and operational reliability requirements for large load customers, with a hub-and-spoke implementation model where the Large Load BPM sets requirements and existing BPMs (BPM-020, BPM-013, BPM-031, BPM-025, BPM-002) supply supporting processes. The framework covers the full interconnection lifecycle from design through in-service operations, with initial focus on interconnection reliability and operational requirements; future phases will address stability assessment, oscillation, PMU, and compliance monitoring. MISO's Tariff filing is targeted for July 2026, and the BPM portfolio is scheduled for finalization by October 1, 2026, with LLWG review cycles on August 27 (first draft) and mid-September (near-final). For hydro and PSH owners, this matters because large industrial loads competing for interconnection queue positions, transmission capacity, and grid reliability resources (particularly voltage support and ride-through capability) may face new facility-data, modeling, and operational verification requirements that shift cost allocation or delay service commencement—affecting the economics of co-located or adjacent hydro/PSH interconnections and increasing modeling/compliance burden on existing hydro plants if brought into Large Load validation scopes.

documents.ai_summary: MISO establishes detailed network and commercial modeling requirements for large load facilities (those where a single breaker opening/closing changes load by >50 MW), requiring explicit device-level representation of generators, battery-energy storage systems, and demand-response resources rather than aggregation. Behind-the-meter generation ≥5 MW must be individually metered and modeled; generation at large-load facilities can participate in markets via traditional GIA, pseudo market generation, or ZGIA (zero-injection generation interconnection), with dispatch instructions flowing through MISO's centralized mechanism. Large loads must establish separate CPNodes (pricing/settlement nodes) to prevent load-distribution skew between day-ahead and real-time models. This directly affects hydro owners with co-located generation or storage at large industrial facilities—they face clearer rules on whether plant-level generation participates in MISO markets or remains behind-the-meter, and how storage (BESS) and ramp-support devices are metered and dispatched. Feedback is due Monday, July 31, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: MISO has launched its 2026 Long-Range Transmission Planning (LRTP) process for the Midwest and South regions, with issue identification and solutions development following a seven-step process; solutions proposals are anticipated in 2027. The LRTP will assess reliability and load-serving needs across a 20-year horizon (CAGR ~1.5% annually) using Future 2 and 3+ scenarios that show resource and energy adequacy under MISO's 1-in-10-years Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) criterion. Hydro owners' revenue and dispatch flexibility are affected because transmission bottlenecks identified in LRTP feed into the solutions phase — constraints on interregional transfers or load pockets in the South region (Louisiana/Texas) directly impact where MISO can call on existing hydro for scarcity pricing and ramping services, and load growth shapes the baseline scarcity against which hydro's flexibility premium is valued. Feedback on Future scenarios is due June 17, 2026; solutions will be developed in 2027, making this the foundational study for MISO transmission expansion over the next decade.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is revising its interconnection study process (PAC-2024-3) to replace Summer Shoulder charging cases with Light Load charging cases and will continue studying storage charging across all three phases of the Definitive Planning Process (DPP). This affects pumped-storage operators by expanding the operational scenarios in which their charging patterns are studied during interconnection, reducing prior constraints on when PSH charging can be evaluated. Simultaneously, MISO is updating its Long-Range Transmission Plan (LRTP) base topology using the Summer 2035 February Cycle model and requesting stakeholder review of transmission projects 230 kV and above for inclusion; this determines which transmission infrastructure gets planned around PSH and conventional hydro export capability. The PAC will review the BPM revisions in July 2026.

documents.ai_summary: MISO finalized tariff and business-practice-manual changes to its MHVDC interconnection procedure and clarified Necessary versus Network Upgrades definitions and Multi-Party Facility Construction Agreement (MPFCA) terms; it also updated Attachment GGG redlines and is targeting two FERC filings in the next 30 days and Q3–Q4 2026. The portal automation system (Generation Interconnection Application Automation, or GIAA) has completed Release 1 (April 2026) and Release 2 (May 2026), with Release 3 scheduled for July 18, September 15, and November 15, 2026; stakeholders requested release notes and front-end sorting/download options. documents.ai_summary: MISO reports four tariff actions in progress: (1) BPM-015 on removing storage charging limitations in generator interconnection agreements, targeted for PAC Q3 approval—directly affecting how pumped-storage hydro can charge in MISO; (2) GI Queue Improvements (Attachment X), Q4 targeted; (3) MISO-SPP JOA updates (Rate Schedule 06), Q3; (4) ZGIA/Large Load definition reassignment to LLWG, with FERC tariff filing planned July 31, 2026. Separately, MISO is filing a 205 tariff change to decouple Affected System study timelines from DPP-2022 and -2023 queue cycles, aiming to avoid 30–90 day Phase 2 delays and cascading queue congestion. Storage accreditation studies for all four Futures scenarios continue, with final values expected end of summer 2026—these will establish RA accreditation for storage in MISO's long-range transmission plan. The document signals MISO's intent to accelerate interconnection processing and modernize storage-charging treatment, but hydro and PSH owners should track Q3 PAC outcomes on BPM-015 and monitor the 205 filing timeline (end of July) for queue-acceleration details.

documents.title: Item 04b – Michael Kurtz Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: PJM's proposed bifurcated capacity market directly affects how existing hydro and PSH generators are paid for capacity — the proposal would maintain short-term pricing with caps/floors for existing resources (including hydro) while creating uncapped long-term auctions for new entry, fundamentally altering existing-resource revenue certainty and scarcity pricing signals in a resource-constrained era.
documents.ai_summary: Michael Kurtz (Boehm, Kurtz & Lowry) presents a proposal to modify PJM's Path A, Option 2 capacity-market reform by creating a bifurcated market: a 'Legacy Auction' with one-year auctions and maintained price caps/floors for existing generation (projected 95.4% of capacity), and a 'Reliability Auction' with no price caps/floors for new generation (projected 4.6%), with blended pricing passed to non-Reliability-Backstop consumers. The proposal is framed as a middle path between PJM's conclusion that even $625/MW-day may be insufficient to attract new entry (versus real-world CC financing needing $633–$2,070/MW-day) and the risk of paying existing generators the premium needed for new construction, which Kurtz argues would constitute a windfall and violate the just-and-reasonable standard under the Federal Power Act. Existing hydro and pumped-storage generators would remain under the capped short-term regime, preserving their current rate treatment but constraining their upside if scarcity pricing rises; the proposal is presented to PJM's PRTMDW (Pricing, Risk and Transmission Market Design Working Group) on July 15, 2026, and reflects ongoing PJM resource-adequacy tensions triggered by supply-demand gaps and data-center load growth.

documents.title: Item 01a – Ron Mcnamara Phd Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Addresses PJM capacity adequacy and investment dynamics in a scarcity-driven environment shaped by data-center load growth and accelerated retirements — directly affecting hydro revenue through capacity-market pricing, resource-adequacy constructs, and the strategic value of dispatchable generation.
documents.ai_summary: Ron McNamara (First Principles Economics) presents a conceptual framework for PJM's capacity adequacy problem to the PRTMDW, arguing the root issue is inadequate investment, not market design per se. He emphasizes that restructured markets eliminated the guaranteed cost-recovery and stable counterparty that regulation provided, forcing capacity investment to compete as economic/commercial ventures bearing price, policy, and rule-change risks — a fundamentally different risk profile than pre-restructuring. McNamara recommends PJM adopt an agreed end-state vision (5–20 year horizon) against which all capacity proposals should be evaluated, with preferences for decentralized solutions and accelerated permitting/build timelines. The presentation does not propose specific rule changes but frames the investment-scarcity nexus as central to hydro's strategic positioning: in a market now "managing scarcity," the value of reliable, dispatchable generation (hydro's signature) rises, but only if the market and regulatory framework create stable revenue streams and counterparties for that capacity.

documents.title: Item 04b – Bifurcated Capacity Market Under PJM Path A Option 2 – Michael Kurtz Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Proposal to bifurcate PJM's capacity market into separate auctions for existing and new generation directly affects revenue certainty, accreditation mechanics, and pricing for dispatchable resources including hydropower in a scarcity environment.
documents.ai_summary: Michael Kurtz (Ohio Energy Group) presents a proposal to modify PJM Path A, Option 2 by creating a bifurcated capacity market: a "Legacy Auction" continuing short-term (one-year) Base Residual Auction pricing with caps and floors for existing generation, and a separate "Reliability Auction" with uncapped, long-term pricing for new generation. The proposal addresses PJM's transition from surplus to scarcity management—the December 2025 BRA cleared at the $333/MW-day cap with 6,516 MW UCAP below reliability requirement—but avoids paying existing generators the premium long-term rates needed to attract new merchant capacity, instead using RMR authority and flexible pricing floors to retain older dispatchable units. Existing hydro and dispatchable resources would remain on short-term capacity pricing with caps, avoiding windfall effects, while new merchant capacity would access long-term revenue certainty in a separate clearing; a blended wholesale price across both auctions would flow to retail markets. The proposal implicitly treats all dispatchable generation (including existing hydro) as reliability units warranting cost-of-service or floor protection during scarcity, and no vote or comment deadline is stated in the presentation.

documents.title: Item 04c – Initial Considerations And Recommendations – Maryland Opc Presentation

documents.ai_summary: Maryland OPC (Offices of People's Counsel) presents initial recommendations for redesigning PJM's resource adequacy construct, arguing that uncertain large-load growth is artificially inflating capacity procurement requirements and cost allocation. The presentation proposes three design paths—(A) risk allocation, (B) reliability consequences, (C) E&AS reform incentives—and an alternative "Commit-to-be-counted" model requiring large loads to make verifiable capacity commitments, fund/bring new capacity, or accept priority curtailment before being added to shared RA obligations. This reframes the capacity market's demand side from forecasts to binding commitments, directly affecting which resources (dispatchable hydro, PSH, and storage) compete for RA accreditation and what price signals they face when loads have uncertain, non-binding demand profiles. The recommendation prioritizes cost-causation allocation—meaning new large loads, not ordinary customers, absorb reliability and cost risk—which can shift the investment incentive landscape for existing hydro and storage resources competing in capacity auctions.

documents.title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - Scarcity Pricing - Jul 14, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's scarcity pricing proposal directly affects energy price formation during system stress, which is a primary revenue mechanism for hydro and pumped-storage resources that supply emergency flexibility and reserves.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal on scarcity pricing (Day 2 of Phase 2 Price Formation Enhancements, July 14, 2026) modifies two mechanisms: (1) load-shed pricing extends the scarcity signal into both real-time dispatch (RTD) and 15-minute forecasting markets (FMM) when a BAA enters EEA Level 3 emergency and operators shed firm load, treating curtailed load as unserved demand to prevent market prices from collapsing; and (2) armed-reserve pricing adds an opportunity-cost adder in RTD to reflect when reserve capacity is released into energy markets, capturing the scarcity value that the 15-minute ancillary-service procurement (RTPD) process already recognizes. Both mechanisms include operational safeguards: operators can pause either mechanism, and the load-shed signal turns off after four cumulative hours of load shedding in a 24-hour window. The proposal defers comprehensive scarcity redesign to a future phase. Feedback on grouping, CAISO BAA treatment, load-shedding implementation options (verified MW vs. forecast approach), and whether the mechanisms adequately preserve scarcity signals without over-mitigation is requested before the draft final proposal.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal reforms BAA-level MPM by grouping BAAs via Marginal Export Capacity and export-transfer connectivity (instead of testing each in isolation), subtracting interval-specific load-serving obligations from withholdable capacity, and mitigating only pivotal suppliers after a grouped BAA fails the 3PS test. CAISO BAA retains default-competitive status and will not be subject to the BAA-level test as a group — a deferent to concerns that economic intertie imports are undervalued by the current framework. The proposal advances grouping and LSO changes near-term but defers comprehensive scarcity pricing and CAISO BAA mitigation to a broader future phase, with Day 2 stakeholder feedback to focus on scarcity-pricing mechanics, implementation choices, and safeguards. For hydro operators, especially those with multi-BAA footprints or export capability (e.g., Northwest PSH and reservoir operators), the grouping and LSO logic could narrow the suppliers subject to mitigation during tight intervals, raising energy prices and ancillary-service value when genuinely pivotal capacity is constrained — but the deferral of scarcity pricing means no new scarcity-pricing adders are being adopted yet. Most exposed: large dispatchable generators and PSH with withholdable capacity in grouped BAAs; comment deadline not stated in document.

The UDE flag modifies how deviations from dispatch instructions are metered and settled; hydro and other dispatchable resources must now comply with revised settlement rules that took effect June 1, 2026, affecting how they are charged or credited for off-dispatch performance. The mechanism is live; no further stakeholder action is requested, but operators should verify their settlement systems align with the June 1, 2026 rules.

documents.ai_summary: MISO reports quarterly Transmission Customer Metric (TCM) results measuring what portion of day-ahead congestion revenue is returned to transmission customers via ARR/FTR credits versus retained by non-transmission customers. The 2025–2026 planning year shows 60% TCM, with 2026–2027 at 95% (partial-year data through June 29, 2026). The metric tracks total DA congestion revenue ($1.845B in 2025–2026), splits between transmission-customer returns ($1.102B) and non-transmission-customer revenue ($743M). Seasonal variation is substantial: winter 2025 TCM was 50%, while summer 2024 peaked at 92%. This directly impacts reservoir and pumped-storage hydro located in congested zones—a higher TCM means more congestion rent flows back to hydro owners with ARRs, improving revenue from transmission-constrained dispatch; lower TCM diverts that rent elsewhere. The metric has trended upward since 2020 lows (55% in 2020–2021), suggesting improving transmission-customer treatment, but shows high volatility by season and year.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's demand curve updates for regulation, spinning reserves, and up-ramp capability directly affect the ancillary-services revenue hydro operators earn; the co-located resource dispatch rule affects strategic dispatch options for hybrid and co-located hydro; and uninstructed deviation settlement changes alter operational compliance obligations and economic incentives for all dispatchable units including hydro.
documents.ai_summary: MISO filed three tariff changes: (1) Demand Curve update (ER26-2705-000, effective August 4, 2026) revising the demand curves for Regulation and Spinning Reserves and the Up Ramp Capability product in Day-Ahead and Real-Time Markets — hydro's core ancillary-service revenue streams. (2) Interconnection Service Limit Constraint for Co-located Resources (ER26-1915-000, filed 3/25/26, amended 6/11/26 for later implementation) allowing co-located resources to dispatch more efficiently within their interconnection limits — relevant to owners of hybrid hydro-solar or hydro-wind plants seeking optimized dispatch. (3) Uninstructed Deviation Settlement Charges (ER26-1521-000, accepted by FERC 5/29/26, effective 6/1/26) modifying settlement rules to incentivize reduction of uninstructed deviations — affects all dispatchable units including hydro by changing the economic penalty structure for unscheduled output. Ancillary-service demand curves are particularly material to large, responsive generators; co-located rules widen strategic options for mixed-renewable portfolios; uninstructed-deviation incentives reshape operational discipline across all hydro plants.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Distributed Energy Resource Working Group reported on operational coordination among MISO, distribution companies, transmission owners, aggregators, and load-balancing authorities for DER deployment; the Local Enrollment System (LES) is in multi-phase rollout beginning with emergency DR and expanding to demand-response aggregators (DERAs). FERC issued a Notice of Withdrawal of Inquiry and Termination of Rulemaking on Order 2222 (Docket RM21-14, April 16, 2026), ending the rulemaking on aggregator participation in RTO markets. For small hydro and pumped-storage owners, the termination of RM21-14 closes the federal rule-making pathway for aggregator participation but leaves MISO's tariff-level Order 2222 compliance in place; the LES framework and DERA enrollment phase are the next operational gate determining whether small hydro/PSH can participate at scale through aggregators or remain subject to full-resource-model registration. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this status report.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 14b DAMAP Reduction Total - Presentation (MSC-2026-7).pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 14b DAMAP Reduction Total - Presentation (MSC-2026-7).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: DAMAP Reduction Total calculation affects how derated or manually re-dispatched hydro units have their day-ahead schedules scaled, directly impacting revenue recognition and ancillary-services stacking for dispatchable resources including pumped storage and reservoir hydro.
documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to change how the Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) Reduction Total is calculated for derated and manually re-dispatched units, replacing a summation of all cleared day-ahead products (Energy + Regulation + Contingency Reserves + Ramp + Short-Term Reserve) with the maximum of two DART constraint-clearing values that reflect which products can physically share megawatts. The current method potentially overstates the Reduction Total by double-counting shared MWs across products, resulting in lower adjusted day-ahead schedules for affected units; the proposed method aligns the reduction calculation with actual physical constraints that limit product combinations during day-ahead clearing. MISO also proposes a conforming change to one Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee Distribution component (DDC_NDL_CAP_VOL). Stakeholder feedback is due July 24, 2026, with a target FERC filing in Q3 2026 and effective date 60 days thereafter. This principally affects dispatchable thermal and hydroelectric units that regularly clear ancillary services alongside energy, and pumped-storage facilities that rely on accurate product-stacking calculations for profit optimization.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to correct the Day-Ahead Margin Assurance Payment (DAMAP) Reduction Total calculation, which currently overstates reductions by summing MWs across shared products when units are derated or manually re-dispatched. The correction would base the reduction on physical unit limitations instead, yielding more accurate adjusted day-ahead schedules and affecting the Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RSG) Distribution calculation as well. Both changes require a tariff filing; the Market Subcommittee is adopting this as a new issue (MSC-2026-7) for proceeding to tariff modification.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's 2026 biennial review recommends keeping nine market-design issues inactive, including three with direct hydro impact: MSC-2020-1 (Using Storage as a Transmission Asset to Provide Market Services), MSC-2020-3 (Enhanced Hybrid Resource Participation Model), and MSC-2021-9 (Uncertainty Product in DA, RT, AS). These issues, once active, would expand PSH's ability to offer grid services beyond energy and ancillary services, unlock hybrid participation in MISO's markets, and introduce flexibility products that could shift PSH's revenue sources—but no work is scheduled before the next biennial review in 2028.

documents.ai_summary: The MISO Independent Market Monitor (Potomac Economics) presented stakeholder feedback on proposed Module D revisions to market-monitoring authority, duty-of-candor requirements, transmission withholding surveillance, and cost caps on startup/no-load offers during emergency-energy events and tight conditions. Key findings: Entergy and OMS MWG support IMM verification and capping of startup and no-load costs during emergencies (addressing very high offers submitted during winter storms not otherwise validated under tariff); the IMM is developing clarified authority to assess reference levels for demand-response and validate opportunity-cost components of startup offers (including costs from regulatory or emissions-based start restrictions). Redlined tariff language addressing stakeholder concerns on duty of candor scope, transmission "full capability" definition, and rule clarity is expected. Most affected are generators offering into tight/emergency conditions and demand-response resources used to validate reference levels; no vote date is stated.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 06 IMM 2025 State of the Market Recommendations.pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 06 IMM 2025 State of the Market Recommendations.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Independent Market Monitor recommendations on capacity accreditation, emergency-range penalties, storage dispatch optimization, real-time capacity products, and interchange optimization directly affect hydro and PSH revenue through RA/accreditation rules, ancillary-service and reserve payments, and real-time energy pricing mechanisms.
documents.ai_summary: MISO's IMM presented 2025 State of the Market findings and six new recommendations to the Market Subcommittee on July 9, 2026. Key proposals affecting hydro and PSH include: (1) improved capacity accreditation with corrections to maintenance-margin calculations and modified off-control unit treatment (2025-5); (2) penalties on units failing to provide emergency output, with estimated impact of $5.6M on coal and $12M on gas/oil emergency-range capacity payments (2025-6); (3) reduced make-whole and reserve payments for deviating resources to strengthen dispatch-following incentives (2025-2); and (4) revival of existing recommendations for a real-time capacity product for 2–4 hour start resources (2020-1) and look-ahead dispatch optimization for storage management (2021-4). The report also flags 26.6 GW of projected load additions by 2030 and evening ramp demands up 50% year-over-year, driven by solar growth. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this summary document, but the recommendations are now before the Market Subcommittee for consideration of tariff filing. Hydro and PSH owners benefit from tighter accreditation rules that reduce overstated capacity claims by competitors, from enhanced real-time products that play to their flexibility, and from optimization of storage dispatch timing; they face potential penalties if emergency-range claims are overstated.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 07 IMM Quarterly Report.pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: IMM quarterly market-monitor report documents energy price formation volatility, storage resource participation and dispatch efficiency, contingency reserve shortages, capacity accreditation methodology, and interchange optimization affecting real-time pricing—all directly material to hydro revenue and PSH dispatch strategy.
documents.ai_summary: Potomac Economics' Spring 2026 IMM quarterly report to MISO Market Subcommittee (July 9, 2026) identifies rising evening net-load ramp demand (averaging 15 GW between 3–7 pm, up 45% year-over-year), 20 shortage-pricing intervals (nearly double prior year), and 187 intervals with negative system-wide prices as solar penetration increases. Energy Storage Resources (ESRs) now comprise 1.3 GW capacity, setting system and local prices in 5% and 16% of intervals respectively and providing 28% of regulation; a software flaw caused 7% ESR unavailability when outside state-of-charge limits, dispatching units inefficiently (e.g., above-max ESRs discharging into negative-price hours, below-min ESRs charging at >$200/MWh), now addressed with a July software fix. The report recommends optimizing MISO–SPP/PJM interchange through alternate real-time dispatch cases to lower volatility and average energy prices by ≥$2/MWh (saving >$40 million/year), and shifting existing-solar accreditation from 2–5 pm (68% summer) to 4–7 pm (∼50%) to correct over-crediting that artificially suppressed 2026 PRA clearing prices and reduced summer bids by $240/MW-day. Hydro and PSH owners should track storage accreditation methodology changes and price-volatility patterns as ESR fleet grows; the interchange optimization recommendation indicates MISO may adopt real-time co-optimization mechanics that would affect locational value and ramping-product revenue.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 12 Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Market (MSC-2026-2).pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 12 Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Market (MSC-2026-2).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO's Regulation reserve market performance and clearing mechanism directly affects hydro and pumped-storage revenue from ancillary services (the largest and most volatile reserve product in MISO), the treatment of battery entry into Regulation markets, and potential automation of performance-based disqualification rules that could reshape how dispatchable and storage resources compete for reserve procurement.
documents.ai_summary: MISO staff presents an analysis of Regulation reserve clearing and performance deterioration: Regulation requirements roughly doubled on July 1, 2024 (to ~800 MW base), Regulation reserve prices rose 53% and mileage prices 71% year-over-year in 2025, yet non-performance penalties reached 31% of total Regulation revenue by 2025, with gas resource penalties rising more than 2x year-over-year. The document identifies that (1) Regulation performance is assessed only in settlement, after-the-fact, with no automated real-time feedback loop to disqualify poor performers (unlike offline Supplemental and STR); and (2) coal and gas performance has deteriorated while batteries have entered as significant Regulation suppliers. MISO staff indicate they are evaluating options to improve real-time clearing and performance monitoring, with next steps to follow. Pumped-storage operators should monitor this closely because: (i) rising Regulation prices increase PSH revenue exposure to that product, but (ii) potential automation of performance testing and real-time disqualification could advantage faster-ramping technologies (batteries) and penalize PSH and conventional hydro more heavily if response-time or consistency standards are tightened without accounting for hydro's multi-hour operational flexibility constraints.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 11 FTR-ARR Market Enhancements (MSC-2025-5).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating the Auction Revenue Right (ARR) nomination and Financial Transmission Rights (FTR) allocation process, which directly affects how transmission-hedging revenue flows to generation owners, including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities that rely on point-to-point FTR positions for congestion hedging and revenue certainty.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is conducting a holistic review of its ARR/FTR market under FERC Order 681/681-A compliance constraints, with focus on the ARR nomination process (Reference Year, definition of baseload supply resources), changes to the allocation of ARRs into monthly MPMA auctions, and improvements to transmission-outage reporting incentives. The current ARR allocation uses a fixed Reference Year tied to historical transmission usage to balance stability against gaming and accords long-term (10-year rollover) financial rights to Load Serving Entities for power supply hedging; MISO is evaluating whether the Reference Year, RSP definition, or tariff execution rules should be modified, while ensuring full funding of existing LTTRs and no introduction of new gaming opportunities. MISO requests stakeholder feedback by July 23, 2026, and will present next steps and proposed outage-reporting mechanisms at the August MSC meeting. Most exposed are generation owners (particularly hydropower and storage) whose ARR holdings and FTR self-scheduling optionality depend on stable path valuations; changes to Reference Year or baseload definitions could shift which generation types retain long-term transmission-hedge access.

documents.ai_summary: MISO filed tariff revisions (ER26-2705-000, effective date August 4, 2026) to update demand curves for Regulation, Spinning Reserves, and Up Ramp Capability (URC) in response to rapid solar penetration and net-load ramping stress. Regulation and Spinning curves are being simplified to a single $98/MWh value, and the URC cap rises to $96/MWh to strengthen market signals during tight conditions. Separately, MISO is advancing 'Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Markets' (MSC-2026-2) with most stakeholder feedback supportive, and pursuing updates to the Freeze Date congestion-management construct along MISO seams (jointly with PJM, SPP) to improve interregional coordination. These changes directly affect the price and procurement of flexibility and ramping products hydro supplies; URC and Regulation are primary revenue streams for dispatchable hydro and pumped storage. No comment deadline is stated for the demand-curve filing beyond FERC's statutory review.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes revised rules for allocating Real-Time Revenue Sufficiency Guarantee (RRSG) Constraint Management Charges to electric storage resources, distinguishing treatment by day-ahead and real-time commitment status (Charge, Discharge, Available, Continuous). The rules separately govern deviations prior to and after the Notification Deadline, using Economic Minimum/Maximum Limits and Hourly Integrated Forecast constraints to determine which storage deviations trigger charges. PSH operators face altered settlement exposure depending on whether they are committed to charge, discharge, or remain available — with charges assessed when real-time dispatch deviates from day-ahead schedules in ways that increase active transmission-constraint flow. Most exposed are pumped-storage facilities with multi-hour round-trip commitments, where transitions between commitment states and forecast adjustments near the Notification Deadline will materially affect hourly net revenue. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this excerpt; this appears to be a working redline under MSC review.

documents.title: 20260709 MSC Item 13 Evaluation of Updates to Congestion Management and TCDCs (MSC-2026-6).pdf
documents.filename: 20260709 MSC Item 13 Evaluation of Updates to Congestion Management and TCDCs (MSC-2026-6).pdf
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MISO is evaluating transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs) and congestion management during reserve shortages, which directly affects how dispatch and pricing decisions treat dispatchable generation—a core revenue mechanism for hydro—and how make-whole payments (DAMAP) are triggered when congestion and reserve scarcity interact.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is evaluating updates to transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs), which cap the shadow prices the market will pay to enforce network constraints, with particular focus on how undersized TCDCs interact with operating-reserve shortages to cause manual redispatches and Day-Ahead Marginal Assurance Payment (DAMAP) uplift. The document illustrates how reserve scarcity can overwhelm congestion signals, forcing resources down post-facto and triggering make-whole payments (e.g., Winter Storm Elliott example). MISO is considering expanding TCDC breakpoints, adding steps that increase during reserve shortages, and adjusting weighting between base and contingent constraints; a feedback request and implementation plan will be shared later in 2026. Dispatchable generators (including reservoir hydro) are most exposed: when reserves are scarce, high MEC penalties can force dispatch back to EcoMax despite binding constraints, then manual redispatch down creates the DAMAP liability. Hydro owners should track this work because enhanced TCDCs or dynamic reserve-shortage scaling could improve real-time economic dispatch and reduce the frequency of out-of-market corrections.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Market Subcommittee management plan lays out the 2026–2027 agenda for market-design work. The plan also tracks MSE (Market System Enhancement) program completion and resolution of inactive/backlog issues post-UDS upgrade. Voting items and feedback deadlines span May 2026 through Q4 2026; next calendar and biennial reviews are scheduled Q3 2027. No specific hydro position-taking is documented here.

documents.ai_summary: ERCOT is revising its 2027 ancillary-services (AS) methodology with board approval targeted for September 15, 2026; stakeholder feedback is being solicited through July 2026 ROS and WMS subcommittee meetings. The report shows ERCOT's minimum synchronous inertia has declined from 143 GW·s (2016) to 114.7 GW·s (2026) despite rising non-synchronous generation penetration (now 81% of system load), while fast-frequency response (FFR) awards have ramped from zero in prior years to 430 MW in 2026—indicating a structural shift toward synthetic/storage-based frequency support to replace lost synchronous inertia from retiring thermal units. For hydro operators in other RTOs considering their own inertia and frequency-response portfolios, this documents ERCOT's precedent-setting approach to pricing and accrediting FFR as a substitute for synchronous reserve margins, a model that may inform future NERC standards or multiregional frequency-adequacy assessments.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ has adopted and clarified a Revision Initiative Request (MIR) Process (effective November 13, 2025; current version 2.0 as of May 12, 2026) governing how stakeholders submit and advance proposals to change the Markets+ Tariff, Protocols, and related documents. Qualified Entities—including any Markets+ Participant, SPP Staff, the Market Monitoring Unit, governmental authorities, and SPP Members—may submit MIRs via the RMS using a standardized Submission Form; incomplete submissions are rejected and resubmitted by deadline. Submissions are routed by Primary Policy Coordination staff to the appropriate Primary Working Group (MDWG for Tariff/Protocols/MIR Process itself) and Secondary Working Groups; comments must be filed within five business days of Primary WG scheduling and are posted within three days. The Primary Working Group (e.g., MDWG) approves or rejects changes, which then route through Secondary WGs, the Markets+ Participant Executive Committee (MPEC), and the Markets+ Independent Panel (MIP) for final approval; system-change MIRs receive impact analysis (scope, budget, timeline, staffing implications, alternatives) within 30 calendar days of Primary WG approval. This process is the formal gateway by which hydro and PSH owners can propose market-design changes—faster than new tariff proceedings but still multi-stage—and affects what rule changes are feasible to pursue in Markets+.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes a new Co-Located Resources Constraint mechanism (MIR8.2-R) that formalizes 'clipping' — transferring MWs between co-located resources behind a single interconnection point when their combined capacity exceeds the injection limit. Critically, must-offer obligations for co-located resources use the same lesser-of logic, meaning a PSH facility paired with solar (for example) could see its must-offer requirement capped by the injection limit rather than its full capacity. This changes the dispatch flexibility and revenue recognition for PSH in portfolios with injection constraints, and improves market visibility into actual MW availability at the point of interconnection. The update includes tax-law adjustments (100% bonus depreciation reinstatement) and revised overnight-capital and fixed-O&M assumptions from EIA 2026 and the 2025 Quadrennial Review. For hydropower and pumped storage operators, the revised Gross ACR directly impacts the offer cap applied to their existing units; a lower ACR narrows the band within which they can bid and may compress margins, while higher ACR provides headroom. The preliminary Gross CONE values span from $298–$4,403/MW-day depending on technology and delivery year, and Battery Energy Storage is preliminarily set at $502–$696/MW-day, which establishes a competitive benchmark for long-duration storage against which PSH will be evaluated for capacity qualification.
