documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's ESR model design directly determines how pumped-storage hydro and battery storage compete for capacity accreditation, ancillary-services revenue, and energy-market dispatch—the core mechanisms by which storage owners recover fixed costs and optimize multi-hour operating decisions.
documents.ai_summary: PJM presented its current Energy Storage Resource (ESR) participation model, covering opt-in market participation, state-of-charge tracking, ancillary-services eligibility, cost-offer development, and capacity accreditation. The ESR model is a self-schedule framework (no PJM commitment); resources offer as one continuous resource with charge/discharge modes and optional SOC parameters, but PJM does not track SOC in dispatch and offers very limited opportunity-cost recovery for forward energy-limited constraints—a structural gap that disadvantages use-limited resources like pumped storage competing against batteries. Capacity accreditation uses class-based ELCC (4, 6, 8, 10-hour durations), and PSH with shorter physical duration can derate to match a longer ELCC class, but there is no explicit mechanism for PSH to reflect seasonal or hydrological variation in available energy. This presentation supports an active stakeholder issue charge on ESR model enhancements; no vote or comment deadline is stated in the slides, but the mention of a published position paper and ongoing stakeholder process signals that PJM is revisiting the model as the battery storage pipeline grows (8.4 GW under construction or in Cycle 2, 66.5 GW proposed).

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes three solutions to close a perceived gap in its 24-hour lead-time accreditation rule for offline resources. The problem: thermal generators increased their start-time lead times approaching Winter Storms Fern, Enzo, and Heather, rendering 3.1 GW unavailable for commitment in the Day-Ahead Market and Forward Reliability Assessment Commitment (FRAC) processes while still receiving full accreditation value, despite contributing to emergency deployment of LMRs. Solution 1 (12-hour max lead time) aligns offline-resource accreditation with the Operating Margin calculation but risks uneconomic commitments. Solution 2 (zero availability for lead-time increases within 48 hours of the operating day) would penalize changes near emergencies but allow longer-lead resources to participate in multi-day FRAC. Solution 3 (sliding scale: full availability at 4 hours, declining 5% per hour to zero at 24+ hours) offers graduated incentives. MISO will select a recommended solution in August 2026, file revised tariff at FERC in October 2026. Stakeholders should comment by July 22, 2026. Pumped-storage and conventional-hydro operators should monitor because the same accreditation rules govern their RA value; any tightening of lead-time rules that penalizes start-time flexibility, or that creates asymmetries between thermal and hydro accreditation, could compress the capacity credit PSH and peaking hydro claim during peak-scarcity periods.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE introduced a potential two-year transition mechanism for its Capacity Auction Reforms—Seasonal Accreditation (CAR-SA) proposal, which shifts resource accreditation from current Qualified Capacity (QC) values to seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values. During transition, resources would sell a weighted average of current and MRIC-based accreditation; the full CAR-SA design includes auction seasonality, auction-timing changes, and a winter gas constraint. The Committee raised concerns about equity across resource types (some resources face larger derate than others), lack of concrete year-by-year formulas, and treatment of resources with seasonal asymmetry, higher MRIC than QC, or changing MRIC year to year. The ISO clarified it does not plan to delay the core seasonal framework or deactivation changes, and offered to provide impact analysis and cost information; stakeholders broadly supported a transition for planning certainty but demanded transparent mechanics before final CAR-SA rules are adopted. No comment deadline or vote date was stated in these minutes.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) with a three-year transition beginning in CCP 2028–29 (Q2 2027 proposed effective date). The reform shifts accreditation from a long-standing annual Qualified Capacity (QC) methodology to seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values that reflect resource contributions to each season's adequacy. During transition, each resource's accredited capacity will be a weighted average: Year 1 (2/3 QC + 1/3 MRIC), Year 2 (1/3 QC + 2/3 MRIC), Year 3 (full MRIC). Hydro owners—particularly seasonal resources like winter-peaking or pumped-storage operators—will experience year-by-year accreditation shifts; some resources (e.g. passive demand response and winter solar) will see accreditation rise under CAR-SA, while others (especially summer-peaking hydro) will experience lower recognized capacity. The demand curve for procurement will also shift leftward across the three-year glide path, mirroring supply-side accreditation changes to maintain unit consistency and cost equivalence. Next steps include stakeholder review of transition mechanics and expected board/Markets Committee approval in coming meetings.

The mechanism directly affects hydro's accreditation and capacity revenue: by capping non-firm gas capacity and pricing it separately, ISO-NE reduces the volume of low-cost gas capacity competing in winter auctions, tightening supply and raising clearing prices for all resources—especially valuable for pumped-storage hydro and reservoir hydro with winter peaking capability. The filing to stakeholders occurred in July 2026; the ISO notes it will "assess potential enhancements... in the months to come and after the CAR-SA filing." Most exposed are PSH and winter-peaking conventional hydro in zonal export-constrained areas, which benefit from reduced gas competition in winter RA auctions.

ISO-NE's capacity demand curve and Net ICR would adjust accordingly, but the price-formation mechanism (reference-unit recovery at Net CONE × rMRI factor) would be preserved. This proposal, if adopted, would fundamentally change how all accredited resources including hydro, pumped storage, and thermal units recover capacity value, with most exposure to resource types whose value depends heavily on modeled energy availability in GE MARS software.

documents.ai_summary: FirstLight Power presents technical analysis of interconnected design flaws in ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation and Reserves-Seasonal Attributes (CAR-SA) proposal to the Markets Committee. The core issue: the current design allocates seasonal capacity payment rates proportional to Marginal Reliability Index (MRI) at Net ICR for each season, driven by an administrative 50/50 seasonal risk split, weather-year weighting that overstates winter event duration, and accreditation at 'at-criteria' conditions (demand-curve location inconsistent with actual clearing risk). FirstLight demonstrates that under this design, a reference resource may not recover Net CONE annually even when the system is tight in one season, suppressing entry signals for seasonal capacity. Potential solutions offered include dynamic seasonal risk splits aligned to actual system conditions, accreditation within a feasible clearing-point range, revised weather-year weighting, and payment-rate approaches that ensure annual Net CONE recovery. No deadline or vote date specified; this is positioned as urgent discussion to prevent compounding design errors before CAR-SA implementation. Pumped-storage operators—particularly those operating in winter-constrained regions or managing seasonal energy constraints—face material revenue exposure: if winter accreditation and payment rates are structurally overstated relative to summer, then summer-constrained capacity and flexibility are undervalued, and winter-heavy PSH assets may receive artificially elevated seasonal payments that don't reflect true entry incentives.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE Markets Committee voted to recommend support for manual conforming changes implementing FERC Order 2222 (M-11, M-28, M-RPA) and the SATOA project (M-28, M-RPA). The vote passed with no opposition and one End User abstention; recommendation now goes to Participants Committee. For NHA members, this action signals that ISO-NE's rulebook is moving to accommodate smaller hydro through DER pathways and may reshape how pumped-storage assets are contractually and financially treated if designated for transmission-only service—affecting both revenue models and operational flexibility.

documents.ai_summary: MISO Reliability Subcommittee reports on the top 10 cost-generating congested constraints in its footprint as of July 2026. Seven of the ten constraints are M2M (Midwest-to-Market) coordinated flowgates, and six of the top ten stem from planned outages. The document presents a baseline congestion topology but does not indicate proposed mitigations or next steps. The relevance to hydro lies in flowgate binding and outage scheduling: tight M2M flowgates limit transmission capability for exporting generators (including hydro from the upper Midwest or neighboring regions) into constrained zones, and planned-outage timing can either relieve or exacerbate scarcity pricing windows when hydro's ramping and energy offer highest margin. Operators in hydro-rich neighboring RTOs (e.g., PJM members with hydro capacity, or DSOs considering MISO seams) should track whether MISO's congestion profile shifts—persistent binding on M2M corridors may signal interregional transmission expansion opportunity or pressure for storage-as-transmission alternatives.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Large Load Working Group (LLWG) is developing several rule packages in 2026–27 that will shape how large loads and co-located generation participate in MISO markets. Key active issues include: (1) Market Participation and Registration of Co-Located Load and Generation with zero-injection GIA consideration (PAC-2024-4, feedback requested May 14 and June 10); (2) Large Load Firm Service Step Up (LLWG-2026-1, tariff redlines due August 27); (3) Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG-2026-2, evaluation and cost-allocation recommendations due Q4 2026); and (4) Interconnection Reliability Requirements including stability assessments (LLWG-2026-3). The co-location rule package directly opens a pathway for hydropower and pumped-storage facilities to register and dispatch co-located load behind the meter, potentially unlocking new revenue streams from load service and reducing network-cost exposure. Reserve-product enhancements and firm-service mechanics will change the mix of flexibility and capacity products available to large, controllable loads—affecting how hydro-connected or hybrid-sited PSH competes for reserve and flexibility revenue. LLWG meetings are scheduled through Q4 2026, with tariff redlines and final recommendations due by December 2026.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ GHG Task Force proposes replacing EPA eGRID and EIA fuel-type emissions factors with two superior backstop sources: GRETA (a real-time heat-rate curve model already used by MISO, SPP IM, and APS) and Open Grid Emissions (OGE, a peer-reviewed, generator-specific annual dataset). The proposal would establish a four-tier pecking order—Market Participant submission first, GRETA second, OGE third, and Market Operator calculation as fallback—shifting away from outdated annual averages to dynamic and sub-plant-specific emissions accounting. This matters to hydro owners because zero-carbon hydro and pumped-storage assets will receive more accurate (and favorable) emissions-factor treatment in clean-energy programs and multiregional GHG accounting; the use of real-time heat-rate modeling and open-source peer-reviewed data strengthens the defensibility of hydro's zero-carbon claim in export markets and capacity-procurement contexts where GHG attribution determines eligibility and value. No vote date or comment deadline is stated in the document.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing automatic eDART (Outage Database) ticket creation in September 2026 to capture all unavailable MW from committed capacity resources in real time. The system will auto-generate forced-outage tickets when a unit shows unavailable in Markets Gateway but lacks an active outage ticket in eDART, closing a gap exposed by Winter Storm Elliott and reinforced by Winter Storm Fern where unplanned outages went unreported. This directly affects hydro and PSH operators' obligation to report unavailable capacity timely and accurately under Schedule 1 Section 1.10.1A(d) (must-offer rules); the auto-creation logic will flag operators whose availability data in Markets Gateway diverges from eDART submissions, and forced-outage rates derived from eDART feed into capacity accreditation, reserve calculations, and PJM's forecast accuracy to stakeholders. Hydro and PSH owners dependent on accurate outage reporting for capacity value and performance assessment should monitor the Tech Change and eDART forums as details are formalized before the September 2026 implementation.

documents.ai_summary: MISO's Independent Market Monitor presented findings from the 2025 State of the Market report showing all-in prices rose 67% to $53/MWh, driven by natural gas cost increases and capacity-market reforms. Key findings for hydro owners: (1) MISO transitioned to a reliability-based demand curve in capacity markets and reformed resource accreditation to reflect resources' marginal contribution to reliability in riskiest hours—shifting value from solar/wind with declining accreditation to dispatchable resources, including hydro; (2) shortage-pricing reforms in Fall 2025 improved energy and ancillary-service price signals, and MISO filed recommended penalties to improve incentive for units to follow dispatch setpoints; (3) real-time congestion costs rose 23% to $2.2B, driven partly by conservative transmission ratings and MISO's manual re-dispatch—highlighting transmission constraints that affect hydro deliverability; (4) MISO projects 26.6 GW load additions by 2030 (3.1–5.1% CAGR), with guidance that co-located generation and load should not avoid capacity or transmission costs, and siting at weak network locations should be non-firm pending upgrades—affecting co-location economics and interconnection strategy; (5) renewable penetration peaked at 45.7% in 2025, creating ramp-demand volatility and voltage-support constraints that favor dispatchable resources and storage; (6) marginal accreditation for new renewables is falling sharply, making continued investment in dispatchable generation essential—directly elevating the system value of existing hydro and PSH in MISO's reliability planning.

documents.title: 03b IPPNY Comments on NYISO Demand Curve Reset Methodology Improvement Project
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: IPPNY comments on NYISO's Demand Curve Reset (DCR) methodology directly touch capacity-market accreditation and proxy-unit design, which set the reference prices for NYISO capacity revenues — the 'missing money' mechanism on which dispatchable hydro and pumped storage depend for cost recovery and investment signals.
documents.ai_summary: IPPNY, representing 80% of New York generation, submits comments on NYISO's preliminary DCR improvements, urging four changes: (1) require proxy units to meet firm-fuel winter-availability requirements (minimum 8 hours daily operation December–February, or 56 hours on-site fuel storage); (2) adjust the Level of Excess to close the gap between market and planning assumptions; (3) shift the zero-crossing point (ZCP) of capacity demand curves rightward to reduce price volatility with small supply changes; and (4) improve annual escalation factors for financial parameters while retaining the quadrennial reset cycle, using New York-specific data for cost-of-debt and market-return indices. The core grievance is that NYISO's 2022 switch to a 2-hour battery as proxy unit excluded firm-fuel costs needed for winter reliability, causing capacity prices to fall below levels needed to retain or invest in generation — a signal deficiency that IPPNY argues has induced retirements and underinvests in reliability. Status: IPPNY feedback on preliminary recommendations; no vote or implementation date stated. Most exposed are any hydro/PSH operators relying on NYISO capacity-market revenues for cost recovery, particularly if they have winter firm-fuel capability that the battery-proxy ignores.

documents.title: 2 DADRP/DSASP Cleanup Tariff Revisions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO tariff cleanup affecting market participation pathways for aggregations (including DER/small hydro) and energy storage resources; removes deprecated demand-reduction program language and integrates aggregations into cost-based reference-level framework, which bears on offer-development obligations and mitigation-offer rules for non-traditional participants.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is cleaning up Market Services Tariff (MST) and Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) sections to remove obsolete language from the sunsunset Demand Aggregation/Demand Reduction Provider (DADRP) and Demand-Side Ancillary Service Provider (DSASP) programs. Key substantive change: aggregations (including small hydro and DER) are now folded into MST 23.7.3 cost-based reference-level framework, replacing a prior special exemption (MST 23.7.4) that had carved them out because NYISO previously did not calculate reference levels for demand-side resources. The removal of MST 23.7.4 means aggregations must now develop cost-based reference levels for mitigation-offer compliance, aligning them with generator standards. Other revisions correct grammatical errors, restore erroneously deleted BPCG recovery language in OATT 6.1.12, and clarify minimum-generation-bid and supplier definitions. Filing timeline: BIC discussion 7/15/2026; Market Committee vote 7/29/2026. Small hydro and distributed hydro resources participating via aggregation must monitor this closely, as it resets the compliance baseline for offer development.

documents.title: 3 ICAP Demand Curve Reset (DCR) Process and Methodology Improvements
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's ICAP demand curve reset methodology directly affects capacity accreditation and pricing for all resources including hydro and pumped storage, which depend on accurate CONE (Cost of New Entry) calculations and proxy-unit definitions to determine their capacity value and revenue.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is redesigning its Installed Capacity (ICAP) demand curve reset (DCR) process and cost-to-build methodology, with initial recommendations evaluated against reliability-based valuation, transparency, investment efficiency, and ease of administration. Key proposals include: using EIA overnight capital cost data to streamline cost-to-build estimates (rather than consultant-driven bottom-up approaches), codifying proxy-unit screening criteria to increase predictability, implementing more frequent indexed updates to financial parameters, and adjusting demand curve structures (kinked curves, zero-crossing informed by Minimum Reliability Index). The document is an interim presentation (July 1, 2026) building to an initial concept proposal in August and a complete market design with tariff updates by year-end. For hydro and pumped-storage owners, changes to CONE inputs and proxy-unit definitions directly affect capacity accreditation values and the price signal that drives the DCR clearing price—hydro's primary revenue mechanism in NYISO; any shift toward faster reset cycles or non-consultant methodologies could increase or decrease the accuracy of cost-to-build estimates that anchor their capacity payments, and technology-prescriptive proxy choices (e.g., mandating a gas turbine) would exclude alternative dispatch profiles that might better reflect hydro's actual value.

documents.filename: 09-10-MIR8.1 and MIR8.2 Update to MORWG June 2026.pptx
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MIR8.1 restructures how pumped-storage and battery resources manage state-of-charge forecasting across Markets+ unit-commitment studies, shifting from market-participant prediction to market-operator calculation of SOC trajectories — a material change to how storage revenue exposure and dispatch predictability are handled under Markets+ rules.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ MIR8.1 proposes to introduce time-coupled intervals in all unit-commitment studies (Day-Ahead Market, Day-Ahead RUC, Intra-Day RUC, and Short-Term RUC), allowing market operators to calculate state-of-charge for all intervals after the first, rather than requiring market participants to submit a SOC forecast for every interval. The change is optional: participants can elect either the current design (submitting SOC forecast for each interval) or the new coupled design (submitting SOC forecast only for the first interval, letting the market operator time-couple and calculate subsequent SOC values). The proposal targets a FERC filing timeline, with MPEC approval targeted for August 2026. For pumped-storage owners, this addresses a key exposure: misforecasting dispatch leads to infeasible SOC trajectories in real-time, triggering capacity shortfalls and financial penalties; time-coupling within studies mitigates that risk by ensuring the market solver respects physical charging/discharging constraints. The optionality preserves flexibility for hybrid resources and those charging/discharging outside the market (where the operator lacks full visibility). MORWG convened June 30, 2026; MPEC approval is scheduled August 25, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ Markets and Operations working groups will discuss and vote on six Market Implementation Requests in June 2026, with August 2026 MPEC approval targets for most items. MIR8.1 (State of Charge Management) and MIR8.2 (Co-Located Resource Constraints) introduce new participation and operational frameworks for multi-hour storage resources—both drawn from MSR (multi-service resource) subgroup whitepapers and directly affecting how pumped storage and hybrid generators (including co-located hydro + solar) can operate and earn revenue. MIR9.2-R and MIR9.3-R expand dynamic-scheduling and pseudo-tie pathways, opening participation for neighboring resources and potentially enabling smaller or out-of-footprint hydro to access Markets+ balancing. MIR60-R and MIR81-R address real-time transaction settlement and dynamic multi-transaction-interchange pricing, altering how interchange flows (critical for Northwest-to-SPP hydro exports) settle and are valued. Comment deadlines range from June 18 to June 25, 2026; August MPEC vote is the approval milestone for most items.

MIR9.1-R (Non-Dispatchable Physical Resources) creates a framework for resources whose owners are legally or contractually unable to submit financial offer information, allowing them to be modeled in the market without unavailable offer data—directly relevant to run-of-river hydro and other variable resources that cannot control output. documents.title: 04-MIR75-R SPP Comments-20260520.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This MIR75-R proposal directly affects high-priority export scheduling and adjustment procedures for hydro and other dispatchable resources in SPP Markets+, touching revenue realization for exports and operational constraints on resource commitment and discharge.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ MIR75-R proposes clarified mechanics for adjusting high-priority export e-Tags when a resource's maximum economic limit or Variable Energy Resource forecast falls below committed export volumes. The proposal specifies that adjustments will be made pro-rata when multiple e-Tags share a single resource source, with a 1 MW minimum threshold and whole-MW rounding. Hydro and pumped-storage operators exporting power into or through SPP Markets+ will face automatic downward adjustment of export schedules when their available capacity (Max ECOL for conventional hydro, Maximum Discharge Limit for MSRs, VER forecast for wind/solar) cannot support the export commitment — a constraint that directly reduces realized export revenue and requires operators to manage export bids against real-time resource availability, especially during low-water or variable-generation conditions. The language resulted from an April 2026 MSWG/MDWG policy decision; this MIR specifies the operational algorithm. SRP supports the threshold addition.

documents.title: 05-MIR9.2-R Dynamic Schedule Resources June 2026.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Markets+ Dynamic Schedule Resource rules establish how dispatchable hydro and other resources physically located in one balancing authority but serving load in another are accounted for in dispatch, power-balance settlement, and interbalancing-authority transfer accounting — directly affecting how hydro output is cleared, metered, and compensated across BA boundaries, particularly for multi-state/multi-BA hydro operators.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ proposes a new 'Dynamic Schedule Resource' participation type (MIR 9.2-R, June 2026) to solve a double-counting problem: when a dispatchable resource in one Balancing Authority (Native BA) is dynamically scheduled to serve load in another (Attaining BA), current rules treat its dispatch change in both the dynamic net scheduled interchange (NSI) and the market-to-interchange (MTI), forcing both BAs to regulate redundantly. The solution links a Dynamic Schedule Resource to a Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface; the resource remains dispatchable by Markets+ in real-time (RTBM), but only the interface value (not the resource's full output) is counted in the Attaining BA's power balance, preventing double-counting. The proposal defines five use cases: participating-to-participating BAs (resource-coupled or not), participating-to-non-participating (resource-coupled or not), and non-participating to participating. Most exposed are multi-BA hydro operators and pumped-storage facilities dynamically scheduled across BA lines; use-case 1a (participating-to-participating, resource-coupled) preserves dispatchability and shifts regulation responsibility via the interface, altering how dynamic hydro transfers compete in dispatch and how their locational and marginal-loss signals propagate across seams. Tariff and protocol sections are newly drafted; implementation timeline and stakeholder comment opportunity are not detailed in this presentation.

documents.title: 05-MIR9.2-R SPP Comments-20260602.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Dynamic Schedule Resources clarifies how Markets+ will treat dispatchability and real-time ICCP management of hydro and other resources subject to physical energy transfers across BA boundaries—a revenue and compliance issue for hydro sellers using dynamic dispatch to serve load or other BAs, and for multi-state resource compliance with e-Tag and regulation-burden rules.
documents.ai_summary: SPP staff proposes tariff and protocol revisions (April 2025/1.0a) to clarify registration, e-Tagging, and operational treatment of Dynamic Schedule Resources and Interfaces across Markets+ timeframes (DA, RUC, pre-RTBM, RTBM). The proposal distinguishes resource-coupled versus non-resource-coupled dynamic schedules and specifies when a resource may remain dispatchable under a dynamic schedule (internal transfers) versus when transactions must be non-dispatchable (certain exports). Key change: MSRs (multi-state resources, of which hydro is the canonical example) registered as Dynamic Schedule Resources can represent import or export depending on dispatch, but must coordinate separate e-Tags with the Native and Attaining BAs and accept ICCP-reported real-time quantities as fixed; Dynamic e-Tags referencing these resources are ignored by settlements, shifting compliance burden to the Market Participant. This reduces regulation burden on receiving BAs by eliminating pseudo-ties but locks the Dynamic Schedule Resource's output into the native BA's power balance and removes it from real-time economic dispatch in the attaining BA—a material constraint for hydro operators managing multi-BA export strategies. Status: tariff/protocol revisions have been proposed; next step and comment deadline are not stated in this excerpt.

documents.title: 06-MIR9.3-R Dynamic Schedule Resource Pseudo-Ties June 2026.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Markets+ is refining pseudo-tie registration rules for external resources, which directly affects how hydropower and other dispatchable generation located outside the Markets+ footprint can participate, be dispatched, and settle — a strategic option for NHA members operating in non-participating balancing areas seeking access to SPP Markets+.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ (SPP's combined market and reliability coordinator) is adopting a new registration pathway (MIR 9.3-R) that allows external resources physically located in non-participating balancing authorities to be modeled as pseudo-tied within Markets+ using dynamic schedules instead of formal NAESB pseudo-tie agreements. External resources registered under this new option will be dispatchable by Markets+, settled at their physical-location LMP, and participate identically to formally pseudo-tied resources, but the underlying dynamic schedule between native and attaining balancing authorities will remain in place (and ignored by the market system and settlements). The change preserves all formal pseudo-tie requirements and adds two new attributes: the market participant must designate the resource as a "dynamically scheduled pseudo-tie" in the registration workbook, and the participating attaining BA must provide an attestation letter confirming its understanding that the resource will be modeled as pseudo-tied. This creates operational flexibility for BA arrangements that cannot or prefer not to establish formal pseudo-ties, potentially broadening external-resource participation. The document shows protocol language updates to sections 9.1.1, 9.1.9, 9.1.9.1, and 9.1.9.2 but states no vote date or comment deadline.

documents.title: 06-MIR9.3-R Dynamic Schedule Resource Pseudo-Ties submission.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: External resource pseudo-tie registration and modeling rules directly affect how hydropower resources outside the Markets+ footprint (including those in adjacent balancing authorities) can participate in the day-ahead and real-time energy market and settle, and clarifies the framework for pseudo-tied hydro to remain on dynamic schedules while competing in Markets+—a critical pathway for cross-BA hydro participation and revenue capture.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ (SPP's organized market launching 2027) is codifying registration and operational requirements for two forms of external resource pseudo-ties: formal pseudo-ties with binding BA agreements, and dynamically scheduled pseudo-ties where the resource is modeled as pseudo-tied into the attaining BAA in Markets+ commercial and network models while energy continues to flow as a dynamic schedule under NAESB/WECC standards between native and attaining BAs. The MIR (Markets+ Initiative Request 9.3-R) adds a new resource designation ('dynamically scheduled pseudo-tie') and defines meter-agent, attestation, and settlement responsibilities in Protocols Sections 9.1.1, 9.1.9, 9.1.9.1 (new), and 9.1.9.2 (new). SPP staff rates this as medium design, implementation, and operational complexity; MPEC approval is targeted Q3 2026 with Q1 2027 go-live. This standardizes a workaround already in Markets+ base design, reducing ad hoc handling and participation ambiguity for external hydro resources seeking to serve load within the footprint—directly relevant to northwest hydro exports and cross-border hydro from Mexican utilities or other external basins.

documents.filename: 07-MIR60-R Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) submission.docx
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) establish a new framework for import/export transactions across the Markets+ boundary and internal transfers within the footprint, affecting how hydro and other resources can participate in interregional energy trading and settlement — a direct revenue vector for hydro owners seeking to export power or manage interchange scheduling within the expanding Markets+ footprint.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ is implementing the Markets+ Interchange Transaction System Points Schedules (MITSPS) framework, which creates generic system points (MPSP) within each Markets+ Balancing Authority Area to facilitate scheduling and tagging of import/export transactions across the Markets+ boundary and internal market transfers. The protocol revisions establish registration, operational, and settlement requirements for MPSPs as sources and sinks for interchange transactions, with optional hourly limits managed by each BA in the Day-Ahead and Real-Time Balancing Markets. For hydro owners exporting from or importing into Markets+ BAAs, MITSPS enables participation in interchange transactions that are not pre-scheduled bilateral trades but are cleared by the market — expanding the scheduling and revenue-participation pathways available to hydroelectric resources. The MIR seeks MPEC approval in Q3 2026 with implementation targeted for Q1 2027, affecting how existing hydro plants can access interregional markets and how new capacity (especially in growing Markets+ footprint) will schedule transactions.

documents.title: 08-MIR81-R Dynamic MTI-MOTI in RTBM submission.docx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: MTI/MOTI tagging and BAA Scheduling Constraints directly affect how SPP Markets+ dispatches interregional power flows in real-time; distinguishing Normal (DA-locked) from Dynamic (RTBM-only) transaction types changes the sequencing and flexibility of resource commitment and redispatch — a structural change to market dispatch that hydro operators use to optimize revenue from flexible ramping and interregional sales.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ (MIR 81-R) proposes to distinguish Normal and Dynamic MTI/MOTI transaction types, with Normal types locked after Pre-RTBM SCED and Dynamic types eligible only in RTBM. This allows BAAs to create separate BAA Scheduling Constraints on Dynamic paths without retroactively constraining the day-ahead and RUC commitment plan. The change is ranked High priority, with MPEC approval targeted Q4 2026 and implementation Q1 2027. Hydro operators in the SPP footprint benefit by avoiding artificial redispatch and binding constraints when BAs adjust transmission limits for reliability mid-day; it preserves the optimization value of DA and RUC schedules and lets BAs manage incremental transfer changes without forcing costly RTBM repricing and potential VRL violations. Most exposed are pumped-storage and flexible reservoir operators using MTI/MOTI paths for interregional arbitrage and capacity sales.

documents.title: 08-MIR81-R Dynamic MTI-MOTI in RTBM.pptx  [in MORWG Meeting Materials 20260630.zip]
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Modifies balancing-area scheduling constraints and market-transfer-interface (MTI) rules that affect real-time dispatch flexibility and locational price signals — hydro's revenue from ramping/flexibility procurement and locational scarcity pricing depends on how transmission constraints are enforced across market intervals.
documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes MIR81-R, which distinguishes Normal (day-ahead/RUC/pre-RTBM) and Dynamic (real-time only) MTI/MOTI transaction types to allow balancing authorities to set different scheduling constraints in RTBM than were used in DA commitment, preventing large NSI swings without undermining DA/RUC optimization. Normal MTIs become fixed quantities in real-time; Dynamic MTIs operate only in RTBM with nonbinding limits (defaulting to 99,999 MW unless constrained by BA-to-BA scheduling restrictions). The proposal updates tariff sections 4.2.7, 8.2, 8.2.1.1, 8.2.2.1, 8.2.6, and 9.4.1 to implement transaction-type registration and constraint-submission requirements via the MUI. This affects real-time dispatch optimization and price formation: by allowing separate constraints for incremental transfers, the scheme constrains BAA scheduling-constraint binding in RTBM while preserving DA-cleared transfers, potentially reducing real-time price separation and limiting the incremental scarcity premiums hydro can capture on flexible ramping in congested intervals. All market participants must submit Normal MTIs/MOTIs prior to DA market close and register at least one Dynamic MTI at resource registration.

committee: Department of Market Monitoring Market Issues and Performance Report
meeting_hydro_reason: CAISO's annual market-monitoring report typically analyzes price formation, ancillary services, energy-storage performance, resource-adequacy outcomes, and market-power mitigation—all core revenue and strategic-option axes for hydro and PSH operators in the Western markets.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 Fourth Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Apr 02, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO market-monitoring report on Q4 2025 real-time pricing, regional generation mix by fuel (including hydro), transmission congestion, and interregional transfer flows — directly bearing on hydro revenue (price formation and regional scarcity signals) and strategic positioning in the West.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring reports Q4 2025 market outcomes: electricity prices in the West fell 7% year-over-year; less frequent high-price intervals occurred; Pacific Northwest shifted to net exporter across all hours; and California prices remain elevated by greenhouse-gas costs rather than congestion. The report shows generation-mix shifts by region (Slides 8–11) but does not propose tariff changes. For hydro owners, the data reveals that interregional transmission capacity and fuel-mix changes—especially lower prices and reduced Northwest scarcity—signal weakened export value from the PNW into California, while California's GHG-driven premium persists. Analysts using this as a reference point would identify market conditions affecting hydro's locational revenue; no comment deadline or action item is stated.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 Third Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Jan 08, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO market-monitoring report analyzing Q3 2025 price formation, congestion patterns, WEIM transfers, and generation mix changes across multiple Western regions — directly informs hydro revenue via locational pricing signals, interregional trade dynamics, and operational conditions that shape dispatch and scarcity.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring presents Q3 2025 market performance: Western region prices down 4% year-over-year; California dominated by south-to-north congestion and GHG costs; Northwest saw higher solar-hour prices while California peaked in non-solar hours; WEIM transfers flowed from CAISO mid-day and from Intermountain/Desert Southwest in non-solar hours, with assistance-energy opt-ins increasing transfers for 8 of 10 entities. Real-time three-pivotal-supplier test found 4.2% of WEIM 15-minute intervals uncompetitive; RTD mitigation errors added ~37 MW incremental dispatch. Hydro owners should track the pronounced shift in congestion direction (north-to-south peak in Q3 2024 vs. current south-to-north pattern) and the interregional transfer behavior, which directly affects locational scarcity pricing and arbitrage opportunities for reservoir and pumped-storage resources positioned to move energy across the Western interconnect.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 Second Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Oct 09, 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO market-monitoring report on Q2 2025 energy price formation, congestion, interregional transfers (WEIM), and resource dispatch patterns—directly informative for hydro owners assessing revenue drivers, transmission constraints affecting their exports, and strategic positioning across the West.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring reports Q2 2025 real-time market conditions: electricity prices in the West rose 12% versus Q2 2024, driven by south-to-north congestion and California greenhouse-gas costs; Northwest prices were higher during solar hours, California during non-solar hours—indicating hydro's value shifts with solar generation patterns. WEIM transfer congestion into or out of Pacific Northwest areas occurred over 20% of 5-minute intervals, and Mid-Columbia and Palo Verde bilateral prices converged with ISO market prices, suggesting arbitrage opportunities narrowed. Pacific Northwest coal output rose despite more outages, and transfers from the Intermountain West during non-solar hours declined Q-o-Q, signaling reduced availability or changed dispatch incentives. For hydro owners, these trends show tightening price signals in hydro-export corridors, persistent congestion reducing transmission access to California, and seasonal shifts in the regional generation stack that affect dispatch positioning and revenue timing.

documents.title: Presentation - 2024 Annual Report on Market Issues and Performance
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO's 2024 market-performance report provides comprehensive data on hydro generation patterns, regional price formation, congestion outcomes, and ancillary-services procurement mix — all drivers of hydro revenue and dispatch value — plus recommendations affecting storage bid-cost recovery, default energy bids, and local market-power mitigation that extend to hybrid resources including hydropower.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring presents 2024 annual performance data and forward recommendations. Pacific Northwest hydro generation increased in 2024 relative to 2023; Northwest prices rose mid-day during solar hours and followed net-load patterns, with transfer-congestion elevation noted (page 7, 11–12). Battery participation in ancillary services grew substantially (page 43), while overall flexible ramping product prices remained infrequent at system/BA level (page 42). Recommendations include extending local market-power mitigation to hybrid resources, enhancing default energy bids for batteries to reflect intraday opportunity costs (with standardized bids for WEIM batteries proposed), and revising bid-cost recovery rules — changes that would apply similarly to hydro and PSH if codified (pages 46–47). No specific vote or comment deadline stated in this presentation; this is a published annual report. Most exposure: pumped-storage operators subject to bid-cost recovery and default-energy-bid rules, and larger reservoir hydro in the Pacific Northwest tier where congestion pricing and seasonal price patterns drive revenue.

documents.title: Presentation - 2025 First Quarter Market Issues and Performance - Jun 26, 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO Q1 2025 market-monitoring report documents flexible ramping product procurement split by fuel type (hydro vs. solar/wind/batteries), WEIM interregional transfer patterns involving hydro-exporting regions (Pacific Northwest, Intermountain West), and price formation across WEIM footprint affecting hydro export value.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring Q1 2025 performance report shows hydro and batteries supplying the bulk of upward flexible ramping product (FRP) procurement, while solar and wind dominate downward FRP demand in the 15-minute market. Intermountain West and Pacific Northwest became dominant WEIM exporters during non-solar hours in Q1 2025, with PacEast and Idaho Power identified as main peak-hour exporters; transfer congestion into/out of those hydro-rich regions occurred in ~20% of 5-minute intervals, creating locational scarcity signals. Electricity prices in the West dropped 39% year-over-year but remain driven by south-to-north congestion and greenhouse-gas costs within California. The report is observational and carries no proposals or compliance deadlines, but provides a baseline on how hydro's FRP-market participation, export positioning, and regional pricing have shifted in the WEIM footprint — useful for understanding Q1 2025 hydro revenue dynamics and transmission-constrained export opportunity.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is filing revised Tariff language by end of July 2026 to impose interconnection reliability requirements on large loads (≥50 MW new, ≥25 MW cumulative increase) and computational loads (≥1 MW of data-center-type digital demand), implementing FERC's show-cause order. Requirements include basic facility data, modeling, hourly forecasts, telemetry, and PMU data; computational loads face additional phasor measurement, ride-through (voltage/frequency), and ramp-rate controls; MISO will install and charge customers for remote disconnect equipment and control systems. A transitional provision exempts loads with service commencement before 11/1/2027 from ramp and ride-through requirements for their lifetime unless they upgrade by ≥25 MW after 10/1/2026. This affects hydro owners because (1) it establishes a co-location precedent — large loads are now defined as discrete withdrawal points, creating opportunities for hydro to site behind-the-meter generation and enter direct load-service arrangements; (2) the ramp-rate and ride-through enforcement on computational loads (AI, crypto, HPC) creates a demand-side flexibility requirement that could be partially satisfied by hybrid hydro-storage systems and (3) the remote-disconnect and PMU mandates on loads set operational-control expectations that may extend to dispatchable generation. Stakeholders expressed concerns about applicability, transition, and specific language; feedback has influenced the revised Tariff language.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes to require large loads (data centers, industrial facilities, campuses) to submit short-term operational forecasts at hourly (next 1–168 hours) and 5-minute (next 6 hours) granularities, feeding into MISO's Multi-Day/Next-Day/Intraday reliability commitment and look-ahead commitment/real-time dispatch processes. Forecasts are submitted at the Commercial Pricing (CP) node level by the Tariff Customer; MISO will monitor timeliness and accuracy against telemetered actual load and is considering incentive mechanisms (ranging from escalation to settlement-based penalties). Status: requirements finalized for LLWG feedback by July 13, 2026; accuracy incentives and BPM implementation to follow. For hydro operators, the mechanism is load-side variability management: large loads add volatile demand that MISO's standard weather/calendar forecasts cannot capture; if these forecasts are inaccurate, MISO's commitment stack and reserve procurement tighten or loosen unpredictably, affecting the scarcity signals and ramping/flexibility value hydro receives in real-time and look-ahead markets. The settlement-based penalty option (SPP precedent cited) could create a parallel market-discipline framework applied to demand-side forecast accuracy, potentially informing future treatment of hydro forecast errors and opportunity-cost offers.

documents.ai_summary: MISO has established a dynamic reserve requirement methodology that quantifies net uncertainty and derives seasonal reserve requirements for Regulation Reserve (4 sec–5 min timeframe), Ramp Capability Product (10 min), and Short-Term Reserve (30 min–3 hr), with requirements varying by season, region, and time of day. Large loads exhibiting non-conforming behavior (volatile industrial or storage-adjacent profiles) were evaluated as a source of net-load and tie-line uncertainty; however, MISO's correlation analysis (sampling February–November 2025) found weak or negligible relationships between non-conforming load profiles and reserve-product uncertainty requirements across all three products, suggesting existing large loads have limited impact on reserve sizing to date. MISO will continue to monitor uncertainty patterns periodically and revise reserve methodologies if non-conforming load impact reaches criticality. Stakeholder feedback (six respondents, May 2026) was mostly supportive, and further engagement will occur at the Large Load Working Group.

The mechanism: larger, more variable loads will increase MISO's procurement of regulation and ramping reserves; if MISO adds new reserve products or expands regulation requirements, traditional hydro and PSH owners will face higher competition for those product revenues and greater uncertainty in which resources are called upon to provide regulation—particularly affecting resources with ramp-rate and regulation-eligibility constraints.

documents.ai_summary: PJM's Interconnection Process Subcommittee presented market participation options for Mixed Technology Facilities (MTF)—facilities with multiple generation or storage types behind a single interconnection point. Resources can participate as independent Co-Located Resources (each a separate market unit) or as a Hybrid Resource (single market unit with unit-specific accreditation). A closed-loop hybrid with storage can charge from grid; an open-loop hybrid cannot. Facilities with independent components can elect either model; those with significant interdependency (e.g., storage unable to charge from grid) must use the hybrid model. Classification must be declared 6 months before in-service date; capacity resources must choose the same model for both capacity and energy markets and must re-elect within RAA Schedule 9.2 deadlines; energy-only resources can change election once per calendar year with notice by May 30. For any MTF, the site Maximum Facility Output (MFO) cannot be exceeded in real time and capacity-must-offer obligations apply to the original Certified Interconnection Rights. The four use cases illustrate that inverter-gen + storage (like solar + battery or wind + battery) and non-inverter gen + storage (gas + battery) can form hybrids, while non-inverter gen + inverter gen (gas + solar) must participate as co-located resources. This framework directly affects pumped-storage hydro owners considering co-location with other generation or considering participation in paired-resource models, constraining how PSH state-of-charge management interacts with capacity accreditation and must-offer rules.

documents.ai_summary: The Independent Market Monitor (IMM) presents its interim reserve-redesign proposal for PJM's Reliability Committee, opposing PJM's parallel proposal. The IMM recommends three sequential implementation packages: (1) incorporating net load forecast uncertainty into reserve calculations (near-term priority); (2) reserve performance measurement and settlement changes; (3) reserve eligibility and market-clearing engine changes. The critical difference is the online/offline reserve mix: PJM proposes all 10-minute reserves be online-only, significantly raising production costs and clearing prices; the IMM proposes maintaining offline reserve capability (primary reserves) and synchronized (online) reserves separately. The IMM contends PJM's approach reduces market efficiency and jeopardizes reliability if current fast-start generators drop fast-start capability to avoid the online-reserve requirement. Solar generation in PJM has grown dramatically (14.3 GW maximum hourly output in 2026, 2.4% of annual generation), driving net-load uncertainty that both proposals address but with different reserve adequacy methods — the IMM's approach captures generator performance uncertainty in 30-minute reserves and includes demand response as eligible supply. No vote date or next-step deadline is stated; the presentation positions the IMM proposal as the operational-necessity baseline against PJM's preferred-design alternative.

The Full Case scenario (updated ORDCs with Primary Reserve not clearing) showed 10-minute Online reserve prices rising from $10.25/MWh to $13.04/MWh (+$2.79), energy LMPs rising $0.80/MWh, uplift declining 3.8%, and load reserve payments rising $216M for 10-minute Online reserves—with greatest price pressure during peak hours when reserves are most needed. The simulation found that prepositioning units with ramping products in the multi-step ORDC case reduced scarcity-event frequency compared to the base case, particularly during two modeled shortage events (3/3/2025 and 8/12/2025), suggesting improved reserve-positioning efficiency, though the analysis carries limitations (PROBE PD simulation tool, combustion-turbine-only commitment, 30-minute Online requirement added to SR requirement rather than separately modeled). Document presented to RCSTF with no stated vote or deadline; further results posted post-presentation.

On capacity-zone formation, the ISO proposed removing gas-only resources from objective-criteria testing to trigger price separation signals, but members from the Alternative Resources, Supplier, and End User sectors raised concerns: Alternative Resources opposed removing all gas-only resources; Suppliers requested application of the methodology to FCA 18 for transparency; and one Supplier advocated that all zones be modeled at all times. The removal of gas-only resources could reduce seasonal import capability assumptions and tighten capacity zones in winter months—raising accreditation and RA value for dispatchable resources including hydropower and pumped storage during peak-scarcity periods, particularly in constrained zones. Votes on both seasonal tie benefits and capacity-zone formation are scheduled for a future meeting (no specific date stated).

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has established a Probabilistic Energy Adequacy Tool (PEAT) and Regional Energy Shortfall Threshold (REST) framework to conduct 5- and 10-year energy assessments (study years 2031 and 2036). For 2026, the ISO is running 19 selected sensitivities spanning load variations (+10% net load, +100% large load), resource-mix changes (offshore-wind deletions up to 3,650 MW in 2036; RFO and NG retirements of 2,000–4,000 MW), and fuel/import constraints (-50% imports, ±10% oil/LNG inventory). The replacement strategy for retired resources uses interconnection-queue composition (70% batteries, 15% PV, 15% onshore wind) scaled by nameplate-to-capacity factors, not direct assumption of hydro replacement. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, the most material scenarios are the large-load and import-constrained sensitivities, which will reveal energy-shortfall risk periods and durations under high-scarcity conditions — data that affects seasonal accreditation exposure and the likelihood of sustained high-price regimes. The methodology explicitly excludes offshore wind from the replacement portfolio due to buildout uncertainty, leaving a net-generation gap in retirement scenarios that hydro supply could fill. No formal comment deadline or next action date is stated in this overview.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ is revising the OASIS Queue Pause design (MIR82-R) to allow individual Transmission Service Providers (MTSPs) to pause, limit, or manage transmission-service requests flexibly — rather than mandate a uniform pause — during the window between Day-Ahead Market close and Energy Schedule updates. Hydro operators in SPP Markets+ should assess whether the proposed flexibility in queue management creates new opportunities or risks for intra-day transmission-service requests (e.g., for storage recharge or ramping adjustments) or whether MTSP-specific procedures may disadvantage certain resource types.

documents.ai_summary: SPP Markets+ proposes MIR81-R, which distinguishes 'Normal' MTIs (active in day-ahead, RUC, and pre-RTBM; then fixed in RTBM) from 'Dynamic' MTIs (active only in RTBM). A BA may register separate scheduling constraints for the same path using different transaction types, allowing it to restrict incremental real-time transfers independently of day-ahead commitment without disrupting the prior optimized dispatch plan. The mechanism allows BAs to limit swing in net scheduled interchange (NSI) between RTBM dispatch intervals while preserving the DA/RUC commitment. documents.ai_summary: Markets+ is establishing tariff and protocol language (MIR 9.2-R) to create a new "Dynamic Schedule Resource" participation type for dispatchable resources physically located in one participating BA but dynamically scheduled to serve load in another BA. The proposal addresses a double-counting problem in current power-balance accounting: when a dynamically scheduled resource is dispatched to a new output level, both the MTI (market transmission interface) and the dynamic NSI (net scheduled interchange) reflect the change, forcing both BAs to regulate separately. MIR 9.2-R introduces a Dynamic Schedule Resource Interface tied to each such resource, so only the interface — not both the output and the NSI — enters the attaining BA's power balance, eliminating double regulation. The framework allows resource-coupled dynamic schedules (Use Case 1a: participating BA to participating BA with a specific dispatchable resource) to remain under Markets+ dispatch control while transferring regulation responsibility to the attaining BA, with e-tagging requirements and registration mandates for market participants. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in the document; it appears to be a technical briefing of tariff and protocol changes already adopted or in final preparation.

documents.ai_summary: CAISO proposes three refinements to its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology: (1) modeling proposed resources identified in transmission planning as needed for local reliability in the base case dispatch (rather than only when they relieve constraints), conditional on reasonable certainty of completion before deliverability is needed; (2) including existing demand response in the base case to avoid over-allocating deliverability; and (3) reducing the dispatch value of generators in the base case from 80% to 70% of maximum study amount to reflect the increased planning reserve margin (from ~15% to 25%). The refinements affect how new hydro and PSH projects are studied during interconnection—projects that would need to compete with modeled proposed resources to secure a deliverable position in queue. Comments are due June 25, 2026. Most exposed are developers of new hydro or PSH seeking interconnection in California who will compete for deliverability allocation against projects CAISO assumes will be built to meet identified local needs.

documents.title: Draft - On-Peak Deliverability Study Methodology - Jun 03, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO refines its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology — the mechanism by which generators (including hydro and storage) qualify for full or partial capacity credit toward resource adequacy; changes to Pmax assumptions, scenario hours, and dispatch modeling directly affect how much RA capacity hydro and pumped storage can claim and at what cost.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO has refined its generator on-peak deliverability study methodology, effective January 2024 and documented here as of June 2026, to address bottleneck risk as the generation fleet diversifies and solar penetration shifts peak net load. The methodology now assesses two distinct scenarios: (1) highest system need (hours 19–22 in summer, peak sale with low solar), where non-intermittent generators' Pmax is set to highest summer Qualifying Capacity in the prior three years, and intermittent generators at 20% exceedance level; and (2) secondary system need (hours 15–18, peak consumption with high solar output), where Pmax for intermittent resources is 50% exceedance level and energy storage Pmax is 50% of 4-hour discharge capacity. For hybrid and energy-storage projects, Pmax is limited by requested maximum output. Hydro and pumped-storage owners face a direct revenue impact: the Pmax values used in deliverability studies directly determine how much capacity credit they can claim in RA markets and interconnection queues; storage capacity credit in secondary scenarios is capped at half the 4-hour discharge rating, potentially disadvantaging long-duration or seasonal storage relative to short-duration batteries.

This change tightens enforcement of offer compliance for all dispatchable and storage resources subject to cost-based offer rules—hydro and PSH are typically among resources required to submit cost-based offers, so stricter penalties and elimination of negative-penalty loopholes increases the cost of offer errors and reinforces compliance discipline. documents.ai_summary: PJM approved Manual 13 Revision 98 (effective July 23, 2026) updating emergency operations procedures to align with NERC EOP-011 standards and address capacity-deficient conditions occurring outside traditional weather-alert triggers. Key changes include: (1) a new Capacity Advisory mechanism providing advance notice when available generating capacity approaches demand requirements, leveraging forecasted peak load, day-ahead reserve requirements, and net interchange; (2) Attachment O establishing a conditional procedure for emergency use of backup generators (triggered only by DOE Section 202(c) orders) with coordinated PJM and Transmission Owner actions during capacity and transmission emergencies; (3) clarifications separating transmission-security emergency procedures from capacity-based procedures, removing capacity-specific actions (Emergency Bid Process, export recall, capacity load shed) from transmission-security triggers; and (4) updated language for Advanced Scheduled Resources under cold- and hot-weather alerts. Hydro operators must understand the Capacity Advisory's forecasting inputs and threshold logic, as early signals of tight capacity may activate voluntary or mandatory dispatch obligations; pumped-storage operators should note the manual's treatment of generation scheduling during emergencies and any implications for charging-window availability. Most exposed: all dispatchable hydro and PSH participating in PJM's real-time market and ancillary-services offerings. No member comment deadline is stated; the revision was endorsed by the Operating Committee on June 4, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes to refine the definition of "Flexible Resources" to require that all available operating schedules meet the flexibility criteria (combined startup and notification time ≤ 2 hours, minimum run time ≤ 2 hours), rather than permitting flexibility on only some schedules. Under current rules, a unit committed day-ahead on a flexible schedule but holding an inflexible backup schedule can still receive Flexible Resource Lost Opportunity Cost (LOC) credits if not called in real-time, even though it may be unable to start under real-time dispatch due to its inflexible schedule(s). The proposal would classify such units as inflexible for real-time and LOC purposes, restricting LOC eligibility to units that meet flexibility on all schedules and are not called due to transmission or reliability constraints. Tariff and Manual updates (Attachments K, 11, and 28) are under review; the Markets and Reliability Committee is scheduled to endorse the proposal on July 28, 2026, with FERC filing to follow. Fast-start hydro and PSH units with multiple offer schedules are most exposed: those unable to configure all available cost-based schedules as flexible will lose LOC protection and be held to inflexible day-ahead commitments.

documents.ai_summary: PJM's Manual 11 redline updates the business rules for Market Sellers, with particular emphasis on Hybrid Resources and Energy Storage Resources (ESR) participation, flexible-resource definitions, and offer-capping procedures under the Three-Pivotal Supplier Test. The revision enables cost-based offer stickiness (once dispatched on cost basis, unit remains cost-capped regardless of updated offers) and clarifies the initial capping determination period. Most exposed are pumped-storage and other dispatchable hydro resources that compete with CTs/diesels for flexibility revenue; any PSH owner using PJM's ESR model or treating a hybrid asset will need to audit self-scheduling constraints and mode-change notification procedures. documents.ai_summary: PJM presented its pro forma Reliability Must-Run (RMR) Agreement framework, streamlining the process by which generators—especially old or transmission-constrained units—can receive cost recovery to continue operating after leaving the market to address thermal, voltage, or stability violations. The pro forma approach pre-approves non-rate terms and conditions, requiring FERC acceptance of only the rate component (either the Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit formula or a full cost-of-service filing), eliminating the need for hearing and settlement judge procedures and reducing process friction. Hydroelectric facilities, particularly older reservoir-based units prone to becoming stranded as markets shift, may use this pathway to recover operating costs when transmission upgrades are pending; revenues from energy, capacity, and ancillary-services sales are credited against RMR charges, creating a hybrid cost-plus mechanism. The framework applies to units regardless of fuel type and is effective only upon FERC approval; PJM terminates the RMR when it determines the constraint is resolved. Critically, the amendment limits this automatic $0 offer through delivery year 2028/2029 (unless PJM and FERC extend it), and excludes such resources from performance-bonus eligibility and balancing-ratio calculations. All capacity revenues flow to the zone that funded the asset's reliability mission, not to the resource operator. This affects any hydro asset retained for transmission reliability or deactivation-avoidance—particularly reservoirs and run-of-river plants in constrained zones—by locking them into below-market revenue recovery and removing upside from performance incentives. For hydro operators, this agreement determines whether aging run-of-river or reservoir plants facing retirement can be forced to remain online, what capital repairs PJM must fund, and how long the contract lock lasts — directly affecting retirement-planning flexibility and revenue certainty during the reliability-need window.

documents.ai_summary: PJM Part V tariff revisions (first read at June 24, 2026 MRC) govern generation deactivation notice, reliability-impact review, and continued operation under must-run arrangements. Generation owners must provide 12 months' notice; PJM then has 4–5 months to assess whether deactivation would harm transmission reliability. If reliability impacts are found, owners can elect either cost-of-service recovery or a Deactivation Avoidable Cost Credit (DACC) formula—a monthly payment that escalates from 110% in year one to 150% by year four of the deactivation-delay period, less actual net market revenues. The formula applies to generation (including hydropower) that continues operating beyond its desired retirement date to support grid reliability. Most relevant to aging hydro plants facing retirement but needed for transmission support or seasonal energy adequacy; the DACC structure and multiplier schedule directly determine whether an extended operating life is economically viable.

The changes aim to ensure RMR units do not face performance obligations without clear cost-recovery pathways prior to FERC rate-setting. This reshapes the economics of mothballing versus operational reserve retention for owners considering exit — a material decision point for aging hydro and storage assets in PJM.

documents.ai_summary: PJM has circulated a revised pro forma Reliability Must Run Service Agreement (tariff Part V, Subpart A) for discussion at the June 24, 2026 Markets and Reliability Committee. The agreement establishes the contractual framework by which PJM can compel continued operation of generation resources (including hydro and PSH) that have submitted deactivation notices but are deemed necessary for transmission system reliability. Key terms include: (1) Generation Owner may terminate only on Catastrophic Force Majeure, if PJM denies necessary Project Investment, or by exercising standard deactivation rights with 90 days' notice; (2) PJM may terminate on 61 days' notice if the RMR Resource is no longer needed, with full recovery of prudently incurred costs; (3) PJM may extend the term unilaterally, requiring Generation Owner response within 14 days and permitting renegotiation of compensation; and (4) PJM retains dispatch authority over the RMR Resource for transmission limits, system restoration, capacity emergencies, or operational testing, subject only to owner-disclosed operating limitations. The document is currently in working-draft, FOR DISCUSSION PURPOSES ONLY status. For hydro and PSH owners, this revised form directly affects exit optionality: the extension clause (Section 2.5) and PJM's unilateral termination right (Section 2.3) determine how long a resource can be held in operation and whether compensation can be renegotiated mid-agreement. Owners with plants facing retirement but offering essential voltage support, black-start capability, or ramping—a common profile for aging hydro and PSH—should monitor whether Section 4 (compensation mechanism, not fully excerpted here) provides adequate coverage of Project Investment (repairs, NERC compliance, maintenance with overtime) and whether the 60-day termination notice gives sufficient runway to execute alternative retirement or repurposing strategies.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual M14D to clarify and tighten reactive power (VAR) control requirements for all generators in response to the May 2026 NERC ERO Enterprise CMEP Practice Guide (which lowered IBR registration threshold to 20 MVA/60 kV) and emerging low-voltage stability risks highlighted by the 2025 Spain blackout. The revisions require: (1) generators operate exclusively in automatic voltage-control mode unless documented exceptions are approved by PJM and the Transmission Owner; (2) define acceptable volt-VAR boundaries and VAR control ranges per MW output (32.87% of max MW capacity); and (3) establish a three-party investigative process (PJM, TO, and generator owner/operator) for reactive control performance issues, with PJM empowered to direct AVR and inverter settings changes. For conventional hydroelectric and pumped-storage facilities, this narrows operational flexibility in reactive-power dispatch—generators can no longer operate in constant-MVAR, constant power-factor, or manual modes without PJM/TO approval—potentially reducing the ability to optimize reactive output for revenue or water management. The revision moves to OC and SOS for first read June 24, 2026, with MRC review June 24, and endorsement timeline extending through July.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual M14D (Generator Operational Requirements), sections 7.1.2 and Attachment D, effective July 23, 2026, to incorporate NERC's new Category 2 GO standard and clarify reactive-power control requirements. The revision adds references to Category 2 GO generators, specifies allowable automatic voltage regulator (AVR) modes, and introduces volt-var and watt-var performance graphs with acceptable operating ranges, along with monitoring procedures where PJM may direct gen owner/operators to address voltage issues. The change is driven by PJM's dual operational pressures: rising solar/IBR penetration and load growth exceeding new generation, both exacerbating voltage stability risks. Hydro operators in PJM (primarily PSH and conventional generation) must update their VAR control procedures and performance commitments to comply; MRC voting is scheduled for July 23rd, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: PJM's Planning and Operating Committees have jointly approved a Storage As Transmission Asset (SATA) framework, now moving to Markets and Reliability Committee review (first read June 26, 2026, endorsement vote scheduled August 26, 2026) with FERC filing to follow. The design creates a distinct operational mode for energy storage—including pumped hydro—dedicated to mitigating RTEP-identified transmission violations: discharge occurs automatically when the violation occurs, charging is coordinated post-discharge, and the asset is settled under transmission cost-of-service (Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits) rather than energy or capacity markets. Most exposed are pumped-storage owners considering or operating transmission-constrained locations; the framework could redirect PSH toward guaranteed cost-recovery transmission-relief roles at the expense of merchant energy and ancillary-service revenue streams. The mechanism locks storage owners into a single operational purpose (voltage/flow support) tied to planning-study assumptions, with tariff conforming language expected September–November 2026.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE has redlined Section II of its tariff to establish a formal Deactivation Notification process for permanent resource retirements, effective for the Capacity Commitment Period beginning June 1, 2028. Generators seeking to retire must file a deactivation notice by the first business day within 12 months of each CCP start; resources >20 MW are subject to a 90-day reliability review, after which ISO may delay deactivation if needed for local transmission reliability and offer net going-forward-cost compensation. Key mechanics: (1) resources that never held Capacity Network Resource Interconnection Service (CNR or equivalent) can deactivate by simple written notice; (2) resources inactive for three calendar years are deemed automatically deactivated unless repower-application protections apply; (3) Lead Market Participants must submit detailed cost workbooks and officer affidavits, subject to Internal Market Monitor audit. Most exposed are Northeast hydro owners contemplating retirement, especially run-of-river or peaking units currently holding CNR capacity — the reliability-review gate and potential delayed-deactivation obligation (with only net-going-forward-cost recovery) can trap owners in the market longer than planned, and the three-year automatic-deactivation clock creates planning urgency for units on extended outages.

documents.title: 2026-06-24 TC A05 NEPOOL Counsel Memo Summarizing FERC Show Cause Order to ISO-NE & PTOs (Docket No. EL26-72)
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FERC's show-cause order to ISO-NE on large-load and co-located-load integration directly affects hydro's strategic options — co-location rules, new transmission service definitions, and generator interconnection pathways for resources serving co-located load will reshape how hydropower (especially pumped storage and run-of-river) can participate in transmission service markets and capture value from load-proximate generation.
documents.ai_summary: FERC issued a show-cause order (June 18, 2026, Docket EL26-72) to ISO-NE and Participating Transmission Owners, preliminarily finding the tariff unjust and unreasonable for lacking provisions on large-load and co-located-load integration. ISO-NE has 60 days to propose tariff changes addressing five categories: application procedures for large loads (defined as ≥50 MW peak at single site, ≥69 kV), cost transparency and cost-recovery agreements, rates and terms for co-location (co-located load defined as end-use customer load physically connected to a generating facility), new transmission services (interim NITS, firm and non-firm contract demand), and generator interconnection for resources serving electrically proximate or co-located load. The order defines three interconnection approaches for generators: new study process matching output to load forecast, use of existing service at existing POI, or load-limited service with no injection. ISO-NE must also file a 30-day informational report on resource adequacy for new large loads. This order parallels concurrent FERC actions in PJM and SPP and builds on Secretary of Energy ANOPR RM26-4-000 (October 2025). Hydro owners should note that co-location rules and new transmission service architecture will determine whether existing or new hydropower facilities can serve co-located or electrically proximate loads, and how ancillary services and BTMG netting are treated—directly affecting revenue models for pumped storage and run-of-river plants positioned near emerging data-center loads in New England.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook, presented to the Management Committee on June 24, 2026, projects 20-year system conditions, demand, generation mix, and transmission congestion across New York. Key findings emphasize that transmission capability increasingly determines whether new resources can serve load, and identify the Central East interface and Northern New York as targeted upgrade opportunities for bulk transmission to enable zero-emissions and firm-capacity development. The Outlook recommends establishing a path for firm, dispatchable capacity (including potential hydrogen-based generation) to provide grid services alongside renewables, coordinating resource additions and retirements to avoid tightening system conditions, and enhancing dynamic voltage support across Central East. documents.ai_summary: NYISO Rate Schedule 1 governs the allocation of the ISO's annual budget between withdrawal and injection billing units, currently set at 72% withdrawals / 28% injections since January 2012. The tariff requires a Management Committee vote in Q3 each year to decide whether to commission a cost-of-service study to evaluate whether the allocation should change; from 2015 through 2025, successive votes declined to fund a study (most recent study was Black and Veatch in 2011, costing ~$215K over 6 months). The next vote is scheduled for July 29, 2026. Pumped-storage owners are directly affected because the withdrawal/injection split determines their share of NYISO operating costs: a higher injection allocation would raise PSH's charging costs relative to discharge revenue, and a shift toward withdrawals would burden conventional hydro operators more heavily. Management Committee members representing hydro interests should track whether any party moves to commission a 2026–2027 study, since the allocation mechanism is active and the cost-of-service framework can shift under the tariff's standing provisions.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO is revising Section 26.4 of its Tariff governing Operating Requirements and Bidding Requirements—the credit and collateral amounts customers must post to participate in ISO markets. For hydropower and pumped-storage operators, lower credit collateral requirements reduce working-capital drag on dispatch flexibility and frequency/ancillary-service provision; the prepayment option may particularly benefit smaller hydro participants.
