documents.title: Presentation - Price Formation Issues - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAISO Market Surveillance Committee presentation on price-formation issues and reserve-product design directly affects hydropower revenue through scarcity-pricing mechanisms, reserve-procurement rules, and co-optimization of reserves with energy—all core inputs to hydro dispatch value and ancillary-service compensation.
documents.ai_summary: Scott Harvey, CAISO Market Surveillance Committee member, presents two critical price-formation issues for the California ISO balancing area: (1) real-time price signals in stressed conditions (August 2020 case study shows low real-time prices failed to incent import supply despite high day-ahead prices, and current rules cap prices at $1,000 during non-spinning-reserve dispatch, understating shortage value to suppliers and consumers); and (2) absence of explicit 30- or 60-minute reserve products, forcing CAISO to procure thousands of MWs of buffer capacity via expensive load-conformance purchases (energy bought in FMM and settled at RTD imbalance prices, with costs varying wildly). Harvey recommends CAISO adopt a tiered reserve product with graduated demand-curve pricing (referencing NYISO's 10-step design: $0–$750 depending on shortage MW), co-optimized with energy, but cautions that existing flexiramp and imbalance-reserve implementation flaws (battery state-of-charge accounting, nodal-delivery tests, locational modeling) must be fixed first—work that will take years. Hydropower operators (especially pumped storage and flexible dispatchable units) are directly affected: better-designed reserve markets with co-optimization and scarcity-responsive pricing would raise the value of fast-response capacity and reduce reliance on out-of-market load conformance, increasing revenue certainty and reducing demand-side rationing risk.

documents.title: Market Surveillance Committee Draft Opinion - Gas Resource Management - Dec 12, 2025
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Gas-fired resource offer rules (reference levels, commitment cost caps, default energy bids) directly affect CAISO's mitigation framework for dispatchable generators; the proposal's expansion to EDAM participants and its implications for offer flexibility and cost recovery touch hydro's competitive position in energy pricing and dispatch, plus the proposal's stated concern about not enabling locational market power is foundational to how use-limited resources like hydro are treated in cost-based offer caps.
documents.ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issued a draft opinion (Dec. 5, 2025) on the CAISO's Gas Resource Management (GRM) proposal, which addresses gas price volatility challenges for gas-fired generators participating in EDAM, including changes to reference-level calculation methods, after-the-fact cost recovery, and multi-day advisory market runs to improve fuel procurement forecasting. The MSC supports most enhancements as low-cost measures to help EDAM participants reflect true gas costs in offer prices, but flags a critical gap: the absence of any market-power test for commitment cost mitigation means all gas units are mitigated in every interval, creating inefficient caps for non-dominant units while potentially over-protecting dominant ones—a structural issue that directly parallels hydro's chronic mis-treatment under opportunity-cost-based mitigation rules designed for thermal units. The MSC identifies EDAM timing (day-ahead schedules posted after morning gas nominations close) as exacerbating these challenges across the expanded Western footprint, and recommends development of a workable market-power test for commitment costs as a high priority going forward. No vote or comment deadline is stated in this draft opinion.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Changes in transmission infrastructure (CHPE HVDC addition, Smart Path Connect upgrades, interface limit redistribution) and generation retirements affect hydro dispatch patterns, interregional transfer capability, and revenue opportunity from exports and locational scarcity pricing—all of which touch hydro's strategic deliverability and the value of flexible ramping capacity.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Summer 2026 operations study reports 1,225 MW of generation retirements (including large thermal units like Danskammer 532 MW and Narrows 352 MW) offset by 225 MW of solar and storage additions. Major transmission projects—Champlain Hudson Power Express HVDC, Smart Path Connect 345 kV stations, and Hertel–Astoria additions—are now modeled in service. These changes redistribute flows and alter interface thermal limits: Total East interface limit decreased 125 MW, UPNY-ConEd increased 250 MW, UPNY-SENY increased 225 MW, and Moses South increased 250 MW. Sprain Brook Dunwoodie South interface limit was raised to 4,225 MW and Total East to 4,050 MW. The study's status is a June 2026 presentation update to the Operating Committee; no forward deadlines are stated. For hydro owners, the net effect is mixed: retirement of thermal generation reduces dispatchable competition and may elevate real-time energy prices and ramping value, while the HVDC and transmission upgrades improve northern import capability and may compress NY price separations, affecting both in-state dispatchable hydro revenue and Northwest-to-NY export economics. Pumped-storage operators should monitor how the reduced Moses South thermal limits and increased UPNY interfaces change the voltage-support and frequency-response service opportunities in those zones.

HVdc converter schedules list in-service status for Champlain Hudson Power Express (1,250 MW), Sandy Pond (1,500 MW), and four other TransÉnergie HVdc links (total ~3,300 MW). Phase-angle regulator dispatch on key NY interfaces (Ramapo, Uniondale, and cross-Sound) is specified to manage congestion. This study informs summer transfer limits and is foundational for RA adequacy and reserve requirement calculations; export-dependent hydro owners (Northwest suppliers to WECC/California, Quebec hydro exporters) should verify their assumed dispatch levels match actual operating conditions and test sensitivity to transmission constraints.

documents.title: 06a Expedited Deliverability Study 2025-02 - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO Expedited Deliverability Study determines which generation and storage projects can deliver power without system upgrades — directly affecting interconnection timelines, costs, and deliverability certainty for new hydro, PSH, or co-located resources seeking NYISO queue status.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Expedited Deliverability Study 2025-02 analyzes three projects (Curtis/Palmer natural gas/hydro hybrid, Soltage battery energy storage, RP New York BESS) for deliverability at requested CRIS (capacity resource interconnection service) levels without triggering system-wide upgrades. All three projects passed their respective interface and byway tests and are deemed fully deliverable at requested capacity: Curtis/Palmer at 58.8 MW summer, Soltage at 20 MW, and RP New York BESS at 5.1 MW. The study is on track for Operating Committee approval with a 5-business-day decision window for each interconnection customer to accept or reject its deliverable MW; non-acceptance triggers re-study of remaining projects. For any hydro or hybrid generator seeking interconnection in NYISO, this procedural pathway offers faster deliverability determination than full Cluster Study if transmission constraints are minimal — but only for projects already through Class Year or Cluster study phases for ERIS (energy resource interconnection service).

documents.title: 06b Expedited Deliverability Study 2025-02 - Report
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO interconnection deliverability study determines whether a hydropower project (Curtis/Palmer Hydro) can inject its requested capacity without network upgrades — directly affecting hydro interconnection timelines, costs, and strategic feasibility of delivery into high-value zones.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Expedited Deliverability Study 2025-02 concludes that the Curtis/Palmer Hydro Project in the Rest-of-State Capacity Region is fully deliverable at its requested CRIS level without requiring system upgrades. The study evaluated three projects (Curtis/Palmer Hydro, Soltage battery, RP New York BESS) using 2029 summer peak conditions, transfer-limit analysis across capacity regions, and contingency screening under NPCC/NYSRC criteria. For hydro interconnection customers, a 'fully deliverable' determination removes the risk of being forced to undersize their injection or fund costly network upgrades to achieve their requested MW — streamlining path to commercial operation. The analysis covers methodology, base-case modeling, and transfer-capability assessments but contains no stated comment deadlines or next procedural steps in this excerpt.

documents.title: 07a Storm Watch Redispatch - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Tariff and settlement methodology changes to Storm Watch Redispatch (Transmission Security Analysis) cost allocation affect how real-time dispatch costs are computed and allocated to load zones, which can influence uplift/make-whole charges borne by dispatchable resources including hydro.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is clarifying its Services Tariff (MST 4.1.8) and revising the Transmission and Dispatch Operations Manual to document a long-term improvement to Storm Watch Redispatch (TSA) cost calculation. The enhancement will use Day-Ahead schedules from the bid redispatch pass (instead of initial Day-Ahead schedules) and real-time schedules to determine flows across TSA constraints, while keeping the real-time shadow-price methodology and Zone J customer allocation unchanged. This refinement stems from review of July 2025 TSA settlements that exceeded $53 million and aims to more accurately reflect the actual redispatch obligation. NYISO is seeking votes on the proposed tariff revisions at the June 2026 Membership Committee meeting.

documents.title: 07b Storm Watch Redispatch - T&D Manual - Redline

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Transmission and Dispatch Operations Manual (Manual 12) redlines the Storm Watch Redispatch procedure, a real-time operational protocol for managing transmission constraints and emergency conditions. The document is in DRAFT status, accepted by the BIC on 04/15/2026 and Operating Committee on 04/16/2026, with an effective date of 05/01/2026. Storm Watch Redispatch is a corrective control strategy that allows NYISO to issue real-time dispatch instructions to manage transmission violations and security constraints — a tool that can override normal market clearing and compel hydro resources to adjust output. For hydro operators, the relevance lies in the operational obligation to accept Storm Watch redispatch directives, which may suppress market-cleared prices during constraint periods or require uneconomic output changes. Reservoir and run-of-river hydro are equally exposed to these dispatch obligations; the mechanism affects real-time revenue predictability and compliance burden.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Operating Committee approves the Expedited Deliverability Study 2025-02 Report and revisions to the Transmission and Dispatch Operations Manual related to 'Storm Watch Redispatch.' documents.ai_summary: NYISO's May 2026 operations report shows hydro (including pumped-storage hydro) at 6,324 MW nameplate capacity, comprising 12% of NYCA generation resources. The report tracks month-to-month generation mix, day-ahead market capacity unavailable in real-time (broken by fuel type including hydro), wind and solar curtailment by transmission constraint, net load ramps, and reserve activations. Two new transmission projects (Smart Path Connect and additional 345 kV facilities) came online in May, and the Champlain Hudson Power Express merchant transmission facility entered the real-time energy market on 5/13, potentially improving deliverability for hydro exports. Hydro owners use this baseline data to assess system balance, transmission constraints limiting their dispatch, and competitive positioning versus wind/solar capacity (11,547 MW intermittent nameplate vs. 6,324 MW hydro). The report shows May 2026 wind and FTM solar curtailment at 2.7% system-wide, with specific transmission constraints listed, affecting revenue for hydro resources competing in the same nodal zones.

documents.ai_summary: Black Hills Energy presents a proposal to align Markets+ High Priority Export surplus calculations with Operations Program obligations, rather than keeping them static across the entire WRAP binding season. Currently, surplus capacity is calculated once per season against forward RA obligations but cannot be updated as operational conditions change, forcing high-priority exports to be classified as non-firm (uncommitted) even when actual operational capacity exists. The proposal would allow surplus recalculation on a near-term basis to reflect real availability, addressing a misalignment between WSPP Schedule C (firm-service language) and Markets+ treatment of uncommitted exports as economically dispatchable. This affects hydropower owners relying on firm bilateral export trades across the SPP-WEIM seam, particularly in constrained regions like Rocky Mountain; the change would restore liquidity of firm bilateral trades and planning certainty for load-serving entities. Status and next steps are not stated in this presentation.

Implementation is targeted for Q1 2027, with MPEC approval sought in Q3 2026. For hydropower owners participating in Markets+—particularly those seeking to export renewable generation or manage interchange flexibility across the SPP-region boundary—this creates a new operational pathway that could alter revenue stacking (energy cleared in DAM/RTBM plus potential bilateral premiums) and strategic choices around scheduling vs. market participation; the mechanism is most relevant to larger hydro and PSH facilities managing outflow across seams into non-Markets+ balancing areas, since it enables market-cleared rather than pre-scheduled boundary transactions.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: e-Tag confirmation requirements affect interchange transaction eligibility in Markets+, which directly impacts how hydro (especially run-of-river and variable output) participates in interregional energy markets and settlement accuracy — a core revenue mechanism for hydro exports and flexibility sales across seams.
documents.ai_summary: Markets+ is evaluating whether to accept e-Tags at the 'Valid' (pending approval) or 'Confirmed' (approved) stage for import/export/through interchange transactions. SPP and its vendor recommend 'Confirmed e-Tags' — only those with completed multi-party approvals — to avoid settlement discrepancies, divergence between day-ahead awards and real-time operations, and failed transactions affecting market assumptions. The 'Valid' option offers earlier visibility and participant flexibility but creates operational and settlement risk: ~10% of Western Interconnect e-Tags in May 2026 were ultimately denied, and using unapproved schedules in market solutions could force settlements on transactions that never become operational. The recommendation aligns with existing Integrated Marketplace practices and reduces vendor development costs. Markets+ protocol sections 4.2.2.7, 4.2.3.3, and 4.2.4 currently reference 'valid' e-Tags; this decision will either codify or revise that language. Discussion topics and a decision timeline (MSWG → MDWG → MPEC) are outlined but no comment deadline or vote date is stated in the excerpt.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2025-2044 System & Resource Outlook examines how New York's grid will evolve under multiple policy and demand scenarios through 2044, focusing on generation adequacy, resource-mix composition, and transmission constraints. The analysis finds that renewable generation concentration in upstate pockets creates curtailment risk (especially by 2035–2044) and drives bulk-transmission congestion through the Central East interface, with fossil-generation retirements and large-load growth (data centers, etc.) tightening system conditions and raising downstate capacity payments. For hydropower owners, this outlook establishes the transmission-planning baseline affecting deliverability and locational scarcity value; for pumped-storage operators, it identifies whether seasonal adequacy stress and interregional export opportunities (low-cost clean-energy export potential noted in 2035 scenarios) will raise PSH cycling revenue and RA accreditation premiums. The document is a draft for NYISO Business Issues Committee discussion (June 2026); no formal comment deadline is stated, but future comprehensive reliability plans and transmission procurements will flow from these scenarios.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook projects electricity demand outpacing resource additions, with firm dispatchable capacity remaining essential across all decarbonization scenarios to provide energy, operating reserves, ramping, regulation, and voltage support during periods of low renewable output. The study identifies Central East and Northern New York transmission interfaces as bottlenecks constraining renewable deliverability and system efficiency; targeted dynamic voltage support upgrades are recommended. Coordinating the timing of resource retirements and new additions is flagged as critical to avoid tightening system conditions. The findings inform NYISO's biennial Comprehensive System Planning Process and identify scenarios for Economic Transmission Project Evaluation and Requested Economic Planning Studies. Board approval is scheduled for July 2026; the full report and 12 technical appendices (including capacity expansion and production cost simulations, renewable generation pocket analysis, and sensitivities) are available in the data catalog.

documents.title: 2 Draft April 15, 2026 Minutes
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: NYISO capacity accreditation and winter ICAP demand-curve methodology directly affects pumped-storage and conventional hydro revenue through seasonal accreditation factors (CAFs) and locational capacity-market clearing prices; the CHPE UDRs decision also touches interregional hydro deliverability and market-seam governance.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's BIC approved tariff revisions to align winter ICAP demand curves for 2026–2027 to account for potential capacity supply via CHPE (Champlain Hudson Power Express) UDRs from HydroQuébec into New York City, contingent on CHPE commencing summer participation. The proposal resets winter-peak and shoulder ICAP demand curves and their UCAP translations using capacity-accreditation factors (CAFs) that assume CHPE participation ('CHPE-In' parameters). Stakeholders raised concerns that actual winter capacity supply via CHPE could diverge from the 0-MW assumption for winter peaks, potentially inverting NYC winter-to-shoulder price signals and reducing accreditation revenue for existing capacity suppliers. The NYISO rejected a lower-curve stakeholder alternative and declined to impose a prohibition on CHPE winter sales, asserting the proposal maintains revenue sufficiency for the reference technology. The proposal is pending FERC approval under ER26-1431 and will become effective on FERC's permit date; it resets baseline assumptions for the broader Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements design scheduled for 2027–2028. Most exposed are existing hydro and PSH owners in NYC and rest-of-state capacity zones whose seasonal RA valuations and clearing-price signals are recalibrated.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Business Issues Committee approved an Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers proposal (Motion #1, May 13, 2026) requiring automatic offering of surplus capacity at $0.00/kW-month with clearing price payment, with May 2027 implementation. Separately, CHPE transmission line commenced real-time energy-market operation May 13, 2026 and capacity-market participation July 2026 delivery month, triggering changes in NYISO capacity-market parameters that will affect existing resources' capacity availability ratings starting July 2026. The committee also reviewed ongoing Electric System Planning and Installed Capacity Working Group activities addressing reliability enhancements (FERC Order 1920 compliance), 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook updates, DER unavailability methodologies, and flexible large-load wholesale participation. For hydro owners, the surplus-offer rule eliminates the option to withhold resale capacity (historically 2.1 MW unoffered Jan 2026), forcing systematic market clearing at spotauction prices; the CHPE parameter shift reallocates capacity value across the system, requiring owners with reduced ICAP ratings to secure makeup capacity or release excess through July 2026 auctions.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to Attachment N of the ICAP Manual to establish separate summer and winter translation factors for Limited Control Run-of-River Hydro Resources and Intermittent Power Resources. Currently, translation factors (which convert Installed Capacity to Unforced Capacity for RA calculations) are computed using June–August production data; the proposal adds winter factors using December–February data, weighted by hourly LOLE factors from the most recent LCR study base case. The revision aligns with NYISO's Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements proposal (filed with FERC on 2/18/2026, effective 6/28/2026, targeted for 2027–2028 Capability Year implementation) and responds to observed winter LOLE in the 2026–2027 IRM study. The document also proposes a formula clarification to better document the current hourly LOLE-weighted calculation method. Run-of-river and seasonal-variable hydro owners will see their RA accreditation shift between seasons—winter production now counts toward winter capacity needs separately—which may raise or lower total RA credits depending on the seasonal production profile relative to winter LOLE weighting.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FERC Order 1920 transmission planning and cost allocation framework directly affects hydro deliverability, interconnection, and strategic transmission expansion that determines whether existing and new hydro resources can reach markets; long-term scenarios and resource-mix assumptions will drive transmission investment decisions that enable or constrain hydro export capability.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is implementing FERC Order 1920 (and subsequent clarifications 1920-A and 1920-B) through a redesigned Long-Term Transmission Planning Process that expands the 20-year planning horizon, incorporates New York Department of Public Service scenario input, and establishes an ex ante cost-allocation methodology for selected transmission projects. The process creates a new Catalog of Transmission Expansion Opportunities, solicits private-sector project proposals competing against NYISO baseline solutions using seven FERC-mandated benefit metrics (avoided reliability facilities, LOLE reduction, production cost savings, reduced losses, outage-congestion mitigation, extreme-weather resilience, and capacity benefits), and gates selection through NYPSC declaration of Long-Term Transmission Needs before cost recovery is allocated. The framework directly affects where transmission investment flows: hydro owners in New York face a new, longer-term planning horizon and competing non-wires alternatives that may or may not prioritize inter-area hydro exports versus local reliability; the cost-allocation methodology (details not yet finalized) determines whether transmission enabling hydro delivery is socialized regionally or assigned to specific beneficiaries. The compliance mechanics are active — NYISO Board approval of the planning structure is imminent, and the first Outlook cycle and PSC filings will begin shortly thereafter.

documents.title: 5 Storm Watch Redispatch (TSA) Costs: Tariff & Manual Revisions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Storm Watch Redispatch (TSA) cost settlement and uplift allocation directly affects NYISO energy market price formation and cost recovery mechanisms that apply to all dispatchable resources including hydropower.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes tariff and manual revisions to clarify the calculation of Storm Watch Redispatch (TSA) costs—uplift charges triggered by emergency transmission constraints during severe weather. The Long-Term Improvement will enhance Day-Ahead and real-time flow calculations by using Day-Ahead schedules from the bid redispatch pass and real-time schedules to determine flows across TSA constraints, while keeping the real-time Shadow Price and allocation to Zone J customers unchanged. NYISO will seek votes on manual revisions at the June Oversight Committee and tariff revisions at the June Management Committee. This affects how NYISO recovers emergency redispatch costs from the market and thus the magnitude of uplift/make-whole payments that hydro and other dispatchable resources encounter during scarcity events—clarifying the calculation methodology may reduce settlement volatility following extreme events like the July 2025 storms that triggered $53 million in initial costs.

The document is in draft for Business Issues Committee discussion (BIC acceptance dated 04/15/2026, Operations Committee 04/16/2026) and effective 05/01/2026. Most directly material are sections on real-time commitment procedures (6.1), reserve and regulation requirements (3.1.4), and voltage/reactive support via STATCOM and SVC guidance (4.2.3) — all operational levers that determine whether hydro is selected for ancillary services or energy dispatch in competitive real-time markets.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook is a biennial scenario-based planning study examining how demand, resource mix, and transmission evolve under different policy futures. The Outlook models two demand scenarios (95x and 100x) and varying policy stringencies, projecting load growth driven by large loads (data centers and economic development), fossil retirements, and clean-energy targets; it identifies curtailment risk in renewable-generation pockets, bulk transmission congestion (especially on Central East corridor limiting upstate generation export), and strategic value of interregional flows and energy interchange with Hydro-Québec. For hydro asset owners, this study anchors NYISO's capital planning and can influence resource-adequacy constructs, transmission investment priorities, and the marginal value of flexible/dispatchable generation as load-growth tightens supply conditions. The Outlook was presented to the Business Issues Committee on June 10, 2026 (draft status); formal adoption and next-step timeline are not stated in this excerpt.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO released a draft Production Cost Model Assumptions Matrix for its 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook, establishing modeling parameters for long-term reliability and resource-adequacy studies. The matrix specifies that conventional hydro (excluding Niagara) is modeled as hourly modifiers based on 5-year historic data with 2018 weather shapes; Niagara is modeled as a pondage unit with monthly energy targets; and pumped-storage hydro is modeled with endogenous optimization of pumping and dispatching. Battery storage similarly undergoes endogenous optimization by the production-cost model. These assumptions feed into capacity-expansion models that determine new-generation requirements and economic retirement risk by scenario (Base, Contract, and Policy cases with lockdown dates ranging 9/1/2025–10/31/2025). The document is a draft for NYISO Business Issues Committee discussion on June 10, 2026, and represents a critical methodological snapshot for how NYISO values existing and prospective PSH and conventional hydro in RA showings and long-run planning.

documents.title: 8e Draft Appendix G 2025-2044 Outlook Production Cost Model Results - redline

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's draft Appendix G to the 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook presents production cost model results across four scenarios (Base Case, Contract Case, and two Policy Cases) for study years 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2044. The modeling shows load growth concentrated in downstate zones (NYC and Long Island), with LBMPs rising across the study period and becoming sharply elevated in later years (2040–2044) under the Contract Case due to assumed fossil-generator retirements outpacing new renewable additions; Policy Cases with higher capacity additions substantially mitigate LBMP growth and reduce net imports. Energy storage utilization analysis reveals that battery capacity additions exhibit high zone-level correlation with utilization but experience diminishing marginal utilization per unit as total storage capacity rises, suggesting a saturation point in battery efficacy. This outlook is a reference document for NHA members modeling demand-side scarcity, transmission congestion effects on zonal pricing, and the substitution dynamics between storage and dispatchable hydro in a low-carbon NYCA.

documents.title: 8f Draft Appendix I 2025-2044 Outlook Operational Analysis - redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's 20-year operational outlook characterizes hydropower's flexibility role and ramp-following capability relative to fossil generation and renewables, directly informing revenue opportunities for hydro's dispatchable and ramping services as the grid evolves under high-renewable scenarios.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 operational analysis (part of its System & Resource Outlook) models the generation fleet's hourly behavior under Base and Contract Cases, analyzing how different resource types respond to load and net-load (load minus intermittent renewables) changes across daily, hourly, and seasonal timescales. Hydro is characterized as serving both a baseline and dispatchable role with 'limited capability to respond to changes in load/net load' compared to fossil generation, which dominates ramp-following. The analysis shows hydro–load correlation is the second-strongest among generation types (after fossil), and hydro ramps track load ramps more reliably than weather-dependent renewables, positioning hydro as a secondary flexibility resource. This operational characterization — which NYISO will use to assess future resource needs and market design — affects how NYISO values hydro's ramp and ramping-product contributions and shapes transmission and flexibility adequacy planning that influences hydro owners' ability to monetize flexible output. Most exposed are hydro owners with ramp-capable resources; the analysis provides baseline data NYISO may use to set demand curves or capacity factors for flexibility products in forthcoming market-design reviews.

documents.title: 8g Draft Appendix J 2025 - 2044 Outlook Renewable Generation Pockets - redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's renewable pocket analysis identifies transmission constraints affecting hydro deliverability in northern and western New York; hydro resources compete with wind and solar for shared transmission paths, directly impacting energy-delivery value and strategic interconnection/transmission planning.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's 2025–2044 System & Resource Outlook Appendix J analyzes renewable generation pockets and finds that hydro resources in Pockets W and X (western and northern New York) face rising curtailment and congestion in high-penetration renewable scenarios. Pocket X1 (St. Lawrence hydro corridor) exhibits the second-highest congestion among all pockets; hydro curtails before wind and solar because hydro is ineligible for Tier 1 RECs and therefore carries no negative-bid cost in the production-cost model, putting it at a competitive disadvantage when transmission is constrained. The analysis is draft (dated June 10, 2026 BIC) and used to inform longer-range transmission-upgrade planning; approved Phase 1 and Phase 2 transmission projects in Northern New York (Smart Path Connect) are expected to alleviate some congestion, but Policy Case scenarios with 13–35 GW of additional land-based renewable capacity by 2035 will intensify resource-concentration pressures on hydro energy deliverability.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Market Operations Report (June 2026) shows energy and ancillary services cost composition for NYISO customers through May 2026, revealing material shifts in price formation and uplift structures. LBMP (locational energy price) has risen sharply to $43.63/MWh in May 2026 YTD average vs. $36.99/MWh in May 2025; year-to-date NYISO average cost/MWh stands at $102.99 (May 2026) versus $80.72 (May 2025). Uplift (make-whole payments) shows month-to-month volatility, with statewide uplift share swinging between positive $1.68/MWh (January 2026) and negative values in subsequent months. Voltage support and black start services remain stable at approximately $0.14–$0.38/MWh monthly, while reserve and regulation costs track energy scarcity. The report's detailed monthly breakdown by LBMP, NTAC (transmission), reserves, regulation, uplift components, and ancillary services provides visibility into how NYISO's price-formation mechanisms and market-mitigation rules are translating to customer costs — critical for hydro operators managing opportunity costs and dispatch decisions.

documents.ai_summary: Markets+ is revising how must-offer charges and credits are calculated and reported in settlement systems. Currently, must-offer assessment occurs at the Market Participant (MP) level only, creating gaps in Asset Owner (AO)-level determinants for shadow settlement and invoicing. The proposed resolution allocates MP-level must-offer charges proportionally by load ratio share across each AO modeled under an MP, preserving MP-level assessment (and financial responsibility) while enabling AO-level reporting. Changes affect sections 2.6.17, 2.6.18, 2.7.26, and 2.7.27 of the Markets+ Settlement Calculation Guide. A two-week public comment period runs through June 24, 2026, via the SPP RMS system; comments require no formal tariff vote if the guide changes stand alone. Most exposed are hydro operators managing multiple asset owners under a single market participant profile, since the new load-ratio-share allocation will determine how aggregate must-offer penalties or credits flow back to individual facilities for purposes of settlement reporting and invoice tie-out.

The proposal addresses interconnection planning (using familiar surplus/replacement/ERAS processes), resource adequacy accreditation (ZGIA resources offset only their associated local load's capacity obligation, accredited under current MISO rulesets and eligible for zonal resource credits limited by Schedule 53 Direct Loss of Load accreditation or local load obligation), market registration (independent metering and telemetry required; market resources must maintain offer limits ≤ local load demand; MISO will monitor injections and consider charges for overage), and transmission planning (ZGIA included as Non-Transmission Alternative in MTEP). Draft tariff language has been posted; formal feedback is requested from the PAC (pending) and LLWG (June 10, 2026), with a FERC filing planned for late June 2026. Most exposed are owners of on-site generation (including small hydro or pumped storage sited at industrial or utility facilities) seeking to participate as co-located resources or hybrid assets; the framework clarifies accreditation caps and injection limits that will govern revenue from capacity and energy markets.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Large load interconnection and interim service step-up procedures materially affect hydro's strategic options for co-located load participation, transmission deliverability, and resource-adequacy obligations, and establish precedent for how RTOs structure partial-service pathways that could extend to storage and other dispatchable resources.
documents.ai_summary: MISO is formalizing a Firm Service Step Up process to allow large load customers to begin service on partial load blocks before full transmission upgrades are complete, using only interim available capacity. The process requires each partial load addition to pass NERC TPL-001 reliability studies (90-day cycle, quarterly submissions, first-ready-first-served prioritization) and mandates that the load-serving entity procure generation capacity in MISO's Planning Resource Auction to cover the interim load. Approved partial loads become effective at the start of the planning year and persist until the full load interconnection is operational; service is revoked if a load block fails to energize within 90 days of its approved date. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, this is strategically relevant: (1) co-located hydro can now supply large-load customers incrementally rather than waiting for full transmission readiness, shortening payback and improving investment returns; (2) the requirement that interim loads participate in the PRA means the resource-adequacy framework now extends to partial-service loads, establishing that generation must be procured at each step, a model that could define how storage and other flexible resources are accredited in segmented operations; (3) hydro deliverability and transmission-constraint management now explicitly account for multiple overlapping interim-service blocks, which affects zonal scarcity pricing and ramping-reserve demand. MISO requests stakeholder feedback on the prioritization methodology, submission granularity, study frequency, and generation-availability accounting by Monday, June 24, 2026, with tariff language to follow in August.

These establish the rules under which conventional hydro and pumped-storage hydro can compete to serve large loads co-located at or behind load centers, and define the operational obligations (ramp, stability, ride-through) that such service requires. The firm-service framework may create new contracting or capacity-accreditation pathways for dispatchable resources, particularly in load-growth regions where large loads are interconnecting.

documents.ai_summary: MISO is finalizing tariff language for Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements, targeting a June 30, 2026 filing. The framework distinguishes between Computational Loads (digitally driven, requiring advanced modeling, PMU, ramp, and ride-through requirements) and Non-Computational Loads (baseline data and telemetry only), with applicability triggered at 50 MW or expansions of 25+ MW. For hydro owners, this matters because (1) co-located data centers, cryptocurrency mining, and HPC workloads with which hydro may be sited or co-operate are now subject to detailed telemetry, PMU, dynamic modeling, and forecasting requirements that will flow upstream to the interconnecting hydro facility; (2) large-load definition and transition provisions now allow flexibility for in-flight projects, creating windows for strategic positioning; and (3) the distinction between computational and non-computational behavior may allow run-of-river or variable hydro paired with load to avoid some advanced-modeling burdens if properly characterized. Stakeholder feedback significantly shaped the revised language, particularly on applicability date, transition timelines, and load-type distinctions.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT's proposed changes to NPRR 1214 directly affect price formation (LMP and AS MCPC determination) and indifference-payment settlement mechanics that would apply to any dispatchable or storage resource participating in a similar market structure; the pricing and settlement innovations are instructive cross-market comparison points for how RTOs handle reliability deployments and the distortion between dispatch (actual) and pricing-run (counterfactual) awards.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT proposes revisions to NPRR 1214 that eliminate energy and ancillary-service price adders by using SCED Pricing Run prices (LMPs and AS MCPCs) directly when a pricing run is active, rather than calculating adders as Pricing Run minus Dispatch Run prices. In parallel, ERCOT introduces an ancillary-services indifference payment (previously energy-only) using actual offer/bid curves instead of linear approximations, and extends indifference-payment consideration to RUC, RMR, and MRA resources whose real-time revenues were previously overlooked. The proposal also expands locational modeling of reliability deployments to Load and SOG resources under certain dispatch scenarios. Although ERCOT has no hydropower, the design—separating binding dispatch awards (from actual grid state) from binding prices (from hypothetical state absent reliability deployments), and compensating the resulting financial mismatch via indifference payments—illustrates an alternative settlement architecture that contrasts with how other RTOs (including those with hydro fleets) handle the same tension between dispatch realism and scarcity-signal accuracy.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes targeted adjustments to its day-ahead ancillary services (DA A/S) design, effective October 22, 2026, based on February 2026 Internal Market Monitor recommendations. The changes include: (1) reducing the Forecast Energy Requirement Demand Quantity (FER DQ) by expected uncleared front-of-the-meter wind and solar supply to better reflect actual reliability needs; (2) setting a daily floor for the DA A/S strike price (K) based on the marginal cost of an efficient, distillate-fired combustion turbine, including regional emissions costs; and (3) establishing a $3/MWh floor on the Impact Test Threshold. For hydro operators, the strike-price floor methodology is the key mechanic—it ties ancillary-services scarcity pricing to a fossil marginal-cost reference, which will raise the opportunity cost against which hydro's must-offer obligation is evaluated and may increase procurement volume during scarcity events when hydro's regulation and reserve products clear at higher prices. The FER DQ reduction for variable wind/solar will also shift the composition of reliability-based demand, potentially favoring the fast-ramping and continuous-availability profile that hydro supplies. ISO-NE Markets Committee votes on these changes June 9–10, 2026, with Participants Committee vote scheduled June 16–18, 2026.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Capacity IBTs and exports rules directly affect how hydro and storage operators can hedge capacity-market revenues and manage export bids—both central to revenue optimization under ISO-NE's seasonal capacity market redesign (CAR-SA).
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes to implement Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (IBTs)—an ISO-administered financial instrument allowing participants to hedge capacity-market price risk by fixing capacity payments—and to simplify capacity-export rules under the seasonal Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA), effective Q2 2027. Under CAR-SA, capacity clearing occurs ~1 month before each 6-month season (vs. 40+ months ahead under the old FCM), shortening the forward-price visibility window and raising hedging demand. The Capacity IBT would allow a supplier and LSE to exchange fixed-for-floating swaps on capacity obligations, with the ISO settling the floating leg (pegged to seasonal clearing prices or CLO charge rates) and netting it within ISO settlement, while the fixed leg stays off-ISO books. Separately, ISO-NE would discontinue rarely-used export-bid curtailment exemptions (III.1.10.7(f) and III.15.8.1.2) and consolidate export functionality under simpler rules (III.1.10.7(i)), allowing capacity exporters to submit opportunity costs that determine MRIC eligibility. Hydro and PSH operators using export strategies or managing capacity revenues through bilateral hedges will see changes to both pricing instruments and export curtailment priority; the proposal suggests March 2027 implementation and is under stakeholder feedback.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04j - CAR-SA: Interactions with PFP - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) reshape accreditation methodology and Pay-for-Performance settlement mechanics — directly affecting capacity market revenue and performance-payment exposure for all resource types, including hydropower and pumped storage, through changes to the Balancing Ratio cap, CPP calculations, and seasonal stop-loss limits.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presents three approaches to cap the Balancing Ratio (BR) under its seasonal capacity auction reform (CAR-SA), addressing a FERC order requiring the BR cap at 1.0 to prevent resources from being obligated beyond physical capability. The migration from Qualified Capacity to Marginal Reliability Impact (MRI) accreditation will reduce total capacity supply obligations system-wide, raising BRs and causing the 1.0 cap to bind more frequently, which shrinks Capacity Performance Payments (CPPs) to overperformers due to funding deficiencies. ISO-NE's preferred Approach 3 would cap the BR at a seasonal ratio tied to net maximum capability divided by net MRIC (1.355 in summer, 1.444 in winter), preserving stronger performance incentives for overperformance while complying with FERC's logic. Additionally, ISO-NE proposes conforming the annual PFP stop-loss limit to a seasonal market by capping seasonal losses at two times (instead of three times) a resource's maximum monthly net loss. Stakeholder feedback is due to Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026, with ISO-NE targeting July for its final proposal. Large-duration and seasonal-flexibility resources (including pumped storage and multi-week-capable reservoirs) are most exposed, as their value in CAR-SA depends on accreditation during scarcity hours; how the BR cap settles will determine whether they receive full or reduced CPP rates during performance.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes a Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) transition mechanism (target Q2 2027 effective date) that will gradually shift resource accreditation from current Qualified Capacity to proposed seasonal MRIC (Minimum Reliability Impact Contribution) values over two transition years (two summer and two winter seasons), with full phased design taking effect in Capacity Commitment Period 21. The transition uses a weighted-average approach: in Year 1, a 100 MW QC resource with 70 MW summer MRIC and 40 MW winter MRIC would be accredited at 90 MW (summer) and 80 MW (winter); by Year 3 it falls to the full MRIC floor (70/40 MW). Hydro owners will face material accreditation volatility during transition because MRIC values depend on seasonal performance during modeled Minimum Reliability Interest hours, potentially creating seasonal mismatches between what resources can offer and what demand curves procure. ISO-NE is still assessing demand-curve transition mechanics and whether to transition the winter gas constraint; comments and questions are due to Markets Committee Secretary Jasleen Singh (Jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026, with further stakeholder meetings scheduled through Q3 2026 before FERC filing.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) establish resource accreditation modeling that directly determines how much capacity hydro and storage resources can sell and at what value — the foundation for their RA revenue.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is modeling accreditation outcomes under its proposed CAR-SA design using a 70-year weather-adjusted load dataset (weighted subset of years 2000/01–2022/23 for winter; 2007–2023 for summer) to capture long-term weather variability and peak-load scenarios. Sensitivity analysis shows that explicitly modeling all 70 years of winter hourly loads produces nearly identical net ICR, reliability metrics (LOLE, LOLH, EUE), and accreditation results (rMRI) across all resource types — including Daily/Weekly Hydro (96.1–96.2%), Energy Storage (20.9–21.7%), and IPR-Hydro (59.9–61.0%) — compared to the ISO's proposed weighted-year approach. The ISO assessed and rejected FirstLight Resource Management's alternate block-based weighting methodology, concluding it ignores inter-block weather correlations and temporal heterogeneity, understating the likelihood of severe winters and distorting the upper tail of the load distribution where resource adequacy is most critical. The proposed framework will remain in place for CAR-SA implementation targeting Q2 2027; FirstLight's alternative approach was a stakeholder submission rather than ISO proposal.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes not to adjust the non-firm gas capacity demand curve in response to firm gas contracts, treating all firm contracts as fully incremental. The proposal is part of the Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA), with effective date proposed for Q2 2027 and expected filing in the coming months. This design prevents gas resources from artificially inflating capacity market clearing prices through uneconomic firm gas arrangements; however, it may result in procurement of more gas capacity than the actual gas available during tight system conditions. The proposal also links gas contract requirements (16-hour hourly minimum for December–February) to energy-limited resource accreditation methodology, meaning hydro and other energy-limited resources will be treated analogously to gas capacity with similar fuel-availability thresholds. Hydro owners in ISO-NE should monitor whether this gas-constraint treatment influences how seasonal accreditation is applied to conventional hydro and how winter capacity pricing evolves.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04m - CAR-SA: Seasonal Offer Construction and Mitigation - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) establish seasonal capacity-market offer formation rules and seller-side market power mitigation affecting how all resources, including hydropower and pumped storage, must construct and submit capacity bids, with direct implications for revenue recovery and mitigation risk.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE presented seasonal offer construction methodology and seller-side market power mitigation rules for its Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proceeding. The ISO proposes applying a Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) methodology conformed from the FCA's Dynamic Delist Bid Threshold, capped at 25–75% of net Net CONE, plus a pivotal supplier test that automatically reduces bids above the threshold if the supplier is deemed pivotal. For the first seasonal auctions in CCP19, the ISO will use an initial COPT of 37% of annual Net CONE (derived from historical FCA16-18 ratios) rather than prior-auction pricing. The presentation illustrates offer formulation for generalized resources and gas-constrained resources by showing how next-best-alternative analysis drives capacity bids — resources whose NBA is temporary exit must cover netGFC plus expected PFP costs, while resources profitable in energy markets offer only the PFP common-value component. Hydro operators with seasonal revenue constraints (e.g., run-of-river or PSH facing winter/summer energy-market disparities) will need to validate whether their avoidable-cost calculations and PFP recovery assumptions survive the pivotal supplier test; if mitigated improperly, FERC cost-recovery procedures are available. Status and next steps are not stated in this presentation; the proceeding remains in detail-design phase.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04d - CAR-SA: FirstLight Power Alternative Load Weighting cont. - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: FirstLight Power proposes revised methodology for winter load-shape and weather-year selection in ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation Resource (CAR) framework, directly affecting how energy-storage (especially pumped-storage hydro) accreditation is calculated and thus revenue under winter-peak capacity commitments.
documents.ai_summary: FirstLight Power presented a revised approach to winter load-shape and weather-year selection for ISO-NE's CAR-SA (Capacity Accreditation Resource – Storage Accreditation) at the June 2026 Markets Committee. The proposal revises FirstLight's earlier methodology to incorporate aspects of both its own and ISO-NE's original approaches: it targets 5-day blocks (not single days) to capture multi-day consecutive-cold-day effects critical to storage discharge modeling, and it optimizes fit across the entire load distribution rather than only the extreme tail (>95th percentile). FirstLight argues ISO-NE's current methodology over-represents frequency of extreme multi-day events and under-represents fit in non-extreme conditions, leading to material but not massive discrepancies in storage accreditation outcomes, with larger potential impacts under different risk splits or future resource-mix scenarios. The document shows no explicit next-step date or vote, but positions FirstLight as a technical stakeholder in an active accreditation-methodology debate directly affecting how pumped-storage hydro is credited for winter resource-adequacy showings.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04f - CAR-SA: Impact Analysis, Market Clearing Preliminary Results - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: CAR-SA fundamentally redesigns ISO-NE's capacity auction accreditation and payment structure for seasonal resources, directly affecting hydro and storage revenue recognition, clearing prices, and capacity market participation rules.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is analyzing market-clearing outcomes under its proposed Capacity Auction Reforms–Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA), with preliminary results presented for three stress scenarios (Lower, Medium, Higher). The reform splits the annual capacity demand curve into separate summer and winter curves with distinct payment rates ($8.82/kW-day summer vs. $19.01/kW-day winter) and introduces a gas-supply constraint in winter clearing. Hydro and storage resources face altered accreditation formulas tied to seasonal peak contribution rather than annual ELCC, and the model shows winter price separation increases as non-firm gas resources displace other capacity. The ISO expects to present sensitivity analyses (80/20 risk split, alternative gas assumptions) in July; the proposed effective date is Q2 2027. Pumped-storage operators and seasonal-variable hydro owners should monitor how the seasonal split and storage accreditation methodology affect their cleared capacity and winter-vs.-summer revenue streams.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A03 - DAAS Post-Implementation Adjustments - MA AGO Comments in Support
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Day-Ahead Ancillary Services market design changes directly affect reserve procurement costs and pricing — hydro's core revenue stream for regulation and reserve provision — through adjustments to reserve requirements, renewable-integration parameters, and strike-price thresholds.
documents.ai_summary: Massachusetts Attorney General's Office supports ISO-NE's proposed post-implementation adjustments to the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services (DA A/S) market, citing cost overruns in the market's first year (actual incremental cost $921–974 million vs. $140 million forecast). The proposals are: (1) reduce the Non-Performance Factor for Total Ten-Minute Reserves from 120% to 115% to right-size reserve quantities; (2) adjust the Forecast Energy Requirement downward to count full expected real-time Front-of-the-Meter renewable generation, not just cleared DA quantities; and (3) set a Strike Price floor based on efficient Combustion Turbine short-run marginal costs, which would better align with actual generator costs and reduce closeout risk. ISO-NE targets October 23, 2026 implementation. The adjustments would have reduced costs by an estimated $292 million (30% of incremental costs) if applied retroactively. These changes alter the supply curves and clearing prices for reserves hydro typically supplies, with greatest impact during low-load hours and periods of tight system conditions.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04e - CAR-SA: Flatiron RAM cont. - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: ISO-NE's proposed resource accreditation model (rMRI methodology) directly affects capacity revenue for all resources by changing how marginal reliability contribution is calculated and how seasonal payment rates are set; the proposal fundamentally alters whether hydro and pumped storage can earn capacity payments based on their actual energy availability and flexibility value during extreme/scarcity conditions versus synthetic stress scenarios.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE and Flatiron RAM consulting present a proposal to align resource accreditation modeling with expected system conditions rather than synthetic 'at-criteria' stress scenarios in the Capacity, Accreditation, and Reliance (CAR-SA) initiative. The core concern is that current modeling assumptions over- or under-accredit resources (especially those whose value depends on energy availability in the GE MARS software), and risk paying for a resource mix optimized for conditions that never occur; Flatiron proposes accrediting based on 'expected clearing' or 'forecasted load' scenarios where system visibility is better and resource mix is known. The proposal includes three options to address situations with few simulated resource-adequacy events: load scaling to reliability targets, scaling based on forecasted load growth beyond the delivery year, or setting accreditation floors based on empirical data (e.g., EFORd) when simulated risk falls below threshold. The document flags that any marginal accreditation approach creates volatility and forecasting burden for market participants, since rMRI values are sensitive to resource mix, penetration, interactions, and load shape—factors outside individual participant control. Next steps and comment dates are not stated in this presentation excerpt.

documents.title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04n - CAR-SA: AEU Conceptual Amendments - Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ISO-NE's seasonal accreditation methodology directly affects how storage and flexible resources are valued in the capacity market, with specific proposals on weather-year weighting and intertie modeling that would alter the MRIC (Minimum Revenue Impacting Capacity) accreditation signal for pumped storage and other flexible resources.
documents.ai_summary: Advanced Energy United presents two conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's seasonal accreditation reform (CAR-SA). Amendment 1 argues ISO's weather-year weighting based on peak-load days overstates the frequency of sustained cold snaps, causing storage (especially pumped storage) to be disproportionately penalized in accreditation; CAU proposes weighting years by the frequency of multi-day cold-weather blocks instead. Amendment 2 contends ISO's flat import-capacity block for intertie modeling obscures when actual imports are available (often overnight, between MRI hours), understating storage's charging opportunities and thus its MRIC value; CAU proposes modeling hourly import-availability profiles tied to load shape. The submission also flags a potential inconsistency between ISO-NE's use of LOLE for resource adequacy but EUE for accreditation, which could systematically undervalue storage. Storage accreditation is directly material to investment signals and RA sufficiency in New England; these amendments are being advanced in the context of ISO-NE's broader seasonal accreditation reform process.

documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's seasonal capacity accreditation (Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements) and must-offer rules directly affect how hydro and pumped-storage resources are credited toward RA obligations and when they can be dispatched.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Installed Capacity Working Group will discuss Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements (seasonal UDR/EDR accreditation), must-offer requirement changes, and ICAP Manual revisions on June 9, 2026. Seasonal accreditation mechanisms determine how much RA value hydro and PSH claim in winter versus summer, a critical lever for use-limited resources whose output is constrained by water availability. documents.title: 2 Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements – Seasonal UDR/EDR Elections and Must Offer Requirement: ICAP Manual and Attachment Revisions (Incremental Changes)
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO capacity market design adds seasonal must-offer requirements and UDR/EDR elections that directly affect external resource commitments and penalties for underutilized capacity rights — a novel compliance obligation touching revenue and strategic flexibility for hydro and storage resources holding deliverability rights.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes seasonal (Summer/Winter) elections for Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights (UDRs) and External-to-Rest-of-State Deliverability Rights (EDRs) starting with the 2027-2028 Capability Year (effective May 1, 2027), filed with FERC February 18, 2026 in Docket ER26-1431 with requested effective date June 28, 2026. Holders must submit separate seasonal return-to-NYCA elections by August 1 prior to each capability year; capacity associated with external UDRs/EDRs not returned must be offered in ICAP spot auctions or certified for LSE compliance, with sanctions for failure — including a revised must-offer penalty calculated monthly. This reframes deliverability-rights holders' compliance posture: seasonal elections create a new obligation to commit or forfeit, converting a flexible holding into a binary choice with penalties. Pumped storage and large reservoir hydro holding external rights face the most direct impact; small hydro with external positions must track August elections and ensure compliance or incur monthly penalties.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Capacity Market Products has issued incremental edits to ICAP Manual Appendix Q, updating maximum allowances for external installed capacity and deliverability rights for 2025–2027. The document revises ICAP allocation limits for neighboring control areas (PJM, ISO-NE, Ontario, Quebec), details Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights (UDRs) for major transmission interfaces including 1,250 MW Champlain Hudson Power Express (Hydro-Quebec to NYC Zone J) and 660 MW Neptune Cable (PJM to Long Island), and specifies External-to-ROS Deliverability Rights (EDRs). Hydro and storage resources in NYCA seeking external-area capacity credits or import rights must navigate these transmission-constrained allocations; the inclusion of intermittent-resource and run-of-river translation factors (Attachment N) and energy-limited resource procedures (Attachment M) indicates the manual also governs accreditation mechanics for variable hydro. This is a draft for discussion; no comment deadline or vote date is stated in the excerpt.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Capacity Market Products issues an updated ICAP Manual Appendix Q reflecting 2025–2026 and 2026–2027 maximum external installed-capacity allocations by control area and interface, including grandfathered and conditional rights. Key routes for hydro exports: Quebec via Chateauguay (1,110 MW of External CRIS Rights, with seasonal variation November–April); Hydro-Quebec Cedars Interface (80 MW EDR to Rest of State Zone D); Champlain Hudson Power Express from HQ (1,250 MW UDR to Zone J); Cross Sound Cable from New England (330 MW UDR to Zone K). The document is in draft form for discussion by the Installed Capacity Working Group (meeting 2026-06-09) with highlighted revisions from the 2026-05-27 version. Changes affect which hydro suppliers can qualify for capacity revenue and at what seasonal limits into high-value zones (NYC Zone J, Long Island Zone K); owners exporting Quebec or run-of-river Northeast hydro must track these allocations and any ICAP auction implications.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Installed Capacity Manual (Manual 04) is being revised with incremental changes effective April 2, 2026, after BIC acceptance on March 18, 2026. Key sections touch energy-duration limitations and duration-adjustment factors for ICAP suppliers (4.1.1), dual-participation rules (4.1.2), DER and aggregation provisions (4.1.3), and dedicated treatment for co-located storage resources (4.1.4). For pumped storage and hybrid hydro owners, the document signals that NYISO is codifying distinct accreditation pathways for storage paired with generation: co-located resources face specific DMNC/DMGC testing requirements (4.2), operating-data reporting obligations (4.4.10), bidding procedures (4.8.7), and capacity-supply calculations that differ from standalone generators. Storage owners should review sections 4.1.1 (duration factors that constrain RA value) and 4.1.4 (state-of-charge and co-location rules) for direct impact on accreditation and revenue; the manual's treatment of energy-limited resources and intermittent resources also establishes the framework by which run-of-river hydro is accredited.

documents.title: 2a ICAP Manual Incremental Revisions (with highlighting)
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO ICAP manual revisions directly govern unforced capacity accreditation, duration adjustment factors for energy-limited resources (hydro's core issue), co-located storage rules, and operating data/certification requirements — all determinants of how much capacity revenue hydro and PSH can claim.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO has revised its Installed Capacity Manual (version 17.0, effective 04/02/2026, Committee Acceptance 03/18/2026 BIC), with incremental changes highlighted as of the 06/09/2026 ICAPWG meeting. The manual governs minimum unforced capacity requirements for LSEs, accreditation calculations for ICAP suppliers, duration adjustment factors for energy-limited resources, and co-located storage participation rules. Key sections address DMNC (Demonstrated Minimum Net Capacity) testing procedures, operating data reporting requirements (including for municipally owned generation and intermittent/energy-limited resources), and provisions for co-located storage resources — all mechanisms that directly affect how much capacity hydro and pumped-storage facilities can supply and at what accreditation level. The revisions appear to be in draft/discussion phase as of the June 2026 working group meeting; the document provides the current manual text with yellow highlighting indicating changes from the prior 05/27/2026 version.

documents.title: 3 Highlights from the 2025 State of the Market Report for the NYISO Markets
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO Market Monitoring Unit analysis of energy price formation, ancillary-services co-optimization, shortage pricing (ORDC), reserve-requirement allocation, and demand-response settlement rules that directly affect hydro revenue through energy and reserve pricing, uplift mechanisms, and locational scarcity signals.
documents.ai_summary: Potomac Economics (NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit) presents highlights from the 2025 State of the Market Report addressing energy and ancillary-services market performance. Key findings: energy prices rose 66–79% in 2025 due to higher gas prices, peak loads, reduced OOM commitment, increased exports to Quebec, and reduced hydro availability; the MMU identifies $221M in misallocated costs annually, including $40M from statewide allocation of local reserve charges and $38M from largest contingencies not paying their impact on reserve requirements; the MMU recommends urgent reforms to shortage pricing (Rec #2017-2: raising NYCA 30-min ORDC to $2000/MWh up to 150% of largest contingency) to prevent economically unjustified exports to ISO-NE and PJM, and to dynamically adjust reserve requirements and model locational constraints in day-ahead commitment. Hydro operators benefit from higher scarcity pricing and better locational reserve signals, but face exposure to large downward corrections if demand-response baseline issues and cryptocurrency-miner over-consumption (paying full LMP despite uneconomic curtailment) are fixed; the report documents $34M annual uplift from paying demand response as if it generates electricity, which competes with traditional ramping and flexibility revenue.

documents.ai_summary: MISO launched the Generation Interconnection Application Automation (GIAA) portal in November 2025 and is executing incremental releases (April, May 2026, with July/September/November 2026 planned) to improve application processing automation, data migration from the legacy Grid Unity system, and user experience. The portal now supports Surplus and Replacement applications, Inverter-Based Resource (IBR) uploads, and expanded transformer and Point of Interconnection voltage-level fields. Known issues include file-size limitations, lack of project-list sorting/filtering, and unclear user-type account options—problems that can slow application review or create friction for interconnection customers (generators including hydro and pumped-storage developers). A dedicated product team was established March 1, 2026, with ongoing focus on bug resolution and data cleanup from the legacy system. Generators relying on timely queue processing should monitor the portal's usability and watch for the next release cycle (tentatively July 18, 2026) to assess whether validation and automated-review improvements reduce application review delays.

documents.ai_summary: MISO proposes final tariff and business-practice-manual changes to Attachment GGG (MHVDC Interconnection Procedure) to clarify the Module B transmission-service injection pathway as an alternative to Attachment X external Network Resource Interconnection Service, distinguish between Necessary Upgrades and Network Upgrades cost recovery, and update the Multi-Party Facility Construction Agreement. Stakeholders in the April 28 IPWG meeting expressed general support but raised concerns about the scope of Necessary Upgrades in connection studies and cost-recovery pathways for Module B versus Attachment X. MISO plans to file the first tariff change to FERC within 30 days (introducing Limited Operations provisions and clarifying injection/withdrawal-rights scope) and a second filing in Q3–Q4 2026 (updating application forms and clarifying Module B as injection-only, not restricted to External NRIS). Most affected are outside generators—including remote hydropower and pumped-storage facilities seeking to export into MISO—for whom these pathway and cost-allocation rules determine interconnection feasibility and return on investment.

documents.title: Draft Final Proposal - Interconnection Service Capacity and Deliverability Retention for Non-Operating Generating Facilities - May 11, 2026
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Establishes mandatory timelines and conditions for retaining interconnection service capacity and deliverability rights when hydroelectric or pumped-storage facilities cease operations, mothball, or repower — directly affecting whether a hydro owner can preserve its grid position and capacity value during outages or strategic transitions.
documents.ai_summary: CAISO's Draft Final Proposal (May 11, 2026) codifies rules requiring non-operating generating facilities to either return to service, enter the generator interconnection queue, or begin repower construction within specified timeframes to retain deliverability allocations and interconnection service capacity rights; failure to act within these windows forfeits the rights, releasing capacity back to the system. MECHANISM: The proposal creates a hard-deadline retention regime that affects hydro owners planning extended maintenance, mothballing, or repowering. Facilities reaching physical derate (reduced maximum output) lose deliverability commensurate with the loss if the derate exceeds 3 years; those exiting wholesale markets to serve behind-the-meter load are treated as permanent retirements triggering reliability reviews and potential RMR (Reliability Must Run) obligations. SCOPE: All hydroelectric resources in CAISO territory, particularly those contemplating maintenance windows beyond 3 years, repower projects, or transitional mothball periods, are exposed. Generators choosing not to follow notification processes forfeit their rights, and the proposal strengthens ISO enforcement of 90-day advance notice and retirement affidavits. Next step: Draft Final Proposal status indicates Board action is pending (typical CAISO timeline ~Q3 2026); stakeholders should monitor for final tariff vote and implementation timeline.

documents.ai_summary: PJM and Constellation jointly proposed a SATA Phase II solution, with Monitoring Analytics also presenting a competing solution proposal, both reviewed at the May 7, 2026 Operating Committee meeting. The revision mandates automatic voltage control mode as the default for all generators; defines volt-var control boundaries and reactive output ranges tied to MW output; specifies two new required reactive capability curve data points ('Maximum AVR capable MW Output' and 'Unit Minimum MW Output with Reactive Control'); and establishes a three-party investigative process (PJM, transmission owner, generator owner/operator) for reactive control performance issues. For hydroelectric owners, this tightens the operating envelope for reactive power supply: hydro units must now document and receive explicit approval for any AVR mode other than voltage control, and must define their reactive capability limits with new precision, constraining dispatch flexibility and potentially requiring retrofits or AVR reconfiguration on legacy units. The revision proceeds through SOS (June 15), MRC (July 1 and July 9), and OC endorsement (July 23), with education and Q&A sessions between June 4 and July 9. The compliance timeline is not yet stated in this first-read presentation.

documents.ai_summary: PJM is implementing Phase 2 of its Regulation Market redesign, effective October 1, 2026 (pending FERC approval), splitting the single bidirectional regulation product into two separate RegUp and RegDown products, each with its own requirement, clearing price, and settlement. Key findings show separate regulation products improve ACE (Area Control Error) performance and reliability metrics, though summer conditions remain challenging; improvements stem from changing resource mix and generator movement behavior. The implication for hydro and PSH operators is that the new product structure will change how their regulation capacity awards are determined and priced — previously a single award covered both up and down service; under Phase 2, RegUp and RegDown awards and prices are independently cleared, potentially altering the revenue profile for units providing regulation. documents.title: Item 02 – Storage As A Transmission Asset – Sata – Phase 2 – Package Summary
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: SATA establishes a new participation model for energy storage as a regulated transmission asset in PJM, fundamentally altering how storage resources (including pumped-storage hydro) can be deployed and valued — either enrolled in SATA (transmission-only, cost-of-service recovery, no market participation) or remain in competitive markets, creating a strategic fork for PSH owners.
documents.ai_summary: PJM's Operating Committee reviewed the Phase 2 framework for Storage as a Transmission Asset (SATA), which allows energy storage (including pumped-storage hydro) to operate as regulated transmission facilities to address localized RTEP violations without participating in competitive markets. Under SATA Phase 2, eligible storage assets would discharge automatically to mitigate identified contingencies, charge via owner coordination afterward, and recover costs through transmission rates (Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits) rather than market revenue, with metering and telemetry matching standard energy-storage requirements. The framework explicitly prohibits SATA resources from queuing for interconnection or claiming capacity value, and expects assets to be small (≤10 MW) and short-duration (≤4 hours). The document advances to MRC review in July 2026, with FERC submission expected September–November 2026. This creates a new revenue pathway for pumped-storage owners willing to accept regulated-utility-like cost recovery in exchange for operational control and transmission-rate certainty, but forecloses market-participation optionality (energy, AS, capacity) for enrolled assets.

documents.title: 11. PDCWG-Report-to-ROS_060426
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT frequency response and inertia management, particularly FFR procurement and PFR performance monitoring, demonstrate a market-design approach to frequency support that contrasts with hydro-rich RTOs and informs NHA's cross-market analysis of how different regions value synchronous and fast-response capability.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT's Primary Frequency Response (PFR) performance monitoring under BAL-001-TRE has stalled due to too few Frequency Measurable Events (FMEs) — the criteria used to evaluate PFR performance are generating only fewer than the desired 20–35 events per year. ERCOT has proposed revised FME selection criteria to increase event counts and improve oversight of Responsive Reserve Service providers; revised criteria have been shared with the PDCWG and ERCOT has begun using them immediately while retaining discretion in selection. The ERCOT system inertia trends show a structural decline: synchronous inertia at minimum-load points has fallen from 143 GW·s in 2016 to 114.7 GW·s in March 2026, while non-synchronous generation has grown to 81% of system load and Fast Frequency Response procurement has expanded from zero to 430 MW. This illustrates a cross-market contrast — whereas hydro-rich RTOs rely on synchronous hydro for inertia and primary frequency response, ERCOT's low-inertia, high-renewable grid is increasingly dependent on FFR procurement and stricter frequency-event metrics to maintain reserve adequacy and response capability.
