documents.ai_summary: PJM staff proposes enhancements to its Energy Storage Resource Participation Model to accommodate rapid battery-storage growth (4,800 MW expected by 2030). The proposal addresses four issue areas: (1) a standardized opportunity-cost calculation for real-time energy offers capping cost at max(incremental energy cost, maximum DA LMP) up to $2,000, with emergency override to $2,000; (2) SOC accounting in day-ahead dispatch (rolling calculation to prevent infeasible dispatch) and ancillary-services clearing (recognizing SOC depletion from AS deployment), but explicit rejection of centralized SOC optimization; (3) no change to inter-day offer rules; and (4) complementary work via the Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force. A stakeholder process begins July 2026. The opportunity-cost cap directly affects how pumped storage (and batteries) offer into real-time markets—tying the cap to max DA LMP rather than real-time conditions or a multiplier makes cost-based offers more predictable but may suppress PSH discharge bids during high-priced hours when SO-C is low. SOC accounting prevents infeasible dispatch but stops short of RTO-led optimization, preserving operator discretion. The proposal affects both standalone storage and MTF configurations (including hydro-battery hybrids). Comments and next steps are embedded in a July 2026 stakeholder launch.

documents.title: 05. NPRR1214_ERCOTComments_20260610 v6
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ERCOT's proposed changes to NPRR 1214 affect energy and ancillary-services price formation (LMPs and MCPCs) and indifference-payment settlement for reliability deployments—mechanisms that set precedent for how real-time pricing and out-of-market payments are structured in other RTOs, including those with significant hydropower fleets.
documents.ai_summary: ERCOT proposes modifications to NPRR 1214 to streamline pricing and settlement for reliability deployments. The changes replace energy and ancillary-services price adders with direct use of SCED Pricing Run LMPs and MCPCs when active, and introduce more accurate indifference payments using actual offer/bid curves rather than linear approximations. New reliability deployment categories for Load and State-of-Generation resources will be modeled locationally. The proposal modifies how binding prices are determined: Pricing Run prices bind when reliability deployments are in effect; Dispatch Run prices bind otherwise. Indifference payments are redesigned to neutralize perverse incentives created when dispatch awards reflect actual grid conditions but prices reflect a hypothetical state absent out-of-market actions.
documents.hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, ERCOT's framework for indifference payments and out-of-market reliability deployments sets precedent for how real-time pricing distortions are corrected in markets with constrained or use-limited resources. The move from price adders to direct Pricing Run prices, and the shift to actual offer-curve-based indifference calculations, affects how settlement treats gaps between economic dispatch (reflecting actual conditions) and counterfactual pricing (absent reliability actions). These settlement mechanics are relevant to hydro-rich RTOs as they assess similar pricing accuracy and participant incentive structures in their own markets.

documents.title: Item 03 – 1 Manual 14h Revisions Ieee 2800 – Presentation

documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14H to adopt IEEE 2800-2022 requirements for inverter-based resources (Phase 1), including voltage and frequency ride-through, primary frequency response, and enter-service criteria, with application to VSC-HVDC transmission facilities and IBR interconnections. The revision adds Section 9.15 and new Attachment K, specifying mandatory ride-through times (e.g., 6 seconds at 0.70–0.90 p.u. voltage) and default frequency-response parameters (droop 5%, dead-band 0.06% × fnom). While Phase 1 targets IBRs, the standards establish precedent for synchronous resource requirements; PJM endorsement is scheduled for June 2, 2026, with MRC endorsement August 19, 2026. Hydro operators should monitor whether these ride-through and frequency-response mandates extend to conventional generators in Phase 2, as compliance during voltage/frequency disturbances will become mandatory, and deviation penalties may apply.

documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 14H (New Service Requests Cycle Process) Revision 05 becomes effective July 23, 2026. This manual governs the interconnection queue process for generation, transmission, and merchant transmission requests in PJM. For hydropower and pumped-storage operators, the key provisions include: Section 9 sets requirements for generating facilities (power factor, capacity vs. energy resource status elections, behind-the-meter generation, inverter-based resource rules); Section 12 covers surplus interconnection service, the mechanism by which existing hydro plants can access previously-allocated but unused interconnection capacity for uprates or expansion; and Sections 1–5 establish the phased study and agreement process that determines project viability and cost allocation. The manual revision incorporates IEEE 2800 standards (synchronous inverter modeling), affecting how hydro and hybrid resources are studied. Hydro developers and PSH operators in PJM should review Section 9's resource-status elections and Section 12's surplus service process, which determine how much capacity value their projects can claim and how efficiently they move through the queue.

Hydro and PSH operators rely on ELCC ratings to determine their capacity offering value; reformulated accreditation methodologies can shift which resource types (dispatchable vs. variable; duration-limited vs. unlimited) receive higher accreditation factors, directly altering revenue in PJM's annual capacity auction. The manual governs RTO-wide (0.1 days/year LOLE) and LDA-level (40% × Portfolio EUE) adequacy criteria that drive capacity procurement.

The manual itself is procedural and defines no new policy, but changes to UCAP accreditation methodology, outage-rate data collection, or reliability-calculation tools (PRISM) flow through this manual and affect what capacity revenue hydro owners can claim.

Manual 14H is being revised to reflect EIT procedures; PJM's Board ruled on the process in June 2026, with FERC ruling anticipated July 31, 2026 and a requested effective date of July 31, 2026. For PSH and large run-of-river projects with construction-readiness and state support, EIT offers a faster path to interconnection and earlier capacity accreditation timing relative to standard queue, affecting project-timing and RA-portfolio strategy; however, EIT projects forfeit the one-time milestone-extension option available to standard-queue projects, tightening execution risk.

documents.ai_summary: NERC issued a Level 3 Essential Action Alert (responses due August 3, 2026) requiring registered entities to implement seven immediate actions addressing risks posed by computational loads (data centers) causing customer-initiated large load reductions and significant oscillations within seconds — outpacing real-time response capability and threatening BPS reliability. PJM members must comply with this alert and the accompanying NERC Reliability Guideline on risk mitigation for emerging large loads. For hydropower and pumped-storage operators, this creates new dispatch obligations (faster frequency response to load swings) and qualification/ride-through requirements under PRC-029-1 Inverter-Based Resource guidance; it also signals potential scarcity value for synchronous hydro's inertial response and for PSH's second-scale ramping to absorb load shocks — contingent on PJM's eventual tariff implementation of NERC's standards revisions (currently in informal comment period through June 17, 2026).

documents.ai_summary: PJM is conducting capacity-expansion (CapEx) modeling for its 2026 RTEP 8-year case (2034 horizon) to supplement generation assumptions when the system lacks sufficient generation to meet forecast demand (218 GW summer, 205 GW winter peak). The model will select economically optimal resources—solar, wind, hybrid, battery (4–10 hour), CC/CT, and nuclear uprates—from interconnection queues (TC2 and Cycle 1), using ELCC-based resource-adequacy constraints that automatically adjust as resource mix changes. Scenario A.1 (base case) does not build gas in regulated states (NJ, MD, DE, IL, eastern PA) unless projects have ISA/GIA or state agreement backing; Scenario B models policy-driven deactivations and nuclear targets. Results will inform 5-year RTEP solution right-sizing and state commitments, with power flows to be developed for Scenario B. The CapEx approach aligns with FERC Order 1920's long-term regional transmission planning and will evolve over successive cycles. This exercise directly sets the competitive position of hydro (and especially pumped-storage) in PJM's capacity adequacy calculations—any resource sited and given ELCC credit in the 2034 baseline affects scarcity-driven revenue signals and accreditation assumptions that cascade into 5-year capacity-market and real-time dispatch outcomes.

documents.title: Informational Only – 2026 RTEP Assumptions Feedback
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: PJM's capacity expansion modeling methodology for RTEP transmission planning directly affects how hydro and storage resources are represented in future transmission needs assessments, which determines transmission investment priorities and interregional transfer capability available to hydro exporters.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is incorporating capacity expansion modeling into its 2026 RTEP cycle to project future generation buildout and inform backbone transmission investments through 2046. CEBA and FirstEnergy submitted feedback on April 20–22, 2026, regarding technical assumptions: CEBA supports the expansion modeling but urges PJM to model broader storage durations (6-, 8-, and 10-hour batteries and longer-duration systems), age-based retirement curves, and sensitivity analysis on natural gas prices and load growth. FirstEnergy requests clarification on whether the model will incorporate PJM's proposed "Connect and Manage" load flexibility framework, which would materially affect where new capacity is sited and thus transmission needs. The methodological choices—especially the treatment of storage technologies, retirement assumptions, and interconnection queue completeness—will shape which transmission corridors PJM prioritizes and whether interregional paths serving hydro exports are reinforced. PJM is scheduled to discuss 8-year modeling results at the May 8, 2026 TEAC meeting.

The model employs ELCC curves that adjust dynamically based on resource-mix penetration—reflecting how hydro's capacity value changes with higher renewable penetration—and includes expansion candidates: solar, onshore/offshore wind, hybrid, combustion turbine, combined cycle, batteries (4–10 hour), and nuclear uprates. PJM will use Scenario B (policy-driven deactivations and Maryland nuclear commitments) as the baseline, with sensitivities testing gas siting restrictions, state storage targets, coal retirements, and gas cost impacts. Results will inform 5-year RTEP solution selection and may highlight development potential in northwestern PJM (ComEd zone). The approach aligns with FERC Order 1920 long-term regional transmission planning requirements and will evolve in successive RTEP cycles.

The capacity expansion model assumes 218.3 GW summer and 204.5 GW winter peak load in 2034, forcing addition of solar, wind, gas, battery storage, and nuclear uprates. documents.ai_summary: NYISO Installed Capacity Working Group meeting (June 2, 2026) will address four rule changes: DER market-participation enhancements, ICAP Manual Attachment N updates, revised treatment of intermittency in capacity accreditation, and improved duct-firing modeling for fossil units. The intermittency revisions are most material — they modify how NYISO accredits variable and run-of-river hydro in the capacity market, and how storage is modeled in the reserve-margin calculation. Manual updates will be presented by Sushant Varghese and Vijay Kaki; Potomac Economics will discuss 2025 State of the Market findings, which often include capacity-accreditation trends and hydro-performance analysis. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this agenda.

documents.title: 2 DER Market Enhancements
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: DER aggregation participation rules directly affect small hydropower owners' ability to participate in NYISO markets under Order 2222 frameworks; the DADSR concept and proposed telemetry/accreditation changes alter the strategic options and compliance burden for hydro resources enrolled in DER aggregations.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes a Day-Ahead Demand-Side Resource (DADSR) variant within its existing DER & Aggregation participation model, designed to accommodate DSR with longer start-up times and limited real-time flexibility. DADSR would bid day-ahead, lock to a fixed real-time schedule, and be ineligible for operating reserves or regulation service; it would qualify for ICAP participation with 2–24-hour energy duration limitations and potentially reduced telemetry requirements (6-second with 30-second scan rates for sub-1 MW facilities versus current standards for 1+ MW). Small hydropower and run-of-river resources enrolled in DER aggregations face a strategic choice: participation under current DER rules (with full telemetry/ancillary-service obligations) or under DADSR (simpler telemetry, day-ahead certainty, but loss of regulation/reserve revenue and real-time flexibility upside). NYISO is also evaluating MNBT and ECBL enhancements and the 10 kW threshold; stakeholder discussion continues at the July ICAPWG/MIWG meeting.

documents.title: 3 ICAP Manual Attachment N Revisions
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO is revising Attachment N methodology for calculating translation factors that convert nameplate capacity to unforced capacity (UCAP) for intermittent and run-of-river hydro resources, directly affecting hydro accreditation in resource adequacy and capacity-requirement studies.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes revisions to ICAP Manual Attachment N to implement seasonal (summer and winter) translation factors for intermittent resources and limited-control run-of-river hydro, replacing the current summer-only methodology. The change responds to observed winter Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) beginning in the 2026–2027 IRM study and supports the Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements proposal (filed with FERC 2/18/2026, target implementation 5/1/2027 for the 2027–2028 Capability Year). The proposal also corrects the availability-factor formula to apply proper weighted averaging, aligning calculation with current implementation in IRM, LCR, and deliverability studies. For run-of-river hydro owners, this means winter availability will now drive a separate winter UCAP translation factor based on December–February production patterns weighted by winter LOLE distribution, potentially improving winter accreditation if winter production is high relative to winter scarcity hours, or reducing it if winter is a dry season; the revision will be presented to the Business Issue Committee on 6/10/2026.

documents.title: 4 Balancing Intermittency Manual Updates
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's Uncertainty Reserve Requirement (URR) design directly affects how intermittent resources and ramping/flexibility are procured and priced in both day-ahead and real-time markets, creating new reserve products that hydro will be called upon to supply and creating new demand curves that establish payment terms for flexibility hydro traditionally provides.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO is finalizing manual revisions to implement its Uncertainty Reserve Requirement (URR), a new 24-hour reserve product designed to hedge forecast uncertainty for net load, land-based wind, offshore wind, and front-of-meter solar. The design was accepted by FERC in July 2025 (ER25-1998) and is scheduled for deployment in August 2026. The updated manuals clarify URR calculation methodology (incorporated in new Attachment D to the Ancillary Services Manual), specify that URR can be met using 30-Minute Reserve in the day-ahead market, introduce locational demand curves with a new Long Island requirement row (270 MW and 540 MW separately), and refine operating-capacity accounting for seasonal differences. Stakeholder votes are scheduled for June 10–11, 2026 (BIC and OC); comments can be submitted at the June 4 SOAS meeting. For hydro owners, URR creates both a revenue opportunity (new procurement of a flexibility product hydro naturally supplies) and a compliance obligation (must-offer rules in the 30-minute reserve product that backs URR); pumped-storage facilities are particularly positioned to capture value from locational reserve requirements, especially on Long Island where the demand curve now explicitly separates 270 MW and 540 MW tiers.

documents.title: 6 2025 State of the Market Report

documents.ai_summary: NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit (Potomac Economics) identifies structural gaps in the capacity market that undervalue reliability contributions and distort investment incentives. Key findings: (1) demand curves based on 2-hour battery cost understate Net CONE, risking premature retirements even as load grows; (2) seasonal incentives are misaligned—firm fuel/UDR elections locked 16 months in advance don't respond to winter market prices, and elected capacity for 2026/27 (15.2 GW) exceeds planning assumptions (12.3 GW), creating cost-allocation risk; (3) transmission security is undercompensated—downstate LCRs increasingly bind at floor, overpaying bottled generation (SCRs, large units) and underpaying non-firm gas units while creating $74M annual inefficiency post-CHPE. Recommendations filed or pending include raising the demand-curve floor (Rec. 2025-1a), moving seasonal-election deadlines closer to winter (Rec. 2022-2), introducing locational CAFs (Rec. 2025-2), and expanding capacity zones. These touch pumped-storage accreditation (2-hour battery CONE undermines longer-duration PSH value), seasonal energy adequacy (firm fuel elections timing), and locational value recognition (hydro deliverability and transmission-security contribution). No formal comment deadline is stated in this highlights presentation, but the full 2025 SOM Report (posted May 19, 2026) and tariff filing ER26-1431 are the operative documents.

documents.title: Item 02 – 1 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 13 Revision 98 establishes emergency operating procedures affecting how hydropower and other dispatchable resources participate in PJM's capacity and transmission emergency protocols, plus introduces a new Capacity Advisory mechanism that signals resource scarcity — both touch hydro operators' obligations to respond to emergency directives and may alter revenue opportunities during stress periods.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 13 (Emergency Operations) to clarify its roles as Reliability Coordinator, Balancing Authority, and Transmission Operator under NERC EOP-011. The revision introduces a new Capacity Advisory (Section 2.3) to provide advance notice when forecasted available capacity approaches the operating requirement — designed to address gaps in temperature-based emergency triggers and expected to increase in frequency as demand growth outpaces generation interconnection. Revision 98 also establishes Attachment O, a conditional procedure to mobilize backup generation at large data-center loads during extreme emergencies (triggered only if the DOE issues a Section 202(c) order); this procedure was activated during Winter Storm Fern (January 2026) but not implemented. The revision cleanly separates transmission-security emergency procedures from capacity-based procedures, removes capacity-related actions from transmission protocols, and updates language for Advanced Scheduled Resources in cold/hot weather alerts. Endorsement is sought before the summer operating period; the timeline shows second reads at the MRC on June 24, 2026. The Capacity Advisory may increase call frequency for emergency ramping from dispatchable hydro, while data-center load growth (now formally recognized in procedures) creates both scarcity signals that favor hydro dispatch and potential operational constraints if backup-gen mobilization competes for transmission or reserve capacity.

documents.title: Item 02 – 2 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: Manual 13 governs PJM emergency operations including load-shedding procedures, transmission security emergencies, and resource-limitation reporting that directly affect how dispatchable hydro and pumped-storage resources must respond to system stress and what operating obligations they face.
documents.ai_summary: PJM Manual 13 Revision 98 (effective July 23, 2026) updates emergency-operations procedures across capacity emergencies, weather/environmental events, and transmission security. Key changes include: restructured transmission-security emergency procedures that no longer trigger PAIs or EEAs; split of Maximum Generation Emergency into separate Transmission Security–Local Maximum Generation Emergency Alert and Load Management Alert; addition of Capacity Advisory to Section 2.3; updated Advanced Schedule Resources language for cold and hot weather alerts; and new Attachment O on emergency back-up generator use. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, the procedure changes govern mandatory response protocols during transmission constraints (Section 5.2) and capacity shortages (Section 2), and clarify which emergency triggers obligate generation or discharge (e.g., load-shedding directives, transmission relief actions). The removal of PAI/EEA linkage to transmission-security procedures may reduce frequency of certain dispatch signals to storage resources during local constraints. Pumped-storage operators should review Section 2 (reserve and capacity procedures), Section 5.2 (transmission-security load and generation actions), and Attachments E–F (manual load-dump allocation) to confirm charging/discharging obligations under updated protocols.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE's May 2026 regional planning update covers several transmission-planning initiatives affecting New England hydro deliverability and resource adequacy: (1) Loss of Source study with PJM and NYISO concluded without achieving full objectives but established new baseline for system constraints in neighboring RTOs; report anticipated Q2/Q3 2026. (2) 2025 Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) RFP evaluation ongoing, final determination by September 2026; stakeholder discussions on FERC Order 1920 compliance (interregional transmission coordination) paused pending RFP completion, resuming Q3 2026 with June 14, 2027 compliance-filing deadline. (3) Connecticut 2034 Solutions Study underway with preferred solution anticipated late 2026; 2035 Daytime Minimum Load Needs Assessment begins post-May 2026 CELT report release, base-case library Q3 2026. These constraint-relief and long-lead-time transmission projects directly affect hydro's ability to deliver reserve and energy products into neighboring markets and hydro's valuation in resource-adequacy showings; owners relying on New England hydro for interregional exports or RA accreditation should monitor LTTP RFP vendor evaluation (financial viability, construction feasibility) and Order 1920 stakeholder discussions resuming Q3 2026.

documents.title: 2026-05-29 IPSAC A02.1 PJM Regional Transmission Expansion Planning Process
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: TRANSMISSION PLANNING: PJM's 2025 RTEP window selected backbone transmission projects (765 kV lines, 500 kV HVDC) and load-growth driver analysis affecting interregional transfer capability and hydro deliverability in Mid-Atlantic, South/Dominion, and PJM West regions; hydro owners exporting or operating within these zones depend on these backbone routes for revenue realization.
documents.ai_summary: PJM completed evaluation of 134 proposals (57 greenfields, 77 upgrades) submitted in its 2025 Reliability Window 1 and selected regional backbone solutions totaling ~$11.7 billion: a 222-mile 765 kV line from Kammer–Buttermilk–Juniata (Mid-Atlantic), a 185-mile 500 kV HVDC line from Heritage–Mosby (South/Dominion), and three 765/345 kV lines in PJM West (Greentown–Teddy–Marysville, Guernsey–Conesville–West Millersport–Adkins, and 345 kV laterals). The primary drivers are load growth in PPL zone (~5–8.5 GW cumulative), data-center load external to Dominion, and southbound generation flowing to northern VA load centers, all creating 500 kV capacity violations on north–south corridors by 2030–2032. The next FERC 1000 window opens July 2026 with proposal close August/September 2026 and board approval targeted October 2026–February 2027. For hydro operators exporting from the South or West into load-heavy Mid-Atlantic, these backbone augmentations directly increase transmission import capacity and firm locational revenue signals; conversely, the selection of HVDC on the Heritage–Mosby corridor (rather than purely AC) creates a new constraint on traditional hydro exports via 500 kV AC paths.

documents.title: 2026-05-29 IPSAC A02.3 NYISO Updates on Comprehensive System Planning Process
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: NYISO's system planning process and reliability assessments directly affect hydro and storage dispatch needs, transmission-constrained resource valuations, and generator deactivation/RMR decisions that reshape the market environment for peaking and flexible resources.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO presented its 2026–2027 Reliability Planning Process cycle, including the 2026 Reliability Needs Assessment (covering 2030–2036) and the 2027–2036 Comprehensive Reliability Plan. The 2025 Q3 and 2026 Q1 Short-Term Reliability Assessments (STARs) identified persistent deficiencies in New York City (Zone J) and Long Island (Zone K) that depend on continued operation of fossil peakers (Gowanus, Narrows, Far Rockaway, Danskammer) until transmission solutions energize or demand-side/storage alternatives materialize. Generator deactivations are being withdrawn or held in Interim Service Provider status pending solution entry. These assessments directly affect which generation assets receive RMR contracts or withdrawal approval, which in turn shapes the scarcity pricing, transmission congestion, and reserve-procurement environment in which hydro and storage must compete. Any expansion of transmission or storage-as-transmission alternatives in the planning scenarios could displace fossil peakers and alter the revenue drivers for hydro ramping and energy supply in the constrained zones.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE, NYISO, and PJM completed their 2025 coordinated interregional transmission planning cycle under FERC Order 1000, with draft results posted in early April 2026 and stakeholder comments due April 20–27, 2026. The planning process found no interregional transmission projects that are more efficient or cost-effective than separate regional solutions, meaning each ISO will pursue its own system needs independently rather than jointly. This outcome is significant for hydro owners because it confirms the near-term transmission topology will remain within existing regional footprints; interregional transmission constraints will not be relaxed by new joint projects, and the value of existing hydro resources for intraregional scarcity and export will depend on each ISO's separate needs assessments and queue development. documents.hydro_relevance_reason: TRANSMISSION PLANNING: ISO-NE's 2025 Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) RFP evaluation directly affects hydro export capability and interregional transfer limits (Maine–New Hampshire and Surowiec–South interfaces), which constrain the locational value and revenue of New England hydropower and determine whether transmission upgrades will be required to relieve scarcity.
documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE evaluated six Longer-Term Transmission Plan proposals submitted in response to NESCOE's RFP; two proposals (A1, A2) passed RFP Objectives testing (thermal, voltage, and transient stability at ≥3000 MW Maine–New Hampshire and ≥3200 MW Surowiec–South transfer limits) and proceed to No Adverse Impact Screening and Benefits Calculation, while four proposals (B1, C1, D1, D2) failed stability or voltage criteria and remain excluded. ISO-NE expects to present its preliminary preferred Longer-Term Transmission Solution to PAC by September 2026. For hydro owners, the outcome determines which transmission projects advance to benefits evaluation — projects that increase Maine–New Hampshire or Surowiec–South transfer limits would reduce congestion and increase the marginal value of New England hydro's energy sales southward; rejection of four proposals may delay relief of these critical constraints.

SATOA treatment was accepted by FERC on October 19, 2023, and is now being incorporated into planning-study methodology in TPTG Section 2.3.8.1, with conforming changes to Section 2.3.8. This formalizes a pathway for storage (including pumped storage) to compete as a transmission solution in ISO-NE's competitive solutions process alongside traditional wires and other non-wires alternatives, potentially creating revenue streams for PSH owners who can locate facilities to address identified transmission needs. Comments on the draft TPTG are due by June 10, 2026.

documents.ai_summary: A coalition including National Grid Ventures, New England Power Company, and PowerBridge submitted two HVDC-based transmission proposals to ISO-NE's inaugural Longer-Term Transmission Planning (LTTP) solicitation but was excluded from further evaluation after failing stability analysis in March 2026. The coalition disputes ISO-NE's rejection of technical mitigation measures (adding an isolated circuit and transformer to the converter station), arguing the tariff allows non-material modifications and that iterative refinement is standard practice. The broader stakes: all expanded HVDC solutions were eliminated, leaving only HVAC alternatives—eliminating HVDC's claimed benefits of black-start capability, bi-directional power-flow control, and future cost reduction. For hydro owners, HVDC transmission expansion directly affects regional scarcity pricing, deliverability of remote hydro resources, and operational flexibility value; the coalition's exclusion narrows the solutions competitive set and may reduce the scope of future regional investments in transmission features that benefit dispatchable resources.

documents.title: Item 01 – 1 Rmr Resources – Tariff Revisions – Redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Tariff revisions to PJM's RMR (Retained for Reliability) resource capacity-market treatment—specifically, how retained resources clear auctions, accredit UCAP, and receive capacity-market revenues—directly affect hydro and other dispatchable units that PJM may retain to address transmission reliability, and establish the revenue and settlement rules governing their participation in the capacity market.
documents.ai_summary: PJM staff have redlined tariff language (Attachment DD, section 5.3) governing Retained-for-Reliability (RMR) generation resources' participation in the capacity market (RPM auctions and accreditation). The proposal clarifies that RMR resources not clearing an auction on their own offer are deemed to submit a $0/MW-Day Sell Offer in the Base Residual Auction for their full Accredited UCAP (up to Capacity Interconnection Rights), provided they are deliverable, operationally available, and not subject to bilateral restrictions. Any accreditation increase post-auction is automatically offered in the Third Incremental Auction at $0/MW-Day; if accreditation decreases or the resource no longer meets RMR criteria, PJM procures replacement capacity. Capacity-market revenues from RMR units are credited to the load zones paying for the resource's continuing operations under its FERC-accepted rate schedule, rather than to the RMR unit operator; credits cease if the rate schedule expires, the unit deactivates, or catastrophic failure occurs. This provision extends through the 2029/2030 Delivery Year unless FERC accepts an extension. Retained dispatchable and storage resources relying on RMR rate schedules—including some legacy hydro units—will have their capacity revenues redirected to load-serving entities paying for reliability upgrades, fundamentally altering the revenue model for RMR-designated plants. The tariff change appears to be in draft form (redline status suggests it has not yet cleared stakeholder review or FERC).

documents.title: Item 01 – 2 Brandon Shores 12 And Wagner 34 Deactivation And Rmr – Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: RMR (Reliability Must Run) arrangement extending beyond planned deactivation date directly affects hydro and thermal generator retirement decisions and the transmission-investment timeline that determines when generating resources become dispatchable rather than must-run — a core strategic option for fleet planning.
documents.ai_summary: PJM has assessed whether Brandon Shores Units 1&2 (635 MW + 638 MW, BGE-owned, Maryland) and Wagner Units 3&4 (305 MW + 397 MW, BGE-owned, Maryland) can safely deactivate on their current RMR end date of May 31, 2029. Planning studies found thermal and voltage violations would persist through 2030 even with baseline transmission projects in service, because several major 500 kV and 765 kV lines required for reliability (e.g., Morrisville–Vint Hill–Wishing Star, North Delta–High Ridge, Peach Bottom–Conastone rebuilds, Amos-Welton–Spring–Rocky Point, Joshua Falls–Yeat) do not reach in-service dates until mid-to-late 2030 or 2031. PJM's recommendation is to extend RMR beyond May 2029 through at least 2030 to maintain reliability until these transmission enhancements complete; next steps are RMR agreement negotiation and FERC filing. This determines whether 1,975 MW of generation will remain must-run (and thus unavailable for economic dispatch or retirement) well past currently assumed end dates — a precedent affecting all generators assessing retirement timing in constrained transmission zones.

documents.ai_summary: NYISO Management Committee approves revisions to the Market Administration and Control Area Services Tariff governing automatic ICAP surplus offers, with the Board of Directors to authorize filing under FPA Section 205. The proposal changes the rules by which capacity surplus is offered into the market automatically, affecting how hydro and pumped-storage units manage their capacity accreditation obligations and surplus positioning—particularly relevant for PSH operators managing state-of-charge and capacity ratings. The full tariff language and detailed mechanism are presented in the accompanying slide deck 'Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers' (May 27, 2026); the proposal moves to Board filing stage pending Board authorization.

documents.title: 3 Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: MECHANISM: NYISO is revising the ICAP market's surplus-offer rules to automatically resell capacity that load-serving entities and ICAP suppliers procure but do not need, at zero-dollar bids. For hydropower and storage owners selling capacity into NYISO's ICAP market—whether as primary capacity suppliers or via bilateral trades—this rule removes their option to withhold surplus capacity and directly affects the monetization path and price realization for unsold UCAP.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO proposes a new tariff section (5.14.4) that automatically submits zero-dollar offers for any Unforced Capacity (UCAP) surplus held by load-serving entities, ICAP suppliers, and ICAP marketers after the monthly certification deadline, effective May 1, 2027 (Board approval and FERC filing required). Currently, surplus UCAP often goes unoffered, potentially raising market-clearing prices; the automatic zero-dollar offer guarantees resale at the auction clearing price. Hydropower and pumped-storage owners—particularly those acquiring capacity via bilateral trades or selling excess UCAP—will face mandatory resale of any certified surplus, eliminating the ability to withhold capacity or negotiate off-market prices for unexpectedly available MW; however, capacity associated with a physical transmission interface (PTID) and 'unoffered MW' remain subject to physical-withholding rules and are excluded from automatic resale.

documents.title: 3a MST 5.14 redline
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: ICAP capacity-market accreditation and demand-curve methodology directly affect hydro and PSH revenue from capacity markets, particularly the periodic review process that sets accreditation reference points and the demand-curve adjustments that drive cleared capacity prices.
documents.ai_summary: NYISO's tariff Section 5.14 establishes the ICAP Spot Market Auction mechanics and demand-curve parameters that clear monthly unforced-capacity obligations. The document redlines the periodic review methodology (every four years, next review for 2025/2026 capability year), which assesses the levelized cost of a peaking plant, net energy and ancillary-services revenue offsets, and seasonal differences in capacity availability. Beginning with 2025/2026, demand curves will account for seasonal variations in capacity availability—summer and winter curves now reflect different excess-capacity assumptions. The 2025/2026 NYCA summer curve peaks at $21.69/kW-month; winter at $16.39/kW-month, with locational adders (NYC summer peak $41.30). Hydro and PSH capacity accreditation is measured against these ICAP demand curves translated to unforced-capacity terms; seasonal demand-curve splits will alter how seasonal hydro availability and storage round-trip efficiency factor into capacity showings, potentially reducing winter accreditation if available supply diverges seasonally from the reference peaking-plant assumption.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing accreditation reforms for Distributed Energy Capacity Resources (DECRs) under FERC Order 2222 compliance, including Continuous Storage Facilities (CSF) and Binary Storage Facilities (BSF). These rules affect how pumped-storage and battery storage participate in ISO-NE's seasonal capacity auctions effective Q2 2027.

documents.title: Item 02a – Joint Stakeholders Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document addresses capacity market design, resource eligibility, and long-term resource adequacy mechanisms that directly affect how hydropower and pumped-storage facilities participate in PJM's energy and capacity markets.
documents.ai_summary: This proposal establishes a one-time Reliability Backstop Auction (RBA) with implications for hydro resources: it explicitly allows uprated hydropower and balance-of-plant investments meeting a $300/kW threshold to qualify as eligible resources; includes provisions for resources with expiring operating licenses (directly relevant to hydro relicensing); and establishes mechanisms to preserve at-risk existing generation through bilateral contracting and PPAs, which affects how existing hydropower and pumped-storage facilities compete and persist in the market.

documents.title: Item 02b – Constellaton And Vistra Presentation
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document proposes expanded eligibility for PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBA) including new resource categories with ELCC discounting rules that directly affect how energy storage, demand response, and backup generation resources participate in capacity procurement—mechanisms that intersect with hydropower and storage market participation.
documents.ai_summary: PJM is considering eligibility expansions for the RBA that introduce ELCC discounting for limited demand response and backup generator operations. While not hydropower-specific, these proposals establish precedents for how variable/limited-availability resources receive capacity accreditation, which may inform treatment of hydro resources with operational constraints or seasonal variability in PJM's capacity market.

documents.title: Item 02d – Smeco Presentation – Updated
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: The document addresses PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) Phase II rules affecting resource credit, capacity performance obligations, and market participation—mechanisms that directly impact how dispatchable resources like hydropower and pumped-storage are compensated and held to performance standards in PJM's capacity market.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes RBP Phase II credit and deficiency charge rules that would affect planned resources (including hydro) through collateral requirements, abandonment penalties, and counterparty allocation to EDCs. Key issues include adequacy of pre-BRA credit posting, appropriate credit multipliers (0.2x vs. 0.5x), and discount rate selection—all of which influence whether hydropower and storage projects find RBP awards economically viable.

documents.title: Item 02e – EKPC And Exelon Presentation

documents.ai_summary: This proposal concerns PJM's new Reliability Backstop Procurement mechanism for large loads, which creates parallel capacity procurement obligations separate from RPM. The outcome affects how dispatchable resources like hydropower and PSH are credited, accredited, and financially settled in PJM's capacity markets, and whether double-billing or cost-causation misalignment could distort incentives for flexible generation.

documents.title: Item 02e – EKPC Paper

documents.title: Item 02f – Imm Paper

documents.title: Informational Only – Flatiron Energy Proposed Methodology TO Address ELCC Risk
documents.hydro_relevance_reason: This document directly addresses ELCC (Effective Load Carrying Capability) methodology and capacity accreditation in PJM's Reliability Backstop Procurement mechanism, which fundamentally affects how hydropower and energy storage resources qualify for and are compensated in capacity markets.
documents.ai_summary: PJM proposes de-risking ELCC forecasts for RBP resources by fixing payments based on PJM's 15-year ELCC forecast rather than exposing resources to annual ELCC volatility. This is highly relevant to hydropower and pumped-storage operators, as ELCC values directly determine their capacity credits and revenue certainty—a critical factor for financing new or refurbished hydro/PSH projects. The proposal uses fixed-for-floating swaps to guarantee Resource Fixed Payments, which could substantially improve project bankability for storage resources but also creates true-up mechanisms that shift ELCC risk from suppliers to large loads.

documents.ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing Capacity Auction Reforms with Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) that introduce Maximum Capability (MCap) and Dependable Capability (DCap) metrics to replace existing accreditation methodology. MCap represents physical supply capability irrespective of seasonality (including a Global MCap for intermittent resources), while DCap represents expected availability during seasonal peak load hours. These changes will materially affect how hydroelectric and pumped-storage resources are accredited and compensated in ISO-NE's capacity market starting Q2 2027.
